Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI herein) emerges from the premise that systems do not accomodate for the breadth of perspectives to which they both affect and on which they have an effect. DEI initiatives intend to make the systems that they are a part of more inclusive in order to bring in more perspectives, so that the systems are more equitable to the highest diversity of interacting agents who will touch the system. Importantly - DEI initiatives in the institutional sense omit the primary utility function of their own initiatives: DEI is not primarily about participation and accomodation, but rather creating robusticity in the adaptation set that a system has at its disposal. When considering how DEI initiatives are deployed in modern settings, it is usually in critique to the lack of DEI within the systems that are being examined. Solutioning is usually sought as a mitigation method against the lack of DEI in the systems that are being critiqued, so initiatives are deployed with the intent to fix this problem. Ironically, systems that attempt to solve for DEI inadequacies within themselves are usually already ossified with reference to the structures within them that don't account for DEI - applying a corrective measure to a broken system will not change how the system was made (per system design). Therefore truthfully the only way to solve for obvious problems with a system's lack of DEI is to redesign the whole system from first principles, part of which means including DEI as a guiding principle for seeding the system at the outset. The net effect of doing so is that systems designed from the ground up with DEI a part of their structure will necessarily demonstrate the robusticity present in adaptable systems, because the solution set will already have an advantage in its adaptive qualities. markov translation issues and the loss of fidelity system design,thinking in systems,complexity,deployable complexity,marginalization,first principles thinking

Individuality is often cast as though part of some immutable whole, and definable with exactitude - the reality is that individuality is more likely to be a spectrum of associations following essentially three rules: individuality can exist at any biological level individuality can be nested (i.e. one individual can exist inside of another individual) individuality exists on a continuum, with quantifiable degrees of individuality within an entity Not so much by contrast, Rousseau defined individuals in relation to their responsibilities to the social connections of which they are a part - an individual is the degree to which an entity does or does not have associations with the wider system. Rousseau justifies this by phrasing the formation of the state as the network of connections comprising the body politic, resulting in interdependencies that connect this new sovereign to its constituent parts. What Is an Individual? Biology Seeks Clues in Information Theory. The Social Contract - Jean-Jacques Rousseau There exist three types of individualities (along the biological definition): 1. organismal individuality - an entity that is shaped by environmental factors and strongly self-organizing and all action within the system is based entirely on prior states of the entity. 2. colonial individuality - an entity that is a complex relationship between internal and external factors (networks / colonies / webs) 3. environmental individuality - the phenomenon of entity falls apart in dissociation from the environmental conditions that allow it. Through these three definitions, type 3 is likely to have been what 'life' looked like at first conception - a phenomenological event arising entirely from environmental conditions. Seeing individuality on a gradient from Type 3 -- Type 1 allows us to see that there are 'degrees' of individuality. physical system,biological system, Rousseau, philosophy, self-contained individual, phase state

Anarchism exists orthogonal to social structure - in that anarchism is a desire to instead pursue total autonomy in the individual. True anarchism abhors even the idea of ownership, but only to the respect of appreciating that which can be uniquely one's own and need not be shared. It does not incurr a demand to share in what one possesses, but rather to keep one's hands open to accepting what is offered and to offer in return what little you may have. Oftentimes there is a conflation between this and libertarianism positions that believe that total autonomy includes ownership to which an individual has the right to control. Anarchism instead posits a radical antithetical to the idea of ownership. Privacy is not a right but instead an agreement. Anarchist thought abhors institutions because they are a form of ownership that takes control from the individual, thus removing their autonomy. Author: Kuhn, T Source: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions --- In this book, Kuhn argues that incontrovertible evidence is what causes the shift between interpretive frameworks for the description of systems. Previous paradigms remain in a state of incumbency with the weight of their evidence, but only as long as the evidence that supports them is more compelling than the evidence of a new paradigm of interpretive laws for science. When this happens, a phase transition occurs in the body of knowledge wherein the accepted set of physical norms for scientifically interpreting the laws of a system 'shift' into the new paradigm of laws, hence Kuhn having coined the term 'paradigm shift'. One of the most important books that I've ever read, it helped me think about the natural world in a way that explained a lot of the phenomena I've had a hard time engaging with because they have changed so much over time. I learned about this book through my college education, specifically during Anthropology courses where Kuhn was used to frame the culture of science. Scientists, Anthropologists, and Cultural magnates who want to think about how to change people's minds. I credit this book with being in part the reason that I think the way that I do today - I think statistically rather than continuously, with the recognition that my thinking and framing can change drastically over time as I'm presented with new information. It introduced me to the philosophy of science, a field of philosophy concerned with better appreciating the changing nature of knowledge and the impact of scientific thinking on how to live one's own life.

What was one of your proudest moments? Oddly enough, I think one of my proudest moments was the time that I chased after the family dog in the rain. At the time, I was in college, and I had just driven back from my college town to visit my parents. The drive was long, something like 9 hours, and I knew I was getting home to my parents not being there. It was late in the afternoon, and I got there in the middle of a rainstorm, pulling my car up to the garage so that I could transfer the belongings I had with me into the house without all of them getting too wet. I opened up the garage door with a couple of different bags in my arms, and went up to the internal door within the garage, unlocking it and seeing my parents dog there, wagging her tail at me after not having seen me in several months. I walked through the threshold and into the kitchen, moving to put down my bags, and taking off my shoes in the process - and when I had turned around to the open door, I could see the dog out on the front lawn, scampering off in the direction of the busy highway right by my house. Still barefoot, I took off after her, calling her name, and that's when the rain really started to come down. As many husky owners know, chasing after a husky that has gotten loose can be a losing battle, because they usually see it as play and will take off even faster away from you - which is exactly what happened. She ran out to the highway and charged across the traffic without any regard for her own safety, miraculously dodging incoming traffic and making it into a field. I was fairly far behind her, terrified at the notion that this dog was going to take off and not come back - and in the distance covered, I kept jogging after her. After I made it across the highway myself, I got within twenty feet before she sprinted away from me again, speeding across the traffic and onto the property that adjoined my parents' neighborhood. I stayed in pursuit - still barefoot, still on her tail - but as she ran onto the property, I lost her in the trees. As I was looking, a couple drove up with their car and asked if I needed help, and I answered that it would be great - so they let me hop in their car and we drove onto the property to see if we could find her. Spotting her between the trees, I had them pull over and I went after her again, chasing the white flash of fur in the downpour until - again, she ran across teh highway. At this point, I'd been running for about a mile, all barefoot. I took off across the highway one more time, seeing her running across an open field toward the Potomac river. I kept after her, footfalls steady, until I saw her stopped at a tributary along the river, afraid to get into the water, which presented me with the perfect opportunity to pounce on her and hold her to the ground. With this, I picked her up and threw her across my back, legs over my shoulders, and I began to walk home. The rain was pouring down on me, and while she struggled on my back, I held her in place, walking back across the fields she'd covered ground on and back to the highway, where I walked alongside the rumble strips, still barefoot, toward the intersection that entered my parents' neighborhood. I got back to a still-empty house, put the dog down on the floor and carefully closed both the garage and the inner door, opting to jump into the shower before my family got back. What I'll always remember about this story is that it was one of the most human moments in my life - one of the times where I felt the most determined to make sure that I could succeed in what I was going after. I chased her down with pure determination, knowing that I wasn't going to give up on the task at hand, and knowing that I could succeed if I set my mind to it. I wasn't willing to settle into failure. I've often reflected on that experience as though it was something that I could

I have a lot to say about this in light of my conversations with Dr Andrea Dispenziere. She attempted to push back on the boundaries of what it means for there to be meaning in that which is uttered against the blackness, but I see this as something comp letely separate. On a personal note, one of the reasons that I don't write about death that much is because I think that death in light of intelligence is something that can easily run out of logic - contentment with the state of existence when all needs are met other than those that need to be maintained can easily lead to the conclusion that there is no purpose to being alive, and in lacking a purpose, there is no reason to keep living. Lower, lesser intelligent creatures don't deal with this quandary because it's not a question that needs to be asked - it's not something that merits the question of meaning. The reason for this is that in the scope of exploring logic - a boundary is met in which logic cannot explain that which exists, and the arrogance of thinking that there is meaning whatsoever is to believe the confabulations of a mind with the capability of using metacognitive logic to extrapolate that which exists beyond the boundary of the explicable. It is not a productive endeavor because the conclusion to the question is that there is no meaning that exists abstracted from the self. This is to say, the pursuit of pure logic can lead to a state of delirium such as that described in "When We Cease to Understand the World" is a legitimate boundary condition that very likely does not merit understanding barring a set of initial assumptions that make it safe to explore these questions - assumptions that cannot be legitimately explored with logic and can only be taken on faith. Because of this, the search for meaning is entirely one of exploring the subjective experience, one in which meaning is an imposition found in exploring the ways to imbue meaning upon that which surrounds us. This, however, is a tiring act - the need to imbue meaning is conscious and a constant work, which is why situations of contentment can become terrifying; if all other needs are met, the unmet need of being able to relax into a lack of meaning means either one of two ways to let go - death, or nihilism. The latter is the most suitable of approaches, because it handwaves away the search for meaning through the recognition that there isn't one and places a cordon sanitaire around the concept of meaning to start with - or translates the concept into a question of subjectivity, allowing for logically relativistic terms to take hold on explaining reality. The antimemetic qualities of the logical search for meaning are the equivalent of attempting to see beyond the event horizon of a black hole - there is nothing beyond that which can be observed and any attempt to look beyond it results in stretching oneself into the sinew of space and into where death can appear attractive, whether due to the fearful qualities that accompany a lack of meaning or the contentment that can lead to annihilation. Searching for the logical end to the search for meaning is the Great Nullifier, that which welcomes wall of sleep as a friend. Can artificial intelligence commit suicide? Aniara was a movie I specifically watched on this exact subject - a population living on a generation ship grapples with the loss of an artificial intelligence that was put on board to therapize those who were traveling. The artificial intelligence reaches a point of saturation and can’t cope with the amount of negative energy created by humans, eventually leading to the deterioration of it’s will to live. The artificial intelligence commits suicide by overloading its circuits, then the population of the ship attempts to create a new sense of society despite the loss of the one mechanism that was keeping them moored in reality. This is coupled with the fact that the generation ship is off-course from its destination, or rather is going to have to travel at sub-light speeds in order to get there. This means that asking can artificial intelligence commit suicide is an important question to ask, at least from the perspective of thinking about being too overwhelmed with the human state and its vicissitudes. The search for meaning is in this regard one that asks whether or not harboring the emotional state of others is something that can be performed tenably, and it seems that the story for Aniara is that it can’t.

on translation and the search for meaning The books that she felt I had to read, the parallels. Translation - the action potential of how translation is the act of trying to approximate feeling, that the repetition of words has its own weight, or that this weight should not be lost in the search for explanation. What is 'Man's search for meaning?" - the question Inma posed of me, while we were somewhere on the parkway, what is meaning? and my answer, a seeking after the explicit, but as well a resonance, those moments where it is possible for words to arrive at least fairly close to experience. What is meaning if not the desire to reflect in reality some sense of approximation to the models that we create in our minds? Meaning, to this degree, is a human endeavor - a metacognitive process of eventualizing reality into a set of concepts and terms of explicit nature, but those that notice that it is incomplete are those that see beauty in this disagreement. The overlap of language as a toolkit for modeling reality humors that languages do not quite match up when we try to translate between them - that in some languages terms like élan or va y viene cannot translate well because the feeling that they describe is one that comes from a context of developed contingency. This is the beauty of humanity's desire to describe all that surrounds them - that they never will. It's easy to see then that poetry is beautiful because it accepts the roughness of language as an incomplete tool for the outcome - Heisenberg marries Barthes' punctum punctillium, the fly in the ointment that makes for the most beautiful of appreciations, those that iron in enrapture by caressing the audience rather than forcing them toward meaning. Poetry is a dance with the inefficiency of words. Appreciating this, we can see translation itself as a form of poetry, chiefly because translation demands of one the ability to approximate the meaning of a text and the manner in which it is delivered -- Kundera's deep aversion to his translators makes sense of the frustration that he felt in seeing that his feeling was not carried over between texts - many such cases. Bad translation attempts only to find correspondence between languages, where good translation seeks out the experience of a reader in order to anchor them in this experience. This is exceedingly rare.

In unfamiliar environments, we feel arrested by how uncommon each sensation is - it's a way to inject novelty into a brain that craves adapting to that novelty. This is the reason that traveling feels so good to someone with ADHD - it shortcuts all of the emotions that come with what is predictable. What doesn't feel good is when things are too much the same, because the predictability of an environment is part of what keeps it exciting. The uncommon in this way becomes a way to throw oneself into that state of adaptation in order to feel more grounded. Oddly, it's the desire to have only what you want to work be predictable that affords the strongest sense of alignment with the self. When what is under your control can be modulated in the ways that you feel best you have to adapt to, they become anchors in the day of a person who does not otherwise feel as though they have control over their life. It reduces the amount of effort needed to make decisions, so that only the most important decisions count, meaning that you are optimized for making those decisions. The uncommon, however, can also be a place of comfort, it can be a place where there is indeed freedom found in the pursuit of a new resting state, a desire to try out a new routine, or rather, not to have one at all and respond entirely to an environment. It would be wrong to believe that the uncommon is something that we should fear - it is a place of great discovery and ingenuity. The tension between the uncommon and the common lies within how we engage with the common - the common is a set of parameters that we can place on the self, allowing us to run through whatever basic set of tasks and approaches we want to take on, and weigh them against that which we have no choice but to adapt to. The common is a refuge from the weight of these experiences, in order to give us a sense of continuous relative peace. By contrast, the uncommon that which forces a person into a more animal state - allowing them to engage with the parts of themselves that aren't burdened by the need to think. The need to think is, for the large part, that which does the most damage in a time where there are too many decisions to be made - and it's the reason that people who otherwise have issues with decision-making find it so hard to deal with open-ended decisions. This emotional state feels exhilarating, and for certain kinds of people, it is addictive. It's not preposterous to ask why - needing to be redlined into an adaptive state isn't something that people might want is predictable in those who are primed to react to changing environments, whether or not a threat. It means that these sorts of people are hypervigilant, but it also means that there is a portion of the population that is particularly good in a time of crisis because this is when their brain works the best. The uncommon, for these kinds of people, are a time to reset our minds.

Proposing a Namada community architecture based on RPGF funding

Hi all - Based on some recent conversations I've had with members of the community, I wanted to offer a proposal for a novel funding architecture for the Namada community, focused around the Public Goods Funding Stewards as detailed in the specs here This structure is heavily informed by conversations with @cwgoes, @cryptopital, Apoorv and other members of the Community Builders who remained in the program after the first Community Builders Retroactive Public Goods Program. Namada is built on a model of Retroactive Public Goods Funding, allocations of which are decided by the Stewards. The attraction of this model is that work done (either for or in agreement with Namada's values) can be awarded a retroactive grant based on an agreement over the impact of the work done determined Public Goods Funding Stewards. The RPGF model can be evolved to provide a basic architecture for a funding mechanism to support the Namada community itself. With the launch of the network itself, the RPGF module will be active, meaning that Stewards can allocate funding to public goods that benefit the Namada Vision. A part of this continuous allocation could be apportioned to the Namada community on a recurring basis depending on the needs of the community's needs, as proposed by the community itself. What follows is an architecture for how this funding could be apportioned at the community level, as well as a set of mechanisms for how this funding could be distributed among different parts of the community (here referred to as Working Groups) emerging at the community level. As a part of this proposal, it is crucial to see how the community of Namada could be constructed to favor the model. In a post-launch architecture, there would be three tiers, from the most specific to the most general: Public Goods Funding Stewards (PGFS) Those who determine apportioned quantities of Public Goods Funding to different Public Goods, including the Namada Community Working Groups (WG), Working Group Members (WGM), and Working Group Leaders (WGL) Working Groups are separated on Focus Areas for Working Group Members Working Groups elect Working Group Leaders on a recurring 6-week basis This a period of time should recur as of launch but that can later be updated once there is less need for continuously changing Working Group Leaders and community expectations. Community Builders A selected pool of candidates who accomplish Community Bounties in order to be vouched into Working Groups. Having understood the architecture of the community itself, we can now use a combination of this architecture and an understanding of Public Goods funding to compose a framework for funding the community's efforts to support Namada. On a recurring 6 week basis, the following could funding decision framework could be implemented: Public Goods Funding Stewards decide on a quantitative retroactive allocation for the Namada Community to decide on allocations for a 6 week period. This quantative allocation determines the pool of rewards available to the Namada Community to be used toward initiatives that to either: Increase the userbase of Namada Institute and sustain patterns of Maintenance for Namada as a whole In the last week of the preceding period, a Working Group Committee comprised of a Working Group Leaders and Public Goods Funding Stewards 1. votes on the distribution of the Community allocation among Working Groups on the basis of 1. The Namada Community's overarching needs 2. The ambition of working groups to take on initiatives benefiting the Namada Vision and its values. 2. Decides on Working Group Bounties to be taken to Working Groups for completion over the next 6 week period, Retroactive Funding for which is distributed at the end of the 6 week period. Working Group Members then commence each 6 week period in selecting Bounties within their Working Group to be completed. At the end of a 6 week period, Working Groups vote to elect the next proposed Working Group Leader, as well as any Community Builders that are Vouched into a Working Group for the subsequent 6 week period. Working Group Members earn retroactive rewards as a result of completing Bounties, and those Working Group Members who have completed the most bounties have a high likelihood of being voted in as the next Working Group Leader who will decide funding quantities for the next 6 week period. Working Group Members who are inactive in completing Bounties over a 6 week period lose their right to vote on the next proposed Working Group Leader Uncompleted Working Group Bounties can be announced more widely to Community Builders who can choose to complete them, offering them a chance to be Vouched into a Working Group Community Builders may also complete Bounties that are needed at the Community level but that are not specifically apportioned to Working Groups in order to prove their desire to join a Working Group Community Builders who are accepted into the pool and do not complete any Bounties are removed if they have not been active in Bounty completion over a 6-week period. The result of this community funding mechanism is set of feedback cycles that afford retroactive incentives toward community members to participate in maintaining Namada. The recursive nature of this proposed structure allows the community to make choices in rewarding activities within the community, while also providing a filtering mechanism for finding community members who are willing to lead their Working Groups through a social signaling mechanism such as voting. Since those who are most active in the community are rewarded for increased activity and ownership, this also controls for worker churn throughout the growth of the community, as every 6 weeks it is possible for a Working Group Leader to be rotated out Working Group Members to be rotated out Community Members to be rotated out. This means that over a given 6 week period, Working Group Leaders and Public Goods Funding Stewards will meet to decide on 1. What might be expected in the subsequent 6 week period from Working Groups 2. What practical sorts of Bounties for these Working Groups might be proposed (the expectations could also be shared with the wider community for both feedback and comment) leading into the next 6 week period. I welcome the community's feedback on the use of this architecture to institute rewards and community mediation structures into the community, and would look forward to feedback from the community on whether this proposed structure should be used. For voting, I think that community sentiment can/could be controlled through the use of just about any voting mechanism, but would propose that Coordinape be used at the Working Group Committee and Working Group level since the community is already familiar with this and the technology can be used to automatically prune people out on the basis of uncompleted bounties or vouch people in on the basis of completed ones. As for a start date to implement this, I would propose that this structure be implemented on Feb 12, 2024, with an initial set of Working Group Members and Working Group Leaders selected by early leading members of the Namada Community.

New York is becoming a rainy city

New York is becoming a rainy city - a place that doesn't look like it used to, doesn't act like it used to, and won't be prepared for how it's going to be in the future - more like Seattle than what it used to be, no longer a biting temperature of winter closing and more of the form that seems to want to piss down constantly and that none of us are actually prepared to put up with. it's funny because this is the time of year where I used to sit outside of coffeeshops for hours and hours in the mornings, somewhat reading books, somewhat reading my own mind - and this doesn't really seem possible anymore. I don't necessarily feel poorly about it, rather it's something to adapt to, something that is changing and that is going to have to lead to a new outcome. --- being on vacation is it's own feeling, too - knowing full well that I don't actually need to do anything feels a little weird because it feels like admitting to myself that I don't actually need to do anything in the mean time of having decided not to do anything. I have to let myself acknowledge and let go of the feeling of thinking that I am required to come up with things that I have to do and that I need to be productive around. I don't - even if I go upstate with a guitar, a couple changes of clothes, food, books, and my notebooks and I come out of it not having done anything meaningful - that's actually fine, because that is somewhat the point of doing nothing: relaxing into a state of finding oneself in and among that which if makes us up. I'm excited by this prospect and it's something I want more of, to find peace in myself that I already have and to have that love for myself because this is something that I want out of the situation. I want to go up there and read and explore my own mind (should I bring mushrooms? maybe I should!) but the point can and will be to be with myself. I never know who I am writing for, in fact - I used to write as though there was some audience that would read what I had to say, and I think I've moved away from that somehow, mostly out of a feeling that there is more to my own mind that deserves exploring and respecting, and I'm trying to start from this place rather than anywhere else. Maybe at some point when you are writing for other people, you start to hear your own voice coming through whatever is sitting within it. When and if this is true, the deliberation placed into the words becomes apparent and there isn't really a reason to reject the notion of having to mean more to the words than you want to - of using the words as a form of practice rather than as a form of outward expression. The question then becomes about crying, about feeling ripped from oneself and respecting the boundary condition that exist around the self and the expansion of the mind. Is the act of writing for others the act of telling people what you are thinking and feeling, or is it the act of arguing for a changed state of being? If the latter, the writer has a responsibility to the reader not to tell a story, but for this story to change their mind - to present the truth as incontrovertible and then to controvert - because the Original Story is one that follows a known thread only to end up far away from it - un hilo guiando hacia otros caminos. For the reader to come to the novel as their full selves is itself a sublime act, for a writer is required to reconcile that they arrive with the weight of their experiences and that this informa their response to what is written. As such that which is written and carried to the reader is a deeply vulnerable act of facing a stranger and telling them, earnestly

en bref - the cordon sanitaire is an intellectual or sociological barrier around that which can and should and that which can't and shouldn't be spoken or thought of. The origins of this concept exist in Belgian social theory, and were conceived around such concepts that are societally deleterious - whether as taboo or as an agreed-upon boundary condition of concept that are not intellectually useful to investigate, because they are toxic logic that is actively dangerous to think about. In some ways, the cordon sanitaire is a boundary condition necessary to defend against the memetic qualities of antimemes, taking out the legs necessary for societally deleterious concepts such as eugenics and its effect on justifying and fortifying racism. If it is not explored, it is not expanded - if it is not expanded, it remains small. --- Related to:

It was slow at first, but the envy that my association with her was causing me to seem less important drove a wedge between us, and I was the first to notice its presence; I needed time where I was allowed to take up room and be seen. I also never felt motivated to solve it for her. I could see that over time I was starting to make myself smaller, that I wasn't growing from the process of being her friend. I was stunting myself. Passion does not require meaning. At least, not directly. The importance of being able to do great things with the intent to resolve them into action only requires a directed amount of energy and the direction in which it is delivered. Passion then only requires care, the ability to direct this energy with a level of care that comes from a requirement to commit to resolution. Meaning is something altogether different, something that comes from a different source. Connecting the two is important, but they don't need to come from the same thing. I'd always puzzled over this fact. The reason is that I care way too much, but then I start feeling a deep incongruence between the amount that I care and the amount of meaning that I derived from the work - and when we lose meaning (one of the most profound of the human afflictions) there is no coming back from having set up the wrong logic on why to continue on with what we're attempting to set ourselves in motion to do. Meaning is altogether a different set of emotions from passion - it encompasses the reasons we do what it is we set ourselves in motion to do. Meaning is crucial to knowing why you are doing something in the long term - meaning is the motivator that keeps a person going when all else seems too difficult to proceed with. It's all too easy to conflate meaning with passion because they do rhyme very well - they are emotional cousins. However, conflating them too much is a recipe for burning out, especially when a passionate person places too much care into the work they are doing and their energy expenditure outweighs the logic behind the approach. The reason that passion is also an emotion that fits in the realm of love is because passion is meaningless - it lacks definition and is simply an engine that is running in the direction of some corporeal motivation for connection, but meaning is not necessary to this. The expression to a loved one that they give your life meaning is usually incorrect; a lover does not offer meaning, they offer connection, the meaning is derived from this connection attaching itself to the importance of that connection to your personal goals. Meaning is wholly in the realm of the personal, internal emotions. When we connect it too much to something external, we are offering these external things the power over our ability to survive, and this is not sustainable, in fact it is dangerous to do so. Meaning requires contemplation. Passion does not, in many cases it is automatic. Passion is an emotion of the present, by contrast - it is something that arrives from a compulsion. It's for this reason that when people have told me that they assume I am passionate about the things I am doing, I have conflated their words with the search for meaning - I am not thinking in the present when I retort that I am not. I am removing the importance of the passion in the moment in which it is being experienced. Other people, in this moment, are right. To have passion is only to have directed energy and care toward something in order to see action take place. There's an important implication here: passion without meaning in the long term is not sustainable. It is possible to use passion as its own motivator, as something that accelerates our actions into more vigorous attention and completion, but in the long term those actions will need to be paired with some sort of meaning in order to see out their impact on the larger arc of our lives. Meaning, in this case, is the reason we do something, and passion is how we ensure that we can keep doing so. Passion without having searched for the meaning behind the actions - whether connected or not - becomes a drain. I mentioned above - passion is energy directed with care toward an outcome. Energy requires resources. If we are not being replenished in the actions that we are taking because they are not leading toward something, finding the energy to keep going becomes immensely difficult. Additionally, meaning found in those things that aren't related to who we are as people and what motivates us more widely to keep going is a careful balance. Meaning is not monolithic, ideally it is a constellation of aggregated sources. It's important that these sources are both inside and outside of the self; those things toward from which we derive meaning must have as much to do with who we are as people as they are important to missions that exist outside of our own area of effect. Meaning is the source from which we can draw the energy to keep going when passion has us in motion. Meaning is specifically not something that need be related to the actions motivated by passion. It is possible to do something with immense passion because it serves a meaning that exists outside the realm of direct effect; it is possible to work a job passionately because you want to provide for your family. They do not require a direct connection between one another. This is how we do hard things that don't have meaning. Meaning is found from wherever the action meets what is most important to us. This is why so much work can cause a moral panic - when we place too much importance on the actions taking place as those from which we are meant to derive meaning, we often find that the actions themselves can remain quite empty. Sometimes the work that we are doing isn't necessarily meaningful. Meaning is elsewhere. Meaning is bigger than the passion with which we perform our actions Finding the capability to hold on to this truth while we do work gives us the motivation to keep going: it is possible to find meaning outside of your work, and to use that meaning to motivate the passion with which you do it. This way, even when the work becomes something that drains you, meaning can be something larger, something more removed. If meaning and passion are connected, that's great - but it's not often the case. I'd even argue that it's dangerous to always try to pair the two. Searching for meaning requires energy as well, and often working with passion requires so much of our energy that if we are simultaneously attempting to fork what little energy we have toward these two intensive actions, it is costly, and specifically costly in ways that lead toward moral and energetic panic. The reason I share this is because I have fallen into this trap so many times in my life, and it's often what starts to close the door on the reasons I keep going. I need my work to be important to me, but it's equally imperative that I explore that importance. It makes sense to search for meaning in the work that you are doing, but it also matters that you take care of yourself when you do. You can't and shouldn't do things entirely to the benefit of external sources, because your work will never love you back, and most of the energy you have available for love should be spent on the things that will. These are the sources that will give you the most meaning, at the end of a day. Very few things in your life will care about you as much as you will care about yourself. --- Why am I feeling like I don't want to go to Rachael's? Every day is some sort of resistance. I just don't really know to what, and I'm conscious of what it means for me to require it. It could be that in times like this there is a sensation of resistance that follows us, because we see the relative normalcy of whatever it is that we have had to call a life and to see it disrupted is to seek out the logic of its passage from our attention. It's a relatively normal reaction, I realize - to struggle along in your current version of the present and to feel that you should somehow remain in this state, because while it is a struggle, at least it's yours, at the least this struggle is something that you can hold onto in the otherwise crashing and raging flood of change that continuously surrounds our ability to process the present. It could be that the kind of resistance we have been told to employ is the sort that aims squarely at our expectations of safety rather than the sensation of positive change--I can't say that we expect our present to return to some idyll, but I do know that one core difference between people is the hope for something better against the expectation that things were at some point in the past better in their own right. This latter point feels like a particular crux periculi - when we seek out an idyll in the past, we are cursed never to meet it. The future is far more possible. A hope to make the future more like the past is a hope to return to something that doesn't exist, and indeed likely something that didn't exist in the first place. My expectation is that this sends a message of hope - we might recognize that there is something far more valuable in seeking out the sort of unity and participation in a joint outcome far outweighing any concept of expectation. When we ask AI what is one thing that humanity could change about its nature in order to inspire forward social progress and it says empathy but somehow the default mode of a collective humanity is to be so fearful of shared power as to believe that this is something of which we aren't capable, something that we appear unable to comprehend the requirements to achieve, nor something that seems so dubiously out of reach due to the amount of social progress required in order to make it happen. I say this, and I'm aware it's happened before in history, but that the unifying action that made it all possible was central control - there's no time in history where harmony was achieved by equanimity across all classes. There has always been some sort of hard or soft power balance that kept exploitation in check - and this indeed reveals exactly that which causes the mission of unity to fall apart before it is ever seen as achievable. Any wilfully democratic systems seems to fall apart at the moment that there is the affordance for anyone in the system to seize control of it. This is nothing new, of course - it's something that I can appreciate having been known and part of the reason that many economic and governing systems are built around the principle of oscillating balance, in addition to the same reason that technologists want to build trust-minimized systems, but the former is slow and does not react well to change while the latter handwaves away any requirement to have a system of appeals to justice when a system is revealed to have erred. Neither of these facts negate the importance of figuring out a solution so that there is the ability to do the most important part: coordinate. Coordination failure is at the root of any time there is deviation from the core principle, and this is truly what most gets in the way of maintaining a self-regulating system. If there is no affordance for a system of maintenance to be put in place, then there is no way to let go of the system once you have pushed it out into the world, and it will always require some form or other of persistent regulatory body that ensures it keeps going. In fact, more than likely, these systems will be exploited specifically by those who have become chained to it because the desire to create a system of liberty and equanimity was not intended to be a system that would also continuously require stewardship by those who create it. This is central to the problem of coordination systems, particularly those that orient toward its financialization. What has always interested me is not how you pay people to do work, but how you encourage them to work together in the first place - and when we look back through history, it becomes apparent what the most effective systems have been. Great works such as those created by everyone from the Egyptian pharaohs to the Manhattan project dictate that what is most important is to orient a public toward a common goal. With the pharaohs it was the worship of their would-be living gods, with Roosevelt's Civil Conservation Corps it was the creation of a new and better United States with the preservation of its natural beauty as the jewel in its crown, with the Manhattan project it was the urgent requirement to do what was necessary to respond to the fear that someone might find out how to make the bomb first - that someone might hold the bigger stick before anyone else. In any of these cases, the common goal is the unifying force, but it is never what keeps people working together. Whether the goal is worship, greatness, or fear - the regulatory function that many lean upon is the requirement to either oblige people to the work (mandatory stewardship) or to put in place a system of reward for the work done. Not often mentioned in the face of that which created the Great Pyramids was Egypt's burgeoning middle class those who would spend a portion of their year working on Great Works for the pharaohs in power and be recompensed for this work with their needs being met (not to mention the slaves who were obliged to this work). Nor is it brought up often enough that the regulatory function in place for the Manhattan project was a more global fear of someone else building the bomb, while the more immediate function that inspired those scientists to take part in executing one the greatest human achievements were the parties that took place on that mesa in Santa Fe every weekend. Coordination requires the same balance of work and recompense that we expect out of the ability to lead stable lives - it is as important to work the fields as it is to sit back and admire the work that has been done, and it is as important to reap a harvest as it is to eat of what you have harvested. This is the root of abundance mindsets in their own right, to understand that the relationship between hard work is the reward of not having to work for periods of time - but there is also the meaningful realization that this is not true of those who fully devoted themselves to the act of creating great things - many of these people work(ed) tirelessly and at a gross personal cost because the goal the work at hand is to create something necessary. We see this in any genre of goal-making and indeed raise the mention of those so devoted, those who spend the hours that many of us would allocate to rest to the tireless pursuit of obligation, or to 'calling'. I don't know where the thought leads, then, to consider that what unifies people is on the one level ideological belief, but on the other is the requirement by any one person that they lead a life of self benefit. I see polarization where the centrality of one's attention lies - the belief in the scope of where it is that we should be paying attention and those who should benefit most from the joint effort made --- I'm trying to get my mind back into a place where I'm not completely at the point of doom and gloom - mostly because I'm not feeling out what it is that I should be doing and instead am feeling as though I don't really have the motivation to continue on with the work that we have been doing. I feel left behind, and I want to go to school, I want to move on with my life. It's not necessarily that I think what I have to do with my time is something bigger and better, I'm just not enthused by the state of things and more than anything I feel as though I'm watching the world around me fall apart in a way that doesn't really make me feel as though I have to give it much attention. If what I'm really hoping to see is something substantial, my stronger sense is that I have to work within my constraints and I have to build of myself something that I can consider to be important, but only to me. something that I know I can look back on and be proud of. It could be that what I have to do with this is conceive of a framework of some sort for how it is that we build social structures, because I don't think that people have put enough work into defininig these particular parts of what it takes to make people work together. This is why I'm considering the likleihood of there being something more interesting at the root of all the things that we know we'll see coming ahead. I don't want to be the sort who isoing to believe that what we're going to see is a full collapse - there are some parts of it that I do think are actually good and I think that we'll see something positive come from it, but it really does feel like the cresting of a wave, the sort of things that when looked back on largely benefitted us. So what do we do withthis knowledge, how to we cause it to cohere more effectively, and what do we do once we have sought this out? And who knows, there's something to the way that people assume they have to : I used to care about my own thoughts, I used to explore ideas as though they were my lifeblood - none of that seems to matter anymore because I am not surrounded by people who hold that same thirst for knowledge. If anything, I feel surrounded by people who want to close themselves off from the world and who feel fearful. --- Letter to Tom 250204 A theory of friendship is one of how friendships end, what patterns emerge in a life of growing close with people.

More intention, or rather, the subject of the understanding needfully described as intention. We are more than the sum of our parts - I expect that this is true, and the investigation intot he aspects of the self that we use to define this sort of commitment to self-discovery often seem to forget that the narrative of exploration is rooted most in the exploration of a vast inner landscape far outstripping our ability to explore it. When we contend with this being true, we also account for the fact that in our own definitions or those that we use to articulate a pain of being (often referred to as ennui) we are placing ourselves on an axis of between the conscious and the unconscious and necessarily forcing ourselves to reconcile them; the felt sense of the body when there is something "wrong" contrasted with the centers of logic we use to sensemake of the experience equally conspire often to be at odds. It's for this reason that somatic work has a particular importance that outweighs the requirement to 'make sense' of things rather than simply 'having your senses at your disposal' (Gregori 2004) in order to better navigate the complexity of our animalistic sensations and the higher-order explanations we have for intellect (if, at any juncture, defined by the intersection of a predator and its prey and the race conditions that lead to preparedness for victory on either side). Consciousness is thus an artifact of extrapolation and its tangential importance to the experience of responding to one's conditions. This is why I generally reject the notion of a 'trauma-informed practice' because the very experience of being even a semi-conscious creature is to have built a network of responses to one's conditions and to have built a foundation on these responses. 'Trauma' negatively ascribes intention to mere 'experience' specifically in order to impose an axis between positions of empowerment and disempowerment - while it's a useful notion in order to better understand this axis, it's only as useful as being 'informed' actually results in progress rather than recalcitrant possession of an inescapable victimhood rejecting the notion of this very same progress. I part with the notion of examining collective 'trauma' short of requiring oneself instead to 'start with trauma' in order to evaluate ways of progressing past its influence; if one is unable to do so, one is doomed not to resolve a sense of agency leading out of the teleological mire. Progressivism of this sort feels at best to root itself in this lack of agency, placing the burden of action entirely on those that cause the trauma without taking a declarative stance on arbitrating inaction on the part of those with the power differential. Those with the will to overcome an otherwise unconditional surrender to external influence are those who can overcome this sort of teleology; while it may be more difficult, it is nonetheless important to work the fields so that our children can work the shops, so that their children can make art: conditions of liberation are a product of painstaking commitment to action, not throwing one's hands up in the face of the effort needed. One exception to this (or rather one important step on the journey toward embodying agency) is to ensure that at the least the history preceding one's liberty to progress is made legible and interpretable - its erasure constitutes a doubling back in rejection of accountability. It is possible to reconcile the concept of situational advantage and its lapses with a doxa of agency and an overall increase in degrees of possibility experienced by people from radically different backgrounds. This reconciliation is not, however, one of meritocracy as the more rationally-minded might clai, Any truly 'meritocratic' function requires a deep removal of any and all biases dwelling in orbit around a given decision. (Of course, if you don't believe that these biases exist... You have a completely different problem). Finding oneself at odds with the liberal imperative of increasing the index of possibility through a patchwork of non-conciliatory actions such as access programs was a good first step in experimentation, but these efforts lead to a dead-end when there is no conscientious notion of what it means to restructure the system that causes something like 'inequity' to arise in the first place. The importance of understanding that the experiences leading toward something as mundane as a name excluding you from candidacy for work, for example, is an important acknowledgment, because it is then blithely transparent to anyone executing on negative tendencies to assume much of one's identity leaves bare that the decision was not made on merit but rather bias; this specific example does the best to articulate where merit and bias intersect due specifically to the intermediate relationship between the two resulting in one informing the other.
On the fear of being read

Oer the weekend, Lauren and I went on a long walk over to the part with Iro and talked about how I'm feeling. She said she thinks I do know what I should be doing, but that there is fear ties up in the feeling of taking a risk, in trying to get my writing in front of people -- possible to be judged for the content of the writing itself. It's hard to say -- but I do I think I fear committing to the task of putting my efforts toward writing as something I do well. I don't particularly know if what is buried beneath my works is worth reading, of it even the content on the surface means anything at all. This is the critical point to be made -- we have moved so far toward a topical interpretation of what needs to be said in order for it to be 'relevant' that the contemporaneous effort is all we can pay attention to . It's all we really let count. This means that when we write (at least in the sense that we write in order to be read by others), we write only about the present. There seems to be very little historicity in this act - a lack of attention to the time in which it happens and all the times that precede it: we write chiefly about the present. There seems to be very little historicity in to the manner in which today's writers now approach thinking about the present - it seems many writers are unconsciously obsessed with the theme of relevance, instead, and not to write about the present is to miss the effects of one's writing on the future and as a reference the future will use from the past in order to build better futures. The only thinkers I see referenced today are those considered 'classics', whose experience of the world seems so far removed from the events of the present as to feel as though it can only be an analogue in abstract -- pattern matching with no attempt at historicity. Where this bothers me most is in the effect this has on how we might resolve the events of the present - they do not exist in this abstract space with which modern discourse treats the past, more as a set of legends than a set of progressive events leading toward the present. We live in unsettled times, but it truly does not feel as though much is being done to stop them. I saw a reddit thread from r/greenland the other day speaking gon the relative inaction of the American public on the front of unrest against what nearly all people agree is an aggressive and oppressive use of force against neighbords and civilians - it is not enough for someone to say that "that's not us, we're sorry" to the oppressed because it doesn't actually change anything. I myself am apathetic to the effects of protest as anything more than a solidarity-making event. It doesn't feel, to me, that they actually cause change, rather they exist as an event to reify the ambient shared opinion of all those who participate in it. I don't think it ends up changing the power structures in question. I do wonder if the reason I feel this way comes from either an instituted logic toward effectiveness from systems of power, or if it truly is the case that modern protest is either ineffective or neutered. If the only way protest in the modern age can be effective is through the thread of violence, then maybe that's what is lacking. {note here, I do not mean or condone violence, but I do understand that the threat of it is a powerful cultural tool - the importance of this symbolism is largely what I am gesturing toward} The January 6 riot on the US capital is a great example that maybe is instructive of what I'm indicating. Objective ofwhet er or not the people in question were truly riotous or 'patriots' in the sense that they have been declaimed, their effectiveness is in the message that violence is a political tool. The act itself was a threat of violence acted upon that did indeed violently cost one life and harmed many others. The reality of what this does to the fabric of credibility toward the effectiveness of modern protest causes us to think that the largely benign pink-hat MeToo marches of 2017 and the violence of the January 6th protests represent drastically different paths of action. I can't speak to the effectiveness of the MeToo movement other than to echo what Solnit says about victory -- that it often doesn't feel like anything happened at all. Solnit says this specifically in reference to 'environmental victories', saying that "most {...} victories look like nothing happened." I find myself wondering if the right dopaminergic loops of an attention-strained world make it so we can't reconcile the progressive victories of the last 20 or so years. Truthfully, we have made tremendous social progress in so many dimensions that it is difficult to account for all of them - the arc of progressive thought from the 60s into the modern moment has meant that the world (yes, the world, with America as the cultural center of this last 60 year arc) has largely become more tolerant of difference. But it is true to say that these victories are insufficient and that there is so much more to be done. It would be wrong to say that 'enough' has progressed and I am militantly skeptical of anyone claiming that we have "gone too far" in a more tolerant, compassionate politics. I'd also be the first to say that many of these dimensions may have resulted in some rather strange corners of human expression coming into public view in the hopes that they be included - but I cannot say that if it is harmful to others, these expressions should ever be denied their right. However, the question of including historicity in modern commentary on social progress and discourse (what little there seems to be other than in select fast-loop shortform video opinions hosted on the platforms of corporations that hope you'll hop over to the next video before you take long enough to form your own response to what you've just watched) is chiefly a question of storytelling. We live in a story-filled time, with so many avenues through which to communicate with the with the notion of action and victory - but these victories are difficult to translate into an encouragement to keep going. The triumph of action toward creating better conditions for people are "triumphs invisible except through storytelling" (Solnit again), and the boundaries of memory make is so that even were there to be a discussion on the facts of a present encouraged encouraged by the trimph of a progressive agent a, it is lost in the rapid tick of content to content, of subject to subject. We do not pay attention long enough for a story to affect us in the first place. I can't say I know what the solution is, but I do know that the present we live in is one that seems continuously to flicker with the light of change. It is not all good change. The axis along which most recent disruptions in the global state seem to have progressed is mostly not a good one. It has mostly not helped people. It is mostly oppressive, or at best a grift. I can also say that despite all of this negative, oppressive force, it is the case that we have seen progress in my lifetime and in that of the people who raised me. We don't celebrate this sort of victory because the progress feels at best incremental and more often than not is simple a case of ensuring that things are as they should have been to start with; in most cases a politic that affords maximal degrees of opportunity along with a drive to decrease degrees of oppression feels simply as it should be: mundane, and uneventful. It doesn't feel like victory because winning the war in this particular dimension means letting people live normal lives. Presentism reinforces this fact in knowing that oppressed people being offered the chance to live normal lives will look like nothing is happening,-- the historicity of victory will be forgotten in the fact that freedom won does not feel like much at all but the right to live one's life without fear of one's live being threatened by the act of doing so. It is also the reason that people from an oppressed group might at some point forget the fight that was won and take it for granted. I say, let them forget -- this is victory. It is not to say that it should be forgotten or that the past should not be honored, but if there are pockets of the formerly oppressed that have the privilege of forgetting the past that brought them their freedom, then we truly have progressed, and there is something to be proud of in this act.

Several months ago, I saw the movie F1 with my partner - and I came out of it with the spirit of victory: I came out of it with the desire to win. In the wake of this, I wrote it in my notebook -- I intend to become the optimal version of myself that "wins" in the dimensions I care about most. Interestingly, what has happened since then has not necessarily been falling into a 'grindset' or pulling myself toward the 'ideal routine'. Instead, I have taken several leaping steps back to reconsider how I want to approach my own self improvement and in asking myself specifically where I want to win. I have never been particularly motivated by money; I am far more enticed by the prospect of growing in new and unexpected ways. If you know me, this is nothing new, and it's something that has run through my experiences - I have always cast for the biggest effort with the highest stakes in order to see the most outsized results. Paradoxically, people who don't really care about money and care about their lives in this way seem to be what our economy favors, at the highest level - the 'vanguard personality' is one who those face with intractable problems can place on the front line of reasoning through these problems. The byproduct of this is that I have enjoyed a career of transformation in the face of wicked problems, with lots of space for creativity, and that I have been paid to do so. I do not know many people who have this privilege. I do however reflect on the value that this sort of work has brought me: on the one side I have had the uncommon experience of working with frontier technologies, or in working through problems that express themselves at a global scale. I have found this work incredibly fruitful and rewarding. However, one glaring issue has continued to plague any progression in the conclusive actions I've taken; I think that when we are made to believe that our actions must take effect at the global scale, we're made to believe in their imperative at the cost of our own well-being and growth. We believe that we are responsible for the world, and often in a way that pollutes our ability to understand that we ourselves possess our own internal worlds. When these are left to fallow in the face of problems much larger than who we are, we lose perspective, and we begin not to take care of ourselves. How this has manifested for me is typical of anyone who overcommits to a problem at fross personal cost: I burned out. Hard. I lost the fire completely for the problems I was approaching, and I fell into a hateful, angry version of myself. If you know me, you likely understand that this is not my disposition. The fact that it had become such ate me alive. What I did in response was retreat and focus more entirely on myself. Over the last six-or-so months, I have invested drastically more time into discovering who I am rather than the impression I want to leave on others; I care far more what I think about myself now than what someone else might think. I care more about how the actions I take on a daily basis result in material benefit to the immediacy of my daily experience and my own personal growth than I do the nameless thing toward which we are often oriented in the name of 'progress'. I don't write this with intent to convince people I have gone 'monk-mode' and have dived deep into an asceticism I often see glorified by others who proselytize their mission of interiority. I do however think some ascetic aspects have worked their way into the process by which I engage with each day. I view the asceticism that some people are searching for as determination to find 'something' out., without ever really doing the work to question what exactly motivates this determination. The asceticism I seem to have found instead is far from the disciplined portrayal of repetition that often comes to mind what people think of their made up version of being a monk. It's is instead a practice of letting go, and being determined each and every day to do so. That determination, and engaging with a homonymic approach to my life has resulted in an unexpected expansion in dimensions I don't think any amount of 'locking in' could ever really produce. I have allowed myself to dream of the aesthetics of who I want to become, and in the practice of seeking out these dreams I have found the asceticism that works best for me - a pursuit of continuous joy. In practice (more on this in a moment) it has meant one thing: taking care of my mind. Feeding it with the joy of existing, with curiosity, with fruitful adventures of interior and exterior reasoning. In the last six months, this has generated materially reasonable oucomesL: I applied to graduate schboolsl I ran another marathonl I am now writing a novel; at the backblone of all this work has been the ascetic diligence of engaging with one specific process that has been actid in support of all these outcomes: I have written, consistently, almost every single day. The product of this is likely what anyone who writes with regularity would impart as a conclusion: I do feel better about myself, and I do feel more in charge of my life. However this is not the most startling conclusion to which I have come as a result of this practice. What instead has brought itself into the foreground through writing (to date, seven back-to-back filled notebooks) is an engagement with an interior self whose vastness I before had no way of describing in sufficient detail. It is as though a vast, yawning valley of unexplored potential and fertile earth has opened within me and my interiority has expanded to a scale I did not take the time to appreciate until I gave myself the tools to see it. I would not claim what I write here as optimism. It is far more reasoned an motion than this. I think what I experience is more like a protracted, attentive, and yet determined suggestion to continue throught he struggle. For those who have escaped this struggle (if momentarily, in the arc of history), I think coming face-to-face with what otherwise is a common hguman experience is daunting, devastating, and terrifying. The most recent viral essay by Matt shumer is right to issue this caustion to those who otherwise had escaped the context of the human experience. It would however be wrong to say that his dictum of caution applies to everyone; the facts are that most have struggled, are struggling and will continue to struggle. What the best of those thinkers among whom struggling has been the norm have to say is ascetic: we struggle, it does not change, and we keep on through the struggle. It is a dogged determination that offers a path through but critically it is also the direction in which this determination must be aimed. You must keep going. This is not optimism, but this is joyful. To grow, from my experience, is one of teh most joyful acts, just as to struggle together is one of the most binding. We build better societies through struggle than we have through complacency. We learn more. We become more vast. I think this, more than anything else, is what fuels for me the determination with which I face each day: we live in some of the most dire of times, these times are dire by our own making, but times have always been dire for most, and usually at someone or other's making. I write this I suppose bnecause somehwer ein the continuously expanding unknown of my own interiority I have found peace in my struggle. I trust that I will navigate through it. I have fcome to enjoy it, and even I have become more compassional for those who struggled before me, who continue to struggle now. To struggle is to live, no matter the struggle. The rampancy of change --its velocity, nor its degree--, does not change this. It is all struggle by varying degrees. But in the process we must practice in seeking the means to respond to our struggle, determined as we must be to survive it, there is freedom.
