The tree at Herbert Von King

There was a tree that used to fill Herbert Von King's dog park. It was a massive, hulking, old thing with branches that offered shade and divots where the roots poked up from underneath the loam and wood chips. They cut the tree down in 2025. I'm pretty sure it was dying, watered mostly by the piss from 30 years of dogs who frequented the park. It was taller than any other tree I've seen survive those conditions. I was proud of it, and it made me smile every time I entered the park Now the dog park has an open, larger feeling to it --by all measures getting rid of the tree opened up space for the dogs to play-- but I still miss it. I took a photograph of a couple sitting on one of the piss covered benches that used to sit in the trees shade. I sent them the photograph and got back one word of "thanks!" and felt like I got to capture something for them, under the shade of a tree that isn't there anymore. I guess it's not really about the tree or the couple, but the empty space at the middle of the park is its own kind of memory--something so large that used to take up so much room, gone, leaving behind something new, but it's lost still hanging in the air above the park. People who never knew it was there probably don't remember it and don't miss it. I think somewhere in going to that park after they took the tree down, I began to say goodbye to Iro. He still had years left.--I think the feeling was one of encountering the hole I knew would open up in my life and trying to steel myself against it. I hardly ever went to that park. I barely ever sat on the benches that had I had been coming to for years, for all of Iro's life, partially due to the busyness of parental neglect toward our best friends, but also because we've been coming to it his entire life and at some point it started feeling like each time was one of the last times. He was fine. He was in good health. He still ran around, he just that year had begun to speak to me more clearly. The first day I felt like I was saying goodbye, he took me to the door of the dog park, telling me that he was ready to leave. He'd never done that before, never before getting bored and wanting to move on. When we walked out of the park, I got down on my knees, thinking about him, about how he chose to tell me what he wanted, and how I'd finally, ten years in, been learning how to listen. I took his head in my hands and spoke to him, telling him that I don't have words for the space in my heart that he fills. Usually, when I perform that sort of affection toward him, there is a sort of pulling away I feel in him, or he'll whine, wanting to keep walking. This time, he sat there, his heavy head in my arms, and he let me breathe into his fur, letting me kiss his forehead. We started walking home, but he pulled me towards a coffee shop, one that had opened up on the edge of the park just a few years before. He pulled me towards the folding tables. It was cold, the kind of cold that holds on to the memory of winter through the water suspended in the air, the humidity increasing and threatening to jump clear past spring, into the sweating summer of Brooklyn. That was the day after the temperature had jumped up to 70°, then swung back down like a hammer. That previous day, I had walked, sweating in too many layers, between the gym and home, twice. At the coffeeshop, I parked Iro down by the tables, went inside, and as I ordered nine dollars worth of turmeric floating in nut milk, I cried behind my sunglasses, quietly sniffing as though allergic to the season. I couldn't tell why he had taken me there. My dog has been a load-bearing tree in the canopy life for as long as he has been alive. He didn't make that choice - I didn't even get to make the choice as to whether or not it happened. An ex decided I was getting a dog, and made the choice for me, and I still have him. She didn't even send me a message to let me know when her own dog died years after we separated. I found out through a friend's instagram post. I had to unlearn a lot that I learned about training dogs after dating her - too many rules had been written and I realized, too late, they were getting in the way of closeness. He wasn't happy, and I was a bitch to him. I think it wasn't until Iro was nine that I started to actually talk to him and understand who he was. That's maybe when the branches grew a little wider above me, but it was around six that I started to fear what my life would be without him. I started writing this essay about him because in that moment that I had been crossing the street toward that coffeeshop, I felt the intense awareness of how that missing tree felt in the park and how long we'd been coming. The same feeling is easy to simulate when you walk through the forest and a tree has fallen - the canopy has a gap in it, and the sky seems eager to flow in, but the vault of the trees overhead no longer feel like cover; we are reminded that they are just branches reaching up toward the sky, shyly avoiding one another in the canopy - they call 'crown shyness'. When the space of all those branches that don't touch is missing a piece of its puzzle, the absence is obvious, unremitting. I started writing this essay because I knew that one day that massive supporting tangle of branches that held up the sky above me would disappear, and I'd have to sit in the exposed air underneath it, and I wouldn't feel protected anymore. I've never understood why anyone who has had a dog in their life could ever say 'it's just a dog' - my mother said it once and I felt earnestly short of slapping her. Iro was the only reason I survived being broken up with by the woman who got him for me, and maybe the only reason I survived living beyond the gap she left in my life after she left and took the dog I had helped her raise.

Children at times are freeform angels - people unsculpted by expectation, whose frames flop and sinter about in the adoption of movement. I watch a woman coax her child down the sideward; it takes six and a half minutes of ill-fitting communication, the child expressing without words an expectation their mother seeks with which to compete - the child bare-chested under their rebellion as the sweater they wear rides up and away from the mother's grasp, away from the home their mother wants to be enticing. Maybe before children learn words they know better than we do how to be resolute in the expression of their desires. It's more pure a declaration of want than when working in dialogue with a fear of judgment of conflict. I think parents forget this; it is easy to forget. My mother, raising three children somewhere she didn't speak the language just because her husband wanted to chase his career. She wanted to leave as well, according to him. "It was the fastest way out of the United States," in one version of the truth, "we were only going to be there for three years, not twenty," in another. We lived in nine countries. My mother raised us in all of them. My father was there, sometimes, most of the time, and years later before he knew I was a woman he would tell me what he would do when he wasn't. Thirty six years later, it has shaped me not to feel American because of it, to look at the country on my passport with skepticism. My parents love one another more than they ever have, in a sense I don't care about what brought them to this point, even while I bear the marks of how it's shaped me. We are all shaped by people who did not know how to raise children. Maybe that is why I am impassive in my love for my parents; they made mistakes, and I will as well, even when the child I raise will not come from my distended belly: I will not know what to do with a child either. I will not know how to speak their non-language of unawareness of a need to express desire. I will also fuck up. I will still love them. They'll still hate me through my mistakes, until they are old enough to understand those mistakes were impossible to avoid. I will also pull a reluctant child down the sidewalk and not listen. I cannot wait. I cannot wait for the frustration of not knowing how to translate the tense wind of a child's voice expressing opposition. The purring wilderness of wanting something different.

I did it again, I sat in my living room playing video games until 11 in the morning and never actually got my day started, and now I'm writing my journal entry here on this computer instead of in the notebook that I know needs to contain these thoughts, and this computer is about to die. It's been telling me since about an hour ago, and since, all I've done is watch Instagram videos, I started watching a video about how to have a system for the sort of effectiveness that I aspire to have. So what is effectiveness, if that's really what I'm aiming for? That's the real question I've had to ask myself, because I don't seem to be able to figure it out. According to this video, it's the work of figuring out the following: S - Specific, don't be vague, nail down the tolerances. Y - Yours build it for YOUR life, not a general one. You have to be in charge of what you are doing. S - Scheduled not scheduled means optional. It means you don't really need to do it if you don't feel like it. If it's on a schedule, you have to. T - Trackable Make it so that you can actually measure the progress you are making and improve on it. This is crucial. E - Easy to execute All the steps of the process should by tiny M - Maintained Repeat it constantly. The issue I see with all of these videos is that too much of the time I look at them and I don't know what to think other than 'here's something that I have to consume that will eventually lead me to further destroy myself. At some point I had a schedule, but then when I wake up and I feel like shit, or I didn't actually do what I intended to do for the day, I find that too often I'm caught in a loop. I don't end up caring, because I'm not actually accountable to anyone, and no one really cares whether or not I am. That's the hardest part of doing anything for yourself, and I know I know it, because it's something that I've had to encounter any number of times before. So what does this mean: I do need a system. I need something that I can lean on that shows me what I'm doing and how I'm doing it. Everything leading up to my graduate school applications made sense because it was something that I could depend on, and it was measurable. I didn't set things in motion just because. I was training for capability. I came out of it somewhat injured, and I don't think I did what I needed to in order to condition myself for the sort of performance that I wanted to have. I was sold short on myself, even though I still saw out what I wanted to do, at whatever speed it took to do it. I can do that again. My running schedule is something that has to come back, because it's part of the backbone of making sure the rest of it happens. I also need to be strict again. It doesn't matter if I wake up tired, I need to wake up when I intend to, not when I'm ready to. That's a difference from how I've been doing things for the last few weeks: I need to wake up at the same time, earlier than I'm doing it. My dog deserves it, I deserve it. As I write this, it's eleven, and I'm starting my day. Let's not have too many more of those. I'm depressed. That's okay. I need rest to recuperate and figure some things out. That's also okay. That doesn't mean that we can't see out what we expect from it all, and it doesn't mean I can't aim higher. As I write this, my nervous system is coming back to rest. I'm allowing my unconscious to be drawn back into what I need to be doing rather than what I've been doing by default. I have calls today that I need to prepare for. I have the ability to execute on a dream and do more than I'm giving myself the credit of needing to do. This book needs to go through the hard part and I need to see what happens. I started working this morning, then I stopped. That still needs to happen, but only after I do the following: We're going to be okay. I need to come up with the guardrails that ensure I succeed. That's not the right question, babe. The right question is: what version of you wants what you're looking for? years ago when I was switching careers, I read a bunch of books trying to help me figure it out. A friend of mine recommended "What color is your parachute" at the time, it was the perfect exercise. When opportunities came my way, I was sure of what I wanted to do because I'd done the work to figure it out - and I saw a lot of success, because I was fully invested in the work. Here's the catch: Now that it's been a few years, I went so far down the track of the opportunities I thought I wanted at the time that by the end of it, I burned out, tired. I didn't want to do anything anymore. What was the reason, though? It wasn't that the opportunities were bad. It was that I'd fundamentally changed as a person. A huge part of the reason I was burning out is because the job wasn't what I was looking for anymore. This seems obvious, but the reality is that it's not. Our needs change constantly. It's exhausting to realize this, I know, but what it really means is that the version of you that you used to be might still be the version of you guiding you toward what you think you want. It means you have to work inward. this is called 'revisiting your priors' for the decisions you make - with the understanding that your values, demands, and desires, they're all very likely to change. So what am I doing about it? I'm re-reading the Parachute book because it worked for me, and it's helping me get clear on the fact that the present version of me is dramatically different from who I used to be. It means that now, I'm in touch with the fact that the present version of me is the version I'm working for, and means that when something comes by that I know I want to do, I won't have a doubt. So the next time you're wondering about how to get the world to give you what you want, ask yourself first: what version of you is it that wants that? --- --- "Is the version of you that's making decisions about what you want actually you?" Constantly I am urged to solve my wandering attention with some panacea — all I need is a system. All I need is a one-shot solution to solve it all. I'll admit — the prospect is enticing. My inclination is and has been a burden my entire adult life, and I am constantly fighting the foraging action that pulls me off task, only to find myself suddenly (I swear to god this has happened) suddenly playing a violin in my bedroom, the intent to get on with it utterly and blissfully forgotten. As a result, one-shot solutions like keeping a stack of lists, or putting up sticky notes — or whatever else is offered in my direction — are all enticing. I have not staying on task. The number of times in my life where I have been reduced to the indirect realization that I have, once again, been forced to pay the "ADHD tax" is a number so large I wish it was my bank account balance itself. What is worse is the certainty that I am not alone in this journey, and that my experience with four has been long-established enough to recognize that in the flurry of "systems" I have sought to implement in order to change one of my afflictions, there really isn't a convenient solution. To some sure Everything about trying to remember and to struggle through the toil of keeping on is difficult. I say this knowing intimately that I have failed myself so many times as to wince at the thought. Despite this, I have seen success in my life: I was a successful photographer for around 8 years. I have done more than most people might think of doing in several lifetimes, and for a brief period of time, I was a tech CEO. All "impressive" things by most measures, but I am here to say, in explicit detail, I struggled through all of it. It is easy for this to be called "high-functioning ADHD" — or whatever name we want to offer it — but the truth is that I really did struggle. Half the time that I have been "succeeding" at anything, I have been white-knuckling my way through the work in pursuit of its completion. There is a reason that this has worked for me, but it is not a one shot solution. The reason that I've been able to do any of this is that I am stubborn. That's it. It is the reason I have been able to develop discipline and have plunged into the hard work of anything: to do it all not in spite of myself. If we take a step back, we can get a slightly better picture of what exactly this means. I often see (very inspiring) videos about people's journeys toward success, and usually among the barriers to success are framed as being in the hands of other people: they always mention, never identify first "haters." What baffles me just a bit when I see these videos is that I'm often caught wondering who exactly these "haters" are, — who has the level of anti-capital within them so pronounced as to rise in the face of those who struggle toward success and to tell them that they won't. My greatest error is that I don't think "haters" actually exist — or rather they themselves, I do think wondering who these "haters" are confuses me greatly because I know my greatest hater: me. I inevitably believe that I can't do something. It could be that this is some survival function in my brain trying to protect me from harm, but being that the things this part of my brain says to me are so harsh as to outpace anything anyone could ever dream up, it's difficult to manage worse haters. This is why I have I am a struggle: no amount of barriers put up by someone else are worse or more powerful than those I impose upon myself. It would be really easy after this to devolve into a hackneyed, grit-and-determination parable on struggle and particularly struggles with our own afflictions, set of values. That isn't what I am trying to do here. I'm not even sure I am offering advice, rather thinking my way around the reality of my experience to explore why necessity is a heat that I keep stoking up. It is just perspective, which is all we really have in this life. The reason I have been able to keep going despite the difficulty and the mosquito-like whine in my ear to stop is because I am stubborn — I show up entirely in spite of myself. It's a bit of a reaction often to the fact that I have my hard days where I am exhausted and find it incredibly hard to get up, and then am peppered by a world that truly does think that each person's system or perspective somehow can resolve for another. I really do hope that the bullet journals and routines and exercise and psychiatric drugs do work for everyone who tries them. I they do work.c But only if you stubbornly keep showing up to decide that they do.

The effort to be made, the effort to be made, the effort to be made. I do not need to get up at 5 in the morning to write, then grind away my life. I'm not really interested in being the sort of person who needs to show everyone else what I do and how I do. June is the ninth month, it is the halfway point, and it is the point at which it's all going to turn around. I'm not sure what will happen over the next 6 months, but I think I can make it good. The question I keep asking myself is what I want to play. I have not focused on this question enough — I do not seem to know what the end character looks like, to start with. She is strong. I know this much. Her time at the gym is about having the best body she can, on her terms of life. She does not worry about money — not because she makes tons and tons of it, but because she has her finances managed to a point that there isn't much to worry about — things like big dinners might raise an issue here and there, but the baseline will always be safe. She dresses well every single day because it is important to give people the impression that she takes care of herself and that impression's effect on others. People come to her for advice, and it's part of her job — the work of being someone who lifts others up, making them into the best version of themselves. She is not tied to any one thing, but she is very good at what she does. Now in first person: I will direct people on policy contribution. I'll be an expert in the sector because it is crucial, and because it is an area I can talk about for a long time. I will write about this. I will talk about this. I will work on this. I will also be a writer. Not just opinions on, for instance, energy policy, but art and fiction, or on subject matter and its relevance. I will work on contracts, and I will have to travel to examine facilities and how they function in line with expectation broadly set. My intellect makes my abilities, and I will do the work of translating for others what they do not know or understand. I find fulfillment in the work because it makes me feel that we are driving toward a better future for everyone at hand. I will match this energy. I'll take charge of conversations because I am the sort who knows how to navigate them. I like control. I want to do more of it. It is a problem I have: how to work on, and a problem I want to be in there for. I know myself in this way. In the mean time, in my life, I am still writing. I am doing it differently than I used to; now I work in a way that suits my love of the discipline, rather than fleeting as though I have to perform for those that are overly focused on numbers and on impressing others. My sense still continues to be that the direction of athleticism is in the direction of adventure. People want embodiment — and while we are moving in the direction of embodiment — we will praise those who do the work to make the pursuits remarkable — who push beyond the expected. This means I write about two things: endurance, and energy. I can write about either under the other, and part of the reason that I do has less to do with the environments I am a part of: I know these things because I am already doing these things. I am a part of them because I am a part of them, just as I will be in the future. This is an invigorating fact. The version of myself that exhibits these qualities already exists: I am her. I haven't found a way to be in the position I need to be yet, where what I do is what I will be doing, but I feel a certainty for something I need to try: there is something there I want to explore. The person I am is known because I do not mince words and because I am an advocate. I know what I am talking about when given the chance to speak, and I speak confidently. I am the difference between a leader and a boss — someone who inspires, but not someone who requires themselves to manage people on anything more than a mentorship level. I do not put myself in such a position, but others want me there, more often than not. Let's summarize, then: I make probably around 300K a year, but I do not all come from one place. I dress well every single day, without fail, because it is how I want people to perceive me. My personal brand is affable, confident, connected, and attentive. I care about everything that surrounds me. I am determined. The work that I do takes me to exciting places because that is where the work needs to be done, but also because I want to be there. People want me there because my being there means something to what is happening. My presence will mean to the people involved that they are working on the right thing. The question then becomes — how do I take where I am right now and position myself so that I get to be this person? What story do I need to tell about this in order to become her? My career is not confusing. The throughline is essentially obvious: it is energy, and it has always been energy. My fascination with the world is factually rooted in this knowledge, and I don't need to doubt this fact. At that point, I was giving up the lighting industry. I knew it. It moved too fast. I didn’t know how long I’d be gone. But I knew the technology would change. The people would change. Everything would change. [...] Wonder dissolves age. Nobody is old in front of something they’ve never seen before. Career changes are strange like this - the realization that you may have niched down onto the frontier of whatever vehicle is encouraging forward change, then realizing that it requires an enormous amount of emotional and constitutional energy to stay there. It's no surprise that in the modern age we are seeing such an increase in burnout or sabbatical remove in the workforce; we have developed so many new frontiers that anyone who stays at the front of them often runs out of the energy to keep going. The moment that you stop moving with that momentum, it can feel as though you are being left behind. What I truly love about this interview is the fact that you've tapped into the sense of fulfillment she has found in not keeping pace, but rather seeking out how the threads of a previous life might fit into whatever personal frontiers can be made instead, making, I think, for a far more fulfilling life. Gibran once wrote, to the great discredit of those who called him a pop philosopher: You have been told also that life is darkness, and in your weariness you echo what was said by the weary. And I say that life is indeed darkness save when there is urge, And all urge is blind save when there is knowledge, And all knowledge is vain save when there is work, And all work is empty save when there is love; And when you work with love you bind yourself to yourself, and to one another, and to God. There is a pain in knowing oneself — above specifically we leave behind both the judgement of others and their fixed awareness wholly alone in the experience we are having, carrying something that no one or so few can understand. I think I'm getting there, in one sense — I'm beginning to rub up against the soft surface of my own potential and am astounded by what I can see. I don't especially know how that path plays out, but I will— It's just really astounding to see that at 36, I am going to be more in shape than I have ever been in my life. I'm going to be able to do more than I ever have. At this point, I'm just trying to see if I can do it — whatever it is. Meaning myself. I watched a video that said briefly that I am not unmotivated, but rather I need a reason. A reason why I want to pursue something. My immediate reaction is to resist — after all I seem to be getting along fine, but as well — I don't especially want to have to rationalize everything in order to pull it off. Sometimes you just want to do it. I guess the question then is what I want to do, and I have spent months puzzling over this stupid question. I want not to agonize over the injustice of not having the world hand me my next step. I think I do need a reason, but for the large part this reason needs to be something to which I am first internally aligned with. I think that's nature, somehow, but as well it's being outside, it's moving one's body, it's caring about things well beyond that which our society desires of us. That is to say, I want people to care about the world with me. The impression I have is that we're better off chasing the ideas that make us excited about life than those we think we are meant to do because it's the sensible choice. I liked running the goalkeepers today because it made me feel like I am capable, and I'm not especially certain that many people can do what I can. But I don't want to be doing that without a reason — I'm not about to throw everything behind merely just because I'm good at it. I don't want to end up taking it as a result. The question is now of what I want on the balance — is it the pursuit of a wild step toward wilderness first, then a "career" second. Norway does seem in a way most like the place that would meet those desires, but I don't think I would be happy there. My ideal scenario would be going to Trondheim to study renewable or hydroelectric power, then running my ass off in that place, then coming back together with her. It might mean a lot of time (years?) apart, but I could see it being the shape things take. How would I survive the fact that he may not have that many more years yet? Is making decisions around him in my life the right call yet? What if I have to plan in spite of it? On the face of it, what I want to do in the long term is navigate the complex politics of how to make a sustainable future more economically attractive than not doing so. I think we so far only get one earth and the massive challenge of figuring out how to oversee its limitation means that we need to be ready to navigate the work together. The amount of information reaching people each day is notoriously difficult to measure. One researcher tried to measure this in 2012 at around 34gb per person per day, and increasing by 5% each year, but gigabytes aren't a great unit to measure information in. It's easier to measure it in decisions - and today we're constantly forced to make a choice as to whether or not we actually want to pay attention to something. Five hundred years ago, a person's world was small enough that almost everything they encountered came from a few dozen known people and places in a day — nothing like the volume, or the novelty, we're asked to process now. It's too much to fully interact with, but that's what we're dealing with nowadays. It's no wonder we feel underwater. Does a like actually mean what you want it to mean? Are you developing a relationship between yourself and what you are consuming, and what are the results of those interactions? I often begin aging myself in advance

I find that I often begin aging myself in advance of my next birthday by about four months. It could be that this is a function of aging, and I simply don't care anymore; the notion of needing celebrate a given day feels less important when in the wake of accumulated years this single day feels like one among many. Yes this year, I celebrated by birthday with complete strangers. This is one of those behaviors I have earned and kept up with, not exclusive to birthdays, but to other celebrations I've had in life. I first did this by celebrating Thanksgiving with a Christian musician in Georgia in a field at night with two guitars and a plastic tub of chicken tenders we'd bought at Kroger. I celebrated Christmas with a thatch of drunk Chileans, Argentineans, English, French, and Germans on a beach in Ecuador after feasting on wild-caught fish in a local's backyard. The bonfire we build was so high that it seemed to lick the fabric of the night sky with its flames, and in the search for more downed wood my friend (she is still my friend) sat me down and told me to enjoy the night that we'd made. I spent of of those Easters cycling across Japan weith trhee men, and the day of may have been when I had to remove a tick from the skin of one friend's scrotum with a pair of tweezers while laying in a room full of other traveling strangers, having carried our bikes up over a thousand steps to get to where we lay. Another Thanksgiving was during an ice storm in Kansas, where trucks littered the highway median jack-knifed, and I ate a Sizzler at a Denny's where once we left, the rusting towbar of my truck came loose, throwing sparks across the highway, and I pulled over to swing the last bit until it broke off completely, and we slept at a rest stop that played a farmer's weather radio station on a muffled speaker all night until we woke up covered in snow. It's not that I don't like celebrating occasions, it's that I'd rather use their marker as a way to remember something else. My sense is that a meal that acts the same as the same meal from the year before will be remembered that way. I won't forget my 36th birthday. I ran along Col de Fours with three men in a race and whooped as loud as I could with my lungs full of mountain air, and was chastised by a Frenchman stranger who said they don't do that here. I felt like an ignorant American despite my native roots, when we left that man behind, my new Bavarian friend told me that they did the same where he came from, so it was okay. People have different ways of responding to the mountains. I took a photo when we reached the pass with the three of them, and Benni sent me a message afterward, asking forgiveness that he'd placed it among his other memories as a way to mark the occasion. By nightfall that same day, the route I'd made had sent an Italian and an Englishman over a pass between France and Italy into Bardonecchia as the sun went down, and they said it was the scariest, hardest thing they'd ever done, but that they'd do it again in a heartbeat. My birthday ended with a shot from a bottle of Genepy on a folding table next to a brown Renault van at the top of Col de Vars, and the sad, smiling puppy of a Frenchman who'd marked the checkpoints of our race got me a sparkling pair of socks with 'Badass' written on the side as a gift. There are better systems for making memories than those we're told to use. The unimportant things, I'm not as good at remembering, and as I get older I care less about trying to. I make stories from the things that are important, instead. They aid in granting gravity to the experiences with other than I want to share, and for months afterward, ticking into years, those memories work hard not to be filed away. The folders I could tuck them inside feel golden, and on the sorting desk of my mind I can't help but keep them there for a git longer. A bit of suffering, together. A laugh. The dark. Caipirinha or champagne on a beach on a sullen beach, with stranger. Frigate bird wings, ripping through the air like torn paper. Life is richer that way. What I am saying is this: there are systems for memory, and there are good memories. We can make the choice to remembering things, however inane, or we can choose to make memories we will crave never to put away. Think of this. Fo the next time you celebrate the turning of a year, don't try and repeat what you have already done. Ask instead: what is the strangest, most brilliant thing I can do to ensure that it is worth remembering?
I slept incredibly well last night

I slept incredibly well last night. I didn't do the work of remembering what I dreamt (I tried to), but I made it into the morning early enough to say that I love waking up early. The first few hours of the day will always feel freer than the others: they are normally outside the territory of any authority, and they feel unusually liberated from the demands of productivity and capitalism. It's maybe for this reason that these are the hours I treasure most for creativity. My mind is free to wander and be "unproductive," glancing off one thought or another on its course toward or through the reading I've done for the morning. I often feel much more license to explore my thoughts, because there is no one demanding that I put them in service of their work. When I think about what this means, I generally land on the assessment that I have a little demon in my head threatening me with a hammer any time I start thinking about relaxing. The little demon threatens me with the knowledge that any free time not utilized as a vehicle for productive capital is somehow wasted time. I find that even on the days when I have a very legitimate excuse for not being productive (vacations, illness, days when I "just can't"), the little demon with the hammer is even worse, hopping from foot to foot with an impish smile on their face, knowing that I should not by any means expect a moment of rest. Yesterday was one of those days. The night before, I'd slept horribly due to the unexpected consumption of a caffeinated tea at 9 p.m., and I was up until 3:30 in the morning reading as a result. I finished two books in direct succession. It was delightful! And I paid for it all day yesterday, as the little purple imp in my brain demanded I produce something of value in response to the productive late-night hours of reading. One of the books I read was Perfection by Vincenzo Latronico. It sent me into a spiral, and that spiral is what forced me to finish Lindsay Hill's Sea of Hooks, which has a cathartic-while-tragic ending that made its strange micro-chapter structure utterly worthwhile. Naturally, when I woke up yesterday, I was incredibly motivated to write about either. What does it even mean to read a book if you are not somehow turning your enjoyment into some material insight that you can then place in front of others as an indication of personal legitimacy? However, my need for proper rest had other plans. I am 36, practically middle-aged, which means that not getting my structured 7–9 hours of sleep leaves me an absolute pile of grey [slurry?] the next day, and nothing meaningful will happen with the day. Part of getting older has meant accepting this fact and creating room for it, which meant that, as a formerly over-employed ex-tech worker without any meaningful job prospects or vision for my future against the incoming job apocalypse, I could "allow myself to relax" and "do less with my day." Which absolutely did not work. Being utterly exhausted, I resigned myself to thinking that maybe I could simply pick up another book to read, but since my well-rested self tends to over-aspire as to the literature I intend to consume, my pile of to-be-read books is filled with only challenging, vaguely [illegible: two words] books. My brain couldn't do it. [So be it?] I had some accounting to do, and that didn't work either. The moment I sat down to pile my receipts on my desk, my motivation evaporated and I ended up in the kitchen, peering across the shelves of the fridge. (Come to think of it, this is what happens every time I try to do any accounting. I struggle, we struggle.) At this point I resigned myself to free-writing in my notebook to see if I could tease some sort of insight out of my restlessness, thinking that maybe somewhere in this [illegible] would be a set of reflections on Latronico's Perfection. They never came, and besides, what Rosie Spinks had to say on the book is more insightful than anything I'd have had to say anyway (you can and should read it here; in fact, read all of her articles, she's brilliant). When the Brilliant Thoughts failed to arrive, I felt it: the panic of not knowing why you can't be productive. Mind you, this came after the rationalization that I could "relax" that day, and I had attempted to fight the notion anyway with a string of tasks. That panic is infuriating to look back on. It doesn't demonstrate some virtue; rather, it indicates that part of the death drive our society instills in us is the inability to take a fucking break. I'll admit openly that upon realizing I had no cognitive capacity available for the day, I turned even to social media, and the work I have done to wrest myself free of consumption addiction proved itself useful here: Instagram, even, was deeply unsatisfying. Eventually I gave up and stared at the wall instead, my emotions [still?] racing through my chest, and by the time I'd actually checked in with my body, I realized I was incredibly, deeply tired. I fell asleep on the couch within ten minutes. And you know what? It helped. I didn't wake up and suddenly have the energy to write a panegyric essay on Hill's Sea of Hooks, but I felt calmer. I had more clarity. I was better able to accept that the day was not going to mean anything, and I went out on a walk with my dog instead. --- Beyond typos, punctuation and italicized titles: Timeline. related to: Gender Dysphoria, Gender When we find ourselves interrogating gender from the perspective of one who has gone through the experience of either binary identity in our society - I find it's almost impossible not to address the material reality of what a trans experience means in stark contrast to that of someone who grow up cis. One of the cultural norms that I see time and time again are the encultured trans women ( usually in their first explorations of gender) polarizing themselves into the binary representation of what gender means to them, usually through the lens of stereotype. It makes for a startlingly binary and overall diminishing outward appearance to being trans - and it makes perfect sense, as Andrea Long Chu has pointed out, that trans women would look for representation in the form of objectifying pornography. In much of feminization pornography (en brev: sissy porn), the tropes that are held up in representation are objectifying norms of gender - compliance, weakness, and most disturbingly, very often racially charged imagery. Being that a woman is allowed to be a sexual being, the trans woman who explores an identity of being sexual is prone to finding representation of themselves only in this context. The weaponized nature of this experience is one that is damaging to the utmost to someone who is in a fragile place while defining their expectations of gender. As a result, the sexual identity of a trans person is often framed through this lens, and the effects of this identity can be especially damaging - as trans lesbians will likely agree. But more interesting is an underappreciated reality of experience with respect to gender, and it goes too often unrecognized. One of the stark differences in the experience of trans women who transition after puberty is a completely contrasted experience of having grown up - this is by no means the rule of an experience, as many straight trans women who once had to live as men may have had to do so as effeminates gay men, bringing up a completely different reality of experience. But the fact rep In particular here, I direct my attention to my experience - a trans lesbian, observing the acceptance of trans people into the fold of the broader lesbian experience. Jean Kilbourne argues herself that 'the self-esteem of girls plummets as they reach adolescence, partly because they cannot escape the message that their bodies are objects, and imperfect objects at that,' - and to put it bluntly, this is not the experience of a trans woman who passes through adolescence without addressing their transness as a part of identity-building, short of suppressing it. In having had the altogether less objectified experience of maleness in building ones adolescent identity, much of the time trans lesbians are able to avoid the trauma of degenerated identity that comes from having a world around you define you as a sexual object. In identity building, trans women instead explore an identity of supremacy that they (usually) consciously reject - which is a reason that trans women (and trans people at large) do have well-founded understandings of gender dynamics in society. Many of the 'useful' traits of masculinity get held onto through utility - often because they are traits that all (cis and otherwise) women should have access to regardless. Too often, the manufacture of identity for trans women can become a careless navigation of conflating norms - oftentimes upholding a misogynistic view of womanhood learned through external experience in youth. The danger to this is that a trans lesbian community can take part in toxic assumption - i.e. an unconscious equivalence between the cis and the trans experience of womanhood. Cis and trans women who go through a traditional experience of senescent adolescence don't have the same experience as all those women who grew up as cis men through that adolescence, meaning that a post-adolescent view of the experience of womanhood is necessarily going to be different between these experience. I mention this largely and specifically due to a dangerous trend I see in online spaces. Where online spaces have been communicated widely be members of feminist writing as male-dominated spaces - the same can be said for the freedom of cis lesbians to create their own spaces online. The fearful reality of exploring ones own gender (as a trans person) and finding that they belong to an additionally marginalized group (lesbians) can often result in a competitive need for inclusion, and often muddies the safety of what the experience of a lesbian space is meant to provide. In short, it seems pertinent to me that lesbian spaces concentrate on the experience of sexuality rather than the experience of gender - and while these two areas can intersect in terms of a sexual preference, conflating the experience of growing up cis with the experience of growing up trans can result in the erasure of commonality shared between people who grow up as cis lesbians. It's not the same experience. While I greatly appreciate the growth and acceptance of trans women into lesbian spaces, I fear the lack of caution that accompanies this integration because it does not beg a careful recognition of how intersectional experiences do indeed differ. The cis lesbian experience is an experience of a cis person recognizing homosexual attraction. The trans lesbian experience is (more often than not) the experience of a cis-presenting person recognizing their transness and framing their initially heterosexually-defined attraction to women through the experience of their transness.

Mostly I think that I've been seeing a yearning that was born from having faced my loneliness that has turned into a desire for solitude, which has made me feel particularly good about They do say 'it's lonely at the top', and my loneliest place is in leadership. It feels like a place? Every time I've found myself in any workplace, I eventually get coursed toward leadership of some sort because I'm willing to take point on my thoughts or those of others and turn them into action, as though I'm a vehicle that people can use to get to where they desire to go. It's a place that sometimes seems only I have access to and only I am qualified to take on, because as an executive who ended up here through nothing more than apparent will-to-do, I find myself so estranged from people who don't have this in them. When I do meet someone who has similar abilities, it's like meeting a ship in the night, we know that we can't actually possess the same space because we are not meant to. I have a desire to make change and to facilitate movement and I feel as though when I try to encourage others to take on this sort of self-engagement and self-motivation, I can't quite translate that it's not about garnering the necessary energy to do so from a perspective of positivity but rather that it's this relentlessness. There are pockets of this relentlessness that can be gestured toward contentment and even happiness, but it's a willingness to keep moving because if you are unhappy, at least you know your name. I'm reminded of the speculative biology in Butler's 'Bloodborne' wherein there is a biological imperative toward leadership and motherhood over others, and that in meeting others who hold this imperative, you are destined not to occupy the same space because the imperative drives you toward separation from others, a near hostility that feels somewhat like needing to find others who understand, but knowing you can never really occupy that space together because your experience is altogether different in its own right. I find that I can course away from the loneliness of leadership by experiencing glancing blows with other leaders in spaces where the guards are down and the parameters are temporary, where there is a penchant for sharing and collaboration instead, because while I am a leader, I don't want to be one, it's simply what keeps happening to me. I have had dinners with others who have guided teams toward the completion of projects, and understanding or navigating the social dynamics that come with leadership while interrogating them with others can make me feel less lonely - but these times always do have to end due to the nature of the act and the capacity is possesses within us. I had my chart read a few days ago and what really stood out to me was that I am a leader, but I'm like an alien in being one; people follow me but they don't understand me. Knowing this makes me feel more lonely rather than less. It hits me because I don't feel cared for, which answers both questions, when I have a harbored feeling of not having my needs met and not knowing how to meet them, and wanting/begging to go after them in a way that feels like healing. When I'm not lonely I don't feel this yearning, but when I am lonely, I want to solve for it. When Cherefawn broke up with me. When Sara moved out and I realized I was going to have to do everything over again after Cherefawn and I split up. There was a part of me that really wanted to live in aspace of thinking tha tI was going to end up with some sort of life partner, and I find that too often I fall into this feeling of thinking that the love of me life is a person instead of ths idea that they might be within me. The loneliness of this feeling is one of knowing that I have the ability to love someone, but that when I love someone in a way that is the most generative to how it is that I want to be as a person, I have come to experience a reality of those that I have tried to love pushing it away, revulsing from the idea that there is any way to think that far ahead and commit to a life that appears anything like devotion. This has been true enough that I've found myself thinking about whether or not I'll ever find someone who wants that sort of devotion and whether or not it's a devotion that is even logical, because so much of the way I love is tied up in trust and I've had to learn how not to trust people with my heart. Now that I'm an adult and I'm starting to feel more and more like my life is so much further down the track, I feel all manner of fearful between the moments where I feel the least lonely, because I can stare down the feeling of knowing that my loneliness isn't something that limits my life, and that no one can help me solve for that feeling better than I can. I started thinking about how when Sara and I split up, I was going to end up with the whole apartment and I'd have to pay all of the rent, and -- I didn't change this. I kept going, I kept paying the rent because the apartment is comfortable and I like it, but I let someone live with me because she needed somewhere to live and she hasn't left and I love her, but this apartment never feels like it's mine as a result, it never feels like a place where I can take complete ownership over how it makes me feel and why I'm living here by myself, I never really get to ask if this place is mine or not. When Sara moved out and I gave up the room to Tam I was glad for Tam because that's how you support your friends, but now I feel so estranged from everything because the group that used to tie us all together (Rage and Release) is no longer a safe place for us to be, so with that went all of my friendships that were tied up in what that web of connections had become and the effort I'd put into being with these people and holding them in my life, and then in January that fell apart and now I don't have them and I don't know what to do with their absence - it feels like a long sleep where I woke up and the world changed, and I didn't get to decide where it went. All of these times have tied themselves together around a feeling of needing to be desired or thinking that being desired is somehow what brings my life meaning, but then peeling back the layers and seeing that inside it's just some sort of collapsing star that deserved more attention than it got and should have felt better than it has, because look how far I made it on my own. If we live in an age of loneliness, it's because in the act of allowing everything to connect to everything else, we never stopped to ask which connections should be important, and we never developed the tools to navigate those questions without constantly trying to shift attention between the potentials that every connection could generate.

I added colors to it, pictures of places that I wanted to be, and people that I wanted in my life. I couldn't add flavors, but I added pictures of the foods that brought together those flavors, and I couldn't add touch, so I added pictures of the things that I wanted to touch, lower backs, hot sauce, sandstone, rain evaporating from warm surfaces. I added pressure that causes blooming, though I couldn't add this as a picture, so I just added cicadas. I added peace and books because those are things that matter to me, and I added ideas, but I couldn't figure out a picture for it so I added thought bubbles and speech bubbles that came from them. I added the feeling of running forever, but it was just a picture of running shoes. I added what I thought was missing from my life, over and over, thinking that enough of me filling the space with these feelings might mitigate the loneliness that I felt, as though somehow I'd fill the gap of my own intentions by dreaming of something that I didn't have and as though thinking in this way was the correct aopproach to trying to build out hte future that you want. You have to believe it. You have to believe that what is possible is probable, and you have to move progressively toward it. Quiet times are times of action, times in which the effort that can be made outside of the pressures of everyday life are something that can put you on your back in terms of the efforts, that can be made rather than the frustration that girds inaction. I think mostly of hte way that ttime is not osmetihng that we think of as a resource, but rather something that is simply passing. Maksim was the person who told me this, that I needed to stop thinking of time as something that was simply passing, and start thinking about it as something that could be spent wisely - that if your time is being spent cheaply, then you are not valuing your time for the resource that it is. Ho told me that I hadn't been thinking about it enough and the passage of time was something that I needed to pay more attention to, a man in my heart who was both old and young, both wise and headstrong, but a maker, the sort of person who can solve any issues provided they have the tools, and if Maksim didn't have the tools, he would make them out of the other tools that he did have. When I got back in touch with him, he told me a number of things that I had forgotten- that my life is full of limitless potential and that the ways through which I engage in that potential have much to do with my ability to force myself into the future. He also told me that I was not using my time wisely, and he was surprised at how much time had passed since we last worked together. I asked him when we last saw one another and he told me that we worked together a bit when I was 20, but the first time we met was 14. What had I been doing since then? I'm not sure I said, but I think I didn't want to admit that so much of my time had been eaten up by thinking that one pursuit was going to give me meaning and that I got lost in the weeds of realizing that it would never be fulfilling to pursue what others were pursuing. I think that at some level he knew this, and I could see that he was frustrated with the time that had passed, I can't blame him for it - if he really thinks the last time we worked together was over a decade ago, it's probably worth the rust to think that moving quickly is going to be more difficult. He didn't seem as though he was hopeless, though - he seemed engaged, wanting to build something more. That's when he told me about all the things that he'd had to make without knowing their purpose, all the tools that I didn't realize I had available but that he'd handed to whomever was handing them to me. That was you? I asked a number of times, and he would just nod sagely for a moment. I didn't know what I was making it for but I'm glad you put it to use, and I'm glad it was for you and then he'd twirl the ball-peen hammer that always seemed as though it was in his hands. I can make anything you need me to make. When I asked him what he'd rather be doing, he mentioned that there is something really cool that we can make together, I just don't think you've ever put the time into thinking about how we'd make it and I was not sure what he was referring to. He showed me blueprints for a a shape something like a building, a church, a gathering space, where the inside was filled with interleaving surfaces letting the light in from outside, where the power of it was wonder for those who would enter, where things could be said and mentioned for their gravity and to cement people into understanding that there was something wondrous to pay attention to, but that the only way we could get to making this was if you can offer me the time to make it. I left that conversation thinking that Maksim was ready for me to offer him something I didn't know how to offer, because I'd spent so much of my time thinking that what I needed to make was something so much more surrounded by what is around me - and I think this is true, even now as I write this the pressure that I feel from what surrounds me has more to do with other people and other places and expectations that are set on me, not what I hold inside of myself, not what I think I should have inside, and not what I wanted to build back when I knew Maksim at first. You'll have to let me apologize I wanted to say and every time I was about to, he'd stop me and remind me that he didn't need an apology, I exist outside of Time. I can make anything, and I can make it at whatever pace I want to, but you are aging. You are thirty-two. You are the only coming to me with something that you don't have much of, and I want to remind you that while I want to make these things with you, it's you who holds the raw materials with which to do so. You can choose to offer Time to me, you could offer all of it, but I will not ask for that much - but you cannot forget that if Time is a resource and you only have so much, you need to remember how you are spending it. Don't spend it on the things that don't matter, but if it was spent on the things that do, then it was worth the cost.

So I asked Maksim what are you going to do with the time once I have it saved for you and he said we are going to build a church. I wasn't sure what he meant. I've never been religious, and to my recollection, neither was he, but knowing him I knew not to press the issue. When he knew what he had to make, he was dead-set, his ageless eyes pulling in light from around us and sparked bright as though consuming the sun and fueling some fire inside that would kick him into movement. Maksim is someone I have known my whole life, and yet I have never known him well enough - he is the best parts of me, the parts that keep quiet and put their head down on the work that needs to happen, while I spent most of my time in anxiety spirals, gathering information and unsure how it would be used. Maksim - is it worth trying again

Is it worth trying this again I asked, hushed tones, thinking he wouldn't overhear me while he had his head down, drawing. Yes, of course and I heard him put his pencil down, I heard him come over and look over my shoulder, down at my own sheet, and at my own work. It's always worth trying again, he said, it's always worth going through the effort of seeing if there is a better way to do what it is that you are doing, as though there's some sort of meaning to be derived from the practice of being, as though in finding the act of being in the act of having to adapt is the only place within which you find meaning. So yes, it is worth trying again, it is always worth trying again. He said this, putting his hand on my shoulder, the end of the sentence hooked on his eyes, feeding inward, and I wasn't sure anymore, because I was poised above another blank page, as usual. You have done this so many times before, this time is no different. This is another time for you to invent and see out the path forward as though there is meaning in writing this path. So I began to draw, again, etching around in circles, trying to make something of it. You know you will not get it right on this first sketch, sitting beside me, his own hands covered in the charcoal of his own designs, but we know to be forgiving by now. I watched Maksim take up the room of his own thoughts and bear into motion a sense of self that I hadn't made room for in myself. If he was a part of me, he was someone I hadn't taken the time to know, an imaginarium of thoughts and emotions that I felt so much for and from whom I wished so much forgiveness but there is nothing to forgive, I simply need you to remember that you are at the core of yourself. If it feels divine it is because the act of Creation is divine and because you are allowed to feel this feeling of being divine in the act of Creation, you are the God of your own making. We will make this church together. I could not see what he meant by the end of this, what the church was, where it was, what it was becoming within our hands. It was simply intention, an act of pursuing pure will in order to see what became of it. He would repeat these things as though mantras to me that the will is the way and I would shoulder their meaning through the words that inevitably poured out of me in pursuit of a Truth of some sort. No one can make you happy, only you can make yourself happy, he reminded me of the woman I'd met when we lived deeper into Crown Height and I didn't remember telling him, but this is how Maksim is, he seems to remember all of it and how it folds in together because we are making a plan of all of this and it will be beautiful, we simply must keep making and so I did, with him, working toward trying to have more and more of my understanding girded by a commitment to continuation. Is this what they mean by faith? and he smiled at me, nodding, eyes bright Yes, you get it. This is faith. You must continue on. You will find meaning in the movement so long as you have faith in what is there to believe. I'm not sure if that is what turned the tide, if that is what took me from feeling that I'd wanted to let it all go and that there wasn't a purpose to me actions to instead truly leaning toward it. I think I admired him too much not to say to myself that he is right, and that the mere act of continuing onward is worthy enough. We collected all of these meanings together. This is why they are holy, because we agreed upon their holiness. If we are to make a church of this, it is because their holiness comes from the interstitial, that between the collected aphorisms that urge you onward, there is something more that sits atop, hoping to be carried, hoping to show you that you must have faith in your own Divine path, that you wrote this in place. So please, give me the time to build this with you and explore what love can build, what skies we can make above us and how much can come from the love of a sun and a moon sharing the same light. I have you to thank for the warmth you have offered me as I work through the night to balance the shores below, as I tame the oceans and the unruly foam of their children above them, allow me to work for you. Allow yourself to rest and continue warm the surface into action so that I may have the time to show you the places that will be made from your repose. Finally, alow us the freedom to know that time is both valuable and meaningless, that you are learning of its value even while you learn that you can decide how it is spent. We will make much of its passage. But for all of this, you must allow me to show you what it will become given that into which time can be made. It will be made together, with your offering as a gift, your faith in its meaning as a tool. You must forgive yourself for taking as long as you have to pay attention to the degree that you are now. I did not speak because you were not ready to listen, I am only speaking because you have run out of words. So let us not speak, let us move forward, let us make something of this Church we are becoming.

faith is a coordinating technology - it's well suited to the direction of huge groups of people because it is a conclusive and motivated set of traditions and actions that are well-connected to the utility of a common goal this is the most interesting thing about coordination as rooted in faith, and it is indeed what is missing from the human species. the act of believing some set of conditions will improve is based on a common ability to believe in the improvement of these conditions as exclusive of free will -- that is, faith is the act of believing that there will be a better outcome despite not knowing for certain that the outcome will happen. faith is inimitably tied as well to hope, because hope is just as blind, while absolving itself of the lack of agency that faith inspires in some. if a sociological technology of faith is possible (and it is because we have evolved it in several directions as a species), then it's still possible to use that technology for the better; it's possible to use both faith and hope in the service of good things this is in some ways what I think we have lost as a civilization: the inability to have faith in a collectively-held outcome that serves as many people as possible. the effect of lacking an alternative executable collective coordination mechanism that efficiently orients humans in the same direction is that it results in a lack of commonly-desired outcomes: without an effective means through which to point all of us at something that all of us want, we each think that we want something different from our neighbor, either locally or on much larger scales. this results in coordination failure -- we don't move in the same direction, even when it could benefit all of us. this is the danger of not having a meaningful coordination technology at the level of a species; now there is no way for us to meaningfully work together to solve collective problems. this is why I think that we need to reconsider the social definition of faith and it's utility in how we approach collective problems.
A crisis of faith is always a crisis of faith - apophasis, rationalism, and AI

the point of life is not in knowing but it's a nice perk that we get to, sometimes apophatic - to learn of god through negation - knowing that which is not god Emphatic, but empathetic. I do not think mathematics is over, and while the scream that we must be feeling is the realization that a profound change must happen, some part of us must as a species have known it was coming, just as we have had to experience that same despair before. I read an article recently that describes what is happening in mathematics in response to AI. The writing is beautiful, poetic and despairing, and I feel deep empathy for a writer and a mathematician who is navigating the ground having shifted beneath his feet. The despair of knowing that things might change and not knowing exactly how one must adapt to the shifting present is a state of, in many cases, pure terror. In this moment of human history, we are particularly there . I've been pursuing something recently that I think is rendering me immune to the pessimism that comes with it, or rather inured to it, because I just can't bring myself to believe that thinking is over. I recently spoke to a man on the street who stopped me to ask for money. He was sitting in a push walker, and his shirt was clean, as were his socks. Being stopped for money happens all the time in New York, and when you have lived here long enough, it can become easy to shrug off the interaction and keep walking, however callous that makes us, but there are occasionally those who it is clear did not want to be where they are (no one does), and so I stopped, and we had a conversation. His name was Theodore (name changed), and he had only become unhoused in the last 4 days. It was the 4th of August, and he'd been evicted. He said he didn't know what to do, he didn't have a way to make money, he was 56 and the world felt like it had moved on from him. He was trying to get 85 for the shelter for the next 3 weeks so that he would have somewhere to sleep. There is something more obvious in those who are telling the truth of their desperation - they are not practiced in telling their story, so they stumble over it as they tell it. There is no order to what they are saying. Theodore didn't, and so I told him I was going to the store to get flowers, and I'd come back with some money I'd gotten from an ATM at the store. As I was walking, I was racking my brain for all the responses I could have had. It could have been easy not to turn back to him, but I remembered something he had said when we were standing. He said that he knew that God had a plan for him, even if it didn't make sense right now, but he wanted to have faith. When I walked back to him, I had the twenty dollars in my hand. I'd had it when I spoke to him, but in a sense I needed to think through what to say to him. Money does not go as far as it used to, I don't have much of it, but when I got to him, I handed him the bill and I asked him when he'd last gone to church. He looked up at me and thought, saying that it had been a long time. I looked him in the eyes and I said 'Theodore, if God has a plan for you, then you should go to church, and be around those who can help you understand it.' He looked at me for a moment and I felt a sincerity pass through him, so I went on, asking if he knew a church he could go to. He said no, he asked me if there was one I knew. I told him that I don't have that relationship with what people call God, but if he did, that was where he needed to be, and I then said it again, that he needed to go to church. My relationship with belief is very personal. I feel as though I have spent a majority of my life in one or another sort of doubt, casting off from the shores of certainty as soon as I've found it, and then frustrated as I am tossed in with the flotsam of self-discovery. I think the reason I have continually pushed off when I find certainty is because while certainty can feel safe, I'm never safe on those grounds. I grew up moving. I don't trust the ground beneath my feet. My experience of learning to live with my own uncertainty has been more or less the mission of the last decade, and I've had to take large leaps of faith in order to do what I have, whether in my career or in my personal life. I like to think that it has offered me a bevy of tools to use when I'm encountering new insecurity. Ideological shifts are profoundly disturbing, and in the secular (maybe post-secular?) age I find opportunity abounding in seeing that a babel-like structure can generate everything. It is true - if the library of Babel were real, would we give up our pursuits in trying to write our stories (or, more darkly, to find the story of our lives within it?). The adversarial potential of a technology that can finish our thoughts still does not have them for us. Mathematicians have already gone through this. Hilbert, Gödel, and Leibniz did this handily. A shift in how we think cannot decide where we are going, what we are doing with our lives, and how we care about the world around us. The entire exercise of knowledge remains apophatic, and the further we hare reached toward the unknowable, the more divine that unknowable. An aesthetics prizing the use of a self-aware mind is a means by which we embody our own cosmologies, and it is a requirement for any age. It is especially true in this one. The ineffable is something we work to describe because we do not know it. Creating a mechanism to better explore those gaps is an opportunity, both of exegesis in our priors but as well to understand where if at all there is so much more yet to know. The despair in the world around the use of AI is a bit perplexing because I don't understand how this is different from any other time in history where a discovery, a process, a way of thinking has declared thinking and progress over. It instead reveals a deep lack of teleological foundation with which the pure rationality of the modern age has left us. What I am speaking to here is that a crisis of faith is always a crisis of faith. We have known what these look like many times over, and we are still here. I don't mean to be maudlin, dismissive or reductive - but I do think that the faithless are often the first to throw up their hands at whatever defies their belief. Understand me - it is possible not to have faith and to believe something. They are not the same. One thing I have always enjoyed is that the best mathematicians and physicists are indeed wonderful writers. Hampshire is one such example. Strogatz is another. Rovelli writes with incredible poetry. If anything, the very fact that exploring thinking as though it is an exegetical process is particularly irrational - since the first thing many come to realize when deepening their course of study is how steadily the map can grow, despite it only ever approximating the territory. It is not all knowable, much to the chagrin of Aquinas - but it is beautiful nonetheless, and the joy of continuing to probe the dark is exactly the sort of joy that comes from discovery. I feel for rationalists who find themselves in a position of terror at the realization that a worldview founded entirely upon rationalist foundations might have uneven footing. I'd stake the claim that many (all) of those who have claimed themselves as rationalists have sought to bound themselves within the constructs of faith to start with. Rationality allows us to shoo away uncertainty in pursuit of knowing, and when you get very good at rationalizing, it can begin to feel as though all is knowable. Any crisis precipitates despair. But an exegesis of rationalism is not a finished problem, and if those who would call themselves rationalists would pause momentarily from judging the 'irrational' (we in the humanities have had to bear this judgment a long time), it becomes possible to recognize that exegesis continues to spawn new systems of belief. Those exerting hyper-rational ideology might realize that there are, indeed, many ways to interpret the truth for its use as a construct of telos. Now, it could be that just because I've spent most of my life calling myself an atheist that I'm not surprised that we are where we are now - there are claims to be made in and about faith in many dimensions, both ideologically as well as anthropologically, but technologically the concept is all the more interesting. What is the use of faith as a tool, and by what mechanism did it emerge for use by people as a way to survive living? Is it an aberration of the conscious mind? I could not possibly think so. I find faith not only important, but necessary, and what we see in the pursuit of any discipline that becomes one's own purpose is the pursuit of the aforementioned telos - the way of providing meaning to what is being done. It is the reason for anyone who speaks passionately about that which they find beautiful and fascinating in the world to do so with that specific passion. There is something in and beyond the feeling of certitude, because there is also the thrill and joy of unfolding the world around us, interacting with it, and coming into contact with whatever we have come many times throughout history to call the divine. We can call it whatever we like. That little bit of programming in our brains and bodies feels good when we interact with the world, and it feels even better when we feel as though we are meant to interact with it. I do not think that it can be taken from us, especially - only that there are new ways of doing so. One way of seeing has now changed - but of anything that can be made certain there is one in particular deserving of the most attention; there is still yet more to learn. I don't think it is necessarily a 'surprise' to learn this, as a non-mathematician - because whatever reasoning we have developed as a species cannot do more than we use it for. Language is a construct, as is mathematics. Its foundations are not real, in the explicit sense, however heretical it is to make this claim. Everything that we model is an approximation of what we actually experience. It may be because I know enough about mathematics to actually appreciate that about half of mathematics feels like an exegetical exercise of something being read for the first time - of reaching into the fabric of our surroundings and revealing what it's made of, if even they are rules - but I believe it's also because we have been relearning how to evaluate our existence for millennia now, and we continue to make progress in every dimension other than how to actually appreciate where we are. --- Wherever one can create a garden, one must.

In treturn, I'll be supporting her at checkpoint and readying her for each leg - taking in the athletic atmostphere and contracting it, emotionally, to the experiences of the last week. UMB is a professional-level race, and with the trail-running boom in full swing, the running world's many eyes are fixed on the ALps this qeek. By contrast, only a scret few know the names Ilooked gortward to seeing in te mountains between here and Marseille. The Speed Project (TSP) is well-known in running culture, but not as much in the professional running scene. Those in the pro scene who do know about it fall under two camps - those who know it but think of it mostly as being silly, and those who understand that the popularity of running is not merely rooted in athleticism. This is not to say, necessarily, that TSP has in any way directed what we call running 'culture', but it certainly has done so in the past. Those who have done so across the years have been a tight collection of brands and race programs - a small crowd somehow penetrating beyond the fabric of locality into a globally-recognized phenomenon. For my part, I've always thought that the current wave of 'running cool' owes a through-line to some of the first unsanctioned races that were popularized through Orchard Street Runners, with Joe DiNoto's Tuesday night runs out of New York City's Lower East Side having set the tone for the grit of 'urban running', whose aesthetic has reverberated over the last fourteen-or-so years. 2013 OSR was perfect for the Instagram era - grainy black-and-white images of athletes darting through traffic late at night - athletes covered in tattoos who gave off a recklessness built for admiration. At the time, the demographic of these runners skewed toward one group - the majority of those represented on social feed were white men putting themselves up against the risk factor of the concrete wilds. Joe, to massive credit, recognized this and worked to bring attention not only to the women who showed up, but as well the wider (non-white) breadth of runners who were willing to put themselves to the test. For a while, the critique of Joe's races was that while it liked to cast itself as 'urban running' - the permission of who got to call themselves 'urban runners' was open to debate; does urban mean white tattoed guy? Who else runs in these cities? Again, to Joe's credit, he worked on changing this representation, any by the time of his final OSR Midnight Half in 2018, the field was as diverse as one might hope from a race that based itself in New York City. For a while, OSR was in high demand from brands as a crucible for New York running culture. Adidas dangled the possibility of greater growth over everyone who contributed to OSR for years until Joe finally got fed up and shifted his attention to a bigger, more lenient brand in Nike, who continues to back his efforts today.
