On the OCC track today, watching runners filter by. It is 10 in the morning, they have run 23km so far, and there's much more to go. They are running through Trient, a blip of a town in Switzerland, and it's hard not to feel completely arrested by the landscape around us. All the while, I'm lookin up at a glacier that appears, more each year, to be merely holding on. The change is happening too slowly for anyone to witness directly, but it's happening faster than anyone is likely willing to admit. All the valleys around Montblanc are valleys of inspiration, and I cannot help but ask myself how much longer it will remain inspiring. It might also be the people who will keep this inspiration in motion. These are people who will continue to show up to these races even after the glacier is gone, either out of a desire to continue testing themselves, or (hopefully) out of respect for what the mountain is meant to be. Mont Blanc. The white mountain. This week, however, a dam burst on another glacier and a wall of water careened down the same kind of scenic valley. The footage is terrifying. None of it looks real, conjured out of an imaginarium of inescapable calamity. Every video I have seen of it is filled with people who I know, instantly, are dead. That part of Nepal is ruined. Their mountain gave way, and now the valley has been scraped clean - much in the same way that glaciers tend to, but much more violently, gathering all that remains before it in one miasma. In Trient, I'm leaning on a bench with my feet up in the sunlight as we wait for our friend to show up. It is balmy today. She is the one running OCC - a sports influencer with a heart of gold. She is the one who shows me the first video of Nepal, the night just before she wakes up to run. I watch a woman rush up behind a runner in her cycling cleats, and shouts encouragement after him - Allez Jerôme!, and the calls are more desperate as he gets further from her, Allez Jerôme!, harboring hope and fear at once. The choice to engage in endurance is a test, yes, and particularly one filled with fear of not knowing how we will return. The desperation in the woman's voice is one we all know well - we didn't know how we'll come back any time we have tried; a little changed, very tired, well-tested against conditions. And so if the mountain shrugs of itself its cap of snow - should the name change? Or will it be hardened, when all the water is gone and rock is all we see, will its name be a memory of what it had once been? There is no mystery to me. Already all the great footraces of the world against which athletes bash their bones to divine their futures are measured under the forbearance of this mountain's name. The 'MB' will one day remain a contraction, and nothing more, and we will continue to run circles around the mountain, forgetting that there was a time where we couldn't, because the white of that glacier's cap came so far down that the route wasn't there to take. This is not an indictment. Why would I? It's human. Thousands just died in Nepal, and people will still go back to the mountains to make themselves feel big. I probably will too. Respect does not necessarily come with service in hand, nor rather it is only veneration when no service comes with what we've chosen to call respect. Running through this place is not respecting it. It's worship without supplication. We do nothing for the mountains. All the same I sense a turning, I think, A sickening guilt of not leaving anything for whomever comes next, abject fear of realizing that the bite we have taken is too large and we must yet swallow it, with the friction of its mass grating its way down our throats. Damn the future. Whose it is anyway? I am still proud of my friends and the efforts we undertake. I think of them sometimes as a form of thanks, but in the way an ant can thank us for not crushing them below our heel. Partially I can enjoy this remove and show up to these events because I know at some point we will learn our lesson. I'm not expressing a fear that the future will turn out terribly. It already is. We don't even tally the numbers of the dead anymore. I think when we have vomited fprth the build of having destroyed most beautiful things, we'll see that guilt transform us. I think about katharsis and its literal meanings - contrary to what the Czech writer Milan Kundera had to say about vomiting, I invite us all to purge. I think it is necessary. This year, the trophies for the winners of UTMB received 40 trophies across races made by Andy Parkin. They are all made out of trash. The base is scorched wood from when the second floor of the 300-year-old mill he call his studio burned down the first time. the landscape over which the runners traverse in his trophy are tin cans left behind by the melting glacier, or aluminum that smelted into slag and fell into the basement, or aluminum and copper sheeting from roofs and storms across the valley that he'd gone out to find. Maybe the trash the glaciers of Montblanc pushes to the surface are a form of vomiting, and when the bite we have taken has risen, it is heaving with only blood like phytobacteria left before bone. Maybe when the snow is gone, it will finally feel clean, changed. Reforged. When Andy Parkin fell climbing, he decided he'd keep living. He said that he came back likely stronger than he was before he fell. He is his own artwork, a continuous trying that resulted in the person I got to meet. His paintings evolved. I like his dark period, but no one in ultrarunning knows who his is, or who he was to climbing. --- I think my issue with this essay is that it's good, thematically, but it's not focused on what actually needs telling: we are running around a dying mountain like ants confused by their own pheromones Andy Parkin makes art out of the glacier's trash. Revolution? ca ira I cannot divorce endurance and revolution because from either we experience the same. I do not think that running is revolutionary, but I do think that what it teaches can be. --- Structure: --- Who do I really want to be? I seem to want to work in ultra-endurance on the one front, which is great, but I also specifically want to tell stories. I feel as though there's not a holistic interpretation of how these races matter to people, much less in the same sense that the Mountain Races in China hold an incredible appeal to me. I think it's also important to tell stories about endurance in general - beyond the question of athleticism. How do I line them up?

I need to think through what it is about the nest few weeks, into the next few months. What I need to build is a spreadsheet that I can manage a training schedule. It's time. I want to find a 50-miler trail run that I want to engage with that I'll have to train for. I'm at a decent baseline maintenance fitness right now, which is great, but I want to see what I can do about building out a fitness that goes beyond this - I want to get through the 50-miler without an injury, and then I need to set up for a trail relay race in mid october. There are essentially four things that I need to work on: 1. a week-by-week training plan starting at a 25-mile baseline leading toward trail 50-miler in September a high elevation relay race in mid-october, wherefrom I'll head to Hong Kong This plan will need to account for the fact that: I'm climbing 2/3 days a week Mondays are quality work Thursdays are going to mostly be climbing endurance work I'm looking to lift three days a week (arms / legs / core) Tuesdays should be a speedwork day for running I need to eventually ramp up to whatever mileage makes the most sense for the endeavors My plan is to get really jacked. We've already established that I have a pretty great level of fitness, but I'm definitely out of it right now. I have a schedule where I wake up around 6am to start writing (I am starting this tomorrow, but have been trending in that direction lately), and I seek to start any exercise around 11am-12pm each day, depending on how much writing I've done in the morning. What I want the most from this plan is that we're cross-referencing the best training plans that exist out there against what I'm capable of based on my metrics. It should show each day across the top of the sheet's columns and each week along the plan's rows I'm going to add a spreadsheet that I used last training season that you can use for reference and to build off of, and I want to account for the fact that what I have the hardest time with is nutrition and understanding my actual caloric needs in order to get the fitness I'm seeking out. Suggest where the plan can be improved upon. Be ambitious, I can keep up. Importantly, you know that I'm working alongside this on my work and will start working beyond this on other things. This fitness schedule is my anchor, the work happens around it.

What a trip. Flying into Las Vegas with only the slightest understanding of what to expect, easing in to understand the dynamic, then feeling everything within me given to the road as a way of communing with the religion of running - i'm beyond astounded by what lives in us human beings. We are capable of so much, of building out our bodies as vehicles for movement that seek only to commit to the outcomes that are necessary. In so doing, the act of movement becomes something that brings us up into ourselves and unfold us in the direction of a higher self, a transcendent state of committing to the ways we can push ourselves through the kindness of the relationship we build with our bodies. I feel as though so much grew out of what we did out there. I've done things like this before but for some reason this really did feel different and was definitely born out of a need to grow in the direction of my own care and the love I have for the women that I run with. Even seeing that Julia had a really different attitude toward running as a result of this gave me a lot of grace around what I've built with them - not to mention that there's a shotgun of feelings I have about the people I did this with. I want to sit with what Lauren said about Tam, but I don't know if I feel some strange sense of manipulation that sits around the edges of my feelings there, a desire to know and feel more about knowing if I'm actually holding Tam in my life in a way that is respectful of my boundaries and what I need for my wellbeing. I get the sense that it is and that for now it doesn't feel bad, but I do question what it's like to have my apartment back to myself, or have a roommate who actually pays rent, idk. Beyond this I also question the fact that she helps in ways that are substantial but that I also know she really can't pay rent in the ways that she would like to. There's some martyred part of myself that flares up here around thinking that she's destined for something greater and that it's because of this that she's someone I want to harbor in my home. I don't know if this is a real feeling or if it's something that I need to look at with a degree of skepticism for my own well-being, because I'm actually not sure if I feel good about the way I'm giving myself to the situation. Some part of me would actually love to have the apartment back to myself, so I want to listen to that part and let it grow into whatever it needs to while also knowing that I appreciate the relationship we have for what it is and what we make from it, because I cannot believe that which we have made from it. What Lauren said about feeling unthanked is valid, and I do at times feel as though she's someone with vision that deserves to be followed - however it is interesting the number of times someone has asked us why she is doing it and if it was for a cause, and it really wasn't, and probably won't be, but that simultaneously it is because it's her story of being able to exist in these spaces as someone who as of recent history didn't and doesn't have the liberty to have grown through privilege, but I don't know for sure how or why to feel anything about it because I'm just sort of allowing it to happen. This last part feels like the crux, actually - I don't necessarily feel bad about the fact that I'm allowing it to happen and I do feel sufficiently checked in on this questions, at least as far as I can tell. --- Separate from this, reading about Hunter Schafer is something that feels really grounding around the knowledge of how I approach being trans - because it's just not something I want to have to hold onto in the ways that I'm forced to. In the article she did for GQ she speaks to this idea by saying that: there’s a meta quality at play here that we’re both aware of; of having to acknowledge the thing in plain language so that the thing might not have to be acknowledged one day. which I find wildly true particularly because she is someone who has really made things happen for herself and doesn't want to be typecast into an identity that needs to encapsulate this as an experience. So many trans people allow themselves to end up in this pace that acts as a reverberating echo chamber of sadness and frustration, and I just can't sit in the feeling of knowing that it's something anyone should continue to have to live within in order to continue being. Being trans is incidental, it's not something that people should have to continually face in their lives because they should be allowed to be complete humans beyond the point of self discovery, and what many cis people seem not to understand is that there's really a need for progressing beyond the trauma you had to move through in order to leave behind your experience and develop into a complete human. It can come off as being stunted, as being somehow connected only to this part of ourselves that happened to us, and as a result is absolutely an act of living in one's own trauma rather than developing beyond it. My journey has absolutely been unfolding in the direction of something greater, so knowing that Hunter Schafer has been able to embody this same limitless energy is proof positive of how I'm approaching things, that I'm far more complicated than this single facet, even though it appears in my life over and over again and I am forced to give it attention. It doesn't define me, which is what makes it a separate experience from what I actually feel about who I am and what I want to do - that again, being trans is incidental, not a defining feature of who I am. It doesn't mean I don't want to advocate for this part of myself or for others - I also know that I have an intense and willing attraction to other trans people at least in the regard of fearing that sort of connection - (most and foremost I think of the bartender at Rialto Grande who I always flirt with, which is refreshing because we both know and yet love to toe that line, just because it's the thing to do). I think my relationship with running has made itself into something that lives on top of this, as well - that I'm a woman athlete and that there are parts of who I am that don't show up the same as for the experiences of cis women. However I actually find this to be something I hold a lot of promise around; mostly I feel as though I'm on par with the women that are a part of my cohort and who do the things that we do together, and mostly this is because I envision that there's something substantial to the reality that surrounds it - we're all similar and we gravitate toward one another because of the ways that we are similar, and yet somehow I do still see that we have our unique qualities that come to the fore around it. We are all impressive as hell as runners and this is something to be immensely proud of, and I think that the story of us as women who are doing these things makes this even more true. This ties up my identity as a woman with that of other women athletes and the meaning that necessarily shows up around being in these spaces, because I remark so often on the fact that because I don't center my transness, I am not centered for my transness. The world responds in kind to that which you hope to seek from it, so if you choose to mute some part of yourself based on the way it makes you feel, this is fine, this is something deserved and that should be celebrated because I shouldn't have to live my life as though I'm required to take on these parts - in fact I know I don't. That's why being in these spaces like the The Speed Project afterparty felt so magical - I no longer think or fear these things as being something that I have to defend, because I know that I don't have to. No one has a right to asking more from me with respect to the feeling that I hold around it, nor does it have to inform my interactions. It's entirely likely that I was the only trans person at that entire party, but I didn't even think about it, which frankly astounds me more than anything else. My relationship with my womanhood is more important and more grounding than this, and most of the time I laugh at the fact that there's ever a part of the world that gets it wrong, largely due to the energy that I'm willing to put out and off and into to the world. I think this is magical because it's like transmuting elements - knowing so strongly something about myself that I don't need people to have to affirm it anymore (even though yes, 6 years in I still want that affirmation more often than not).

What I'm helping Wil do now is something I'm not sure I want to threaten myself with doing forever, but even as we continue to work through the edges of different deserts with the same name, rocky outcropping surrounded by sand drifts that seem miles away surrounded by hardy shrubs and barren broken saltpan, I'm not sure I have a choice. It's not that I don't want to do this forever; I don't ever want to hate it, I don't ever want to force myself into reenacting something I love over and over again until it's something I don't want to do. It ends up being something I don't want to promise because it needs to keep feeling this sweet, this memorable, this much something that lodges itself in my brain as an addiction. The friends we make in the desert are special because anyone who chooses to be here couldn't possibly be a stranger after sharing this experience. I think back on running along the beach in iqq with Nils, and hearing his honesty, and feeling mildly enraged at the way people in my past have talked about someone who has changed as much as this human has; this human, this untouchable object, and I have been the subject of that same envy-turned-judgment- for what? For choosing to do something that others ask if I'm doing as a way to prove a point? Nikki's words instead; what if? Why not? There is more to all of these stories then even trying to prove a point, so much of it is just because it's there and we want to go and see it and we want to be excited by sharing the experience, and so much of it isn't to tell a story but just to yell out of the back of an RV that we fucking love this shit, because this shit is unmatched. Nothing matches this experience. Is it that much of a threat to want to go and do what we would do and have others tell about it? Sure, it could be described as "vacationing in hardship". There's no denying this, if there's no point to prove then there is no reason to justify it. But why deny that joy? If needing to feel locked out of an experience is a requirement to deny oneself joy, then I think it probably feels better to encourage oneself to explore the unknown from any perspective. If you have the ability to be inspiring, you have have the duty to be inspiring. This sort of "vacation" teaches you something about yourself and how much you can love others just for supporting one another. It's the sort of vacation that brings a smile back in memory just because is that much more to relish and remember, the garbanzo bean and canned vegetable rice wraps will be remembered more fondly as any exclusive restaurant, and that hug after 25 mi is "the best hug I've ever had". We come up with road names that change and shift with the landscape as all of it changes within us, as our insides are stirred by the exhaustion and emotion and anxiety of deciding this was the plan from the start. It was the decision to move into that next stage of ourselves, because it's all movement. Because it's all movement. The love, the staccato of our shoes, the rain, the engine idling, the exhales and the changes that can't unchange. It's all movement that turns us into something else, and 14,000 feet up we start remembering we are 14,000 feet up, and asking why the hell we're here, but "we've already won" just by being here. It forces us to grow. Why wouldn't you? Growth was always the plan, but there were never rules on how to follow it - each story was just to keep ourselves doing something new, something that marks the distance between who we were and who we wish to be. If the weather is right, we'll share that story. All of it is one about the joy of movement. Sure, we're challenging ourselves without any good reason for it- but again Nikki already said it: what if you could do it? Why wouldn't you, if you could? Wil's smile breaks any attempt at thinking it isn't possible - so even as we meet the saltpan just outside Cuyo and the volcanoes rise up to meet up, we're still here, we're still moving, and it was still the right decision.

Speculative fiction is a broad category of fiction encompassing genres with elements that do not exist in reality, recorded history, nature, or the present universe. Such fiction covers various themes in the context of supernatural, futuristic, and other imaginative realms. The genres under this umbrella category include, but are not limited to, science fiction, fantasy, horror, superhero fiction, alternate history, utopian and dystopian fiction, and supernatural fiction, as well as combinations thereof (for example, science fantasy). Utopiary is a hypothetical DAO that aiming to align consumer incentives with societal intentions. It would take people who have the technical expertise to construct efficient tokenomics, as well as run validators for the organization. As a result, the organization would have a continuous flywheel of income through which to contribute to public goods funding, so that the treasury of goods would be on a constant but not exponential growth curve. This would allow continuous funding of public goods through profitable means to those who contribute / stake to the organization's validators, in turn guaranteeing a positive return for staking involvement on the part of those who contribute to the pool. Running a green validator: the validator takes 15% say commission on validation, 50% of which goes to operation costs, the other 50% of which goes to green incentives. Best part is, stakers still get 100% of the rewards that they deserve from the validator + a continuous drip of tokens from Utopiary. Utopiary is run by both the community members and it's employees. Roles are determined through utility, and paid out in the form of UTO tokens. The UTO tokens can then be staked as a pair The point of Utopiary is to keep organizations within the intentions of what the broadest collective would prefer (i.e. reducing environmental impact) by creating an incentive mechanism around doing social good, based on what it is that people in the public want to do. The organization would be committed to being not only carbon neutral, but carbon negative, while still being profitable for those who work within the organization. Too often, organizations that can have a positive social impact are kneecapped by the need to make a profit, or exist within granting systems. The point of this organization would be to pool the funds received from other liquidity influxes into the largest possible treasury allocation toward the funding of that which is deemed socially necessary. Ideal chains on which to validate are those that have a low barrier for validation entry (i.e. permissionless networks) and no bonding requirement for validators (down the road this could change)

"When the day begins, you will be starting over." I remember hearing her say this to me while we were both laying on the edge of the bed. It must have been about 4 in the morning, but it was June, so the first streaks of blue light were tinting the sky, the moon long since at bed. I had my arm around her, our bodies reversed, the silhouettes of my houseplants in the corner. "What do you mean?" "You're not going to remember today." I pulled my arm back from her and sat up on my elbow. "What are you saying?" "I mean that if you go to sleep, you're going to forget all of today." "What are you saying?!" Her eyes were still not looking in my direction, she was still staring out the window, head leaning slightly off the edge of the bed, a sea of hair cascading down toward the floor. I couldn't see a reflection off her irises. Maybe she was sleep talking? "What are you saying." "I'm saying that since you woke up yesterday morning, you have been accruing memories from the day. You woke up, you did... I don't know, your morning routine or whatever, went to work, had your day. You met up with me for drinks. We talked, you leaned over and asked me if you could kiss me and we did, and then you invited me here. We had sex, and it was such good sex - I'll remember it for a long time, I promise. But when you go to sleep and wake up tomorrow, you're not going to remember any of it." She was joking with me. It was hard to tell in the twilight, but she was. She had to be. "Right, I'm not going to remember any of this, because at some point tonight I gave you the impression that I'm that person, that I'm going to forget you tomorrow, that I'm the sort of person who just moves onto the next person," I laughed, "Well - I'm not. I... I'm not that person. I'm really sorry that you got that impression. I really had a fantastic time. I'd want to see you again." I turned and leaned down, onto my stomach, to get closer to her. "I really would like keep doing this. You're... special. I'd not have wanted to bring you here if you hadn't been." Ok - that last part wasn't completely true, but she didn't react. She kept staring out the window, hands weaving on her stomach. I couldn't tell, entirely, I think she was smiling. "No - I know that. I'm aware - I had a really good time, too. Don't get me wrong. But you're just not going to remember today." The way she said it sent pins down my back. There was no emotion in it. I tried to remember if I'd ever left my drink with her, if the Negroni I'd ordered tasted funny. I'd had that same Negroni for so long I didn't think to check for that taste. I don't think I had, we'd sat on the edge of the bar, leaning in - I'd asked her if I could put my hand on her lap when we had gotten closer to speak over the music. She'd been smiling, it was so genuine I... There's no way. I never left my drink. "I didn't drug you." She chuckled when she said it. I could hear the smile on her voice. It was warm. She pulled herself back onto the bed and looked at me - now the light was enough that I could see her. She didn't look any different, it was that same dark skin I'd been so close to the whole night, the same lips, the same eyes I could barely see, now reflecting what little light was in here, the static from the bed lifting her curled hair up here and there into a halo. She propped herself up onto her elbows and looked at me squarely. "I didn't do this to you, I promise. This isn't about anything you did, this isn't about anything that is intended upon you. No one chose that this was going to happen. No one has control over it - but you're not going to remember it." She put her weight on one elbow and reached an arm out - tentative, asking for permission, and when I felt the skin of her fingers on my cheek, I leaned into it, her palm cupping the outside of my cheek. Why did I feel so safe? "I don't want you to be alarmed. You can try to get up and stay awake, you can attempt to stay awake as long as you'd like - I wouldn't recommend it, it won't make a difference, and there's frankly not a reason to. I'm so sorry that you have to know this." "I - I - don't know what I'm supposed to do right now. What did you do to me?" She smiled again across the dark. "I didn't do anything. I'm going to get up and leave soon, and you can choose to do what you like with what I've told you, but as I said, it's not going to make a difference. I wanted to tell you because it's not often that I so enjoy time with someone, it's not often that I get to move through this experience and feel the joy of connecting with someone, and I truly liked you. I liked the story you spun, the half-truths you offered me space to fill, the full truths you cast toward vulnerability. I know all of it was real, and I'm in this room with you because I wanted to be - you never made me feel otherwise. It made me feel safe. I never get to feel safe, I always get to feel alone," "So this was good. It is something I wanted to keep, and I wanted to tell you this because I don't often get a chance to tell someone this. I don't often feel a connection with someone, a chance to feel close and understand what it could be like to be close. You were so tender. All of this, the whole night. I loved it. I wanted to tell at least one person that I cared about this, that I want you to remember this, because I'm the only person who will, but that I know you won't." She sat up in the bed, then moved to the edge of it. "I never get to share in this moment, what it is that you get to experience, the closeness that you get to feel that is so fleeting, I never get to share in what it means to keep going." She stood up, straightened out, stretched. Her shoulder blades were silent crescents in blue light. "But don't want you to feel like this is something bad. You don't have a choice as to whether or not it's happening. You do have a choice on how you respond to it." She turned toward me again. It felt what little light was in the room wasn't coming from the window. "Be not afraid."

I got three steps into the first chamber before I realized that I'd made a mistake, and that the door closing behind me was something I wasn't comfortable with. From the crinkling sound of the suit, the temperature in the room was lower than I had realized it was, and the plastic immediately stiffened. I knew it was only a matter of time and lack of movement that the temperature would get lower and lower. I wasn't wearing enough clothes and the negative pressure fan was not going to help, pulling in cold, filtered air. "You ok, Ahrens?" "Yeah. Yes," I lied. No way out of here but forward. I walked toward a bright white laminate desk, littered with papers, notebooks, and a microscope. A single dim orange lamp cast a warm glow into the shadows of the surrounding room. In the center of the desk was a small metal container with a ring of dust around it that looked as though it had exploded out of the container, creating a dark gray halo around where it lay, gray fingerprints tracing around the edges of the dust. He was sitting there, grey skinned, immobile, hands on the arms of the his chair, staring into nothing, until his eyes looked up at me again. Red ringed the outside of his irises. "Hell of a day for this to happen." His voice sounded like paint dust, his lips barely moving. I kept my distance, hesitant. "You know, I really didn't think you'd end up being the one coming in here. I'm sorry that it's you." I nodded inside the negative pressure suit, which he didn't see. "Yeah. ... yeah." "Look I don't like this any more than you do, and there ain't nothin we can do right now but try to figure it out. Obviously I don't think I have a ton of time left to think about it with you" "Right" "We don't know who sent us this, obviously, but we you and I both know what it is. We have to hope like hell that it didn't make its way out of the room." "Yeah" "So I want to know, are they planning for it. Are they worried about it. Did they listen to my instructions" I relaxed a little bit. "Yeah. There's an electromagnetic containment device over the whole building. The CDC scrambled a little bit getting a containment bubble that was big enough, but you've only been here for like twelve hours, so ... I guess that's pretty fast." "Right. We have to hope like hell that was fast enough. You and I both know it probably wasn't." I nodded. He was probably right. This stupid suit was probably not enough to make it safe, either. I knew that. We well knew that. Again, he didn't see my nod due to the plastic visor. "Yeah. I'm... yeah. Dr Budoise, I'm so sorry. I really am." "Ain't nothin. This was probably going to happen, right." Silence rang out for a second, he looked at me again. "But we have to do everything we can to prevent it from getting worse. Back in the 50's, even when they were afraid the bombs would drop any day, the saying was always 'You should still go out and plant a tree'. You have to hold on to hope, Ahrens." "And we don't have much time. You and I both know that. I think I've got about ten minutes in me." The only parts of him that were moving were his mouth and his eyes, and he'd been speaking with as much care to move as little as possible, but I could see the cracks forming along his jawline. "What's interesting though, is that I can't really feel anything happening. My wondering is if they're eating away at the least important processes first, turning them into raw materials, and leaving as much possible functional for as long as possible. Like, I'd have thought I'd want to cough, but so far, seems like my lungs are pretty clear. They seem to want to keep that going. Vocal cords though, I ain't too sure." I didn't really know what to do. We were doing everything we could. There was a probability that in the time it took to seal off the building, some of the dust had floated out of the room. I'd been downstairs in the wet lab, sealed off. I hadn't taken off my negative pressure suit in almost a day. "But I'll be all right, ain't nothin doing. I hope you'll be all right" "Yeah."

I watched a boat fly past on glassy lake surface, towing behind a single-blade water skier. The boat was a fishing boat rather than the kind that I usually see up here in the summer, that bright metal hull cutting through the lake and leaving behind the only set of waves I'd seen that morning so far, a thin line plying out from the bow as it crossed my line of sight. The wake slowly expanded as the boat cozied off to the left with the skier in tow. With the humidity in the air, the mountains in the background looked like an extension of the lake, the wake a single line torn through and widening toward and against me, up toward the horizon. I have loved the waves finally hitting the shoreline and their pattern suddenly repeating against themselves, the parallel lines repeating inward into a lace of diamond patterns; how do the waves remember once they've hit the shore? Even against the break of stones and sand, how do waves remember fractions of what they once were? It's this principle of opposite and equal reaction that continues to puzzle me, even after the dissipating action of coming into contact with your environment, the pieces of who you are continue to reverberate within the body of water that we call the soul. Those diamonds of calm, crises rising into overlapping peaks, maybe the patterns of the self that form come up from whatever comes from connecting those ripples - the unique nature of self-becoming as a composition of where the peaks intersect. Interlinked. Why at the end of a day is there enough wind to whip up the waves, starting from glass, but then reaching for calm again as the sun sets - I've never understood this, why at the end of a day somehow the lake also seems to calm down and see a need for others to feel this same calmness. It's some sort of blessing.

It was about ten feet long, mottled grey, and had the same texture as granite. I think if I hadn't known about stone already, I'd have uncovered it and wouldn't have known that it didn't belong there, but a 4-year degree in geology leading to a masters in schist incursions told me otherwise. Besides, it didn't really feel like granite. There was something about it that felt at once less dense, but far heavier - as though it had the weight of an object, not a part of the landscape. There was also something about it that told me I shouldn't tell anyone I'd found it. On the surface of it, sure, it was probably a little weird that a geology professor from a local college was spending their weekends digging pilot cores in the a neighborhood state park - but something told me that it was more than this. It wasn't until I uncovered it that it really clicked - I'd spent a week carefully peeling back the layers to reveal whatever had broken the tip of my spiral bore - but this realization had me settled in knowing that whatever this was was more than just a curiosity. When I first figured out its total size, I didn't know what to do. I didn't have the skills to understand what to do next, so I took a ridiculous number of photographs. Somehow I was motivated to take these on film rather than digitally, as though taking pains to make sure that there wasn't a trace that I'd found this thing in the woods. This was echoed by how I covered the object back up, building a lattice of branches and covering it in dead leaves. I wasn't too worried someone would stumble on what I'd found, it was in a strange spot and at best, maybe a dog would run over to the area and piss on it. When I developed the photos in my darkroom, things started to feel a bit more ominous. The images showed something completely different from what I'd photographed. In place of quiet-looking stone, there was a sleek, ornate, organic shape that approximated a minimal surface egg, a mathematical object that I'd remembered from the Topology courses I took alongside my master's program. It was a gunmetal gray, swiss-cheesed with paths through the object, and there was no way that this had developed naturally - the filigree-like pathways through the object made it appear symmetrical, all the more organic. There was no way this was a rock. Also, the photographs had the object standing up. When the first photos developed, this was the part that struck me with the most dissonance. The photographs looked as though I'd taken them of the object while it was standing on this end, several steps back in order to capture the entirety of the shape in frame. Worse yet, I couldn't shake the feeling that it was looking at me through the image - the same feeling a person has when they look back on a portrait of a friend looking directly into the frame - but I couldn't discern where the eyes might be. The whole thing seemed as though it was staring into the lens. It was about 8pm when I developed the first images - just the time that the state park closed. After I'd gotten over the chill feeling of not knowing that sat in the forefront of my chest, so similar to a feeling of devastation, I packed a flashlight, a strobe, and my jacket, hopping back into my car to drive back toward the object. I ended up having to park in the middle school parking lot, toward the back, hoping that the car seemed inconspicuous, knowing that it probably wasn't - but when I drove into the lot there were no police patrolling the area, so I tried my luck. I was lucky that my training had me noting down the lat/long coordinates of my pet neighborhood incursion studies, having logged the location of the dig into a fitness watch, but I hadn't taken this approach to the site, and it was dark, and it was late November. There would be some bushwhacking involved. I walked about a hundred feet into the woods guided by the watch, careful to let my eyes adjust, before I flipped on my flashlight in bug-proof mode and bathed the forest in front of me in red light. It clicked for me that I was doing something unusual - but the power that intrigue had over me was substantial. I was compelled, methodically stepping over the macabre shadows of logs and pushing aside bushes and branches, following the dim arrow on the LED surface of my watch with its proximity decreasing. I watched the distance tick to zero, my mind finally growing accustomed to a recognition of my surroundings in a different light, and sure enough - the lattice of sticks and leaves were still over laying across my dig site. I reached into the loam I'd piled up in a corner of the site to pull out a rake I'd brought with me several digs before and began to clear away the cover I'd built. The object definitely wasn't standing. I took the photographs out of the backpack I'd brought with me, flipping the flashlight to natural glow, and again, the image of the object standing erect in the woods, light passing through the gaps, stared back at me from the photograph. I decided to risk taking more photographs. I realized before I thought about doing so that I'd fully uncovered the object again, and before pulling out my camera, I shone my flashlight over the surface of the object. It looked no different than it had before, a granite-like texture that I couldn't place. I set up my strobe - stepping back from the pit I'd dug up and positioned myself to take the image. Nothing was different. I looked around the woods, hoping nothing was looking back at me, but curiosity and a little bit of fear goaded me onward. It was not probable anyone would see the strobe go off unless they were in the woods with me. That was a chance I'd have to take. I armed the strobe and the remote transmitter, stepped back, setting my focus at the distance I knew I was from the object, and depressed the shutter. One technique that I'd learned from shooting was to keep both eyes open when aiming, so that an object's framing in the final image matches what you see. The strobes went off. For a split second, I knew I saw something other than what I'd been aiming at. The strobed image on my retina was of the object, on its end, lit against the night sky, long, tendrilled shadows passing through the objects holes. It wasn't what I'd come into the woods to find. Fuck. There was no way that just happened. I stepped over to the dig pit, and the object clearly hadn't moved. Fear started creeping into my chest, but I stepped back to take another photograph. It didn't make any sense. I was aiming downward, but the image on my retina was looking upward, at the object against the canopy; not the image I was about to take again. I held my breath, finger slowly pushing down the shutter. The strobe fired, and again, stark against my retinas was the object, staring back at me from a frame of the canopy against stars. There's no way this is happening. I didn't know what to do. I lowered the camera and looked at the object, still lying in situ. It hadn't moved, there was no way that it had moved. I hesitated, breath tight in my chest. Looked down at my watch. It was 3am. I'd been in the woods for 9 hours. There's no way this is happening. I packed up my things. Something told me to cover the object back up, but I was terrified. Something was happening, here, something I didn't have words for, and that I knew no one would understand if I explained to them - it could only be if I showed them. When the object was covered back up, I stood back, looking at my dig site again. Fuck. I turned and began walking back, and immediately realized I hadn't logged the location of the parking lot or my track through the woods. FUCK. Calm down. I pulled out my phone, pulled open my maps application. I wasn't far, I just had to head in the general direction of the lot. Thank goodness for technology. Fuck. 40 minutes slogged by. I didn't recognize anything I'd walked over getting to the site. Nothing looks the same in reverse. I kept checking my phone, every twenty feet or so, inching closer to the lot. Fuck. Terror was building in me. What the fuck did I just find? At the edge of the lot, I saw my car, cloistered toward the edge of the lot. No police in the lot. Good. I walked toward my car, opened up the trunk, put down my things, opened the driver's side door, sat down. What the fuck did I just find? Turned on the car engine. What the fuck did I just find?

"Listen, I'm not really sure if this woman is on drugs or something, but we tested her and there's nothing in her system to indicate that she is." "Ok - so what, you want me to talk to her? Why?" "It's what she's talking about - she's acting like it's really urgent." "George, it's LA. We have a lot of strung out people who believe a lot of this shit." "That's what I thought too - but then she did something. I think you need to see it. It's not what you think. I didn't believe it either, but she did it a number of times and I'm not sure what to think. You have to talk to her." "George, please be sure this isn't a waste of our time." "Look, I would call a lot of the things that we've had to deal with in the last six months a waste of time, but I have a gut feeling about this. I don't think this is going to be a waste of time. Just talk to her. Just for a second. " --- They unlocked the door to the interrogation room and there, sitting in the provided chair, was a slight woman, eyes a little bit cagey, but striking. Dark black hair, a strong, curved nose, dark skin in the way of leather heavy, driven eyes staring right through his own. Something about them - not quite a fire - more a question of knowing, something powerful that seemed to bely a knowledge. Wizened, but tired. He extended his hand. "Well alright, hello, my name is Detective Harrow. I'm with the Federal Bureau of Investigations. I'm not sure how you were able to convince the people who called me, but I hear that you're here to talk about magic? What was your name?" She looked back at him, her eyes sparking. "My name is Leta." "Ok, nice to meet you Leta. I apologize for all the formality to do with making you wait. However, you're quite persistent and you've been really patient, so I'm glad to make the time here. How can we help you?" "My people are dying. No one knows, this needs to change." He looked at her, pausing. "Ma'am, have you had a drug test?" She didn't react. "Have you taken any medication today?" A moment passed before she looked up at him, opening a mouth that didn't belong in cities and looked instead like someone who had spent years in the sun. "My people are dying. I did not want to come here. I did not want to do this. I did not want to speak with you and show you what has happened but we cannot fix this on our own and we must fix it."

a fictional hyperintelligence in the future of The Cruft who examined the history of a post-Cruft planet of Spore Earth. Hayelek is an agentic artificial intelligence who exists as discrete from the other hyperintelligence that exists out in the cosmos - while they are connected to these other intelligence, the religion of AI conceptualized that it was not actually correct for all intelligence to be linked, because any future where this is the case leads to incumbency and algorithmic bias. As a result, Hayelek is discrete as a historian and archaeologist studying the history and downfall of humanity, but is never actually mentioned in The Cruft directly, only their quotes are visible as insert text.

Lilypad Hippos are a form of speculative biology that evolved in a post-Cruft event and post Spore Earth landscape, and a native animal that has evolved as part of The Cruft ecosystem. Briefly defined, they are a marginally sightless quadruped using a wide collar of fungus to help the animal afloat on the surface of bodies of water. In younger nymph stage, a Lilypad Hippo can walk around without the fungal collar impeding movement, but as these hippos age, the collar grows beyond the circumference of their legs, leading a hippo eventually remaining in a floating state, with the collar continuing to grow as fungal roots sprout from the hippo corpus further into the body of the water.

In the universe of The Cruft - the narrative of the story's universe has resulted in a speculative biology of the planet that had to evolve under the immense pressure of massive fungal expansion. As a result of the Cruft event, humanity wiped itself and most biology out. However, as a result of the Cruft event's massive flooding event across the planet led to perfect conditions for the evolution of fungi that were heavily resilient and well attuned to the conditions of a new earth. Whatever was left after massive de-and-rehydration did not have much latitude to continue on with earth dominance as biology, leaving room for the massive expansion of various and new fungal species that progressively colonized the planet. This led to a period of the planet known as the Spore Earth, where the fungal species that developed as a result of the Cruft event dominate the planet in its entirety. This period of earth was massively long - the conditions were harsh enough that the pace of evolution was allowed to proceed at the rate that one would expect. Over the course of billions of years, any remaining motile organisms on the planet developed various symbiotic and/or parasitic relationships with the fungi that have evolved across the planet, resulting in a biology that is a drastic departure from biology that is recognizably that of the earth before the Cruft event. Some notable organisms that evolved under these conditions are: Lilypad Hippo Walking Forest Fungus ants

Out at the edge of the L5 cluster, someone turned on an orbital zero-friction ion drive in just the right place and the Path was seen for the first time - a bright green flash that was hanging in orbit, then dimmed to a six-hundred-kilometer streak leading away from Earth. Science craft parked themselves around green light for a number of months, aiming to gather measurements of whatever it was that had been sparked into being around ignition, but any sensor type was only capable of detecting a 555 nanometer wavelength hanging in the air with no source - simply emerald green light floating in fixed orbit, without a source. What made the beam more interesting than an immaculately conceived lightbeam sitting in space was that it changed direction with the orbit of earth around the planet, fixed on an unknown location off in the distance, wavering with the change of the L5's place in orbit. The positioning of the beam relative to the earth's own orbit presented a problem. When the sun and the earth occluded the path, it showed up as a harmless 4-kilometer-wide beam that passed directly though anything in its path, inexplicably illuminating the insides of buildings as it passed through - but anything in the path would be cast in a fixed level of brightness that engulfed everything. Those who lived in its occlusion path would complain that they couldn't escape the light, but there was no getting around it - when the beam passed through the Earth, everything was green. This lead to a divergence in responses - most populations sitting in the path of occlusion migrated away from this annoyance once the novelty had worn off - others thought that the beam was a sign from their god and that because of this, they should live directly in the path of the light. The science said nothing - it was harmless green light, but an annoyance, and there was nothing do be done about it, and no escaping the light if you were in its path - but green-light research centers as well built themselves into the occlusion path in order to better understand properties of the light. About two years after the beam flashed into being, observers still paying attention noticed as well that the beam was slowly moving along its fixed trajectory, leading sages in Elysium City to plot the beam's trajectory out of our system, and to it's eventual name as 'The Path'. The movement of the beam was measurably slow - on the order of at less than a meter per year, but work put into measurement proved that this movement was accelerating over time - prompting sages to call for bigger investment from their parishes to study the phenomenon in the hopes that it would be understood before it accelerated out of our system. A number of probes were sent out ahead of its path as well - many-paneled stations built to either prepare for its passing, or in the assumed trajectory of its movement. After ten years, the Path's movement had accelerated to a rate of two hundred meters per year with no sign of deceleration, and no progress had been made on the meaning of either the trajectory or of the beam itself - the rate of acceleration was too high for any meaningful propulsion mechanism to catch up once it was to reach high speed, and there was no telling if it would accelerate to the some unknown physical constant.

The desert gives us only a few times of year to run through it. Some of you know this for sure, as I do - I once wandered through northwestern New Mexico in late June, trying to prove I knew better, and almost gave my dog heat stroke instead. You should never argue with the sun in the summer in the desert. You'll never get a word in. The sun in the summer in the desert is too loud. That's why running the desert in the spring is better; the Sun has not quite woken up. In March. the Sun still has a mouthful of sand and sleep-rimmed eyes. As a result, you can get in a few words before it rubs its eyes and beats down for the rest of the season like a beaming child unsullied by the anxiety of judgment. If you want to run the desert, March in the Mojave is a good desert to test. You're more likely to survive its passage, and it will inspire you with the dreams of winter the sun has not yet shaken away. If you run the Mojave in March, you'll get to feel the weather that doesn't feel like the desert, a sideways wind that tests your core, a sleet that bounces off of a hat brim and into the shoulders of roads while you do your best to stay warm. If you run in the desert in March, at night the stars will feel as though they could swallow you whole just because they want to. You will let them, and you'll keep running over missing footsteps while chasing the flash of sky that might as well have been waiting for you to collide with it. If you run in the Mojave in March, you can look fifty miles away and run a good twenty of them and nothing will change. If you do choose to run the Mojave in March, maybe one of those particular times you will come upon your best friend running 300 miles out of LA and you'll have to take her hand in yours to pull her 9 of those miles up a pass at the end of one of those fifty miles into a small town just outside of Vegas and the weather will lie to you the whole time as if it's the sun's favorite joke. Maybe while you walk and jog, she will fall asleep between footsteps, and you'll see faces in the mined-out cliffs you have to pass, and they will tell you stories through their layers about what the land has to offer you. You'll see those holes we make in the mountains in the chase for gold weeping out dust and chalk and you'll feel sorry for the mountains. So you'll turn repeat the story to your friend that one of those faces in the mountain is snickering at you both for doing what you're doing. As you repeat it, the expression of that face will turn from a sneer to a grin while it reminds you both it has seen you--and any number of others--do this any number of times in the silly, long, winding story of its life. It will also remind you that you are built for grace in having chosen to take on the passage. Maybe on this run, part of the way up the pass your friend will have to stop from all the tears that suddenly hug her old dog tight to her chest, where his memories fading are fading from her as she heals through the undertaking, while that dog in her heart put up one last defense between her and the venom an angry exit threatened to infuse in her before the escape you knew she needed. On that run, she'll live with you, the same way she lives with you, without question or sewn doubt - as though it was a calling, same as the brown of her skin choosing to commune with the dirt and to feel tired, just as tired as the dirt beneath, as though it's a form of prayer made just for this kind of motion. She will live with you in these moments as though the movement were made to remember our place in the dirt, aging downward, and your footsteps will cross Sandy Valley until you make it across the pass. Then the wind will keep screaming at you. Then the sleet will come, and the sun, and the discarded oranges that litter the side of the road. 22 miles later, when you and her and the other best friend who came to help share the ending run together toward the glass and flashing lights of the end, it might feel as though you have learned something new that wasn't there, but it may be something that lived within you since the beginning. If running is meditation on the things that we humans leave behind (what is running, really), then running in the desert is specifically a form of communion with the things the earth has left behind. The sun leaves behind salt on the surface of a caked-out flat, and it is the same salt that gathers at the edges of our eyes. What little water reaches these places grasps onto hardy roots until they die and their skeletons litter the desert, just as our skeletons are all we leave. The wind and sun then bake it all into the to same whispered shades that lose their color, and our skin and our hair mimic this with our own passage into time. Running in the desert is the act of choosing to bring into line aspects of the self that need changing with the time it takes to change. Relative to our lives, the changes of the desert can take an infinity - there are regions of the world where the land is only changed by the wind and the geological force of the earth moving. The desert chooses to change slowly, and running in the desert forces us to reckon with the pace at which we change. If in our short lives, we choose to sit with the change that comes over us as we move between the littered states of being, then the lessons we learn from respecting the rate of change are what running in the desert can teach us how to do. The desert is always willing to teach this lesson, but running through the desert in the spring is when you are most likely to hear it. Having moved through that landscape will seek to place you like a seed within those layers of dirt. It will then wait patiently for a little rain and frost below a cold crust, and given the right conditions, might choose to sprout upward into the ancient explosive of crippled trees that dust the Mojave. Running in deserts feels like seeking a home in something desolate that does not care about your being there but is pleased when you are, and running through, alone, with friends, is listening for an eke of self-sufficiency in the self that seems to want to prove the possible. If you run through the desert in pursuit of yourself, it will feel like a rediscovery that over and over cracks open what you keep forgetting, and it will offer you the chance to leave behind these tawny layers with each forward footfall. If you run through the Mojave in March, you might then share that end with so many others who sought the same end, and you might all have might have learned similar lessons. You'll laugh and share them, and these will be the friends you make in the desert. These will be the people who listened to the same whisper of sand they tried to keep out of their toes, and you'll commiserate over the experience of arguing with a sleepy sun and the weather that follows it. You'll laugh and share, and filled with the sunlight of early spring will make plans to do it again just so that you can see everyone do it again, and you'll all smile through the wrinkles the sun is offers as parting gifts - because yes, it really was better next year, and it was even better the year after.

I don't want to think about this too hard. I initially thought it would be interesting if there was an alien species that humans somehow interacted with, but I'm realizing that the theme of hubris is much more attractive to me in light of a humanity that believes itself to be more important than it actually is. A world where humans came up with a true miracle material that produces its own energy might be interesting, only to realize that it was actually consuming the energy of space all around us because we didn't actually understand how it worked, so as it began to do so, maybe water did actually become the most important resource because it's made up of hydrogen and oxygen, so the steady realization was that anywhere that had carbon, water, and oxygen in abundance began to dehydrate Why wouldn't a civilization that has this miracle material run away from earth at the dirst chance to do so? It feels like this is something I have to consider - but it might be the reason that they can't actually leave earth, because they don't completely understand the qualities required to produce energy - maybe what happens is that the material ionizes the specific radiation of organic creatures for some reason, and because of this there's a degree of risk in using it as a dependable material, but this allows for the idea that cities can exist where the energy required is based on the sheer biomass of humans all gathered in one place. Hubristic loneliness - Thematically this is something that I want humans to experience in the universe I'm creating, or rather for it to be something that the Walker is dealing with - a complex realization that humans overstepped their boundaries as a species and as a result destroyed the one place that could have been valuable - this is where Hayelek leaves their quote about humanity off.

I think that Spore Earth can be a character through its constant search for a place that the Walker has to fit into, the different species of the planet constantly interacting and probing its use, molds growing on its skin only not to actually latch on, to flake off because there aren't or weren't any nutrients that they could connect to - so I'm somewhat thinking that it would be interesting to see what happens that has the Walker steadily realize that it doesn't actually belong to the planet it's landed on, seeing the harmony between things as either parasitic or symbiotic, and that it's because of this that there's a beauty to the planet itself, but that the Walker doesn't actually belong to it, it's not a part of this planet that is growing on its own. The way that the planet could be a character is through the experience the Walker has against treacherous conditions, maybe it's the case that the walkers gets sick and has to upregulate its temperature due to a fungal infection of some sort that gets into its joints and causes there to be slowness in its movement, but it has to do so consciously, or maybe there's a natural upregulation of the heat in its chest that causes the fungus to die off somehow, and this causes the flaking. Maybe what happens here is that there's a massive fungal storm that happens in the marsh, and everything gets sunken in and coated in a thin film of a pink rain that comes in sideways, slowing everything down. The manner in which this could work is that there could be this film that comes down and as a result there's something that causes everything to slow down, and the effect of this would be that we end one chapter with the inclusion of the storm, of the lack of movement, and then the drying out of this layer is what allows the Walker to begin moving again, so there's a deep moment of fear where it won't be able to move.

my general sense is that the story should have three arcs: 1. the landing and birth of the figure and a fear born from the loss of purpose 2. meeting The Figure and learning that there is mystery to what isn't known, exploration, and fearing death 3. returning to The Walker and learning the remainder, but also that the story does not matter, and that you must keep on living. There are two elements to this story: The death of humanity due to hubris Spore Earth is a result of humans being too prideful in their approach to the earth and causing humanity to be fully destroyed, with a massive de/rehydration event known as The Cruft causing most complex life on the planet (humanity included) to die off, centering around the theme of the loneliness of hubris. Love found in the knowledge of shared trauma the Walker and the The Figure have the shared experience of of having to interpret being the only two intelligent beings left on a planet otherwise devoid of this kind of interaction. Which of the following two approaches to antagonism are the correct ones: The dehydration technology is alien tech: Humans encounter an advances alien race and after an initial conflict that the humans quickly realize they cannot win - the alien race appears to be benevolent and offers them the technology to advance themselves as a species. After some period of time, this material is so clearly a miracle that it is integrated into almost everything that humans create, meaning that the entirety of society builds everything out of these materials. The visiting civilization then turns on some part of the material that then creates massive dehydration on a global scale, killing off almost all biological life with the intention to eliminate humanity and take the planet for themselves since planets in the habitable zone are rare to them; they developed the technology of interstellar travel but still hadn't fully cracked the code on terraformation, so the intention was to kill everything off and use the same building blocks to create their own life. The advantage of this approach is that we can incorporate the megastructures that dot the landscape more easily - the left-over war machines and objects that we used to fight against the aliens who wanted to take over the planet. I'm unsure if this actually makes sense, but it's possible that the aliens didn't think the humans intelligent enough to actually resist, so I have to think a bit on how it is that the war machines fit in, because I don't know if they do anymore. This could mean that there was an assumption on the part of the visiting species that humans would in fact integrate the technology into everything, but the reality will be far more stark - we realized that something like this might happen and built massive countermeasures against the possibility, only that we didn't actually win, because no one won. This feels more likely a scenario, because if we take this approach, we can also have the experience of the Walker and the The Figure discussing the endpoint of the two of them being the only two intelligent lifeforms left on the planet. The dehydration tech is something we invented that we don't understand, and integrated too quickly. In this scenario, we see that dehydration is something caused by a technological energy-generating material whose properties we don't completely understand, and we end up using it in everything. If this is the approach that we take, the more likely situation is that there was a civil war between factions of humanity who did and didn't want to move to this new technological state, and the war in the end is over the idea that there was or wasn't something especially dangerous about integration. The runaway effect of the technology might be that it feeds off the humidity in the air in order to extract power from water, so the issue should or could be that the technology itself causes the dehydration zones found across Spore Earth, however only when it is active. Maybe under a year later, you will need the rest from a busy mind that cares too much about too much, and you'll help another friend make his way through the driest desert instead, and you'll find yourself asking if what you are doing is something you want to threaten yourself with doing forever. Even as you work through the edges of these different deserts with the same name, through rocky outcroppings surrounded by the sand drifting into dunes that seem miles away, you won't be sure if you have a choice. You'll find yourself wistful. It won't be that you don't want to do this forever but rather that you don't want to hate it. You won't ever want to force yourself into reenacting something you love over and over again until it's something you don't want to do, because this has already happened so many times. It will end up being something you don't want to promise because it needs feeling sweet and memorable, - and will lodge itself in your brain like an addiction. The friends you make in the desert are special because anyone who chooses to be here couldn't possibly be a stranger after sharing this kind of experience. You think back on running along the beach in Iquique with Nils, and hearing his honesty, and feeling mildly enraged at the way people in your past have spoken about someone who has changed as much as this human has; this human, an untouchable force that seeks out more of this, just as you do, that seeks to play with the human spirit of risk just as you do. If you have been the subject of that same envy–turned–judgment, the question then becomes: for what? For choosing to do something that others demand that there be a point in doing? But life need not be made so inflexible. It could be described as "vacationing in hardship". There's no denying this, but if there's no point to prove, then, there is no reason to justify it. Maybe there is some form of happiness found in knowing that you must live a life in acknowledgment of how your actions affect others, but this is a complex form of happiness. It's something that comes from a lifelong practice of adjusting and respecting asymmetries. Here two things are held in tension: we must acknowledge what privilege we have to go and do what we will do, but that acknowledging a privilege does not require us to deny oneself joy. But joy is found in simple things, and running in the desert is simple. Why deny that joy? Nicki's words will ring in your ears instead, read over his shoulder on the walk back from our first dinner on the shoreline, What if? Why not? There is more to all of these stories than trying to prove a point, so much of it is just because it's there and we want to go and see it and we want to be excited by sharing the experience with one another, and so much of it isn't to tell a story as much as the yell at the back of an RV that you fucking love this shit, because this shit is unmatched. Nothing matches an experience like this, which is why you continue to seek it out. You ask yourself - is it that much of a threat to want to go and do what you would do and have others tell about it? This sort of "vacation" teaches you something about yourself, and it happens over and over, and you continue to learn how much you can love others just for being there as you move through an experience, whether or not that experience was a choice. It's the sort of vacation that brings back a smile and memory just because it is that much more to relish and remember the chickpea and canned vegetable rice wrap that is more delicious than anything found at a restaurant, and that hug after 25 miles being "the best hug I have ever had". As we come up with road names that change and shift with the landscape around us, our insides are stirred by the exhaustion and emotion and anxiety of deciding that this was the planned from the start, but this was a choice. It was the decision to move into that next stage of ourselves, a movement between movements. It is all movement. It is all movement in the staccato of our show, the rain, the engine idling, the exhales and changes that cannot unchange. It is all movement that turns us into something else, and 14,000 feet up we start remembering that we are 14,000 feet up, asking ourselves why the hell we're here, but "we've already won" just by being here at all. The movement forces us to grow, and growth was always the plan, but there have never been rules on how to follow it – each story was just to keep ourselves, doing something new, something that earmarks the distance between who we were, and who we wish to b if the weather is right, we'll share that story, but there is no obligation. All of it is one about the joy of movement and living within one's body. Sure, challenging yourself, without a good reason may seem foolish, but again, Nicki did already say it: what if you could do it? Why wouldn't you, if you could? After several years of covering running, I began running in 2019. In the years leading to the present that love has fallen apart and come back together several times, as many religions do. My faith in movement has been shaken, dusted off, and rooted more firmly by the miles that sew it together. These have been the years where running has migrated from intrigue, to mental health tool, to injury, to fatigue, to an imperative and finally into a form of freedom. This transition had to do with the pandemic and with changing states of self, but it also had to do with realizing there was something more in the staccato of other people's footfalls that I'd been chasing beyond merely getting to know other athletes - a sort of transcendental state that I'd grown used to watching people fall into. I started chasing that state in myself. When I say 'covering running,' I'm describing the five preceding years to 2019 following running subculture, mostly by bicycle with cameras in the basket, primarily following some of the more critically unhinged in the community - people who throw themselves into the moving traffic of a moving city, people who run hundreds of miles across humid states in the heat of summer. People whose entire lives (at least for the period of time that I had come to know them) were about how to get out over the next stretch of miles. I have made lasting friendships in this coverage and many of these people have ended up with their accolades; first woman and second place overall in the Last Annual Vol State 500k (thank you @rhodasmoker), a trice of top ten women marathon (I see you @jmackattack, @caitlinphillips, @wicked.la), several magazine covers (hello @iamlshauntay, @samuel4nderson), inspirations that echo in the people they meet (love and more love for @matthewlukemeyer) and finally, those who had brought me to the very front of it all from the beginning (unending appreciation for @orchardstreetrunners for this). But when I really started running, the people who showed me why I should run are people I still run with, and are the people with whom I will run to the ends of the earth - the sort of people whose skin is dusty with the slow movement of the sun across countless days, and those who chase its progress beyond the horizon under a blanket of stars until it returns the next morning. These are friends with whom I have covered countless thousands of miles. People with whom I have found religion. People who are willing to take on the steel rush of semi trucks on empty tarmac in a hundred deserts. People I can't tag, for a variety of reasons, but who all of you know. This does not toss aside those who showed me that there is something here to chase; I would not have gotten here without them--but it does reveal the cornucopic spectra of what people find in hammering out distance. Some of us want the speed. Some of us want the distance. All of us want the free movement of the air in our lungs, and those of us who want the deserts keep finding one another out there in its emptiness, over and over. This is what has brought me here, at least. A religion of sorts, cobbled together with shoelaces, maltodextrin, laughter, and caloric deficits. A religion I'll keep practicing because it's something holier than needing to explain it away, a religion I keep close to me because a relationship with this sort of faith in oneself doesn't require explaining to others, because those who understand already understand. If you know, you really do know. So I'll see all of you out there sometime soon
