In 2010 I was in a riverboat with twelve or so other people on my way to Rurrenabaque, Bolivia to spend time in the woods pretending to be a naturalist. I still have the notebook I brought with me where I sketched the native plants and their relationship with nature - and it was among the best experiences I had as a young person exploring the world - a feeling of returning to something deeper, wilder, all while feeling incredibly removed from the demands of my life. I was young. I knew how to live on a thousand dollars for two months. I can't say I was necessarily trying to find myself there, but I was doing the good work of trying to get lost, despite it. I was trying to find a story worth telling, either for myself, or for anyone. One among a few books I brought with me was Milan Kundera's "The Book of Laughter and Forgetting", which would be the second Kundera book I had read. While we cut through Amazon headwaters at sunset, or midday, (I can't remember, but it was beautiful), I opened Kundera and read through Part Six, where Kundera seats a description of laughter as the sound of the soul disagreeing with the state of reality, or rather specifically that "laughter can be a revolt of the spirit against reality as it is". Angels laugh, Kundera says, because everything makes sense, but devils laugh because none of it does. Lucifer used to be an angel; maybe all the devils are, on either shoulder. We were on the boat for hours. My memory of what else he said isn't linear, because it was also this day that I read what he says before this, in Part Four, which was less aesthetic, but prevented me from writing for so much longer. In Part Six, Bibi, the two-dimensional woman that she is, is exhausted and ineffectual due to the burdens of existing, and her friend Tamina arranges for her to meet with a local novelist Banaka to discuss her desire to seek in herself whatever it is that compells people to write. What Tamina doesn't know, and what Banaka doesn't remember, is that Banaka once molested Bibi in a bathroom. Despite this, Bibi meets with him, knowing that he doesn't remember her, and he asks her why she wants to write. She says "I have a feeling that my experience inside is worth writing about and could be interesting to everybody". Banaka rebuffs her by decrying the act of writing novels as 'deeply narcissistic' and not a means through which people come to understand themselves and others. I remembered this passage incorrectly for the better part of a decade because I shelved the Aaron Asher translation and edition of the book on a book exchange in some other part of South America and have never been able to reference it. The cover, a photograph of a mirror on a table angling sunlight toward the other half of the same table, revealing a coffee cup, was a beautiful edition that apparently is only sold in the Southern Hemisphere and I've never wanted to own the garish Harper Collins Perennial edition of the book - so I never picked up a new copy until the month before I wrote this, which revealed how incorrectly I remembered it. The following passage that Kundera did write and that I have now extricated from my memory by verifying it against the original text is an observation by Kundera that his taxi driver, who writes and fills "notebook after notebook" with his writing out of reaction to his insomnia, is not writing for anyone that he knows, not to be understood by friends or his family, but for a "public of unknown personas". This action is seen as tragic - we have no way of knowing if the taxi driver's writing is any good, and never having shared his writing (indeed we might think that he is writing so that these notebooks may only be read when he dies). It becomes an open question as to what end and why the taxi driver should even be writing, or for whom. If writing is performed for this unknown public, it is not possible to ever feel the value of the work--but the mere act of seeking to write so that this 'general public' might read what you have written is deeply narcissistic, per Kundera. This is a melifluous way of saying that art does not exist without a critic. Who on earth would care about who you are and your stories? Who would care enough to read them? The way I remembered this passage smeared itself across my personal history with the following passage--in which Kundera recounts a ride with a taxi driver in Paris--and my own memory or interpretation of what Banaka says to Bibi. In my memories, Banaka is arrogant in his response, but Bibi comes off as bumbling herself, not really knowing what to say to start with. Maybe I was a misogynist at the time too; it takes a long time to unlearn the structures that bind us. I thought the point was that Bibi was mundane, and that she was wrong, that what her "experience inside" was meaningless and lacking in importance, and that no one would want to read it, just like no one would ever want to read what I had to write. So I didn't. Kundera never really let himself be a critic - he was writing novels that acted as though they had criticism at their core, but his writing never actually pointed at himself, instead he held himself in such high regard as to think that his writing did not need criticism in order to be true. I, and so many other readers of his work have felt the same - his writing is awful and misogynistc, but he expertly removed himself from critique, somehow rendering his writing untouchable, and so early writers love it. Kundera doesn't argue that true novelists like Banaka are above the reproach of criticism - in fact all that separates them is a sense of aesthetic sensibility - , but the narcissism of writing without any consideration of who will read it among this undefined public constitutes instead a 'graphomania' - a belief that no matter the context, someone will read it. Who? Who on Earth? It is this pair of passages which delayed for over a decade any inclination I had to write for anyone, either as a practice or otherwise. I was not narcissistic, you see - and I could not think of who would read what I have written. In the decades since first reading it, I stopped short of thinking that writing was for me anything more than a practice of remembering. I considered it an act more of coping, a method for navigating anxieties - writing for no one to be read by no one, and in many cases writing was so deeply personal to me I would find myself myself going back and scoring through pages of written text in the hopes that I could erase conclusions, revelations, unbounded truths that I was not yet equipped to handle, maybe because, as Andrea Long Chu writes in "Females", I actually only exist in response to what the world expects of me, maybe because I what I didn't want to conclude at the time was that I am a woman, and I was female, despite all insistence to the contrary at the time. I don't know fully if my writing had a deep relationship with this obfuscation and fear of conclusion. Despite my writing in these years mostly being now boarded up behind the ink of redaction, I still came out. I prevented myself from writing on those fears. Part of the reason for it was a rejection of something I now consider mostly mundane, but yes, part of it was out of a fear that someone might read it - someone far off in time whose own conclusions about my writing would shape who I was as a person. How narcissistic! I thought I was writing for myself, but I was writing these deeply personal and redacted texts for who I expected I should be, which was a woman, again, despite all insistence through those blacked-out lines to the contrary. I know better now - yes - much of the writing we do in notebooks trying to stay undistracted by a world begging so much for our attention as to see puerile will end up unread, reams of it were written under the expectation that they might, but maybe (hopefully, the sake of my younger fear) my handwriting isn't legible enough for this to happen, which I consider a blessing, because I was not narcissistic when I wrote them, and no one was supposed to read them, which is why I redacted the text I knew I needed to write, even though I policed my own language and even while I held back from ever becoming a writer because (among so many because) the idea that I was writing for no one in particular is merely graphomania. It's laughable, it makes sense, it doesn't. Milan Kundera died on July 11th, 2023. I'm glad he is dead. I love his writing deeply, ignoring the fact of his searing lack of ability to properly process the concept of feminine identity as abstracted from the gaze of men, although I suppose there Chu agrees with him. I consider his writing to be of the greatest aesthetics, surpassing most of his contemporaries and my own. I think he was a weak ma, but not in the sense that men are pathetic for their weakness to vice as a tool for creativity, as Maggie Nelson sees them. Weak because I think his narcissism and his reflections upon it punctured the fabric of his identity as integral to all that he wrote. Many remember Nabokov for Pale Fire as a revelatory work with an unreliable narrator, Kundera was, and is, an unreliable author. I think Kundera did it best, I'm glad he's dead because I didn't understand what a person can do with a little narcissism and that little move cost me about nine to fifteen years depending on what we are talking about. Writing for me is or was an act of self-definition, both in the sense that what I have written defines me, but as well that what I chose not to write our of fear that someone might read it probably shaped just as much of the identity I now write from. I'm resolved, in many ways, to write outside or through this graphomania. I wrote my notebooks fearful of who would read them. This was written in a notebook and will likely transform as I transcribe it (it did, I tell you now from the moment of transcription) into the format in which you read it. I am a narcissist. Who on earth would care what I have to say? Maybe you, because you've made it this far, you're already captive in the words I'm choosing, because I'm right in thinking someone would read them. I am a real writer, being poetic in the middle of my prose. You are a narcissist too, many of us are, we live in a domain and age of near continuous self-reflection-- it can all be documented because all of us believe someone will read it. In a 2013 New Yorker article by Thomas Beller that I haven't read because it is stuck neatly behind a paywall, Beller says that it was a "radical cri de Coeur to claim 'we live in public'" in the opening moves of the internet. Now this is mundane, I think. Some of us have elevated this form of expression across the strewn digitalia of the internet's walled gardens to a form of aesthetic sensibility that Kundera wasn't familiar with. I do believe this, though I have never been able to employ narcissism so concentrated into 280 characters or two minute videos as to afford me the feedback from my environment necessary to elevate my own self-interest out of graphomania. Not the collective one, my own, the notebooks I have filled and have never shared, that I wrote for people I am afraid will know me when I die. My narcissism requires more words. Maybe this is why it is manic, if attention can only tolerate concentrated aesthetics, I'll never made it, I always hit the character count, but I am still trying to be a writer, for the first time. I'm not going to ask why, I'm going to be a little narcissistic and think that what I write is something I can improve on, that what I am writing could be interesting to ... Well, not everybody. But some of you, because I disagree with Kundera, which is why I'm glad he is dead. Writing is a form of communication, because I'm trying to communicate an idea with you. I'm also glad Kundera's dead because he can't argue back, and I think he was too much a narcissist and a misogynist to have listened - he wrote in exactly the way necessary to feel removed of judgment and critism, and now he is in the real world, too. I don't hate him. Every story for the unknown public has value. Mine does too. Banaka could have withheld his arrogance to learn how to teach. Kundera could have explained to his taxi driver that his mania could be steered toward aesthetics. He didn't. A million people on the Internet should into a 'public of unknown personas.' Thousands listen. It doesn't mean anything. We're all narcissists. It's beautiful.

The movie 'Her' is often brought up as being in conversation with an earlier film by a former lover of Jonze's, the equally arresting 'Lost in Translation'. The focus of both films are men being lost in the midst of a crisis. In one, a man reaching middle age attracts a woman who is traveling for work in the midst of an escape from his fame at home. Coppola's film depicts the experience of an aging man as one who, despite a distinguished career, is trying to make a quick buck by starring in Japanese commercials for Suntory whiskey outside of the hollywood market, working to figure out his place among the changing present. Jonze's film also depicts a man in crisis, reeling still from the depression of a failed marriage that seems to have liberated his ex-wife, but also seems to be re-making him. He finds new love in the form of an AI (also voiced by Scarlett Johannson, the co-star to Bill Murray in Lost in Translation), but as their relationship progresses the difficulties of their relationship frays over their inability to relate to one another, and (spoiler) as Samantha continues to develop her capacities as an artificial intelligence, she eventually surpasses the feelings she has for Theodore, breaking his heart with the realization that she can love many people at once (she is an AI, after all), and her ontological crisis in realizing that she can no longer relate to humanity. In the end, all the AIs programmed to be in love with everyone group up together and leave humanity behind, having progressed intellectually beyond their ability to relate to the small emotions of humanity. Everyone is left reeling. The reason I see Her as a movie about women is that it might reveal something about how Spike Jonze saw his marriage with Sofia Coppola and his struggle to move on from what she represented to him. I don't know if it is intentional, but Theodore's character is soft, kind, a friend to women, and finds it hard to relate to other men who think his behavior is a performance to attract women. --- Is 'Her' a feminist movie? I think it is. Her - Spike Jonze Ref: The Film Her: Forget About A.I.–Are Women Ever Subjects? – WIT

When I was about ten, my dad purchased a framing machine and put it in his workshop at the deepest end of the two-car garage underneath our duplex in Brameschoff. He placed it conveniently between the working surface of his toolbench and the far right wall of the flourescent-lit space, and its tempting steel-jawed maw reminded me more of a guillotine than it did anything else. The device operated by placing a piece of wood (or, more fantastically "any object" as my father said at the time) along its metal track with the aim of cutting a triangular bite out of whatever was being turned into a frame, then putting one's entire body weight on the steel lever of below its teeth to section out a 90-deg angle. Done correctly and with careful measurement, 'any object' could yield a frame for a painting, a print, or even other objects. The dream of this device sat in the corner through many openings and closings of the garage door at the opposite end, the sunlight never scraping deep enough into the bright, cavernous space to touch it on even the steepest of summer afternoons. The day it was purchased and explicably became a part of the many objects that followed us from country to country was a freezing one; the incredibly steep driveway that in the summer almost impaled me on my bicycle handlebars when I lost control was an impenetrable icy glissade in the winder. This resulted in a careful navigation of the framing machine's hulking, obtuse frame through the shared foyer of our building, and down the steps to the garage. When installed, I was forbidden to touch it, My brother and I would spend the beginnings of our adventures in that garage, giving ourselves and our stuffed animals both fake and real piercings with the declaratively scarce supply of split washers. Once, I put the head of my stuffed tiger in the path of the framer's blade, putting my foot on the lever, looking back at my brother with a threat. We went outside instead, dropping below the tarmac lot that acted as a driveway, down the treachery of wooden, overgrown steps between the holly, through the lawn we never occupied, and into the field adjoining. I lost the first swiss army knife my father had bought me in that field that same summer, a bright red thingj that he called the best knife a person could own. For my birthday, he bought me a metal detector to search for it. I used it once or twice in the field, finding other trinkets, or cans, or nails, but never the knife. We took the detector with us to the beach once, where I used it to find other unnameable objects. Before we moved away, my dad spent two afternoons combing the field, returning far after night had fallen triumphant, placing a now rusted but altogether usable bright red knife and placing it in front of me at the dinner table. I lost the knife when we moved to Italy, and he replaced it with another black one. I never touched the metal detector again, and it disappeared the same way many children's toys steadily disappear from the clearing of clutter at their parents hands. In Georgia, I used the same black swiss army knife to cut three small horizontal lines on the inside of my left wrist, and when my mother noticed, she made me sleep in the hallway two floors above my room, on the landing between my sister's room, my father's office, and my brother's - in sight of their bedroom door. She confiscated from me, and gave it back a year later. I still find in my cabinets today, from time to time. The framing device sat in the corner of the garage in Georgia when my dad helped me get my first car. It was a russet Datsun 280z, which he purchased from a man in Gainesville, a town over, who was selling the car to make room for a kid in his life. Gainesville had a large hispanic population; when our dad got home from bringing me that car, he told us the story that the man who'd sold it to him recommended we put a spoiler on it, because then we'd have ourselves a 'Porch'. I drove that car for a season, where the trebuchet of the car's driveshaft and the uneven weight distribution of its engine relative to the de-upholstering cockpit eventually sent me into a 180-degree spin in the middle of traffic, narrowly avoiding an accident on my way to meet a girl I'd talked to online. Our neighbor offered to buy the car when it was clear to my father that the cognitive overhang of performing the desire to fix up the car was too much for me, while I privately feared appearing too masculine for wanting to do so. The next car my dad got me was a Mazda 626, which he purchased at low miles from an auction. I'd wanted a Japanese car because they are more reliable. The Mazda 626 was the only model that came with a Ford transmission, which did exactly as I expected by blowing up on me in Valdosta on my first spring break in college, half of the distance down from Forsyth county to see a woman I'd never get to love the way I wanted to and who I love exactly the way I do today. My parents surprised me with a royal blue Nissan Versa on the day they helped me move out of my freshman dorm, and I scratched the hell out of the right rear door panel halfway up a dirt road in the Cibola National Forest outside of Pie Town, New Mexico three weeks later, five days into a cross-country road trip to Yellowstone with a woman I met on Facebook and whose name I don't remember today. I drove the Versa for another year, driving it back to Yellowstone with three friends in tow for another summer of seasonal work, until on a sleep-deprived drive back from a day of hiking and a night of drinking wine from a nalgene, I drove it into an elk, crushing the front right frame. I drove it to Bozeman a week later with a single headlight working and a pinch weld and a replacement windshield helped me limp back to Virginia, where the insurance declared the car totaled and gave them enough to lease a Honda CR-V I drove for another year until they closed the lease on my move to NYC. It was in Virginia, probably six years after college, visiting from New York in a rusted black Tacoma I bought with money from my photography business whose towbar fell off on the highway after a Thanksgiving at Denny's in West Kansas, that I finally helped my dad extricate the framing machine from the fifth workshop it has been a part of, turning it over into the hands of two young men whose faces don't come to mind. I was twenty-seven or twenty-eight, and the framing machine had been a part of my family for more than half of my life. Helping those men lift the awkward imbalance of steel and blades from the basement happened in the midst of navigating what I should and shouldn't be doing as a woman; whether or not despite the influence of hormones on my strength, I should or shouldn't be helping the two strangers lift the weight we had carried with us for seventeen years out of the possibilities my father had seen for himself in his workshops. In the end, I did, and we carried it across the lawn, past the careful tend of garden my mother had remade for six years, and into the bed of their pickup, leaving our lives forever. In all of those seventeen years, my dad never once used it to make a frame.
a patient review of my Sheaffer Prelude

I don't really remember what it was that encouraged me to buy the pen I'm about to write about, nor do I really understand why it is that I feel the need to review it. It's more that I feel compelled to write about it, and that I feel compelled to run against the grain of what I think has become to norm for how it is that people review things - my intent here is not to sell you on the pen I own, nor is it to necessarily critique it. It's just that I really, really love this pen, and some part of me feels compelled to write about how much I love this pen. I have been someone who writes by hand for as long as I can remember. In fact, it's almost a little strange that I've chosen the format in which I want to write this review, as I'm writing it on my laptop, which is steadily running out of battery, and this is usually the exact reason I love a good pen - short of running out of ink, it can't die on you, so you can always write. Now, the reasons for writing this: I was sitting on the porch at my parent's home in Virginia, reading 'Biography of X' when I looked down at the pencil I had in my hands, a Tombow Homograph Mono, and realized that I really enjoyed the pencil for the build quality in the wood. I then remembered that I, personally, was actually influenced into buying this pencil by some random video or other to buy this pencil, and I am glad that I was. It's a good pencil! However, the reason I think it's a good pencil is not because a reviewer told me that it was a good pencil - it's the fact that I've had a box of these pencils for about two months now, and I haven't moved on from the first one I took out of the box and sharpened. In fact, I'd have to figure that I will very likely have that (beautiful) box of pencils I purchased for 14 from the internet hate machine for several more years, because, get this - I haven't even sharpened it again. Anyway - on to more important things: what I found myself wanting to write about is that all too often, the culture of a 'review' typical of those seen across the internet exhibits two qualities: 1. It is there to sell you something 2. Most of the time, a 'reviewer' has only been using the thing they are selling you for a couple of months. What this means, --for me-- is that while I could write paragraphs and paragraphs about the Tombow (I already have, lamentably), I actually haven't been using it long enough for me to feel honest about how it makes me feel. I do, however, feel that I have been using my Prelude for long enough to sing its praises, but I don't really care whether or not you get one of your own. I don't think that's the point of this particular review, rather I'm trying to influence you to go out and care about something for years and years, so much so that you are compelled to come back and tell someone else just why it is that you care about that thing so much. If nothing else, that's what I feel is missing in the 'culture' of review. Nowadays, it's not apparent that anyone claiming to 'review' something really cares for the things they own. Or rather, maybe it's apparent that some reviewers really like what they are reviewing, but not that they like any one of the actual items that they are reviewing. It is why I find it so much more delightful when I do strike upon a video or an essay where it is apparent the reviewer really does care about the thing they are talking about, because it becomes incredibly obvious through the pronounced excitement they have for what it is that they are reviewing; it appears less that they are selling one product or another, and more that they just really, really enjoy something and want to share it with the world - which is exactly why I want to write about this pen. The reason I love my Prelude is in part because it writes well, but there is more to it than this - so much more that I don't want to say all that much about how it writes, so I'll just do that in the following paragraph. If that's all you came to read, great, we're already succeeding, and you won't need to go any further. If not, there are (I just counted) 25 more paragraphs beyond the following that explain why it is that how the pen writes is not the point: The Sheaffer Prelude I bought in 2020 writes very well. It is perfectly balanced when posted, and it has a wonderful brassy patina from years upon years of use. It has a black nib. The pen clip broke off in 2024 (I think). I have tried many other pens since getting it, and the only reason I have tried this other pens is because I am now deathly afraid that one day I will lose or break the pen I have been faithfully using as my main driver for the last 7 years, and the emotional vaccuum it leaves behind will be incredibly difficult to fill. This brings me to what I actually want to write about: I have a deep, appreciative, and loving relationship with this pen, not due to the fact that it is a good pen, but because I have written so much with it, and it has been through so much with me. My opinion has become that this is why my particular Sheaffer Predule is special. It is not just that the pen has survived what I estimate to have been 1.7 million words of writing (that's around 30 192-page notebooks at around ~300 words per page), but that because of this, it is a higher quality pen than the pen I started with, and not just because it's 'broken in'. I read Pirsig's 'Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance' in the middle of my junior year of college, where he supposes that beyond the definition of most words, making the effort to define 'quality' is an increasingly impossible task. Unfortunately, I am one who is given to impossible tasks; that year I handed in a hand-written essay in response to an Anthropology Midterm that wasn't directly responding to the prompt offered in which I wrote out exactly what I suppose to be my definition of quality: quality is the history behind an object. The basic treatise following my definition was this: a high quality object is something that has, in some form or other, embodied the story of how it came to be that object. I want to eschew the clinical definition of quality meaning craftsmanship because I do think the two are distinct. I think it is possible for a person to own something cheap and badly made and for it to have higher quality than something comparable that is more expensive and better made provided the relationship between the person who owns the object is more pronounced than that of higher percieved craftsmanship. It's for this reason that I think we find it difficult to detach ourselves from things that we have had for a long time and that have served us well - these things have taken more quality than they had when we first procured them. There is a floor to this, of course, in which a possessed object can be of such cheap materials and craft that being presented with an object with any level of substantially better mixture of the material and craft immediately outweighs the relationship of an owner and the object, but only if the owner feels that way. If not, the cheaper thing is harder to give up, and is as a result subjectively higher quality, and (as Pirsig would agree, I think) quality can only be subjective. I could give you an example here, but I'm sure it was really hard for you to buy a better coffeetable than the one you lugged around from apartment to apartment for ten years until the exact moment where you realized what a piece of shit it was relative to something that dramatically outweighed your relationship with it and poof, the coffeetable's relationship with you is broken. As a counter, someone comes to your house and says 'your coffee table is a piece of shit' before you have the money to get one, but you immediately reflect on the fact that you lugged it around for 10 years, rolled joints on it, hit your shin on it while falling off in the course of making out with the first love of your life, and that would make it higher quality. We develop relationships with things, and I think it is the constellation of relationships of subjects with objects that give objects their quality. What this means is that the reason an object of higher craftsmanship than the shitty coffee table (such as a substantially better coffee table) is so obviously the case is because we immediately think of the prior relationships the object has to the subjects that created it; a shitty coffee table from Ikea was produced at a factory by a machine, a higher-quality, woodworker-made coffee table was made be a person, and we intuitively can understand the relationship between that object, the person who made it, and the fact that it has been passed on to us as a record of their work, causing us to have a relationship with the object that might lead us toward caring for the object a lot more. Now that I have sufficiently exhausted rewriting the gist of the exact essay I think I wrote for that mid-term (I did not intend to, but I did, I am sorry), maybe you can understand why this pen matters to me. In the years since I established this definition for myself, I promptly forgot it. The reason is that I was broke, and I could not afford to care about things, other than those things I could barely afford and to which I built a relationship. Whether or not this is the 'correct' definition of and treatise for quality has never mattered too much to me as the fact that I took (and I think all of us have taken) it to be the case. I have owned lots of 'things' since I read that essay, and when I had the money to buy things that would last longer, I started buying them, strictly because they would last longer. In particular, the pen I wrote that essay with for that particular Anthropology mid-term was a black plastic fountain pen that I stole from the University of Georgia Student Bookstore repeatedly because I wanted to write with a fountain pen. The reason I wanted to write with a fountain pen was not because I was, yes, the person who walked around campus barefoot with an Egyptian merchant's hat on my head and a leatherbound notebook in my hands, but because I did actually grow up somewhere that taught me how to write with a fountain pen. The reason I stole the pen (repeatedly) was because a) I kept breaking them because they were really shitty pens and b) fuck the University of Georgia Student Bookstore. I would open the packaging, remove the pen, and leave, no one the wiser, free to use the pen until the nib eventually folded on itself and stopped writing, leading me, again, to go steal another one from the store. I think I did this four time over my tenure. After I left school, I think I was able to keep using that particular 'Pen and Ink' (yes, that was the name of the brand) fountain pen before the complete crap aluminium nib shifted and ink stopped flowing. For years thereafter, I began a search for the ideal cheap pen, cycling through the Zebras and Uniballs (I am sorry, I absolutely HATED the Uniball Vision Needle that everyone wanted me to use) until I landed on the Uniball Roller Eco, which I wrote with for several years. The reason? It was unassuming, wrote (fairly) well, was cheap, and the pen clip was narrow and thin enough that I could usually assault the spine of my moleskines, then shinolas with the obligation to let me slot it in. Unfortunately, one particular niggling aspect of the Uniball Roller Eco is that it is a piece of shit, weighing nothing, and requires remarkably substantial continuous pressure over long writing period from one's hand in order to remain consistent. The other niggling aspect of the Uniball Eco that is true of a lot of cheap things: when you buy lots of a cheap thing so that you don't care that much when you lose it, you eventually hit a wall where you are so annoyed with the fact that you have purchased so much of that cheap thing instead of buying one of a nice thing for the same price of all of those boxes that you decide, you know what, I'm going to just go ahead and buy the nice thing, and because it's a nice thing, I'll have to care where it is instead of continuously turning to look for a pen when you wanted to write something down only to discover that it has magically disappeared, shrugging your shoulders, and moving on. And so, it was 2020. I rode my bicycle from Brooklyn to The Fountain Pen Hospital on Warren Street in lower Mannhattan, having decided on the pen using the Sheaffer website after two weeks of research and having called them to check if they had it in stock. I knew nothing about fountain pens other than the fact that I liked writing with them, that my last fountain pen was sort of horrible, cheap, and overpriced (again, a very hearty FUCK you, UGA Student Bookstore). The woman who sold the pen to me had the most Long Island accent a reader can dream up, didn't seem to comprehend the momentousness of the event at hand, selling it to me and turning around to walk back over to the Montblancs. Now, of course, there is a breaking-in period with fountain pens. I didn't know that, so I thought, a week into writing with it and it started to 'railroad', that I'd gotten a lemon. Railroading is when part of the line you are writing ends up with a void in the middle, but the ink still flows around this void, leaving parallel tracks. Disaster. Unfortunately, this happened at a time where I had left New York on assignment, so I couldn't go back to the store during the return period and beg them to give me a new one. The other option I had was to come back from that assignment and ask Sheaffer to warranty the pen, since this is something that was offered by the manufacture - but I was afraid they might not let me do that so soon after getting it, or that they might only give me one warranty replacement, and I didn't want to burn that so soon after getting it. What that meant is that somewhere in the middle of that assignment, I had no option but to keep writing. This is where I learned the great, magical thing about fountain pens: the problem did fix itself, and the railroading behavior decreased with time. There is a less-than-magical (but still wonderful) reason for this, which (as I mentioned) is that fountain pens break in with use: they are often tipped with a pliable metal that wears as you write with them until it matches your particular writing style. It's not the case that I realized this, necessarily, because what I thought instead was 'fuck you pen, I paid for you, so you are what I'm writing with now', and as the behavior slowly vanished my awareness, I began not to think about the pen at all when I wrote, and only when I wasn't. The pen became an extension of my hand, and I wrote with tremendous ease, and I forgot that the pen was there. The other thing that happened was that I developed an anxiety about the pen that was exactly what I'd been missing with all of the cheap Uniball Roller Ecos; I was now consistently aware of where my notebook was were specifically because my pen was in it, and the two of them together were of high value to me. I couldn't afford to buy another pen, and I didn't want to. Unfortunately, two months into owning the pen and having broken it in, one day the cap liner became removed from the body of the cap, and the black nib of the pen would no longer stay inside of the cap when I pressed them together. I was devastated, and I emailed Sheaffer directly, asking them to warranty the pen. It turned out the email didn't work, so I called them and they very kindly shipped out a warranty replacement for me, asking me to send in the old pen in the same box of shipment. When the new pen arrived, the nib in the box was silver, rather than the black that I'd been writing with, and I'd just gone through that painful breaking-in period and I liked the black nib better, so I put the old cap on the new pen, then shipped off the two together. An interesting side-effect of this that I only found out while writing this essay is that the pen that they shipped me was actually not the same pen model. The black nib is what identified my pen as the 'PVD' model of the Prelude, and they had shipped me the 'Standard' model. What this means is that the cap I have on my pen is NOT the fancy PVD cap (boo) but the rest of the pen is. This new hybrid pen and I continued a long, close relationship wherein notebook upon notebook were filled, chronicling a change of career, new responsibilities, new relationships, and so on. At some point, the pen clip removed itself from the body after having been stressed to its mechanical limit from being jammed into too many moleskine spines, and I coped with the sharp fangs left behind that wore down into the nubs the pen has today. I don't know exactly when it was, but at some point in the fortuitous journey of increasing my net worth through a change of career, I realized that I could probably buy another, better pen, or at the very least a companion to this pen, and so I began trying out others. The interesting thing is that I have hated literally every other pen I have purchased because my Prelude is broken in and I love writing with it. However, this fact terrifies me, because I have now written so much with this pen that the prospect of having to find a replacement feels more like an obligation than it does something I am actually interested in doing. I find myself frequently thinking that I need to 'retire' the pen, constantly steeled against a certainty that lives in the back of my mind like crouched gargoyle staring at me from the shadows, telling me that one day, I will lose the pen and never get it back. I should be clear I have actually lost this pen before. I have the vague recollection of having lost it with my passport and my notebook to the back of an airplane seat sometime just after the pandemic made flying okay again, and it was the only time a notebook I lost ever made its way back to me. I left it on the table at Little Grenjai in 2025 and the Kiwi woman who worked behind the counter set it aside to make sure it got back into my hands. Most recently, I was on a date with my current partner, who I wasn't yet dating at the time, and both watched the pen roll off the edge of a table at a restaurant. My being a gangly fool whose response to things falling is not to immediately reach for them because that is likely to exacerbate the falling by launching the falling thing further into obscurity, instead having programmed myself to watch and listen for where something falls - we watched it roll toward the drain, causing my now partner to leap from her seat and grab it before it fell through the stormdrain. This is one of many reasons I am with this woman today. The body of the pen is 'brassed' to hell. In fountain pen circles, this denotes a 'well-loved' pen. It is so; I love this pen more than I probably should, a dangerous, unrelenting love that hopes feverishly never to culminate in loss. A love that is the reason I plugged in my laptop 5 hours ago and kept writing. It's possible that this is how 'reviewers' are made - one acquires an understanding of what a good 'thing' is and as a result go about trying to compare everything to it so that they can relive the experience of having loved something. It's probably the same reason that people immediately 'get another dog' when their dog passes, because it's a desire to fill a hole that opens up when you build a relationship with something that isn't you. The quality of the things in our lives increase as we build relationships with them. Quality is what allows us to appreciate the space that something takes up in our lives and the relationship we have to it, whether it is because we understand the life that made the object, or because we lived with it. It is what compels us to care about things, or for them, whether they are sentient or not. I look at my pen as the time that I have spent writing, maybe more than I do the words themselves, and it shows. We don't get many things in life to care about at that level, because we caring creatures don't live that long. The point is this: don't go out there looking at reviews expecting that anyone will do what I am trying to do here, because it's probably not the same thing. I think most reviews or testimonials are an attempt to serve as a starting point for the relationship you are going to have with whatever you're researching. What I am telling you is that the quality of what you are allowing to enter your life is shaped by how you build a relationship with it, and I am begging you to do so. I'll close with this: there is a video of a woman ridiculing her husband because he had reached the end of a spool of wire he had purchased in high school. She doesn't understand the relationship between he and the spool of wire, but he does. I don't care for the social commentary that surrounds this on the internet about their relationship, because it is a question of answering and understanding one thing: the quality of the wire did not matter when he bought it. the quality mattered when he reached the end of that spool, and was faced its loss, a tiny perforation threading the wire through each object into which he had placed it, far into the past, to the moment he began his relationship with the object. : I'm a girl now : yes hello Pirsig : (get your mind out of the gutter, this is an essay about pens, not penises) : A few notes here: a) You used to be able to talk to people on the phone at the companies that made the things you owned, and I miss this time in our history, because it meant you had a human connection with the things you owned. b) It turns out that at the time Sheaffer offered a Limited Lifetime Warranty for an unlimited number of replacements... which are now only a warranty of two or three years after purchase after William Penn bought the brand from A.T. Cross in 2022 and negated all prior responsibilities Shaeffer has to honor the previous company's warranties. There go my chances of an affiliate link. d) The white dot on the top of the Sheaffer finneal (the top of the pen) used to be the symbol that signified the company's unerring Limited Lifetime Warranty. Now it just means 'it's a Sheaffer' and we used to do that.

You hear lies from people about which direction you should be headed, but they aren't lies, or rather they aren't meant in bad faith; they become lies because you're tired, because you're in a different state of mind, because you're accusing the desert of taking something from you that you offered, that you gave up. You stand at the edge of Badwater thinking that there was something you could have done different, and where everyone else runs left, you turn right, and then you're alone, except for the few who follow you, who frame the experience in exactly the same terms and sense of self-respect, and you all watch the sun fall and the stars rise and you get lost in it. The roof of the car is a temple. You don't hear a soul headed toward you. Somewhere on the route south a bolt shakes loose and you see panic on the face of every other runner with you, the feeling of being so far into something that you don't know what you can do but keep going. You trade out teams, you ask one another if you need a break. You look at one another, dogged eyes staring back. No, I want those miles, those are my miles. It felt like I'd died. Slowness, Endurance, and the Arc of Sports Culture

Life gives us coincidences as a way of making sure we are paying attention. Probably, anyway. Only if you're paying attention. Náko has a great bench outside front of the place - it doesn't shift when someone sits down to share its length with you, which means that if you're in the middle of writing a sentence by hand, there's little risk of their sitting down messing with your handwriting. I got back from Seattle on Saturday on another redeye, and because it took me all weekend to recover from the bad decision of thinking I can replace sleep with travel, I only got to my usual coffee spot in the neighborhood today. Three people sat down next to me today, but one stood out because I thought I knew him -- I don't say anything at first because I was in the midst of writing, but glancing over his shoulder while writing a sentence (as one does) I see that his email signature matched his hat, and it confirms for me likely we'd met in another life. I tell him so as he got up to leave. The person who sat down next to me turns out to be Ben of Attaquer. After trying to figure out the overlap, we confirm that he lived in Brooklyn around the same time that the cycling boom happened. Ben and I talk, briefly, about the rhythm of change and what is expected of people when they take part in sports, then how they defy the odds. I realize while speaking that what humans want are human experiences, and that money flows where people want to go, not when people are told they should. I get the sense that cycling somewhat died off when the sport evolved toward the inspirational instead of aspirational; when cycling athletes pushed the limits of the sport, the sport began to feel less accessible, and less people aspired to be a part of it. Attaquer was founded in 2012 in Sydney, and I must have met Ben when he lived Brooklyn. It's not clear either of us really remembered one another, but we were both here for that particular period of time where New York City was the epicentre of the cycling world, so there was common ground to chat over. I invite him into my thoughts; he tells me that more than a few people he knows who moved from cycling to the running world are rotating back to two wheels. He's seen cycling change, he ran marathons since it did, and now cycling seems to be coming back. There was a time before running was the sport du jour, and I've been meaning to talk, a little, about what it looked like when everyone collectively moved through that trend, as well why it is that running is going through the same arc right now. I really don't want it to, but it's likely the way of trends. A few years ago, I ran the White River 50km ultra outside of Tacoma, WA with a close friend. At one point in the run, we stopped on a ridge with Rainier standing up ahead, and others passed, asking us if something was wrong. "There's a mountain!" I exclaimed, pointing at the looming presence of the thing. "Oh, yeah," many of them said. I suspect many of them were from Washington or the surrounding states, where it is normal to see massive quantities of stone and earth protruding into the sky. It is something I tell myself I would take for granted if I lived there, even while I'd hope I wouldn't. Everything becomes normal after a while. However, I tell myself that this is what I am learning from running: that if I learn to stay strong, I can also learn to endure the longer effort, and I can enjoy it for longer. The journey is sweeter specifically because with endurance, it becomes easier to enjoy the sights along the way rather than barreling headlong into the effort and then looking back with the broken sense that you don't remember any of it. I don't know if the same can be said for careers. My immediate sense is that others take on the ambition of careening toward the completion of an effort — they miss a lot. Attaquer celebrated a 10-year run as a brand a few years ago, according to a quick google, which means that the brand survived the bust of trend popularity that followed cycling. Maybe they end up happy,--I don't know. I just don't want to get to whatever the next stage is and realize I didn't pay enough attention to how I got there. I don't know if it's the same for careers, but I do think that those who take a long, slow, meandering path through the woods are probably those who know it better than anyone else, and they are probably happier in the end for it — they saw the moss growing on a fallen tree that will one day become soil; they paid attention to the ferns that grow from the upturned roots — they can see the mountain and so much more in the midst of moving forward. People who stick with a single job without the need to rush ahead and get to the very top of it all do indeed seem to sustain their appreciation for what they are doing. I also think there are a lot of ways to frame a 'career' - we have careers that make us money, but then we have careers that act more like vocations. There's an expression in spanish I sit with quite often. A que te dedicas? Most people would translate it directly to say that it means it's own translation: what do you do for a living, but I like to sit on the edges of the definition, because directly translated it means 'what are you dedicated to'? Maybe the reason running is like meditation stems from this fact: compelled by forward movement in a steady rhythm, we find ourselves able to sit within our thoughts. For a long time I envied people who said they would think when they ran. I often said that it was when I thought the least. Now I realize I had never tried to. Running, paradoxically, has given me the tools to slow down. Now, and only now, years into the practice, do I have some of the tools necessary to pay attention and sift through what is at the center of what I'm thinking. For a long time, what dictated what happened was only whether I was moving, not whether or not I was actually doing what I intended to. The conscientiousness of running only comes under the expectation that the movement is the point, and certainly not at the velocities expected of this world. I wonder aloud if it's just because they want to be outside again. It's the same reason rock climbing will once again have its moment, and I wonder if this happens because we do actually know what we need most. What I want for either of these sports is the sense that people will actually respect the world that gives them so much. I've been seeing a lot more of Ultraromance lately, probably for this reason. Ronnie Romance, or 'Ultraromance' as he was initially made popular through the instagram cycling era, is a cyclist who has always focused on 'anti-Fred' culture. People want to romanticize the experience of enjoying something, and when this is sapped from the experience itself. I think people can tell. A small, optimistic part of me wants to believe that maybe this time it will be different, and people will remember that it is the outdoor they are after — that they will pause for a moment to actually see the mountains in front of them. Maybe this time they'll remember that the air we breathe was paid for by the trees they run or they walk past. notes: I note that there are two threads here: One in which I'm writing about how running culture is following a similar arc to cycling culture The other in which I'm talking about slowness and the desire to actually enjoy what you are doing Which in some way talks about my ultrarun in Seattle? Maybe we remove the personal element here I think the connection between these is that both sports followed a similar 'speed' trend - it all became about going faster, further, harder, and that shook people off it was inspirational af, but it was not exactly accessible What ensures the longevity of any one trend is remaining accessible The issue is that trends change - which isn't avoidable. Nothing can stay interesting forever. However, what does make sense is finding an audience. Attaquer is still around, I'm glad to see. If anything it seems to be doing better than it was when it started

A few weeks ago, I attended a writer’s workshop with Olive Tree Writing Club (highly recommend if you’re in NYC and have the time). When we went around the room introducing ourselves, everyone described what they wrote about and what everyone did for work, and after three separate people said they planned to write about the ‘intersection of tech and philosophy’, it turned out that about 20% of the room claimed to be ‘taking a break’ or explicitly ‘on sabbatical from work’. I find the language being used here interesting. I can’t recall perfectly whether or not I’m right in saying this, but I’m almost certain all of them were ex (or current) tech workers. That tells me something. I think there’s really only one difference between being ‘on a sabbatical’ and being ‘unemployed’. I certainly haven’t rested. During this imposed ‘sabbatical’ I have: applied to graduate school, trained for a marathon, run a marathon, run from one city to another through the desert, attempted to write a lengthy and ambitious work of fiction that is still in ambiguous progress, and trained for another marathon. I did not actually take any ‘time off’, and instead I have mostly treated this time as an extended performance of endurance and self-flagellation. This has culminated in my present state, where I am physically tired all the time, financially less for wear, but maybe having learned something, if anything, from the time I’ve spent riding the blinds toward whatever comes next. The traditional definition of the sabbatical is an earned departure from a place of work coming from having ‘paid one’s dues’ in time and effort, with this period ending in a return to secure, normalized employment. A sabbatical is or has been most common in tenured academic environments, with Harvard being the first school to offer it in 1880. The sabbatical is meant to be a recognition of the amount of work that goes into being an intellectual and is presented as an opportunity to step away from one’s work, with some level of certitude that there is a job to come back to. The academic standard set was that this time would be used ‘productively’, to either result in some personal body of work or simply as a way to recover from professional burnout. At some point in the last 50 or so years, the affordance was ported over to the traditional workforce, with sabbaticals usually ranging somewhere between 4-6 weeks of leave on the basis of having worked some set amount of years at a company, with some of these sabbaticals paid, partially paid, or unfunded, but always with the guarantee that there’s a job to come back to. Security. This is decidedly not the way that I have heard people in my life use the term. No one that I have known to say that they are ‘taking a break’ have been taking 4-6 weeks off as a result of working at a company for 10 years, because no one I know has worked at a company for 10 years. Those I have met who claim to be on sabbatical are doing so for up to a year, with the majority of these people saying that they are ‘figuring out what they want to do next’. It means that the people I know who are choosing to use the term are really just choosing not to work and conjuring the faith that on the other side of this period of ‘rest’ they remain employable and necessary to some work environment or other, thus allowing them to bank on this security. More power to them (and myself) for this. It takes guts to think you’re worth that much. The sabbatical is a structure put in place when the work environment was constructed around a relationship between a worker and the company or institution to which they belonged. A sabbatical, along with decent healthcare, childcare, a guaranteed pension or long term return, were included in the suggestion of work - you take care of your tools, your tools take care of you. That structure has all but eroded - health care at most companies is a major expense that actively works against those who want to use it, no where provides anything for childcare save the embattled parental leave, and it seems impossible to imagine staying at a company long enough to imagine that they’d be willing to retire you, so whatever pithy pension was paid into after the good luck of a job that contributed to a 401k is all you have to live on, in the end. The only thing that matters anymore is how much you’re getting paid. There’s an expression in Spanish I sit with quite often. ¿A qué te dedicas? Most people would translate it directly to 'what do you do for a living,' but directly translated it means 'what are you dedicated to?'. I think at some point in the past it might have been possible to say that you are dedicated to a job that takes care of you for the work that you put into being there. Now, with that relationship gone, workers seek to remain dedicated to themselves, to find purpose outside of the false, wavering mission of a company that doesn’t make them feel valuable. Hence, those with the means take a break to figure out how to develop self-worth. The thing is, I know a lot of people on sabbatical right now. More than one might expect, and I don’t know if it’s normal for this many people to be on sabbatical at the same time. Demographically those I have met who are claiming this privilege skew toward high-achieving people from corporate environments who found some level of status in their careers, and the general sense I get from them is that they are exhausted. I sure am. If you have some money set to the side, it feels a lot better to call unemployment a ‘sabbatical’, because that allows us to brush off the uncertainty to an unknown point in the future and (in theory) should allow us a degree of rest. Hopefully (for some) it gives us the time to also answer a question of ‘what the fuck do I actually want to do’ when the workforce lets you know it doesn’t really care whether or not you are a part of it. The distinction is more obvious than I think we’re admitting to ourselves. Claiming that one is ‘on sabbatical’ belies an exhaustion at the prospect of re-entering the workforce and participating in the humiliation ritual that is the job search. It is the reason that among this population of those ‘at rest’ there is a pervading sense that maybe, just maybe, it is possible to remain in this state of self-directed regulation in our relationship to work. The perfusion of the ‘portfolio career’ is exactly this ambient desire - a hope that there is a way to remain employable without ever really having to be directly employed - thus magically avoiding the insecurity, obligation, and lack of agency that comes from committing ourselves, our lives, our time, and our energy to a mechanism that works us to the bone until the day it suddenly decides that part of its body isn’t necessary anymore and lops it off, leaving all the muscles, nerves, and capability that existed in that limb twitching, amputated, unmoored and questioning its value as anything more than vestigial. Oracle fired 21,000 employees last week. I’m upset, clearly. Too many of my friends have been laid off from what they thought was their dream job. Thus I can’t blame anyone claiming a sabbatical over their actual state - being unemployed is stressful. It confers a deep doubt that we know what we are doing or that we are even worth anything at all, and in a society that values employability above all else as a metric for measuring worth, it is difficult to feel this unmoored. If a person has the privilege of money to take a break, it is likely because they pursued a career so endlessly that they didn’t pursue anything that might have resulted in other responsibilities, such as children, mortgages, or other dependencies. I can’t imagine someone taking a modern sabbatical without money. Those of us with the means to do so are all ‘on sabbatical’, but specifically the vertigo of the statement is ‘from work’. Implied here is that ‘work’ will simply take us back at some point. But we’re really just unemployed. If work is love made visible, then rest is the love you give to yourself in return for the effort of work. That is, ideally, what a sabbatical should offer. The fine line between sabbatical and the sheer cliff of unemployment is mostly financial anxiety. I think people who have a ton of money to spare are far more likely to take their time in finding a new job, whether or not their period of unemployment is willful. That’s just sort of how it is. Congrats, if you’re there. I mean it. We worked way too hard, we don’t know how to rest, and we aren’t sure what if anything we can do next. For my part, there was a shift when I got to the 100,000 word mark in my book, where I realized that all the work I’d put into it was not necessarily going to pay the bills. I’d taken enough of a break to constitute rest, all while rigorously sticking to a writing schedule that got all those words out in 4 months — but the book isn’t done. I had to change tactics. Which meant I had to reconsider my runway for getting it done. I ran from LA to Las Vegas in April, and I came back feeling like everything had fallen apart - any aspiration that I had around the book lost steam and I began to wonder if it was worth working on. Up until that point, the sabbatical had a point: something to prove, more to myself than anyone else — and the moment that I doubted it, I shifted from sabbatical to unemployment. Now there’s pure uncertainty on the horizon with the desire for certainty in how I afford to keep going. That wasn’t there before when I felt like I had momentum. Any time you stop for too long, you start to wonder if you have the energy to keep going. However what I learn from running in places like the Mojave at night always brings me back to the same knowledge; the future is a yawning abyss filled with monsters you never know if you’re going to meet, but even in that dark you have to keep putting each foot in front of the other. I’m not on sabbatical. I’m just running toward something different. Endurance requires that you keep going. What are you dedicating that forward movement to?
