She piped up from the back of the room, standing up. "Well - professor, if you'll let me say it - I think all of us agree that none of us knew we'd end up here. I don't think it's fair for us to talk about our current conditions as though there was something we could have done to prevent it. None of us knew that what we were doing would have these results." I cocked a slight smile, keeping my eyes locked in her direction. "Continue?" "So like - We act as though we should all feel bad for how things turned out, but I'm just not really convinced that it was something we could have done anything about. Everything was proceeding to this point, and now we're here. There's not a lot we can do to walk back the idea of changing where we are. It feels like the best thing we can do is start from where we are." Another voice spoke up, a boy sitting in the third row. Rimmed glasses. "It's not really about us atoning for what we did, I don't think that's what the professor is trying to have us understand. We need to know how we got to where we are so that we can work to dismantle the structures that are resulting in the present. We can't really change things right now unless we know how we got here." She hesitated, looked back at me. "Do you want to respond to that?" "Yeah - like, I get the idea there, and I'm not disagreeing with it at all. I think we definitely need to know what brought us here, but look at what we learned this semester. A lot of things are random, some of the reasons that things are happening have more to do with the interaction of two or three events that had unpredictable outcomes. I'm not just convinced that we can find the answer in looking at the past." There was some silence. "Why might that be?" "I - well, I think that there's value in it, but the random nature of our time puts us in the condition of trying to explain a present that is currently unfolding. My impression is that by trying to decipher too much of what it took for right now to happen might result in a constant state of reflection rather than one of action. I think if we're instead looking at the present and deciding what needs to happen next, then maybe we can get ahead of things getting any worse." The boy in the rimmed glasses responded again. "We can't look at the present without understanding how the present came to be the present," "And I'm not arguing with that, I know there's a degree of that, I just - I don't think that it's what we should be obsessed with. There's too much at stake for us to want to get through and too many dangers of us continuing on with the way things are right now." "An obsession with how the past unfolded is what all science is based on, though. You can't solve the present without having done analysis of the past. The idea that you can work from the present without having to know that seems short-sighted." She faltered a bit. The boy with the rimmed glasses sat back down, looking back at me. "Our current condition is a result of the actions we took in our past. This is true. I think Mr Sales is correct to bring up that some degree of analysis is incontrovertibly important to the process of examining any path forward from a disposition. Looking into the past and tabulating the work that took us toward certain ill-conceived outcomes is crucial," "However, while I think you're both right in your own ways, but what Ms Reedin just said is more correct than you are, Mr Sales. What she is right to point out is in opposition to your core position. We cannot recreate the past, therefore we cannot hope to create the future from a knowledge of the past." I could see Sales squirm in his seat, hoping to respond. "This does not mean that we don't need to know the past, it means that we are obliged to understand that correcting course on the issues that are ahead of us requires new ways of thinking that are more resourceful than the ones we have employed so far," "Resourcefulness requires courage, and courage is illogical. It's possible to make measured guesses at what you think will happen in most situations, but some degree of faith is necessary in order to get toward the solutions we hope to see unfold. There is no certainty. That is what I've hoped to teach you all in this course, which is why Ms Reedin's comment on present disposition is where I want us to start from. What are the basics? What are we starting from, and what tools do we have at our disposal?" Sales blurted out "But our tools are the past!" "This is true, some of the past can be used as a tool. However, you are committing the sin of overfitting - you are believing that past trends can somehow predict future outcomes. Any scientist worth their salt will tell you this is not true, and that the results themselves as they unfold are more truthful than a study of the past. Ms Reedin's comment has us understand that we need to consider the variety of optionality that the present offers us, because there is potential in understanding that a path forward from the present can be informed by any approach, meaning that it's possible for us to completely change our approach in opposition to any and all past proceeding. It's very likely that a resolution to our current condition lies in taking the problem from a completely different angle, approaching it with some other tool than prediction. Sometimes, if you want to knock something off course, you need to blow something else up, and this, more than anything else, lies in doing the unexpected."

What makes things all the more confusing was that however hard things were to navigate when we got back to the city in those months afterward, the start of it was pure and from a place that probably liberated us from anything else. It's why when we were back home, all the disagreement that led to me looking back and looking for a different way for things to have played out didn't make any sense, the context for how things started was so completely different that it didn't immediately fit within what was necessary to make it work. When I told her I loved her, I didn't really do so directly. We were sitting on the back of a pickup truck somewhere outside of Truckee Mississippi (the irony was not lost on me) - she had turned to me and had told me that these are the sort of trips I wanted to do for the rest of my life and I found myself looking at her for the first time and seeing in her someone that had been looking at the same landscape as I had and had appreciated it through enough overlap of experience that I could see what was being stitched together. We'd parked in the empty space below a wind turbine, the whistling thrum of the blade whipping overhead - the dogs had been uncomfortable overnight but somehow we made it through their unease, and I'd woken up before dawn. We'd driven here because the idea of going somewhere neither of us had been together but that overall was probably not that exciting of a place seemed novel -- seemed like an experience that both of us could walk way from having felt comforted by. I realize now that this is how you build relationships - you share experiences with people and you make space for those relationships to be built on the time that those shared experiences offers to each of you. The drive had taken 18 hours from Chicago; I picked her up from work with packed bags and two panting dogs and an audio book ready to go, but we didn't start listening to it until 6 hours in, so we'll have to listen to the rest on drive back, yet in the moment that we were sitting on the tailgate, the dogs milling through 4 foot grass after sounds in the underbrush (thank god for tick prevention), I didn't really want to go back anywhere. It seemed easier in that moment to think that freedom comes from thinking that you deserve a space that is entirely your own and with which you can defend yourself against the decisions of a society that are placed upon you. That truck was rebellion, for me, and sitting next to her was the same, even while rebellion is exhausting. I was holding on to an enamel cup with a bike tube wrapped around the handle to prevent the heat from our coffee from burning my fingers, and it was as simple as you know, i think i might we might be in love in the middle of her taking a sip, her hands holding the lip up to her face, and she didn't look back - I just watched her smile slowly and close her eyes because yeah i think that might be what this is, and we didn't say anything else after that, the wind just kept whistling over head. On the drive back, she held my hand and I felt as though I was driving back to something different from what we'd just experienced, and I didn't want to steer the car back toward Chicago. What if we just didn't go back and she looked out the window the same way that you had earlier and it would be nice to give it all up, wouldn't it?

So here is the best part of it all, the dream that I felt as a result of having looked back, when I was on that beach and I was spending time with all of these new friends that I'd made on the beach: Aaron had just left and was on the way out to Quito to fly home for Christmas, while I was planning on spending that time with a constellation of people I'd met on the beach - people I'd worked on a farm with and with whom I'd formed friendships. I can't really remember the people that I met but I remember that we went down to the beach to look for fish so that we could have them with dinner, and we made a feast around the different kinds of fish that I was able to buy from a fisherman on the shore who had caught them that morning - we put them on spits and cooked them, then shared them in an open yard with one another, until finally we all left to wander down toward the beach together. There wasn't a lot for us to do other than drink with one another, but I wanted to get a raging bonfire going, so I got everyone to go with me up the shoreline to find wood for what we wanted to have around us as we spent time together. Once enough had been gathered, everyone was well drunk, and we were enjoying the sense of lost time that comes with passage of other people's lives around you, I remember my friend turning to me and saying you can relax now, you made all of this happen all while allowing me to sit back and enjoy the cachaça that was brought by the brazilians. I remember even now that in those times there was a lot of liberty in being able to live a life like that - I've spent a healthy number of christmasses without my family and it's mostly because I don't think the idea of christmas is something that needs celebrating. It's a nice holiday, but it's not exactly meaningful without there being religious to back it, because I don't think what the point of it is becomes easily discerned without knowing this reasoning, so I don't think that there really is a point. So what can I learn from this story? What is it that I think proves something about me and makes it so that it's clear I know how to do what I know I know how to do as a result of telling this story I t means that I can create community, it means that I can bring people together, and it means that alongside all of these other skills, I know how to keep people happy, I know how to tell stories, and I know how to offer to others the creation of a space that is well shared and comfortable. That's always been true of me, as hard as it can get sometimes. The worst is that now I'm really not even waking up in the morning to go to work. I'm really just... phoning in in at this point. There are no deliverables, so I have nothing to deliver, and I have no way of trying to get myself to move froward a state where that's something that I do. I'm so tired, I really feel as though I'm about to fall asleep in and around this. The point is that on that beach, I felt something that I haven't felt many times in my life- the power of being able to bring people together. Because I was able to speak multiple languages, I was able to get everyone on the same page, and I was able to coordinate us all around the resolution that needed o happen in order to best optimize the situation for the greatest possible group benefit. I don't know if that's something that I should feel proud of, but it's definitely something that I care about a lot so I'm trying to think about what the right way of approaching it is, so here we are.

Per Kundera, M, elliptical writing is the act of not-writing everything that you intend to have as a part of your text, the you should indeed leave some of the imagining up to interpretation on the part of the reader. It's for this reason that slice-of-life style writing is a useful vehicle for introducing people to stories - rather than completely covering an idea end-to-end, there's a way for the writing to encompass only that which is directly relevant so that there's a way for the reader to expand what exists beyond what they have written on their own. In fact, this is one of the more powerful notions when it comes to writing, to give your reader something that they can interpret and build out, and further is the very reason that it's valuable to flesh everything out as a writer, but then only write about what is important. Elliptical writing has us drop into a story and fill in the rest of the characters and setting with our own imagination, a way of building something beautiful out of the idea of beauty itself, rather than the literal imposition of beauty upon the observer.

Metafiction is a form of writing wherein the writer often breaks the fourth wall by playing with the structure of narrative to pull the reader into the act of reading. It’s something that is often seen in the writing of Kundera, M, but as well in Cortazar, J and Labatut, B. With Kundera, M in particular, the metafictional elements are present in his divergences into philosophical footnotes and/or commentary on the story itself, particular with the effort to have the reader understand that the motivation of the story is to have the reader consume the universe that has been created around characters or narrative, but instead as a vehicle for thoughts and ideas that the writer holds. ed: it’s also a form of writing that I particularly enjoy and would like to get better at, because it’s a writing style that I think I’d really enjoy to write in. In particular, I could see The Cruft existing as a piece of metafictional work that uses the musings of a hyperintelligence (currently named Hayelek) who exists in a state of observing or remarking on the phenomenon of a failed civilization that once might have existed on Earth - however the general sense that I get is that Hayelek will be more the observer while The Figure will be the one making philosophical asides - which brings our total characters in the book up to three rather than two.

The emotional regulation does not seem to hold - the desire to stave off anxiety around possibility and it's weight as an emissary of its own peace, all the while in a state of feeling uncommon with one's own surroundings, as though a part of something both greater and utterly uncaring of your participation. This is the feeling brought forth by Saturdays by the feeling of having had to think about one's past in a state of motion even while we are attempting to regulate ourselves against the future and past emotions. As Mo Gawdat mentions, anxiety is a feeling that sits in the future because it is a fear of what will happen next. Happiness is instead found in the present, in the happiness found after recognizing what is in your control and withholding fear that desires to bloom forth through any meaningful consideration of the past and future as features of our lives we wish we could change, and it is only in the present that we can truly take action. So it is a question to me why fear envelops me, why in this moment it is an emotional state that I'm experiencing - and I'm forced to believe that it is a product of anxiety of looking forward and seeing that any set of outcomes are available, any set of outcomes might happen. So we work through the exercise and ask the question - if the fear is that Im going to get off of this train and hear that something devastating has happened, is it real? It is not - it is not something that I need to experience, and because of this is something that I can tell my brain not to experience, it's something that I can push to the side because it is not real. I am in charge of this feeling and I am in charge of what it constitutes. --- Recently, I've been listening to Mo Gawdat - the former CBO of Google who, since the passing of his son at 21, turned his life toward the pursuit of happiness for as many people as possible. In particular, I was listening to a conversation he held with Steven Barlett (Diary of a Ceo) - where Gawdat refers to the time-based notion of emotion. His claim is that most negative emotions are couched in the future and the past as either symptoms of regret or expectation, and that the unhappiness that comes with negative thinking often emerges through an interaction with that which we can't change. This has had me thinking about the general rise in anxiety in present times that seems linked to a well-connected society's general inability to exist in the present - we are in many places at once, but we are never in any of these places because technology is not a substitute for being physically and psychically located in a place and a time. Rather than moving with Gawdat's definition of happiness being a function of that which you cannot change and a lack of imperative to exist in the present moment, I would exact the definition to have it describe a need to be in the physical present. More explicitly, I find that when I'm most anxious while using technology, it's because I am interacting with a present I cannot directly affect. In Mo Gawdat's definition of anxiety or regret, the temporal location of negative emotions pull one away from the present, and the solution for this is to direct one's attention toward the present moment. It's not something that comes easily to people, but it's a meditation on the feeling of knowing - the feeling of examining possibility as something that is interesting, but not that is determinate, because only those things that lie either outside or inside of out control are those that we can think about. Anything else is imaginary and exists outside of those bounds, they are features of existence that reach out for attention but are not tangible; you cannot touch them, you cannot feel them. This is the great mistake that has arisen with creating technologies that exist to reconstitute our presences in several spaces at once. We even call video calling 'telepresence', as though there is a feature of this sort of interaction that constitutes meaningful interaction, when telepresence is likely better termed 'pseudopresence', enveloping a construct of terms that describe the ability to experience anxiety around one's need to exist and affect several places at once - an experience that is not tangible and not real, because at best our ability to telegraph the appearance of presence must be acted upon locally by those who are physically in a location and capable of affecting local reality. This may be the reason for a grand state of deflation washing over us when we get off of yet another 'telepresence' call with someone, and likely equally the reason that despite the rhetoric of liberty desired by workers, there is still an underlying desire among the lonely public despiring in the direction of interacting with other humans on a physical basis, because this better approximates the ability to physically affect one's own environment. We might not want to spend all of our days under the panopticon of controlling leadership that treats us an implement of its desires--this impinges on the human desire for autonomy--but we do still desire interacting with one another. Any form of interaction that takes place with full engagement of both the mind and body interacting with something that is physically present is a predicate for having felt as though we can truly affect our environment. We do not feel this when we have 6 hours of telepresence calls because being 'telepresent' is not the same and being present, else it would be given the same name. While there is an anxiety that exists when sitting with a fear of the future and a regret that couches itself in the past, pseudopresence also places us in a state of anxiety about an inability to interact with and affect the present, inherently leaning us toward a state of forward-leaning anxiety as we sit on the expectation of what should be done next rather than the ability to affect it directly. In the most austere of emotional circumstance, imagine being on a video call while watching someone experience the worst damage of their life - we are utterly unable to prevent the reality of the present that is happening on the other end of the call, and are as a result horrified by the reality that out anxiety is laid bare. As just one symptom of a general anxiety that seems to exist around the use of technology to exist in several places at once, I'm convinced this is the reason that telepresence is so difficult for actually feeling a genuine connection with the people you speak to. Most information technology that concerns itself with informing people about the present is doing so at the cost of habing people understand that the present they are being informed on is not one that they can directly affect. This is the product of millions of news feeds, media consumption, and yes, telepresence that produces this experience. It's also not to say that we should broadly define telepresence as negative - it does not wholly remove of us all ability to have meaningful interactions over digital media. I have cried over text messages and phone calls, I have laughed heartily in the chat, I have been in teletherapy for years - but to depend wholly on this form of interaction as equivalent to what happens in the physical realm feels like an austere rejection of the somatic experience - we have many other senses and they work together to characterise our experience. However It's not to say that you can't; I have had my share of telepresence calls that are meaningful and have actively been engaged in telepresence therapy for about 4 years now - but I'm aware of the truth that an anxiety sitting atop our experience of the present will always remove of us the ability to experience what we are doing at the moment that we are doing it. Our calendars are backed up entirely with back-to-back telepresence such that by the time one conversation ends, we immediately commence another call with a completely different context, starting with the same phrase of 'where are you based?' out of a desire to place the stranger in a physical context. If Gawdatt is right, attempting to 'solve for happy' becomes a question of navigating the utility of technology in our hyperconnected present - developing an understanding of pseudopresence is probably a powerful tool for appreciating modern anxiety in the context of social interaction. Our understanding of modern anxiety and social interaction can be explained by the effect of the technologies that inform it. While technology offers us the illusion of being everywhere at once, it simultaneously robs us of the ability to be fully present anywhere. It's not just about being mentally present, but also about prioritizing physical presence when possible, and fully engaging in our digital interactions when necessary. Instead of rejecting the presence of these phenomenae, we're forced to learn how to navigate their presence consciously by reorganizing our reaction to the limitations they impose and the effects technology have on our ability to be present. Only then can we hope to mitigate an anxiety arising from being everywhere and nowhere at once. --- : : to 'despire' is a confabulated emotion, something I've come up with but nonetheless needs naming - a complex emotion of both feeling hopeless and yet motivated toward action, but only toward things that we can't change.
