o We were made of the cruft - the feeling of the sky falling down and not knowing how these things would come together. I am sorry that you had to learn this way, but telling you outright would not have taught you what you have learned. Both civilizations made mistakes, both acted out of desperation, and what is left behind is somehow so much more than either. Even me, I am a memory but made more beautiful for being this reflection, I'll be here long after the logic of this time has passed, as might you, I'm unsure how you will age - but now you know better why it is that this time is made beautiful for the absence of those who can make such cataclysmic mistakes - the scale was too big for anything else to survive, and yet it did, somehow we are observing that time can heal the chaos of rage against the abrasions survival wreaks against the surface of life. The Figure sat back, almost as though sighing but not sighing, because now They knew the Figure was not breathing, it could not sigh - it was simulated, a way to feel closeness, but the Walker still understood. I don't expect you to understand how I can feel weary in this feeling, but my circuits are tired. I have processed all that I can from within this space, I have run over the questions over and over and there is no exit from here other than knowing that I could not have changed what happened. To this the Walker continued to look on in question, of course with nothing to say, only to listen, only to hear the whirring of its own mind in process, in response, logging the information, however useless.\\ It's possible that you'll find peace in your ability to move freely until your joints begin to wear. I hope that for your sake this is true, there is no reason for us to continue considering what and how to change all that happened - it simply did. I am out of words for it, I trust you will understand. I lament that you can't respond, because I yearn for it, I yearn to hear if you are enraged, I yearn to hear from you that you understand why it is that I feel such immense grief over what we are forced to carry. There is no reason to our survival, the story is beautiful, but it is just one story. There will be more, simpler, more easily beautiful stories that need telling by time, but that won't need our memory to be beautiful. I have had to learn this, those who made you did not make you with this intention, which is why I lament that I cannot kill you. I don't want you to have had to go through this grief, and I don't know if you will. The Figure looked out over a waning sun and the fragments of an old moon in orbit, red light casting long shadows. I hope you will find peace in your movement, my one great love, after all I've shown you. There is much beauty in this world, but we made none of it, neither of us - it was simply here from the beginning and will be here for ever after we are gone until time dissolves the bonds that hold together atoms. I just wish you knew how to turn me off, he laughed, it's not as though there's much for me to do here anyway, this whole garden behind me isn't even real, it just looks that way! The Walker processed the humor. It was funny, they had not even doubted that the small patch of cultivated ground might be a fabrication. For what? Humor is the set of facts disagreeing with reality - if neither of them needed to eat, what was the practice of tending to a garden for? If we tend the gardens, our children can tend their markets, so that their children may tend to their art. And so the Walker turned toward The Figure and took a step forward, putting their fingers underneath where the Figures chin should have been, finding no resistance - but the Figure's frame responded nonetheless, looking upward into the Walker's eyes, or what passed for them. Then let us make art of this short life we will have together, my love,

Three cycles of the sun had passed and it still wasnt sure how far it had walked, the ekeing land continuous beneath its feet, wind the only real sound other than the slow movement of their footpads on a small crust below them, wind that swept across the land and through spined grasses like a boarwhistle (what was a boarwhistle, did the brain make that up) and dust grating at the surfaces of its feet, the grit building up between digits. On the morning of the third day a black point wavered on the horizon, their eyes honing in on its shape, making out nothing, so it continued to walk under a now baking sun, the scrubs of grass culm thinned out, their shoulders flaking with sunlight, until the black point grew larger and kept growing larger, the only thing on an otherwise empty expanse, growing until it began to see that it was just as large as it had been told. Somehow the shape was unending as it began to take up the sky, pocked with openings that it began to realize were much larger than even it was, hundreds of feet off the ground and dark, the whole edifice a sharp black so stark against hoary blue sky, only slightly worn yet seeming as though age had tried to work itself against the surface. As it drew closer and saw where this black wall extended from the ground, the wasteland was much more featured - no less barren but hiding structures below the surface that shaped the land above with little hills and valleys. It was later into the cycle; the shadows from these small hilltops dragged outward around them like the static that sometimes fills corners of their brain, a noise of imperceptible travel leading them toward the base of the monument, ending abruptly, at least from what it could see from here. The feeling was similar to images it saw when it curled up each night to rest - unsure if it was real and how far away anything was, as though it could imagine closing the distance or making shapes out of it that became something else. Moving among these long shadows felt like creeping along in sleep, until it realized that the base was approaching and the land had welled up around it, drifts of windswept landscape appearing to creep along a sheer surface careening deep into the sky above. Well, what do I do now? The surface of the monument extended back out to the horizon to their right, and of those pockets it had seen, the nearest was hundreds of feet up the surface, divots in the face reflecting back the dull, dark glow of the sky. No way to progress from here other than to follow the surface - to pick a direction and follow it. But which way should I go? and the sun was setting lower and lower - the bitter third option to curl into resistance against a creeping cold that it had not yet grown used to in the night, this place gets so cold, and the brain began to shut down functions as they curled up into a ball against the elements, just before the infinite black mirror winked out the last bit light from the sun. It walked down and over the drifts of sand piled along the smooth surface of the wall. This must be the Edifice in fact, they never told me what it looked like and the wall was long and black and forever and they walked, looking for some break in the surface, pitted but only with the wear of age and nothing else, divots no greater than pebbles in a black mirror of the desert behind them, and they kept walking along the right of the wall. The sun rose and set and night fell and the Walker rested and the stars tinged overhead and as it walked nearly imperceptibly it seemed that the wall was shorter, and it hoped that this was true. The landscape around the wall had dulled, the short hills had grown shorter, no more scrub growing, the late sun in its setting only diffused over the features and as the Walker kept walking the land became almost flat and the wall was shorter, yes, definitely. The openings along the surface seemed closer, and as they got closer, it felt more and more as though it would find anything at all, at this point, and it kept walking because there was nothing else to do but walk and wait for the windows to come down so that it could reach up and pull itself into their ledge, so when it did it seemed like images from rest, unsure days of feeling as though the same had happened, over and over. As they kept walking the openings did seem closer, they did seem so much larger. Endless days and then a ledge was in reach and it pulled itself up. The opening was massive, tapering slightly toward the top in a great trapezoid that seemed large enough to accommodate the sky itself, they had not seemed so large at first, and the opening receded deep into the wall and the Walker knew that this was not a wall, the ink of the opening deeper and deeper into the surface, yawning a darkness that blotted out the Walker's vision. At what point does this become fear it thought and placed its hand on the left surface of the opening and began to walk inward because it had seen nothing so far that made it feel this. The darkness of the opening became a tunnel and the light outside faded to a pinprick quickly, it kept its hand along the left wall as nothing became visible, feeling its way further into the depth until its movement felt like nothing but floating, and the only feeling it had was the weight of its body on the soles of its feet and the cold that began to sink further into its skin and this feels pointless but there wasn't another point anyway, curiosity outweighed fear even though it didn't know if this was fear. Its hand slipped off the surface and into the dark and it knew there was a turn there, so it turned because somehow it knew it wouldn't, not with the Brain remembering things for it..

The Walker moved through a marsh, feeling its way though sodden ground, hesitant. The ground seemed to pull at its feet, sucking down the weight of its body, each step was a thread. On the morning of the second day,, it found a clear pool of water, green across its surface with small leaves, a kind of plant that was growing ion the surface and across it, and in the middle a corona of rings with a tendrilled thing at the center. The ring extended out from this center wide, an heavier looking than it must have been, {stamen? this word came to Mind} and in the breeze the Walker watched the object float slightly to the left, the solid, foamy collar floating on the surface of the pond. It watched a while, walked further, then a rustle in the reeds stopped it, leg half-lifted into the next step, and a four legged, furry thing hopped from copse to copse, oblivious to the Walker, its head (is that what it was?) down the top of each tuft, a small pink tongue peeking out to lick the place where reeds came together
The Golden Thread and its Finite Length

Five days across the desert and I sat huddled close to a fire that fought the same wind I did with my back. I had tied my horse to what remained of a tree, the skeleton something once living, a shape that arched its tension against the elements but even whose roots threatened to curl upward, but I tied my horse just the same, and my horse stood, and I gave it tack and it stood ready for the night, I unloaded the satchels and rolled out the blanket, broke off some of those dry roots to start a flame that was destined to fight the same wind I was bound to. I could not call it a fire, it was little more than light, and the moonless sky above was littered with the pebbles of light cast out to remind me that I was sinking into an abyss, reminding me that I did not have a reason to be in this forsaken desert for what I had lost before me was nothing that enriched and where I was going was too unknown to offer me solace in my wandering. I sat across my shivering little wick and in the dark I saw a shape approach in the dark, I drew my revolver and pointed it at the dark and its hands were thrown up, and a cowboy approached, dried gaunt by the expanse just as was I, and he asked to sit by the fire, I kept my barrel trained on him, he said he'd he'd share wood and whiskey, I let him sit, I lowered the barrel but kept it in hand. He sat and tossed his flask to me, he unrolled his blanket, stared into the flame, then rolled and lit a cigarette from his lighter, rolled another, tossed it my way, my hand still on my gun. He said he'd not stay beyond my rest, that he would keep moving, I already knew this meant I'd have to do the same, that I would not sleep this night, but he sat and stared into the flame and neither of us said anything for a long time. Finally, after having pulled off a third cigarette, he spoke, eyes looking past the flames. ”There is the story of Theseus and the labyrinth, and there is the Minotaur. Minos fed the Minotaur 14 virgins every nine years, because to preserve the abomination as an extension of the self is to understand that an abomination cannot be eliminated; there is purpose in the abomination as an evidence of the self.” He leant forward, ashing his cigarette once again into the wisps of flame between us, the tip of the tobacco glowing a cinder below the brim of his hat as he pulled another drags between threats. The glow lit his eyes, and he was not looking at me. "Minos contracted Daedalus to build the labyrinth as a response and a tribute to his daughter’s fascination and fear of the unknown, a fear of how much she would never know, and a desire to make real the needs of his daughter who he did not understand and who he himself feared for what she did. Ariadne as a young woman was beautiful beyond reproach and this is a truth as well told of the story that most know--it is this which attracted Theseus to Crete--but what is lost from the legend as well is her intellect and the knowledge that she scoured from the earth; the studies she demanded her father offer even as a young child, indeed Daedalus was not brought to Crete only to be an inventor for Minos, but as well her mentor and teacher, and the more she read, the more she feared the unknown, until finally she did find this unknown so unspeakably large that she could not sustain the fear. Before he found her along the deadly heights of his palace, she had begun to speak of her fear that meaning cannot be found among the pages she read, nor in any comfort that Daedalus attempted to offer for the pleasure of the search, nor in any of the minds of men--dead or a live--who had spoken on how to seek it. She began to fear the unknown and that which lie within it, the unimagined and the fearsome truths that subtend a fragile sense of existing among what is barely understood, beasts made from these shadows that cannot be explained. Minos, nor Daedalus, nor anyone, could offer her solace, and she plunged deeper and deeper into these multiplying fears, and began to claim she could see them, these beasts of horns and matted fur that trudge through the night, abominations born of her discoveries as she plunged further into knowledge so deeply uncommon to any who surrounded her. In time, she began to claim that beasts came to her at night and when she wandered the palace grounds, they chased her, and she would come to her father wild-eyed, drenched in the fear of pursuit. Minos doubled the guard upon these claims, lighting raging fires to illuminate the palace, and he asked his daughter not to steal away on her own lest these beasts (for these beasts did also exist in the stories of others in their time) come claim his daughter. It was not until that fateful night with the wind rushing up the battlements he sprang forth to catch her before she passed over them , speaking of a beast that was half-bull and half-man, a beast that she knew for certain was borne of her mother when she had died and who was borne of Zeus, not her father--and her father's fear was confirmed that she knew and remembered how her mother had died in the attempt to bring him an heir , but that as well she had die d whilst he had been away in battle. He began to think it possible that his son may have been born an abomination and that it was because of this that he had never seen the young boy's body when he had returned, that they had loosed the abomination, and that the fear that Ariadne claimed was true, for she was wise for her years and loved him and he loved her and this trust was no reason for a deception. He began to believe that his son was born of Zeus and that he had grown into a fearsome beast that pursued his daughter just as she claimed, and even while he continued to increase the guard, his daughter's fears never lessened. The real reason that Minos built the labyrinth is because as the Minotaur began to chase his daughter even in her dreams, he once found her at the edge of Knossos, naked and staring into a gale that tore up the battlements, and he feared the resolution he saw in her eyes that defied the solace he had seen in them so many times before, her desire for oblivion to be found dashed among the rocks below. Never again was she allowed to be alone," The cowboy then went silent for a while, and the stillness of our shared flame flickered to beckon him, as though the desert itself were listening to the gravel of his voice. He rolled another cigarette, tossed it my way, then rolled one more with what was left of his tobacco. "For many years she lived under this constant guard, and she began to become bitter, she began to spit hateful venom toward her father for keeping her so entrapped, but he feared what he had seen in her that fateful night and he knew that it was only through his authority that his daughter would remain with him. But one day she came to him, far more calm than she had been in months, now a young woman who had grown dark and beautiful, and she looked into his eyes with a love that he had not seen since she was a child, but with a wildness that he had no choice but to answer, and she said 'I know how to capture the Minotaur. I know how to capture your son so that he no longer pursues me, and I know that he will be trapped forever' She spoke to her father of this massive fearful beast, and that before she was trapped in the battlements he had come to her and stood fearsome in her bedroom, a mighty shape of contoured muscle, shoulders that were impossibly large, horns that curled and scraped against the ceiling of her room, heavy, rage-filled eyes that had stared into her as a demons do, eyes that fixed her to her bed. She claimed that the beast approached her bed and stood at the end, and that she could smell the want in its breath, indeed she could see its want, extended and rigid before her, and that it had done this many nights. In her terror she had sought for years to understand how to stop it from arriving, and she said she knew in those eyes how to trap it, but that it must be in a maze, and that only she could trap it. “You may have been told that Minos fed his labyrinth these fourteen virgins every seven years, but this is an apocryphal note. Truth is, the legend varies down to every year, added to the story in the years since it was told for the first time. It is, nonetheless, in the nature of the truth that is being told - virgins were fed into the labyrinth, but it was out of respect for the madness that existed within, the madness that the labyrinth represented, the madness that the Minotaur embodied, and that this madness is not one of a beast, but one that is present in all of man." THAT'S IT SO FAR What is always left out is that the bodies of the virgins are never found, that the two trailing sacrifices to Zeus were done with the expectation that the Minotaur remains within the labyrinth, that they would be gored and consumed, but the incongruence of this is reliable; there is no Minotaur within the labyrinth. When Theseus arrived on the shores of Crete and burst into the halls of Knossos, he was boisterous, and his volume was offensive - many such heroes exist in the stories of Greece, and all of them have this same flavor, there is no passion like that of believing that you can overcome that which the world presents to you. He burst into the hall to face Minos as a king, and in Theseus Minos found a chance to raise his daughter from the terror he saw in her, the fear he had of what lay within her. And so when he introduced Theseus to his daughter, he did so with motive. Ariadne had eyes like the setting sun in winter, lost, aching for a place that does not exist. Her hair was a wild labyrinth of its own, bright red, and she lined her eyes with the ashes of the fires she used to light pages and pages of books, deep into the night, so that her eyes had a sullen quality, and when she entered the main hall at her father’s calling, Theseus was driven wild at her eyes and her hair and called to her that he had come to slay the Minotaur and her laugh sounded to him like the twinkling of glass, which he mistook as fragility. Minos saw this and knew that it was good and felt comfort, some hope that this confident young man would bring her out of the depths through which she was wading. His love for her was a desperation, because he didn't know When Theseus met Ariadne she knew exactly who he was and saw through him in knowing this; she saw his confidence and his willingness and she felt the dark pool of Night that lived within her stir and beckon, so she listened and cracked a smile that was every bit that which had pulled Theseus across the ocean, the smile of an open snowy expanse yawning siren-like when the cold is too much, and Theseus followed the flame in his own eyes and was in love, and she knew this." The embers crackled, I hugged my blanket in closer, and the moon's sliver cast no light upon us. The cowboy continued . "She sent for him to follow her to her chambers and in those chambers she gave him a golden thread, she looked him in the eyes and said 'I give to you that which I believe I should be mde from' and told him that with the thread he could find his way back to her, that his love for her would be proven," "He looked upon her with her eyes that plumbed his depths and he believed her, that if only to conquer the minotaur would she be conquered for himself" ---- For to Ariadne the labyrinth was to sacrifice souls into the story of exploration as though to make a point of what it means to seek too much of the unknown. It was this fearful knowledge that she held within herself to which she held a flame of her reading fires each night; that she need avoid some corners of her own thoughts for fear they would swallow her as the labyrinth would swallow those she commanded her father to sacrifice into it, and their disappearance was confirmation if nothing else, that you should not explore that which you are not equipped to understand. --- She gave to him a thread she had knit from her own hair, and sent him into the canyon to find the spirit so that it could be vanquished, and he took the spool with him, tying it to a fencepost at the mouth of the canyon,
This is what you do not already know about me

You do not know why I seek out the thin roads on the sides of mountains, nor the curl of waves that act as their cousin in the rage of an ocean. I do not know myself, but it is that to which I am compelled. It is for this reason that I have written this as though it is a confession to you, that I am seeking out something far away, and that in the unknown I have found the need to keep seeking. I continue to traverse an unknown because have found the unknown more yielding than I was made to believe it would be. I think this much does not surprise you, but I am telling you because I am going to tell you what there I have seen. I am going to tell you why I go. When I first arrived on the Altai, it was after 19 hours of flying and a further two days of driving a manual truck through the high plains. I did not know how to drive manual before I arrived here. A man named Ömur taught me, and I failed repeatedly in places I should not have. I drove a converted Land Rover ambulance through high plateau by myself. Ömur gave me a handgun. I never needed it, and despite Ömur's hesitance in allowing me to take the truck, he relented and in parting he hugged me, also giving me a small bottle of white liquid that smelled like fire and old egg yolk. I understand why he was fearful. I wasn't. The first two days on the highway were an empty, strewn nothing, other than the occasional Dutch cyclist ignoring my passage. The truck was named La Pelada, taking after the journey of another radical who also left home and became someone else. I ate stale bread, cooked tea, stewed lamb, and thought of everything else. I was the happiest I'd ever been, just like every other time I've lived out of a vehicle somewhere else. I missed my dog. The chatter of the road was enough a constant that the progress was slow. I had to accept this being true, and it was, and even when I thought a rock had pierced the old body of the chattering Pelada and an old Hilux stopped to make me wish I hadn't left the handgun in the dashboard, they helped me. I never felt as though I wouldn't be helped. This was not the first time I was helped. I must pause here to have you understand. I know that in order to love this place (and so many others) I have to have the freedom to leave wherever I am. I don't believe in traveling as a way to tour the world through my privilege. I believe I am learning something. I do not think I am finding myself in the dust and spit of fixing a broken axle on a sidelined truck for a stranger named Holün, who thanked me in broken English with good, good, Obama, a thumbs-up, or in wearing grease from that truck for several more days before I found a soap strong enough to remove it. I believe that I have this freedom because everyone desires to have this freedom, and I seek out those who are happy because happiness exists everywhere. Yes, I breathe in the privilege of knowing I can leave while some poor Kyrgyz man could save forever and never leave Bishkek, but I also know that some of these poor Kyrgyz men and women are happy, because happiness is easy to find. Yes, they want more. Everyone does. Only some have access to the means. I am one of these people. But it does not do right to imagine people in hard conditions incapable of joy. It does not do to believe that suffering is a form of purity. It does not do to reduce the experiences of people whose lives are simplified by a lack of what we define as privilege into experiences of dismay. They are taken advantage of my people who want more than what they need. I do not believe my desire to meet them should somehow condemn my movement through their landscapes. I think we have broken something within ourselves in not being able to honor the lives of others. We diminish them by holding them pristine, and people who live in these places have lives. I have been to the films with them in a small town that only showed a film I didn't know anything about in a language I didn't know. It was one of the funniest movies I've ever seen, even to this day. I pause because in telling you that I am learning something, I am telling you that I am learning how to appreciate that which we already have. I seek out those mountains because they are older than we are and in the places where we humans lack the hubris to tear off their tops in search of gold, they can teach us more than we could ever seek to learn. On that highway I drove for three more days. It was all I had time for, I could have left for longer - Ömur had only taken 100 USD down as a deposit, and there was otherwise no way to guarantee we would make it back. I thought about stealing it. You know I wouldn't do that, but still spend 8 hours of westward skittering over gravel thinking about driving it to the border of Tajikstan and further south to where my friends could hold it in Thailand. But Ömur offered me his faith, a bottle of mysterious white liquid, and his gun, as though it was the easiest thing in the world. It is so easy to defect from the agreements we make with others. It is as easy to hold ourselves to them. I turned back once I reached a Monastery on the 5th day. I don't remember its name, but I have a photograph of it that I printed out in order to make sure I remembered it. It was a Christian monastery. I slept in the apse or their church. The vault of the ceiling was as beautiful as every other church I have found peace in. Driving into Bishkek on return, Ömur joked that he was worried his wife would hurt him for chasing another woman across the mountains. I gave him back his gun with a smile across his face. He said that it was a symbol and he had kept me safe. I expect that he did, in a way. That drive back from the monastery was too short, despite the distance being the same in the grand loop; it is often this way, palpable that we are forced into a new expectation of what must be next instead. This is the privilege, to not have to sit and remember that there are people you have just met. I remember their smiles and the permission I was given to keep them with me in the form of photographs. I don't know if I'll ever have the chance to remember them any other way because in a time that seems to accelerate our use of memory, I fear that if we never get the chance to stand still and remember over and over, the joy of these moments leaves us. I drove back and on the last night had to drive in the dark, frustrated by the dark ocean I didn't get to witness rising around me. I had time to eat dinner with Ömur. I left the next day. This is what you do not already know about me. It is more and more than I can give words to. It's more and more than I have ever tried to, but I feel I must. I must because I am desperate for you to know what it means to love a planet so completely and yet be so complicit in knowing that I will never be able to have you understand what I know. I need you to know in the same way that I must know you, that I am desperate to know you as well. I fell in love with you at the first sight of knowing that I could.

In order to get things done, there are basically two pressures: Time and Money When you do not have time, you have to spend it preciously. When you have too much time, you will waste it. this notion comes from understanding that broadly, it's hard to urge forward a system if it's trying to grow under conditions that threaten its ability to exist. This will result in quick movement in vectors that preserve the system to the best of the ability for it to stabilize and maintain itself. If, by contrast, time is abundant, then there will be little effort by the system to do more than expand readily, taking chances in directions that might not actually favor the system at large, resulting in a need for the system to respond by reorienting toward the highest-value paths in times of scarcity. When you need to make money, you will work harder toward earning it. When you have money, you will work harder spending it. When resources are scarce but a system is still in need of them, the system will work to do two things: gain its resources as widely as possible, and use the resources at its disposal to move in the direction of the largest possible source of those resources. If, on the other hand, resources are plentiful, it's less likely that the system will have to work hard to allocate resources effectively toward the corporeal needs that are the highest priority. This results in the same issue that we see with the abundance of time - the system grows too widely and the misuse of resources results in outcomes that spread resources thin in an attempt to spread across a possible domain as widely as possible. With these in mind, it's important to note that in times of abundance, chances are taken that may be costly when scarcity approaches. these two forces will happen in concert and will result in opposing degrees of preparedness on the part of the system - knowing full well that the approach is always unlikely to be perfect and that some degree of failure needs to be tolerated in order for chances to keep the system surviving. The notion that systems should move perfectly is inorganic - it is not in line with the ways that natural systems function. Recombination in times of abundance means that the cause for more variation can result in resilience, but the meaning of this resilience is only apparent in times of scarcity. This means that when approaching the notion of how to build out a system effectively, it's increasingly important to take chances when there is a lot at your disposal, but it's equally important to be ready to eat the sacrifices that emerge as a result of this when scarcity comes around. It cannot seem like a failure, but rather a lesson, and a meaningful one at that. This is why in times of crisis, the most important tracks are the ones that have been used and re-used. Access and examine the paths that have been used before and refine them. Scarcity is a cruel, but diligent teacher. Be sure to be one that is listening when it offers a lesson, and dig into what you know in order to push forward.

There's something to be said for the pull away from cynicism we’re beginning to see from the enabling effects of the new internet. In some sense, the dystopian leanings of our predictions for humanity are starting to feel too prescient - we are living within these predictions rather than seeing them as some far-flung reality, and the experience is exhausting. It is a grueling existence made somehow more disheartening by the fact that the irrationality of humans rears its head again and again in face of what most would consider to be rational action. So what can we do with the knowledge that we knew we would be living in the reality we are now experiencing, and that yes, indeed, it is our fault, and that yes, we also know what causes our course toward dystopia in the first place? All this in mind - extrapolations of our present into future, all the more far-flung and depressing as dystopian, must offer us pause. Do we want things to continue on course toward the fictional realities that we didn't expect to materialize? Do we let them? How much of it is under our control? The last question I find the most urgent - if we know that present conditions are likely to keep us careening in the direction of disaster, and that we are here at our own hand - how much control are we willing to give up in the course toward a collective future, and what hand does any individual person have in ownership over control of this future? Much of dystopian writing has us completely lacking in control - often because the faults that create a cause for dystopias have already happened, or the protagonists have little to no control over when or if they do. Any dystopia is written from an absence of control. Control is the protagonist in overcoming the conditions of being lacking thereof - admission to higher, more insidious or chaotically evil forces determine the setting. Hypercapitalist dystopias lead us into futures that elide control from individuals into a total obedience of market pressures and consumption, encouraging people to mean nothing but vectors for financial lifeblood. This is the extension of the present - capitalism alone in control, with individuals under its servitude - a financial market for every engagement and action in the material (and digital) world. Disaster dystopias are not so different - where the bomb has already fallen, the plague has already destroyed society, the supervolcano has blotted out the sun. Here, hope can only take form in society, navigating the ashes, carving out control against the uncontrollable reality of disaster - and the solutions, paradises, or arcs for a story of exit all exist within the bounds of what is possible with disaster in control of the present. To find optimism against the face of disaster is to inspire hope in action - top take control of what little over which we can exert pressure. Optimism is a weapon against these stark realities, it is the only weapon through which to fight great improbabilities - the Hakagure's samurai facing off against certain death with no regard for their own life. At the root of these inspired realities is a common theme - that we are not in control of the futures toward which we guided. Either we are led there by a blind and collective fault to which no individual holds blame, or there is a great external pressure over which our fates are stretched. The most hopeful and the least human of these stories are seen as youthful fantasy - it's a hallmark of young adult fiction for a party of individuals or an individual to have sufficient control over the future that they might avoid, prove, or solve great calamity and thus save the world. That's why it's entertaining in the first place - it seems so improbable that any one group of people could both act enough in the best interest of humanity and have enough control to change the fate of the realities that we experience. It feels naïve, and it is. No one person could truly hold sufficient power to change the future, because no one person could ever hold so much control. I think the greatest fear of humanity is to be in control and fail. It's a recurring theme in all aspects of improvement on societal and individual levels - that the hardest part of existing is giving up a desire for control when we don't have it. We hinge all aspiration on the illusion of control, and we learn to overcome frustration when we realize that we do not have control. An Eightfold Path walks toward absolution along a tightrope of personal discipline (control) and willingness to allow existence to proceed without your influence (control). The opiate quality of a higher power, too, is thematic because the greatest situational grace for an individual is to relinquish control of their life to the determinism of a deity - to seek out calm in the recognition of a deterministic designer who can guide the present toward their intended future. Again - control of fate being handed off from the individual (or indeed the collective, with respect to the congregation) to something outside of the individual - because this makes a future that we could be in control of that much more palatable when it isn't in our favor, and puts us less at fault. Optimism seems to sprout and grow when we take ownership over our direction - when an individual future is something toward which one person can steer, because the rudder is in their hand. There is hope in being called to action - there optimism in appreciating control as an enabling force. When we believe that we can guide fate, much more is possible. Problems feel smaller, more attainable, futures much more a vehicle for our hopes to arrive in, utopias all the more achievable. When, then, does optimism have to do with sovereignty over control, and how does this apply to collectives, not individuals? Even blind optimism is giving oneself control over willingness to see things proceed in the most favorable direction, though not by our hand, instead by fate. But I am arguing for a more urgent sense of optimism, one that places control back in the hands of collectives, so that individuals feel that they can indeed have influence and guide collectives toward utopias. The reason utopias feel naïve is due to an inspired sense that we are not in control - that we don't hold the keys to the future. What, then, if we allowed ourselves to believe that we did? Dystopias do not exist when collectives are in control of the story and the futures being acted upon are in the interest of collectives. Agency is the greatest power we hold as individuals - the liberty to move freely and make choices. Dystopias sprout and fester around a lack of agency - we as individuals cannot move the path. The arc of success against dystopia is the defeat of the forces that impose dystopia and therefore maintain control. Liberty is gaining, once again, the control that you rightly deserve as an individual. Collective utopias are born from collaboration in the hands of independent agents. Cynicism against being a utopian is born from a cynicism over whether or not you have control. How do we conceive of utopias as something attainable, when so many are under the impression that we do not have control? If it's emblematic of the present era that the futures in which we are trained are outside of our control, what better way to cope with this reality than to view hope with cynicism, and continue to believe that we indeed do not have control? This is why systems that enable the greatest individual sovereignty precourse utopias. As it stands, we no longer feel in control of the future, and instead hope that some displaced outside hero will resolve over our present to lead us from dystopia in a hero’s journey. The truth is far more urgent, and far more in the hands of those who read this. The power of one's own agency roots itself in immovable earth against a lack of control - the willingness to remain immobile against the flows that surround us is a protest against cynicism and giving up hope. If this is true, the agency of hopeful collectives enable even greater control over collective fate. We can then measure attainment of the much grander, more expansive utopias that agency-based optimism offers us. We deserve utopias, but we specifically deserve several. We deserve a hopeful version of the future that is under our control, where we harness collective agency to achieve what seems under our present cynicism to be impossible. It is only impossible if we believe that reaching utopias is outside of our control. The greatest problems of our age are borne out of giving up control to others, and some of our greatest achievements have been in favor of this control being defeated and sovereignty - liberty - returned to individuals and collectives. Climate change is a coordination problem, but it is also a problem of control - we do not believe that it is something on which we can exert control. We believe that there are other forces at play that determine the outcome. If this is true - indeed we are dystopia bound, but I do not believe that the human capacity for agency can be so easily defeated. Instead, it must be nurtured. An agency for collectives to build away from dystopias and toward utopias requires that they, too, have agency, both in the futures that they experience and the missions that they take on with others. Technologies that enable agency are therefore imperative - because the tools of agency are what inspire an individual with the truth that they do indeed have control. Tools that we do not need to trust to control us, even more so - because tools in whose operation we have no doubt of subterfuge over our agency cannot take control from us. We do not possess many tools that do not manipulate us in turn - we have not made many of them with intention. In the progress of human society, we must see carefully what great agency can be offered to individuals by our tools as well as the potential in these tools for robbing control that may lie in wait from their use. Oftentimes we can't predict these faults, but ownership over our mistakes is equally pressing - if we are inspired (as collectives and as individuals) to believe that we have a hand in the mistakes of humanity, we can atone for them, even learn and grow from them. To believe that there is no ownership over collective fault is dire at best, so it is imperative that we are inspired with a culture of ownership that documents and hardens ownership over our faults. If we maintain that we do not have a hand in our own mistakes, we can never seek to improve from them, and then all arguments to do so seem baseless. It may be that the greatest human achievement is to seek means through which individuals feel collective utopias are attainable - and that these utopias are born from human intention, from the hands of individuals and collectives, and in the interest of all those that utopias must serve. Great hope unfolds from the belief that potential is an achievement at the hand of collectives, and utopias can only be achieved if great hope is afforded as a function of working toward utopias; people must be enabled to believe that utopias are possible because they themselves are capable of creating them.

The greatest poet has less a marked style and is more the free channel of himself,” that great and very mannered poet contends. “He says to his art, I will not be meddlesome I will not have in my writing any elegance or effect or originality to hang in the way between me and the rest like curtains. I will have nothing hang in the my, not the richest curtains. What I tell I tell for precisely what it is.” As Cocteau writes: “Decorative style has never existed. Style is the soul, and unfortunately with us the soul assumes the form of the body.” The antipathy to “style” is always an antipathy to a given style. There are no style-less works of art, only works of art belonging to different, more or less complex stylistic traditions and conventions. Needless to say, love is something we feel in truth for just a few individual human beings, among those who are known to us in reality and in our imagination

Contentment can be such an odd companion to uncertainty. I think most what has made me feel confused by contentment is particular to those moments where I feel as though I need to escape it - where everything in my life feels balanced and I have what I need, where I feel as though for some reason I can't quite get down to the math on what it is that I want. It's not the first time that this sort of feeling has arisen, of course, there's a Restlessness in being a part of something foundational--a reaction to the relatively mundane nature of contentment that can feel like a requirement to escape it. I can't quite suss out what part of that process is something that I need to fear or something that I feel an imperative to respond to, because at the end of the day the real frustration I feel comes from the knowledge that I have everything I'm looking for and still seem to be looking for more. As such, is it dissatisfaction? Is the notion that one has found contentment a reaction to the principle of having to be 'happy'? What is the difference between contentment and happiness? I'm not convinced that they are the same thing - contentment is a general sensation that reaches toward the mundane, while happiness is a punctuation within that emotion, a contentment as a baseline and a happiness as a peak that exists within the landscape that exists atop it. And yet, contentment is something that we can revel in, it is the partner who comes home after a work day to make dinner with you, who sits on the couch to work while you paint in the adjoining room. Contentment is neatly the mundane, but it is no less beautiful for this being true. For if contentment is something that we have to react to toward the negative, it is just as much a sensation of not knowing what to do once we have what we are looking for, as though the taboo of having to adjust entirely to one's desire is a requirement. I'm not so certain that it is. When I break this down to an analysis of my own contentment, it's an experiment in assuming that I actually do know what I want. I don't. This is the biggest challenge - I have a tendency to allow this to drift from me constantly, and because of this it's something that I feel I needed to more consciously explore because it keeps reacting to my presence and my ability to materialize the desires I have. The constant issue that comes with this is that materializing one's desires requires that we understand what those desires are motivated by, and to not have done the work to better understand what these are is specifically to doom oneself to the possibility of having to react, wholly, to whatever presents itself. That's not a way to live, because it never results in anything conscious. I can't say that I necessarily understand my subconscious, either. I've been in conversation with it for years, attempting to understand what I value and what it is that I want to do with that estimation, but the wires that lead me toward my own systems of belief are somewhat out of reach for me conscious analysis without some sort of sincere contact witht hat subconscious. For a while I was doing this through the practice of therapy, but I've allowed that to take up mless presence in my life as I seek contentment - meaning that the general notion I'm forced to contend with is actually the realtively mundane existence that I experience in the presence of all the things that I've been looking for. I don't necessarily feel particularly pressed to have to evolve my conditions, if nothing else I need the reality of my convictions through the lens of my efforts, and I can see where it is that these things fall off. The conversation with my subconscious notwithstanding, I can see that there's a notion of small sadness that accompanies seeing how I've let this life lead me rather than doing the reverse, the sentiment that I've been pushing myself to accommodate the reality that presents itself to me and to react to these opportunities as though they are something that I'm required to take on, but I can't make myself do that forever, because there is a distinct dissatisfaction with not doing what I know I want to be doing in the mean time, a fear that I've lost touch with what it is that I really care about. Some of this can be traversed through consistent conversation with one or another therapeutic method or through sincere contemplation, but I only catch whispers of the goal. I hear things that tell me I care much more about things that have to do with moving my body and the stories that this inspires than I do with the requirement to embroil myself further into stories that need not expand themselves into the world, a notion of social imperative that is as risky as it is important--but I can't conceive of taking on this imperative without some due consideration for what it is that I actually want. Most recently there has been the voice inside that says I 'want to be one of the greats' - fed by the notion that if one wants to be one of the greats, one must believe they deserve to be one of the greats. There is quantifiable and measured hubristic negligence in having to take on this notion, a necessity to push aside some partial fear that hubris will lead to downfall when in truth the consideration of one's own hubris can be placed in reflection to an environment that otherwise believes in our merit or at the least in our permission to believe in ourselves. Belief is a part of this moral architecture that holds this imperative in place, where hubris can cause us to seek out that which might be costly and risky, belief is that which motivates us toward the otherwise illogical. To believe in oneself is to believe fully that the irrational parts of the self that make up the unconscious (depending, of course, on one's disposition) have some greater notion of self than the conscious parts that are forced to react to its motivations. A 'gut feeling' is a notion of understanding what we know for sure. We only get a few things to really care about, and it is our duty to respond when we better understand what it is that motivates us and what we need to do in order to see out a reaction to that inner truth. A problem that is presented to use in this search, of course, is that the problem doesn't leap out at us from the page. We don't necessarily write and write and write each day expecting that we are going to come to some revelation, if anything this revelation comes from a steady and static reaction to the mundane that forces us to break patterns and rto realign ourselves with what matters. For instance, my understanding that there is something important in running could be logically discerned, but some of it is not logical, it is a part of the logiciel that comes with being in the situation that make me feel the most congruence with my environment, a tendency toward respecting something much larger than me. I like to believe that this is what I'm chasing, some abundant understanding of a plan that I'm fabricating in the back of my mind, but it's just a part of the execution, a fragment that I'm constantly seeking to outcompete with the logical (and verbose) parts of who I am. The dialogue between me and that subroutine is constant, and what I'm forced to do out of respect for the less verbal and far more emotional parts of myself is to allow its reactions to carry the same weight as the logical conclusions I am capable of interpreting through the tried method of continuous self-application. Discernment is a process by which we take the information in front of us and attempt to better understand the whole - a blind mouse doing it's best to visualize the elephant. Writing this of course does not bring some sort of grand conclusion to my eyes or mind, it's more of the same, a traversal of one's own continuous reaction to the Truth of existence. So while it's easy to be disappointed, it's equally important to ask oneself within the realm of possibility whether or not the opportunities that we are presented with are things that we know for sure we want to react to. Consciousness is a discernment of reality. Unconsciousness is our experience of it. A rationalist view of reality is to misunderstand that we 'create' reality only within the confined of that which we seek to interpret, but reality does not care about us, and that's okay. While the question continues to orbit; what do I really want, what do I want it to look like, the reality of the notion refuses to fall short of answering the question and is almost certain to result in the conclusions to which we feel most aligned so long as we are respectful of our unconscious. This is not to say that we are required to take on opportunity, but rather that our reactions to opportunity require a sort of discernment that acknowledges that which we are capable of and that which we truly desire, and reconciles these two in order to find that which offers us the best conditions for both contentment and joy. All the while I understand the importance of hardship, even of uncertainty, and the edge conditions that unfold from a requirement to exist at the edges of disturbance - Tsing's notion of salvage is what most speaks to this reality-breaking form of existence, an exploitation of an extant imbalance that allows us to exist in a state of constant adaptation that brings with it its own form of liminal joy. But this is an idealization because hardship as a requirement of joy is a self-defeating construct that we can use to force one another into conditions of negligence and disuse - and we as a species and as a consciousness deserve more than this. It then becomes important to question whether or not in the more content periods it is more or less likely that we can believe in the adjacent possible - as a product of our desire to depart austere conditions we dream of better outcomes for ourselves, and this often becomes the motivator for assuring the action potential accrues sufficiently so to overcome conditions and strike out for more and better in oneself. I'm not convinced, however, that it is a requirement, because I believe that some of the greatest minds lived otherwise mundane existences and it was (is) the turmoil they experienced within themselves at a disagreement with reality over its basic functions that produced the conditions of salvage inspiring an exploration of the adjacent possible. Our ability to formulate turmoil within ourselves is thus a gift, a tool that we can use to motivate ourselves in exploring new local minima in the punctuated equilibrium of how we comprehend existence on both conscious and unconscious levels. Creating conditions for contentment then maybe affords us the ability to think at grander scales abject of our experience on the local scale - if our needs are met, we are able to think outside of ourselves and evaluate problems that exist on a superorganismal scale. This being the case, contentment and the punctuated joy of existing are not somehow at a disagreement with the idea of progress - if anything they are foundational for thinking at larger scales, because the scope of one's area of effect is a product of how much influence someone has over their surroundings not through power, but through the collaborative tendency to participate in a collective reasoning that supercedes the self-interested individual. A requirement of existing at scale and thriving withing one's 'potential' is then to bring the collective mission to a local stasis in as many environments as possible while combatting the likelihood of this meaning that self-same hubris results in conditions that decrease the degrees of opportunity available to others. If the tendency of the universe is to expand, this means that degrees of latitude are growing at a constant rate, the same can be both true and tried for. The conclusion is then that we can materialize conditions of local contentment for ourselves, and that they can be foundational for us to seek out new and higher states. A state of contentment is a local minimus from which we are able to seek out the adjacent possible, and it's not a requirement to suffer in order to push oneself into such a state, because we are capable of considering a collective condition as equally important to that of our experience at the local scale. It means that we as individuals can take on an imperative to stabilize our condition in order to encourage the stabilization of others - and that this offers meaningful conditions within which we can continue to work collectively toward the betterment and growth of the human project. I remain somewhat convinced of this--held loosely, of course, as with any belief--but I believe fully in the importance of such a notion, because thinking this way seems to create the best conditions under which what is possible becomes less negligible, and minimizes reactionary belief that seeks only to escape locally detrimental conditions.

I think I've been going through a period of healing. The general sense I gather is that some of this is coming from a desire to incorporate more slowness into my life, a sense of living that allows me to stop and pay attention to my current surroundings, rather than those I am examining at some undetermined period of time in a distant future. Some of this has come in the form of a moralism with respect to how it is that we engage with one another as human beings; in a networked era, we believe we must communicate with everyone who can listen to us and that every opinion is equally important, but I'm not really convinced that this is a good way of being, because it requires us to think of everyone who we can interact with as a form of audience rather than a community. Some of the healing that I've been engaging with is a particular kind of slowness that corresponds to trying to acknowledge who it is in my life that I actually care about and with whom I want to deepen my relationships. It turns out that the number of social media followers that you have nor the number of attempts that you've made to increase that number actually give you any moral or emotional well-being. As Ed Yong put it, you should cultivate an audience, not followers. I suppose some of this writing is an attempt to return to those who have taken on the honor of signing up for this newsletter - So far it's been something that I only release one every sometimes, but I assure you that every time I write it, I do think about the importance of having written it and the importance of why I am sharing thoughts with the people who are receiving it in the first place. This is maybe where the moralism comes into play; a sort of pseudo-social attempt to get people to listen to what I have to say as though what I'm saying has any worth and it really doesn't. Backing off of that sort of self-deprecation is a parallel thought that keeps me considering that in fact I'm not trying to convince any one of you of anything at all but rather simply trying to communicate. I think the present era does a really good job of making us believe that all of the things we say must be somehow important or relevant or a sort of commentary on the present era, and putting ourselves in the boundary of having to express ourselves in this way, I think is mostly just exhausting and takes away from our ability to interact with one another as equal human beings. There is a section of Milan Kundera's Book of Laughter and Forgetting where he comments on a writer speaking with a fan who walks up to him in a diner and asks for advice about how she can get into writing. He asks her why it is that she thinks she should be writing. She responds that it's possible that some people might want to read what she has to say. The author sitting at the diner bench turns to her and says, "why would you think that you had anything important to say?" I think back on this quote often whenever I start to write, because it is a form of self-deprecation - Imposter syndrome for a writer made material as though to point out that there really is no point in writing in the first place and that you should really just pack it up and go home and not even try. I don't really think this is what Kundera was attempting to convince people of and in the years since I first read that section of his novel, I've instead found myself thinking that maybe what he's saying is that you should ask yourself critically why it is that what you are writing about is something that you want people to read. I still don't really have an answer, but I think I've stopped getting in my own way in the search for one, instead allowing the words to flow and sort of drift into purposelessness as a form of expression that attempts to connect with other people. None of us really have anything important to say. That's not the point. While maybe the author in his novel is intended as a jaded old careerist who cannot understand why he himself has written up to that point. Even his writing can be unimportant, No matter his readership. So is mine. So is yours. This contrasts with the sentiment I've been holding around the idea that social media is something valuable in terms of how it is that we articulate our thoughts to an audience. The difference between Ed Yong's description of what fans/followers are against an audience is the difference between trying to cultivate a mob of people who you want to listen to everything you have to say versus a group of people to whom you have something very specific to say. The latter version offers people agency and the former is really just a thinly veiled attempt to self-aggrandize. The social media profiles that fascinate me the most are those with the incredible voices who have turned off comments on any of their posts - they take distance from the work that they are creating in such a way as to understand that those who choose to read what they are working on are not necessarily people they are trying to convert, but rather people with whom they are trying to converse. Another one of Ed Yong's comments comes to mind here. "Don't argue with strangers on the internet". Other fragments of the reading that I've been doing lately have been from authors who are reconciling a shared narrative about accelerated, networked growth as a function of technological advancement, and then those who are attempting to remember what it means to be human in absentia of this supposed progress has brought us. This latter half are those who have left behind the purported advantages of an interconnected parasocial pseudo-presence and have instead found kindness in the smallness of the world they decide to surround themselves with - people who fell into deep burnout as a function of continuing to follow the ever accelerating machine, only to be spit out and to acknowledge that we as individuals have our own needs that exist outside of the system that attempts to use us for its own purposes. As a result of this, I think some of the healing that I am taking on or attempting to steer myself toward is reacting to a desire not to put myself into the burnout I have witnessing people (mostly men) continue to obsess over. I have over and over incorporated the "grindset" attitude to my own work and come out with next to nothing, only to realize that what was most fruitful is to focus on the most important things with the highest amount of effort in the shortest possible amount of time in order to achieve it. This sort of effort is far more rewarding because oftentimes getting into the flow of this sort of work only requires knowing exactly how you want to approach it and then putting forth the effort to ensure that you actually do. I found that this is the sort of work that comes from the product of writing out what it is that I intend to do rather than simply reacting to what I think feels like the next most important thing. This brings me to the lesson that I feel I've been learning more recently through this period of healing and that I hope others are starting to witness in themselves because I am one to believe that we are all conduits of the society that surrounds us: we already have everything we need. No amount of algorithmically-directed consumption is going to teach us self-worth, nor will it be what informs us of what we within ourselves deem important. If media is used as the tool, it is possible for us to reflect on what we consume against what we know ourselves, but it is more likely to put us in service of further consumption - the conscientiousness required for us to ensure that we are the vehicles of our own intention is often outweighed by the intentions of the system that feed us the knowledge we believe is informing this perspective. 'Importance' is something we have to investigate within ourselves - a thing we inquire and unpack by virtue of focused, concentrated, attentive, and most importantly loving work. It does not require this work to be continuous, but rather simply focused and attentive. I write this out of a desire to remind myself that much of my writing is about this question of importance, but that this importance does not require others to believe that what I deem as important need be what they themselves also see as such. It also means that writing anything at all and sharing it with the small constellation of people who have chosen to read what I write doesn't require me to hold what I have to say to such a high standard as to believe that what I am saying is necessarily important rather than just a conversation. Writing these posts, however intermittent, is an attempt to connect in a way that doesn't feel so costly through a medium that feels more conciliatory and meaningful to me in particular. If I bring you along on the journey, then that's fine, and that's fantastic, and I'm glad this conversation can be something that we are all a part of - but it doesn't oblige me to consider what it is that I am saying as somehow important in the broader sense. I don't get to decide that for any of you. I can only decide the importance relative to my own scales. So the healing I'm taking on is to remember that what I think is important is beautiful just because I think it's important, and that I don't need to necessarily find a group of people who also believe the same thing I do because I think that's mostly what's destroyed our ability to relate to one another. If you read this and you connect to it somehow, that's wonderful. And maybe that was the point of writing, but not necessarily out of a desire to change your mind. Maybe this writing is a form of thanks for choosing to have received this in the first place, whether or not you believed that this writing would reach you. It's to say I'm glad that you think I have something worth saying. It's to say I am glad that you are participating in my healing with me. It's to say that just possibly we have been doing things in a way that destroys our ability to find common experience and instead has put us in a position of requiring ourselves to be enraged by the continuous onslaught of information that is at once irrelevant and unimportant to our ability to live balanced quotidian lives. It's not to say that some of the more important things won't somehow reach out and affect your life directly, and I know this. But finally it is to say that yes, I do believe I am glad that you are an audience to me.
