Last night, New Year's Eve, my close friend Lauren and I met a man who was out to drinks on his own. It was a celebration of the new year, we had just come from another overly fancy cocktail bar that thought too much of itself to a neighborhood haunt with decent latin techno spinning on LPs, and we met the man just after we came in, ordering whiskey sours at the bar. This sort of thing happens to Lauren a lot when we are out - she is both conventionally and startlingly uncommon in her attraction - a woman exhibiting all the traditional-seeming traits of femininity and all the musculature of a woman who believes in shaping her body into that befitting an Amazon raised on Mount Olympus - a Greek goddess I get to call my best friend. The man she was speaking to immediately honed in on this 'difference' - it's a line I have heard many men express in our presence, and as I ordered the drinks, I leaned over, cracked my own smile, and was introduced to him (for the purposes of this story, his name will be Morris - not his actual name). He mentioned to the two of us that he could tell we weren't regulars to the bar, that we didn't seem like the usual white crowd that occupies the space. I've always appreciated when people say this to me, because I am mixed, nearly ashamed (and dealing with the shame) of my whiteness - it is a high compliment when people who are not white themselves see immediately that both I am not only white but as well that I take pride in the parts of me that make this difference. It didn't take long for Morris to speak to us about his child through the photo used as the background of his phone: a milk-chocolate skinned young boy with eyes like nebulas. At our expressed excitement, Morris showed us more photos of him, unlocking the screen, opening his instagram, and showing us photos of the child with a short-shorn white woman with the child in her arms - immediately clarifying 'we're on the outs though, we're on the outs'. Lauren and I said more about how beautiful his son was, about how proud we are of the friends we know who have children, a pride that we as women feel in seeing other women take on the challenge of raising people into adulthood. Morris, for his part, turned from the thought, "yeah but I miss this, I miss being out, I miss being at the parties" - his child is one and a half years old. He went on to say that he loves his child, that the boy matters most to him, but he wanted the freedom of being out at the bars on New Year's. Lauren and I watched Morris move on to other women, making out with a woman he didn't speak a word to on the floor, coming up to me after my asking 'how was that', and him responding 'I wasn't in love with her'. He tried to kiss me downstairs at the bathroom sink, only getting my neck. Desperate. He tagged on to the next bar as the night began to drag to a close - Lauren and I had wanted to dance, and the floor closed at Doris around 3. We walked to Friends and Lovers, getting to the door around 3:20, where the doorman tried to charge us each a 30 cover, Lauren and I playing an unintentional good-cop/bad-cop to get us all in for 40. Morris tried to buy us more drinks, we denied them, we danced with three other people on the floor until the music died fifteen minutes later. Morris put his hand on the waist of a passing woman who he didn't speak a word to, we watched her lift his grip from her skin, and he sat down at the bar. The last scraps of conversation between the three of us were in telling him to go home to his son. I reminded him that he probably has less than a year of his child not remembering whether or not he was home for holidays and that this will start to become important soon. The forlorn expression on his face is what we left him with, and as we walked to Lauren's apartment, she mentioned how she felt he was suspect, faithless, her distrust of him framed through the phrases he used. I found him pathetic in a way that I still feel sympathy for. At the age of 35, I have heard more and more women in my life deride the relationships they have with the men in theirs. My sister says to me (not for the first time) as we visit her over the holidays that were it not for the marriage she is already a part of (to a man she claims truly to love), she would not be dating another man. At a writer's workshop in Mexico, a black woman tells me that she chose to be in a relationship with a man to raise her kids because it's hard enough to be raised black, but not because she wanted to. A close friend's husband struggles with his own freedom to write because they have a child and this incurs responsibilities that he becomes responsible for when he's 'finally off for the holidays', which my friend doesn't have the luxury of getting 'time off' from under her employ as a mother. Another close friend, this one a man, tells me how lost he feels in relationship with his wife, who finally came out to him as both non-binary and queer; it feels like an attack on his masculinity, and they have not had sex in a year because she is protective of her body in a way he doesn't know how to react to - but they are still married, she is still with him. It could be that all of this is symptomatic of a society slowly learning to deinterlace the relationship between being a woman and the oppressive structures that womanhood places upon us in a world built by and for the advantage of men. Women have seen significant concessions and reformist progress; Sontag says in her essay 'The Third World of Women' that "{a}s otherness is reduced, some of the energy of sexual attraction between the sexes will decline". She wrote this in 1972, and in the same essay she describes the sorts of progress that a patriarchal society will offer to women as concessions, what she called 'reformist' policies of which we should be suspect. We have seen many of these concessions come to pass - our equal-ish access to executive roles in workplaces, a heavily diversified set of roles made available to women, a broader (though shaky) access to abortion, equalized or equal-ish pay. These are all outlined as the sorts offered to women to keep us placated in a society that wants to keep us functioning as a part of the engine. However, Sontag also balks at any assertion that the gap of equality between the genders (I am conscious that at the time of her writing, speaking of all the genders was not common parlance) should be subsumed under the struggle for freedom from the oppression of class - indeed it is a reformist stance to say that there is 'no war but class' war, and women are offered "merely liberal improvements in their situations" when the struggle against bourgeoise oppression uses the freedom of women as a political tool. The struggle of women, per Sontag, is a longer, deeper question than any of liberalist politic - the separation of the genders and the structures this entails roots beyond class and in a different dimension from that of a liberation from the axis of power; it does not encompass the struggle for collective freedom, because the freedom of women is a question of axial power between the sexes. In a modernized argument, it is one of comprehending concessions to the explicit loss of power under the dynamics of a society structured around men, for men, and by men. She lays a finger on a feeling I witness in men today: "If women change, men will be forced to change. {...} The structure of society is founded on male privilege, and men will not cede their privileges simply because doing so is more humane or just. Men may make concessions, reluctantly, granting women more "civil rights". In most countries now, women can vote and attend institutions of higher education and are permitted to train for the professions. Within the next 20 years, they will get equal pay for equal work and be granted effective ownership over their own bodies. {...} but these concessions, however, desirable they may be, do not challenge the fundamental attitudes that maintain women as second class citizens nor touch the root of male privileges." She precedes this by laying claim to the same feminist position I have heard before in the presence of other more consciously-minded women who are aware of the structures against which they abrade, that "it is not for women to assume the task of liberating men, when they first have to liberate themselves. [...] Supposing that these changes can be undertaken in collaboration with men minimizes (and trivializes) the range and depths of women's struggle". I witness this from the remove of fifty years and the understanding that concessions have been made; we as women in this society do enjoy much more liberty and access to equality, but I broadly agree with Sontag's opinion that "it is about power". My sense is that the concessions of a reformist society have however offered us some remarkable progress in the delimitation of women's agency, and that this is resulting in the threat to the power of men against which current political divides seek to inoculate themselves. Sontag predicted this, she is not the only feminist to have done so, because the convergent evolution of an educated class causes the emergence of collectively held opinion and the structures it begins to build. 2026 has raced far enough into the new millennium for us to understand that we have made progress on the acknowledgement and some degree of reconciliation of how widely splayed are the dimensions of human expression; I would not be writing this so safely were this not to be true. I believe we are, as women, more free, even while freedom is an ur-goal underlying more efforts to be made and is unattainable in its lack of definition; structurally an aspirational lacuna toward which we patiently labor in the manner of Foucault's definition of enlightenment. I also think that the effects of this slow liberation, even those that exhibit the qualities of 'liberal improvements in (our) situation' make themselves apparent in how women have chosen to express themselves, both in terms of aesthetics and in the teleological assertion of aesthetic as an expression of internalized belief. The photo that Morris had shown us of his wife was one of a woman who had chosen to tacitly reject traditional expressions of gender that define her as feminine - I mentioned her short hair, but both Lauren and I agreed, while laying on the floor of her apartment in the 5am stupor of a night's summary, that were it not for his explicit mention of her as his wife, we might have assumed her queerness. To be clear, she may well be queer, raising a child with a man with whom she is 'on the outs', a man who seems to be reaching for a time in his life where his own freedom was less limited. In the morning (afternoon, really) I sit on my chair opposite the couch and recount the night to my partner, and we conclude that Morris exhibits all the qualities of a man nostalgic for a time where clubbing meant being able to touch women in some presumably benign manner. She explicitly defines his kiss on my neck as assault, I don't disagree, but I found him benign. I found him benign and further felt so when as we turned the corner toward Friends and Lovers, Lauren immediately dangled a practiced question in front of Morris to see if he would bite, asking him 'what is your relationship to masculinity?' Morris leaned away from us as he walked, not quite stumbling, maybe taken aback, saying that he doesn't think about those things, that he 'doesn't like to get political about things', and I clapped down on the use of this language, saying that it is not a question of politics, rather a question of rights, because we live in a society that has been built around masculinity. The question is as a result not politically charged, but direct, a personal question to someone we want to know more about - do you ask yourself this question? You must. Morris responded by saying he had thought of these things, that his wife is a Columbia graduate, that he himself went to Stanford. My partner mentioned upon hearing this that our interaction over this question sounded like two cats playing with a ball of yarn, and I do think there was a certain cruelty to the question. We didn't get an answer from him before reaching the doorman of F&L. It could be that the relationship Morris has with with his wife did at some point exhibit some consciousness of how gender and race play into the realized experience of their relationship to one another - it would surprise me if someone Stanford educated would truly feel that avoiding the question of his relationship to masculinity would be due to its 'political' implications, -- but some part of me witnesses in hindsight the use of a vocabulary designed deflect the question. I do not personally believe that he does not have an opinion on the matter, rather my sense is that he feels harmed by the presence of the question and its effect on his existence as a man. It could be (and here I truly cannot make the assertion to this likelihood) that his relationship with blackness and a the painfully slow unfurling of freedom for black men is affronted by the loss power as a man. It could be that this is just as well a worthwhile question to be asking, regardless of whether or not he thought so himself - either way I view his use of a language attempting to deflect the question as one of emotional worry, of a tiredness. As I said, I found him pathetic in a way I felt sympathy for,. The dynamics of gender and liberation are questions foremost over the concession of power, not concessions of superficial improvements to the surface of an otherwise unchanging and unprogressive society. These are not my words, they are Sontags, but I do believe them to be true enough as proven by the experiences of oppressed peoples seeking their own liberation to warrant speaking them as though they are my own. However, I think we are, today, in revolt. It is the reason that the two most qualified candidates for presidential leadership in the United States have been women, and they have both lost handily to a man who represents the most idealized expressions of gender by men. Power is being threatened. Sontag is right, "Women cannot be liberated without reducing the power of men". Men do not know what to do about this. The first quarter of the New Century was one that offered us the chance to create concessions in the right of race to power; Obama was elected, and the Mechanism has sought to inoculate itself to this transgression. Culturally, this progress still made way for other concessions in the access to power for women, and it turns out this is more threatening, and truly we aren't ready for it. The second quarter of this great Century will continue to ask the question. Broadly what I witness in women now is an expression of gender as though to reject, much of the time, the signals is broadcasts. I think I witness in men an unmooring in response. I may be overly focused on the expressions Morris used to avoid our rhetorical hook-and-reel, and maybe it was cruel of us in a certain way to pose the question given the security of our temporary friendship to a man who by most accounts we should have found societally reprehensible - out on the town from his wife, leaving a child at home - but I do think there is something to a 'tiredness' I saw in Morris when the question was asked, because I see it in many other men perceiving disabuse of their power by a society attempting to equalize gender. I see it in my aforementioned friend seeming threatened by his wife's willingness to share the dimension of her sexuality, but Andrea Long-Chu takes this to its extreme in "Females", saying that "if sexual orientation is basically the social expression of one's sexuality then gender is basically a social expression of someone else's sexuality. In the former case one takes an object in the latter case one is the object". I cannot explain why she protects herself from my friend's advances but remains in relationship to him, but I understand why she does because I see in many newly queer people the same foundational rejection of a relationship with the dynamics of gender, expression, sexuality, and the dynamics this produces when too consciously brought into the purview of physical interaction. My friend's wife's hair is also shorn short to her head in a 'pilot's cut'. She is a strong woman, any time I've ever spoken to her. My friend is exhausted and thinks his marriage is failing. Maybe it is, and maybe it is because masculinity does not know what to do under the circumstance that power is ceded to women. The exhibition we are witnessing in our society of power's concession is different from what Sontag specifically describes as 'liberal improvements', I think. I return to the question of whose duty it is to educate men on what to do when their power is diminished, but men do not know what to do, from what I can tell, They themselves seem quite bewildered by what it means to view women as equals. I describe this feeling on the floor of Lauren's apartment as we close the night, gesturing with my arms to the removal of cobwebs around my fist held like an anchor in the center. I think men are confused by having the lead themselves through the unknown of women's liberation, because women's liberation will leave them behind if they do not work to liberate themselves. If they are not confused, it is because they are rejecting the notion that there is something to work on.
On Suffering and the Aesthetics of Power

I've been reading a lot of Sontag lately - primarily because it's a book that was mentioned by Maggie Nelson in her book 'On Freedom', where Nelson speaks to the differences that exist for women or men in the pursuit of what she selects as the best definition of 'freedom' - Foucault's "patient labor giving form to our impatience for liberty". Sontag's On Women includes an essay on Leni Riefenstahl's career. Sontag is practically derisive of all the work she produced, focusing heavily on the aesthetics of how it reflects a fascist ideology. She then repeats something I hear her say in an earlier essay in the collection, where she says, explicitly, that any improvements in the relations between the genders will require men ceding their power to women. Particularly, she quotes: I'm fascinated with this description of specifically fascist aesthetics because it leads me in a different direction than that I think Sontag was implying. Much of the time, the sort of logic that I hear espoused by people who are addressing their frustration with the unknown and the burden of having to calculate one's own purpose with in the search for meaning, people turn to Buddhism, and particularly toward an interpretation that 'all life is suffering'. I don't end up seeing how different this is from what Sontag is saying here - because I think there is a sort of 'mindlessness' in taking an approach to the experience of being a person that comes from the nihilist approach of believing that nothing matters and that there is somehow something 'blissful' about letting this go. A book that I haven't read yet but that I have on my shelf right now is Schopenhauer's "Studies in Pessimism". I bought it and have intended to read it because it describes a contrarian view to the body of work I have been pursuing in the last few months - writing and reading embattled mostly with a quiet pursuit of hope. The personal reasons I have for this are that I tried working on something hopeful and —surrounded by an industry and a culture primarily populated by men—ended up starting to feel as though it wasn’t worth actually working against the grain of a society built by and for men. The frank truth was that in the midst of all the ‘hard work’ I’d found myself doing over the last few years, I had begun to feel that I was in the pursuit of other people’s goals. Maureen Murdock’s “The Heroine’s Journey” acts as a counterpoint to the well-known Joseph Campbell book of a comparative subject. --- I want to talk about how power and ‘suffering’ have an intimate relationship Particularly I’d like to focus on the idea that ‘suffering’ is giving up one’s power, and in fact the aesthetics of fascism might be to lean into the idea that one ‘must suffer’ in order to attain a degree of absolution. While this may be me cherry-picking the commentary that Sontag has chosen to highlight, it causes me to think that maybe in agreement with her, I
I wonder why it is that the intellectualism of the years in which Gibran was published has waned such that seeing his writing as lacking in depth is no longer an opinion that people hold.

You know what would be cool? If a person could hold a device up to their face and speak with abandon, moving through the mildly connective fabric of their thoughts in order to tease out a meaning, then tell their device to arrange those thoughts spoken into an essay that others might read, taking out all the difficult intermediate steps of what makes writing an essay so hard, then post it to social media and manage all the posting that is also so hard, and then, finally, all the critique that comes with having released a thought into the world - which is also so, so hard. That would be great, wouldn't it? To have optimized all the thinking out? A couple of days ago, as though the poles reversed, I found myself thinking that I no longer want to use AI to check my work or any of my writing, ... or any of my thoughts, either - because I think I finally understand the itching sensation at the back of my neck that feels wholly unsatisfied by AI's claim to be a digital mirror. I'd been using Claude for that purpose, and now I get why I can't - it can't give me what it is that I'm actually looking for, because what I'm really looking for is validation. The reason was in part the fact that while reading an article by Sam Kriss, I realized that he was going to kill me for doing what I've been doing. I immediately threw up my hands - I don't want to die!I don't really use Claude to write, necessarily. I use it to convert my handwritten writing into text (it's remarkably good at that) and I use it to... shamefully, make myself feel better about my writing. I use AI for validation that what I'm saying is something that anyone might read. I'm realizing that writing and reasoning is exactly the wrong place for a tool that strings together ideas without really understanding what a writer is trying to get at, or without actually paying attention to whether or not there's a connection in the first place (fun fact, there's a name for that). I'm done doing that, because it doesn't lead me anywhere. Despite those who created AI hoping that it can do so. the sort of reasoning AI is capable of is the sort of reasoning required for mechanism - an answer to a question that is generated by a pattern. That is where it serves the purpose, and I think it's very good at that - good enough that What this means, to me, is that Sam Kriss probably won't come to my house to kill me, or at the very least won't stand in my living room shouting a tirade of well-phrased cwitticisms (I'm reaching) about how it is that writing is holy and important and deserving of protection. I already get it, and he's right to post a reactionary screed designed to cause outrage. We are outraged. That's the point. Part of this is that I can tell, from reading his words, that he's a human, because he holds positions that I disagree with, and in fact that I hated. I hated the fragmented reasoning in the middle of Kriss' screed when he says of writer Hanania that "whenever I see anything from Richard Hanania I’m seized by an overwhelming desire to demolish his house", "because I'm Jewish and he's Palestinian". I hated it because it felt human, because I could imagine a person at the other end of the digital tangle sitting in front of their computer and dreaming up the most rage-inducing sentence he could come up with, and because it's the whole reason the essay works. It is, of course, the exact section that has been clipped and reposted in the day or so since he posted what he did, exactly because it's a horrid thought, and because the circular reasoning that makes it simultaneously anti-semitic and racist against Palestinians is exactly the sort of wordsmithy that causes anyone to stop and contemplate a little longer reasoning period Claude cheerfully puts below a query. I'm still thinking about it, and I read it yesterday, turning it over and over in my head because it was designed to make me angry and because everything else Kriss says in the essay is compelling enough to go back and read again; I excitedly want to express that I do, in fact, appreciate that a horrid opinion about how to treat a group of people is something that makes his writing feel human. The humanistic impulse in me to say that the two things are not connected--that belonging to a faith shouldn't mean that he wants to commit xenocide--, are the nuclear missile that Kriss is sending to my house from across the internet. It might have been a self-deprecating joke, but it was a bad one designed to be bad, and that's great, and that's my point. Slow clap, it worked. The rest of the essay is fantastic, for the same human, angry reason that jumps out of the text and that I, for one, am still dwelling on. I've already seen any number of rage-fueled takes to the fact that he wrote those words for us to consume, but hey, at least it was human. This is not an essay against AI, necessarily. I don't want to it to be (I don't even know if it's an essay), but it might end up that way. It seems stupid and ill-conceived that I feel compelled to bring it in to the discussion, because maybe there really is a compulsion within all of us to comment eternally on the present moment. I know that those among us who care about the sanctity of the word should never hazard to touch the stove on which the kettle is whistling just to see if it's hot - not because I think it's normal to touch the stove, because we're purists and idealists and all the other lists that we use to make ourselves up, but I'm also a realist. I know that sometimes the intrusive appel du vide shows up unbidden and asks us if maybe we should try touching the stove because there may be a quantum chance that just this once it won't be too hot to touch. It's the reason that I do use AI for other purposes - I can tell there's a place for it, and I do use it that way - it feels like a superpower to use it in ways I am undereducated to do otherwise. However, I am realizing that AI's utility does not belong among my words, my thoughts or anything that urges me toward presentiment and experience and tries to tease out meaning. It's not me doing performing the action and hating the process, it's a machine that I want to do the hard part for me. I am not an AI apologist, because I don't give a shit what you think about me, so I'm not going to describe myself that way. These are just words I'm using to navigate a thought. That's what writing is, after all. See, readers and writers fall in love with sentences. It's not the paragraph or even the arc of the novel, the essay, whatever, that attracts us. It's the reason that one sentence stood out to me from the many other very good ones Kriss wrote in an essay that had nothing to do with the core subject matter. Most good thoughts are an attempt to reach across the blackness of space between ideas and draw out inference from their connection, and then the hope is that by having drawn that connection, we can derive meaning from the pattern we see connecting them. A good sentence is a window into how a writer sees the world - but there's a thing about windows; if we know that people are going to be looking in, we arrange the room with this knowledge in mind. We use our taste (hah!) to decide what we want people to see in that room and how we want it to be received by them. A good sentence is and act of synthesis, compressing a body of knowledge into a pane of glass. Every stereotype of a tech bro is a mattress on the floor because no one will ever see the inside of their mind and the machine we are building is more important than our wellbeing. That's the reason the room we're looking at doesn't look like anything, why the takeout boxes haven't been thrown out, and what justifies the impulse to throw this entire fucking essay in the trash before publishing it. We cannot expect words to do this on their own, even if we draw a semantic map of the likelihood that one word will be connected to another, and then use that map to automate the performance of connection. Part of the promise of AI is that it can do this - that the semantic map will somehow generate the patterns we seek. In some circumstances, it works -- but when we're trying to come up with something that matters to us and outsourcing the reasoning to a pattern generator, it's really just graphomania. It doesn't mean anything specific, because it was written by no one, for no one, from no one's perspective, with the mixed expectation that an unknowing public will read it. Graphomania as a condition was described long before Milan Kundera asserted that it is a symptom of a society too docile and comfortable to do anything other than write and believe that their writing is worth reading. I've been realizing that people have fallen out of knowing the term - but there's even a clinical definition that comes from having one's temporal lobe affected - an affliction that causes words to spill forth from someone's hand and onto the page without actually reaching a point. I have a long history with that particular fragment of The Book of Laughter and Forgetting - it was what caused me spend the last fifteen years thinking I couldn't write because my impulse to write was really just a manic impulse. I spent fifteen years mulling over the impact of those few sentences in order to conclude that I fucking hate Kundera for communicating an egotism that delineates the difference between writing with an impulse to explain something and writing because one has an impulse to write. While I am glad that happened, it's also incredibly frustrating to think that we should somehow stop short of expressing ourselves. There's a balance to be struck, after a --- When I think about Vivian Maier's photography, it gives me a similar sensation to that when I think of graphomania - a compulsion to have created something, but uncertain of why. Maybe it was just a hobby that she got good at, maybe even something that had to do with teh dynamics of privilege while living in a society that did not deem women legitimate in teh creation of their art (indeed, she and Virginia Woolf were contemporaries, which I don't think is brought up often enough) I think of the urge to document, ot keep everything that comes with wanting to live in a society that has given us the means to doso. I think it's atrocious, in some sense, biut I also think it's rpbobably the case that living in the midst of society causes us to think that society is pretty gtreaty a nd that because of that it's somethign that needs to be preserved - so maybe there is, in some sense, value to the action.

I think I would like to get really really good at something. Meaning: I would like to learn what it takes to become someone that people see as being very good at something. I got there with photography and while I do think that was an important medium to explore, I do think it was not sufficient for me. In part I feel this way because in Sontag's Regarding the Pain of Others, she addresses the importance of the caption. She says, in the midst of a paragraph where she divides the use of the caption by the impact of the image, showing that the image does not matter when it is placed in absentia of its context. "To the militant, identity is everything. And all photographs wait to be explained of falsified by their captions. During the fighting between Serbs and Croats at the beginning of the recent Balkan wars, the same photographs of children killed in the shelling of a cillage were passed around at both Serb and Croat propaganda briefings. Alter the caption, and the children's deaths could be used and reused." In explicit terms, an image of a child dying or dead does not matter in terms of the emotions it creates in a viewer unless that viewer has an understanding of what they are witnessing: a mutilated child is placed in the abstract can elicit emotion, but it is not emotion tied to any one event. A mutilated Gazan child is another story. I think it is for this reason that I found it hard to sit with photography as a compelling medium. Likely it is because I have spent so much of my career trying to pry apart the meaning of a photograph on its own, hardly having paid attention to the caption, despite Sontag's counsel. I read this excerpt in Sontag many long years ago, and it means so much more to me now because I have pivoted from pure representationalism within art toward the importance of an artistic context. I'd argue, rather forcefully, that many photographers in the modern age have fallen victim to this - the caption gives context when we are flitting through a language of images, but it does not give meaning. What give meaning is narrative, or 'story'. I discuss this with friends in private - that we think art is somewhat devoid of meaning in an era that allows art to be generated with abandon, and that because of this artists who create with the desire to imbue their works with meaning are found not to be palatable by the wider market. I find this to be true; it is art without caption - however I do think that the idea of the 'caption' exists beyond the bounds of that which we choose to describe as simply words below the page. It is the context itself, that within which any art or expression exists in order to confer upon that art meaning; the same is true of history and its impact on the medium, It is less that caption is that which makes the image important and more that caption confers upon the image its context. What is context? In Spain, my partner and I go to see Joan Miró's permanent exhibits at the Fundació, and our (maybe my) impression is that his work must exist in the context of the history that creates it. I stand in front of Miró's 'Painting on White Background for the Cell of a Recluse', where he sat with the canvas for weeks before deciding how to strike the line across the panels. There is another where he did the same, but there was as well a red, a blue, and a yellow splotch in the painting. Miró is the perfect example of the artist whom others may think representationally is not one who had skill, but once one understands the full breadth and constraint required to do what he did, it becomes obvious that anyone with that impression is wholly mistaken. Particularly in its context, Miró's work exists by requirement in the context that produced it. The form of expression he chose as a skilled artist resulted in work that reflected the time that caused him to create the art, and it is in dialogue with the time in which it was created. This cannot be overstated, because without this context, the art may feel good, but it has no valence. Valence is probably important to define, here - because it's a chemistry term rather than one used in the production of art, but I think it maps. Valence is the degree to which the relationship between what is being witnessed and what actually happened are made visible to the viewer. The art I created never really held valence specifically because I stopped short of giving my art the context it needed for it to have a relationship with the narrative I was hoping to translate. A friend of mine recently had an exhibit of their own, commendably presented in a public forum at the center of many other exhibits. I'm excited for them, and the images are very good. I can tell the body of work is going to do very well, in the traditional sense. But while it was poignant and the captions were well written, I felt the presentation of the narrative was insufficient; the captions did not do what we need them to as an observer. I was not moved. I don't know if he had the chance to talk about the images and why they are important. This is where I diverge with Sontag - I do think that while the caption is important, the narrative and method of presentation for the context that they offer is doubly so. Captions without the effort to seat themselves within narrative lack valence. When we as viewers can sense the valence between what we are consuming and what we are meant to feel, we are moved; we can sense the meaning behind what we are witnessing. The ability to sense meaning in an image due to the valence offered by its attachment to context is what probes deeper into the emotional landscape of how we overlap our own experiences (emotions and their triggers) and the experiences of others (eliciting similar emotions, but for different reasons). As an example, there is a difference between reading something in a book that has images (in which the images supplement the writing) and a photo book. A photo book or a monograph of an artist's work on a subject matter is inherently vain, but that vanity has it's own motive, and I think is what I find detestable about the caption when used not to motivate the viewer toward understanding and caring about the subject, but instead only to share a perspective. Sharing only a perspective without an opinion attached to it is, in its own right, weak. It's, per Kundera, 'graphomanic'. A writer who uses their images to supplement the work that they are doing not with the desire to compel one or all people toward action but rather simply to 'tell on their lives' are not giving their images this desired valence, rather they are engaging in an indulgent act. I am not arguing that this should be avoided, to be clear - there is importance to the manner in which the caption is brought to someone's attention. Meaning - I think it's important to examine how a caption is used to invoke meaning in the context of a photograph. If Sontag is right, the caption is necessary because it's meant to draw a viewer into the story that the image is depicting. --- Sontag's claim: the caption determines what an image means Your extension: the caption is necessary but insufficient — narrative is what actually confers meaning Define valence: the degree to which the relationship between what is witnessed and what produced it is made visible to the viewer Miró as proof that context transforms perception (skilled artist whose work is meaningless without the history that produced it) Your friend's exhibit as proof that absence of narrative flattens perception (good images, good captions, but no valence) The personal pivot: why photography felt insufficient as a medium — it made it too easy to stop at the image The implication: in an era of abundant images and scarce context, the artist's real work is building the narrative, not making the image

I wasn't going to write about this, but I think it probably makes more sense than it doesn't. Before anything else, the UCI ruling does a ton of harm to a sport whose inclusivity I have seen evolve extensively over the last couple of decades. When I first entered athletics, I was hesitant for the exact reasons that the UCI is now choosing to rule around - I just don't want that much attention on me when I'm doing something I love. Even though I'm not racing anymore (and I was never anyone significant when I was racing), this ruling confirms the feelings I'd been having around competition in the first place - dissuading people from participating in the ways that they can or should, and overall polluting the sport. What I could understand is a nuanced argument made around parties expressing a nuanced opinion, but that's not what we got. We got men (once again) expressing their opinions on what can and should be done with women's bodies. I'm in running now, because running makes me feel free, because it makes me feel less anomalous - but as I've started to compete recently, I've started to wonder to myself ifthere's not a possibility that at some point they'll jump back and decide I can't compete anymore. Do I think I'm good at the sport? Sure - the reason for this is that I have worked for it. I train five days a week, I go to a personal trainer, I have a group of like-minded athletes who I compete alongside me and push me to be as good as I can me. This is the heart of sport, in the end, or at the least it's meant to be. Competition is a chance to challenge yourself - less about competition against others and more about competition against oneself. The greatest athletes that I've known approached the sport this way - taking on the challenge for themselves first, with the results second. While there is competition between people in sport, part of the effort is to show some degree of sport[person]ship between parties, in order to encourage the notion that competition is not about measuring yourself against others. I think that's why this ruling rubs me particularly wrong - the possibility of having to look as this as a question of 'fair competition' feels like an incomplete take on the question. Fair competition is a question moving through the field to evaluate from the position of those involved as to what is fair. I know any number of cis athletes who compete alongside their trans counterparts - and it's never them who stand and complain about athletic performance, because all of us understand the work that goes into being an athlete in the first place. None of this was ever about trying to win. It was about competing alongside people we admire and being understood on the same level for the effort made. This being true, I don't understand why it's the place of a collective of men to make decisions about women's bodies, cis, trans, or otherwise. To categorize anyone's ability based on their experience is to reduce us to those experiences, and if anything, Caster Semenya's recent victory in the sport should be an indication that the experience and reality of gender are varied enough such that we shouldn't be asking these questions, we should be allowing people to be who they are. For the love of the sport, I'd have expected that there was better measurement and adequate consideration given to people's lived experiences rather than any degree of armchair science that studies athletics. This is maybe where I have gotten the most frustrated - in an era of rationalism, we now like to turn to numbers to justify our decisions, instead of remembering that we are social creatures and that because of this there is probably more value in actually speaking to one another. Our experiences don't lie, which is probably why I feel, personally, so much more solidarity with the experiences of my cis counterparts. We share so much overlap and the further I move through my life of not being believed, not being listened to, not being attended to, and not being respected, the more I understand that we share these experiences because they are the same experiences. If we were to be listened to, maybe this might be understood in the ways that would resolve situations like this. I can only speak for my experience, and I'd hope I would hear more from all those who have comparable experiences, from all those who I know share fragments of mine and want to share their own. Rationalism is a tool, not an ideological cudgel with which to make decisions; the decisions are meant to be separate from the information that we use to support them, we are meant to weigh data against the consensus of public opinion in order to come to our conclusions. That's not what is happening here, unfortunately.

Photography functions in a fairly obvious sense: one points a camera at a world outside of oneself and imposes perspective on it through the action of taking a photograph. Despite this, life has had its way of imposing doubt on me as a photographer, and it's part of what caused me to walk away from the practice. However, that's not what I'm writing about today, and it's not what you're going to read about - it's just a lens through which we're going to discuss what itched at me when I was trying to leave photography behind and gave me my reasons for leaving. For a number of years, I thought photography couldn't do this. The reason I didn't was that I assumed photography was inherently self-limiting; an image is a trapped moment in time, a small death of the present: good images bewilder, great images sink into the fabric of the soul and beg us to wonder what else happened, or what should happen next. What I see a lot of these days is the These days, I see a lot of the first, and while I truly love the stories of those that have found a way to make money with a camera, my sense is that images that only serve an aesthetic purpose don't really compell us. If they do, an age that focuses on optics is one that tries fervently to flaunt our individuality, forcing the image-maker to consider the image as an extension of the self rather than an attempt at observation. Neither approach is necessarily the 'correct' one, but I do think that we have lost something when we consier images purely as a matter of perpective. Art is meant to ecoke a sense of awe, I think. Are we meant to believe that all matters of awe are purely at the hand of their creator? What happened to the conduit? I want to widen our perspective here a little bit: when I refer to this later phenomenon, I'm speaking to an artistic moment that I believe to be the motivating force between the work of many artists: it is as though by the mere act of creating, the artist is speaking to something larger than themselves. We have a variety of names for the impetus that comes over us in the act of creation that compells us forward I have tapped the pressed-foam ceiling tiles of this feeling a few times in my life, and I have never known exactly what to do with it. I backed away from it for a period of years, for instance, due largely to the fact that despite the fact that I knew I was on to something, I didn't really know what to do with what I was 'on to'. It's as though in the moment one realizes that what they are creating might actually hold greater significant beyond the self, it imposes an existential dread or a great reckoning: what is this 'source' from which we are drawing in our most creative moments, and what does it mean for us to have been the person who dredged it up? The feeling is electric: it's so striking as to feel one has struck diamonds or the elixir of life itself. The unfortunate conclusion to which some arrive here is, I think, the source of my complaint. I don't like it when an artist's response to having created something significant and memorable is to immediately think 'well then, I found a way to make something beuatiful, therefore I am the source of this beautiful thing'. Don't get me wrong, I do believe that every artist deserves credit for the work they do to perfect their craft, but we as artists are not the source of the art we create. I say this with impunity: artists are mere custodians for what life inspires within us. The core argument I'm trying to make is this: I think great things take time, but they also take commitment to tamping down the hubris of believing that we are the reason they are happening. Inspiration requires that we pay attention to the world, either as a participant or as an observer, and I think that the greatest work we see surrounding us comes from having sit still long enough to take in the greater wonders of life and to have made something of them. As with every self-doubting photographer, mulling over the importance of the image brings Sontag's quote from Regarding the Pain of Others to mind: " To the militant, identity is everything. And all photographs wait to be explained or falsified by their captions. During the fighting between Serbs and Croats at the beginning of the recent Balkan wars, the same photographs of children killed in the shelling of a village were passed around at both Serb and Croat propaganda briefings. Alter the caption, and the children’s deaths could be used and reused."

The real question, I'd suppose, is whether or not the life I have lived has really gotten in the way of who I am. By most stretches, I've had a very accomplished career - there are not many people who can say that they worked with National Geographic and held a flash bulb over Tutankhamun's forehead, there are not many who can say that they became the CEO of a tech project only 6 years later, or that whilst doing either of these things I ran several marathons and eventually several ultramarathons. My most stretches, I can respect the assumption that I've been able to make do with the experience that I've had, and that I'm doing just fine. However, the issue is not whether or not I've been able to achieve things - it's that I've been able to accomplish these achievements despite what I would consider to have been fairly significant hurdles in the large scope of things, and possibly even because of them. I'd make the argument that the reason I'm able to pull off the massive efforts that I have in the past is because I have more experience putting up with a bad experience than most people do, so when the time comes to choose some or other difficult experience, I'm already prepared by my experience with fear, disappointment, trial, and exhaustion to endure whatever amount of effort it takes to accomplish something. It does not devalue the achievement, in my regard, to acknowledge this; I am proud of the efforts I have made and what it has taken for me to achieve them, and I will continue to take them on. In large part, they are the reason you are reading this body of text which otherwise I probably wouldn't have written due to a mild shame I feel in recognizing the exhaustion I have felt, time and again, so soon as stopping for a moment to understand the path charted toward the present. Partially, the reason for my inclination to beat around the bush with 'how hard it has been to be me' is because of what I've been able to accomplish, and since what I've been able to accomplish has been substantially more than that most people can lay claim to, I usually push the hurdles and challenges to the side as though they aren't quite deserving of the attention this letter demands. However, if there hurdles to be acknowledged, there are three: I moved 9 times across 8 countries before I was 16; I have diagnosed, unmedicated, yet well managed ADHD; I am of mixed latina ethnicity; I am a transgendered woman. I'd pause here for a moment and recommend that you ask yourself, before reading any further, if any of these three call up biases in you. I could understand it, especially given the current stretch of time in which you have read those words, maybe more for the latter two than the first - identity politics has run rampant in our society to such a degree as to devalue the impact of these experiences into a normalizing minimization - but I feel these experiences frame the brunt of why it is I have taken until the age of 35 to follow the academic career I'm now seeking to pursue. Further, I lament that they are the case, because under the ideological regime with which we now examine people, I find that utilizing words like 'transgender woman' and 'ADHD' are highly reductive on the basis of the exact biases I am asking you, the reader, to interrogate. The primary affliction of being a third-culture kid is probably less commonly understood, as is being of mixed ethnicity, so they deserve priority - particularly due to their relationship with the latter experiences and how they have framed my career so far, academic or otherwise. I've lived in the Netherlands, France, Canada, Connecticut, Dubai, Luxembourg (two different homes), Italy, and finally Georgia, where I graduated high school. What this meant, for me, was that I moved between 8 different school systems before finally graduating high school in the last county in the United States to desegregate (Forsyth County did not have a significant black population until 1987, and when I graduated in 2008, my AP physics course was taught out of the answer book chained to the wall at the back of the classroom). It meant that by the time I graduated high school, the particular frustration I had to endure was the lack of compatibility between international systems of academic evaluation for mathematics that resulted in, on one hand, my taking algebra and trigonometry three different times in three different countries, and on the other hand, a general apathy for continuing on with mathematics. It meant then when I got to university and had almost forgotten the time I'd spent huddled across a table with my primary school friends, excitedly competing with one another to get to the end of our algebra problems. It meant that overall, my parents hadn't thought that I should prioritize this sort of thinking - so I didn't. I went to college, I got a degree that I am proud of, but that didn't require substantial quantitative reasoning beyond statistics. I regret this. University presented me with another difficulty - throughout much of my adolescence I had kept a secret. Queerness prior to the 2010s wasn't publicly spoken on in meaningful ways outside of a fight for acceptance, and trans people especially were not spoken about with any degree of respect; the secret I had been keeping, and that I would continue to keep until I was 27, was that while raised as a man, I am a woman. In university, I tried to address this a few times - I spoke to counsellors in free sessions offered by the school to see if it was something that was real, that it wouldn't be dismissed out of hand. Being that I went to school in the state of Georgia, I wasn't given any meaningful support there, and I buried it deeper. This exacerbated another part of my identity that I've had to struggle with, in the form of my ADHD. ADHD is an anxiety disorder - as much as people understand it as an issue of attention (it turns out that ADHD is not a lack of attention, but rather an abundance of it), it is usually attention that flickers between subjects on the basis of an underlying nervous tendency. Keeping my gender identity under wraps during my college years meant that while I was able to get through college, it was against a tide of anxious repression that often deeply impacted my schoolwork, meaning that the only good semesters I had were those where I was able to grit my teeth and ignore the storming unrest inside of me to make progress on my grades. This never fixed the depression that comes with repression, and usually the depression won, more semesters than not. The unfortunate result of this is that by the time I graduated school, the parts of me that needed the most attention weren't given what they asked for, and what I was supposed to be doing in the mean time suffered for it. I continued on with repressing my identity for another 5 years after graduation, struggling through the impact it had on my ability to pursue more complex work, and I succeeded despite it; I had a burgeoning photography career, taking me to incredible places that I was probably only safe to visit with people perceiving me as a man. I don't regret these experiences, they are some of the most memorable I've ever had - but I know that my safety was protected in large part by the gender identity that I was showing the world at the time. When I turned 27, I had just terminated a relationship with someone I had tried to come out to, and I was ready, finally, to address what was going on within me. I didn't want to continue shouldering the burden of the effect it had on who I was - and the act of telling the truth to myself and then beginning to tell it to everyone else opened me up to everything else about myself that I could address. I was also fortunate - in 2017 people were truly beginning to speak about transgender people as though we should be recognized more legitimately, and with this came a comfort that coming out would bring me closer to myself, and that my identity was legitimate without being some sort of idealization of gender. It is remarkable for me to look back on the effect that coming out had on me. I pivoted entirely within two years of coming out: I stopped being in photography, I worked very hard on understanding my ADHD and how to address it, and I pivoted to a quantitative career. I look back on the history that got me here and I acknowledge that I had a very interesting successful career despite my burdens, but that I am now doing what I actually care about. I am incredibly proud of this progress, because it isn't something that many have the privilege (and honestly, the stubbornness) on which to hold fast. I have now been a female CEO, which in itself in an achievement, and the brunt of the reason for this was because I have had the experience that brought me into the present, a knowledge of a patriarchal world that disadvantages those it is not made for. Learning from my burdens made me better at what I do. I think this last point bears repeating: I am proud of who I am, but I also recognize that everything I've had to deal with,--either isolated to my experiences of life in having moved so many times, in what society has only recently become comfortable with accepting-- is still a challenge. It's made worse today by an ideological regime that seems to be resistant to this sort of flexibility and acceptance, but we know why this is: when new truths are made evident, it is always the case that the dominant power structure will resist change before it is made inevitable. I have won against odds and with the support of a family, friends, and a society that is coming to accept people with my experience, and I am glad for having it, but I also know it is a major factor in what has prevented me from pursuing who I now aim to be.

Fundamental intelligibility is a predicating requirement that a concept be intelligible at first pass - meaning that if someone is to understand what any given thing does, it does not require any additional effort. A quick example of this would be the term 'heart attack' going through the process of synthesis before and after the dawn of modern medicine, with the term 'heart-attack' being itself fundamentally intelligible without further examination: a heart-attack is the act of the heart being attacked by some affliction, leading to a complete understanding of what is happening. Other examples might be 'stop sign' or 'head-phone', where there is no additional logic needed in order to understand something. --- Related to:

The act of synthesis is the composition of information into the most important concepts for understanding. A good understanding is as follows, using the fundamentally intelligible term 'heart-attack': 1. Prior the explicit knowledge of what happens in the body when the some one dies of a heart-attack, people simply died without anyone understanding why this was the case. 2. Some early physicians explored the problem, establishing a knowledge of the human body and recognizing what happens the heart fails. 3. This lead to deeper knowledge of things like the heart as a muscle, the nerves that lead signals to the heart, and what happens when these structures are interrupted 4. The physicians use this knowledge to interpret the event at hand, leading to descriptions such as myocardial infarction cardiac arrest etc. 5. This knowledge is then synthesized by the public to be understood as a fundamentally intelligible concept - the 'heart attack', wherein the event of someone dying from this condition is the result of the 'heart being attacked'. 6. As a result, the knowledge has been synthesized into the term 'heart-attack' . --- Related to:

I want more people to talk about forgetting. I want more people to think about the past and recognize that what they remember is only what was necessary, and that their lives are something that comes from the construction of a personal narrative, not from what we specifically chose to remember. I think this is what troubles me the most - that at some point we conflated the idea of memory with the idea of permanence and because of this caught ourselves in the trap of remembering everything. Now, overloaded by the burden of this sort of rationalist thinking, we're trying to work our way back to a place that can make more sense of the world using heuristics rather than what we've been told to do - attempt to keep it all in our heads and then fault ourselves with the loss of what wasn't important. A friend of mine sent me an article this morning about how it is that Gen Z people filter for information in the modern age, that it's no longer about the process of trying so hard to filter for truth and instead filter for what it is that their peers say about the subject, because truth has become so maleable. It purports thats what we used to consider sources of truth are now so lacking in credibility that we've reached a point where an entire generation has essentially written off the idea of traditional journalism, making way instead for something that approximates relative truth, or what one could call 'truth by local consensus'. Even the more current thinkers decry a state where this feels like something that should spurn concern rather than excitement - Klippenstein just wrote about it in his substack - but I find that there's something more fearful and less reasonable about taking this approach over, say, optimism. In some ways, the trend toward truth by local consensus heartens me - it points toward a distrust of authority that feels more democratic rather than one explicitly oriented toward institutional credibility. When we step back to take it in, this says more about the lack of credibility in institutions as it stands. There's some trepidation that can be had around the idea that local consensus can lead to disinformation as communities trend toward echo chambers that reflect back their own logic, but I have more optimism than this. I see those who participate in this form of truth-seeking as inoculating themselves against a firehose of institutionalized (mis)information - and it's this part that makes me think that maybe forgetting is something that we're supposed to do more of at the organismal level. To me, forgetting does not mean that information is being lost and can't be retrieved - it's something more nuanced than this, instead its a process of pruning information for what is actually relevant. This is why it rhymes with the process of seeking truth, but more importantly it is how humans participate in making sense of the world around us. Forgetting is the process of taking what is relevant and allowing ourselves to settle into what the current of time pulls away from us - and I think there's something to embracing this as a natural process. There are further implications to this that aren't so woo - thinking of forgetting in this way is valuable for practical application - and it's valuable to consider how this affects the landscape of logic that exists around how we create technology. Biomimicry was once (and should remain) a staple of forefront design, so there's no reason not to think about forgetting as an evolutionary process first and foremost (it literally is). The present era is one that focuses so much on storing boundless amounts of information from even deeper wells of truth, and this is, broadly, a deviation from how information is managed in most natural systems. No one can tell me that every permutation of a tree was important to an oak, and no one can tell me that all the ways that a river can run are important to the way that one particular river flows. All information is local and adapted to circumstance, and the fidelity of that information is a product of its relevance to the environment it's a part of, not the entire body of possibility that precedes it - this would be immensely inefficient. It's for this reason that I think forgetting is important - it's something that we need to learn how to do gracefully. Truth by local consensus is the human species adapting locally to the flow of information across the entirety of the internet. Zero-Knowledge Proofs are a mathematical repercussion of the same conclusion - a striving toward remembering only the truth that is relevant on the basis of the local information that proves it. Even the learning methodologies of the Machine Learning algorithms that support artificial intelligence depend on setting paths through knowledge, regardless of how their datasets can be polluted. It's not a question of doing so aimlessly - there's value in learning how to forget gracefully. Truth by local consensus is a form of adaptation, and on the landscape of an internet that by any measure of human history is still incredibly young, humans are still figuring out how to adapt to consuming more information in a week than someone 100 years ago might have consumed in their entire lifetime. It stands to reason that we need to learn to trust the process of forgetting and to learn how to do it in a way that doesn't compromise our ability to reason. There's also a finer point to put on this - I don't mean by any of my writing up to this point that you should throw caution to the wind and forget everything that you've learned. What I'm saying is that there's a significant cognitive burden in thinking that you have to remember it all, and this is not only unhealthy but is also something that you should release yourself from thinking you have to keep up with everything. We're not designed to think in terms of everything we've remembered, we're only meant to remember what is important to us based on the circumstances relevant to direct experience we have of living. Forgetting is a process of accepting that access to boundless information does not mean maintaining access it all. More expansively, it also means treasuring that which you do remember, because it is likely that the natural course of things is to remember that which is most important to you. --- : there's an irony in here mentioned in the article - that Google's technology called 'Perspective' filters these same comments for their own and stacks them against 'toxicity' - but this is a digression because truly what an abysmal reality we live in). : LM Sacasas speaks on this in his essays around 'Reading Ivan Illich' - particularly when speaking to the tendency for any institution to ossify and become an object that seeks to self-preserve rather than something that will always benefit those who created it. There is a way of remembering things called a 'memory palace'. It functions by taking a concept that one might seek remembering and setting aspects of what you seek to remember into a hypothetical physical space. For many people, the reason a 'palace' can function is because palaces have many hallways to walk through, but if one has enough the ability to conceptualize, it is possible to conceive of these hallways and their connections, offering one the ability to mentally traverse through the construction in order to see the connections between a concept otherwise difficult to remember. If this is true, New York City is my memory palace, and the thing I am constantly remembering is all the ways it has broken my heart. Winter in New York City is invariably difficult. If you have a normal job, it's a time that cascades forward from of the urgency of End-of-Year Reviews, the anxiety of unfinished work or a perceived lack of progress, a week or a few days of pause (whether taken or not) -- directly into the blank expectation of the a cold, gray new year. The only time New York is truly beautiful in the winter is when it snows, but specifically when it snows the sort of storm that buries cars to their windows. It is the only time that blank expectation of the new year actually looks like something to work with. Shortly thereafter, the snow starts to melt, the grey ponds of sludge at the heels of each block become obstacles. If you're lucky, it stays cold enough that instead you are forced into queues by walls of snow on either side in an attempt to the cross the street. I love New York City in Winter. The last time it snowed to this point, I remember people calling it a 'Snowpocalypse'. This was around 2014, I had just moved to the city, I was just over a year and a half out of college. I'd met the first love of my life. I was riding a bicycle everywhere in the city. It was the first time I heard the expression 'brick'. I learned it from a Facebook comment. The most recent time it snowed this way was this year. The intervening years brought nothing like this - none of the frozen river that accreted strange circular floes, nor the level of cold that made me respect the latitude of this city. I ran in shorts the entirety of the winter of 2024 into 2025. I remember thinking that the world was ending. When it snows in New York and they suspend Alternate Side Parking for weeks at a time, I can fool myself into thinking otherwise. The intervening years also brought me a sort of respectful understanding of a city that seems to take pleasure in making things difficult. I have had two careers here, and both have been successful. I have loved three women in the time I have walked, run, taxied, and bicycled across this city. Maybe four. I remember all of them by the places I pass by years after those loves ended. I'm reminded of the hurt constantly. New York has a way of reminding you to stay humble, and the shape of memory is in the buildings that don't disappear, until in some deep level of surprise you see dark green cladding wrap itself around one of your favorite pre-wars, where the Bulgarian man used to sit on the stoop every week, cigarette in hand, with a new Belgian Malinois he was training at his side. Full demolition. It never happens anymore, just like the snow never asking you to posthole your way to the closest grocery store because your hubris made you think you wouldn't need to replace the toilet paper after the storm. One of the other facts of living in New York is the acute awareness that everything is happening around you, all the time. Even in January. The anxiety of feeling trapped in the mire of grey sludged winter in New York is the reason people leave when it gets cold. That history of the 'snowbird' started here. Miami wouldn't be what it is without that snow. Anyone who is too poor to head south or to ship their skis to Aspen instead is subjected to the anxious pell and uncomfortable mell of created expectations, of setting oneself up for what we expect to come next. Meanwhile, this winter, I was unemployed. It's the longest I haven't worked; I careened into burnout in my second career after not feeling like there was a point to the first, and that snow that finally fell feels like the blank sheet I need to think about the third. Resting hasn't been easy for me, but it's given me time to think. Depression is a symptom of needing to recuperate from trauma. I extracted myself from a career that was sucking the soul out of the intentions I had for myself. I came out of it on top, but it left me listless. The palace of this city is the number of times I, while bundled to the gills with my giant black dog, have run into my ex walking with her partner-now-fiancé is as though this city doesn't want me to forget that I was taught something. Eleven years since the last time it snowed. I am a different person than I was then. Only partially for the better.
