I have to remember what I have learned and why it is important to read theory and fiction. "You should read more" comes from a place of deep misunderstanding about the generalized unrest people it is not a question of a life lived in the context of new ideas, but rather the people can or should be learning constantly. It's my loose contention that learning constantly provides us with the tools to deal with the problems with me encounter, but I am deeply cognizant of the teleological gap that arises in not having one's own needs, met at a basic level and the encouragement to educate oneself. After all, we cannot fill stomachs with words. This is maybe the place from which to make the most significant inquiry of what uses education if the utility of this education cannot be implemented due to systemic barriers placed in the path of resilience the pen is only mightier than the sword given the paper on which to communicate ideas without the means to transmit into action, the philosophy, we hope to inspire people with violence seems well positioned to take the shape of action little inspired by anything other than a desire to cease or ease one's suffering. It is often addressed in films this way how do the well-intentioned deviate from the morality when pinned like a fly to the Styrofoam backboard of a world so feebly built to support us? Morality is in this case situation--we can only build better worlds if we have the means to. But we do continue to fight. We remember that those who have fought longest and hardest are those who continue to do so when every other person ceases to this is because it is the case that people who have never felt safe, will forever stay the course of seeking such safety.--and it is my contention that apathy(including my own) likely comes from a place of significant privilege. That is--I know I will be fine and this is the reason I have the security to feel ease: I can only do so because I can consider the absurdity of having to make choices to keep myself alive, further under emphasizing that I experienced an increased degree of general attendance in the circumstance of any threat to my well-being. I will in almost every frame of reference (save one glaring circumstance, obvious to those who know me well) be fine, probably. This is the reason I can sit back on my heels and feel frustrated not with whether or not I have the means to survive, but instead how I specifically would like to survive. Meaningfully it very much, could be the case that the reason I possessed the self-awareness to acknowledge this truth is due to the singular and unique circumstance of my own personal oppression--maybe I would otherwise be completely ignorant to my security if I didn't have to face one particular imposing fear upon my existence that call into question the security otherwise experience. I don't know because I only know my own experience to start with. However, this last observation is important and serves to represent the final tail-eating point of what I write here. I can only speak to my own experience and it's commonality with that of others.--but I could not conceive of the relatability of my experience to parallels or lack there of without seeking out that same parallelism. It is critically this seeking out that impart to the act of reading and learning about both the real and fictional experiences of others it's critically importance. I may not be conscious of it, but every time I imagine the existence of the "other", I glean some small understanding of the parallax between our identities, and my hope is that with each of the perambulations into the possibility space existing between experiences, I am opening up just a bit more to the possibility within me to engage in a sympathetic residence with them I do not know if this is true, but it is what I like to believe. A combination of qualitative appreciation between the differences of shared realities, and most importantly, the sheer obligation to utilize my imaginative skill, requires me an obligation to as well grow as a person. This, if among less weight and morally oriented, justifications, is why I read. I read to better understand myself, and to understand other others, and it works, more often than not. Better yet, I think (I think) it gives me hope. I'll close by invoking someone else's words from a book I needed to read when I did: Rebecca Solnit -

There is no unifying moment across all of this writing from the last week, from what I can tell. Some of it was in thinking about the artistry of words (the sidelong education found from the manner in which Powers' wrote "Playground") to the more hopeful notions of how we reshape our control of the planet. George Carlin once said that "The world doesn't care about you. Save yourselves!" implying that in the end, the world will not care about us when we are gone. Powers seems to have said the same thing. Arco, the movie I saw with Rachael this last Friday articulated the same post-disaster perspective: humans will eventually build islands in the sky to escape the destroyed surface of the planet in order to 'let the Earth rest'. The latter of these gives in to disaster - or upon reflectiion, they both do, if we're honest with ourselves. I think there is much to be done as a result. Today, even, I saw a news artcile showing that degradation claims on the effectivelness of solar cells over time have officially been debunked; solar cells appear to remain 80% efficient after several years of use, and the magnanimity of this result should be revelatory. In theory, it means that we can trust panels to proceed in their efficacy for longer term use than any nay-sayer might want to claim. These are the sorts of results from within a dismal present I try to pay attention to, while still consuming my fair share of the dismal. We should celebrate victories. However, it turns out that the interesting thing about victories is that most of them are really just a fight toward normalcy, so when we are victorious, it doesn't feel like much has happened. I've written about this before (not here, in another notebook maybe no one will ever read), but writers like Solnit are those we should probably be listening to if we're really to think about how we advance through the dismal present while still holding steadfast onto the flaming torch of Hope. I've been examining her work closely in this time because it is easy to come to the conclusion that there is no point in trying to fight. It's drawn, to me, the conclusion that maybe we should be listening to people who have already done the work. Solnit offers exactly this conclusion: we tend toward fighting for things to be normal. The issue constitutes of asking what it even means to express this normalct across teh scope of human (or even natural) experience. It is difficult to distill the notion of "normal" into relateable terms that don't leave someone else's definition out in contrast -- but I'd make the claim that maybe when we contine on the endless march toward panyt parallel freedoms, we are really trying to bring things into stability. I think what I'm arguing here is that in teh scope of long marchest totward freedom, it isn't a question to any one victory or set of victories that the outcome might be normalcy. By another word: peace. All stories we tell charge toward the vision and desire of a society, one seeking out this final point of 'greatness' that is really just the chance to live a normal life. Unfortunately some permutations of this 'great society' (often those coming from those already in power) do think in such zero-sum terms. For some, 'great societies' must always come at the cost of others freedom, rather than the fortune of all within tolerant outcomes. Such thinking is reductive, of course-- and doesn't consider the modalities of a world that treats resources as abundant under the same regime as intellectual abundance, at best becoming narratives of conquest-as-path-to-freedom that only think in terms of scarcity. This worldview emerges from a place of fear, and is ultimately a short-term plan. We might be able to harness the power of the sun. WQe might be able to avert the worst - given the time, intention, and effort of telling the right story. Thinking only in terms of local victory (said local freedom) is myopic. We are beyond the myopia of regionalism as an exclusive perspective because it is too late to create a world of isolatio; we bulldozed through that possibility when we invented the steam engine, then the telephone, then the electrical grid, then the internet. The world's trash washes ashore the most remote island beaches. I'm not sure we can say the same about AI yet - but I do think that when we come to the point that all knowledge is available to everyone on the basis of nothing more than a bare-bones device that hosts all of human knowledge, there's no going back to locality. The only version that exists is bucolic; it doesn't exist except for in the imagination, or in the world that reflects values that acknowledge the uncommon scale at which any one person can truly affect the lives of any one other person across a connected planet. I'm casting stones after the latter. In the typical syntopic sense of any good reader, the books that I've been carving through with intention reflect a parallel conclusion: what really matters is the story we are telling ourselves in response to our conditions.Solnit says this from the position of a participant, someone who has themselves shown up in situations requiring her help. Powers does this from a position of theory, but his writing seems to inspire attention to the outer reaches, where the effects of human hubris seem to make themselves felt. Powers, however, also reflects back what George Carlin says: if you want to save it all, save it for yourself. The world won't care whether or not you do, it will keep dancing whatever game it's got in mind a good while yet. It means that the reading I did in the last week oriented toward a common outward-facing conclusion: most of the mistake we make or the harm we intent to commit, are largely the result of the story we are telling, either to ourselves or to others. To get specific, 'Playground' has Rafi - a caricature of blackness explained away by being an AI fabrications of his best friend's memories (maybe for good reason, we'll see) lives in competition with his surroundings. This could go one of two ways if we draw it out to its conclusion: either he wins and feels self-satisfied, or he loses and redoubles his efforts to win the next game. This is the dismal conclusion - but there is a third way he can play: continuously, playing forever, never actually reaching a conclusion, so that he can avoid ever having to stop playing. His life is framed through the escape from conditions, and the constant pursuit of this escape is blatantly sisyphean. Maybe he is happy, but to do so at the cost of achieving normalcy and surviving into whatever calmer version of existing victory could provide could cost all the energy it requires to do anything else. If Sysiphus is indeed happy, is he ever hungry? Do we conveniently leave this out of our narratives for freedom? Maybe he would have been happy working for the CTA, but it killed his mother, the same way it might have killed him, tablet in hand, reviewing for the nth time his own thoughts; the cause of deal that kills most black men: a heart attack, for both of them. Beating, again and again, frightened of life, until the stress of that repetition exhausts them both. It may well be that the outcome I have drawn is that the stories we tell need their conclusions. I have not read many books that conclude otherwise: Hernan Diaz's "In the Distance" comes to ming -- but the stories we tell still need their victories to bring about at rest the ability to punctuate the local with the need to survive, given stress. Tolkien thought this was the reason that there was no point in writing more about Middle Earth - peace breeds eventual unrest in the hearts of men, and they'll find something new to fight about. The charge of the unknown is littered like shorelines with the patient labor of exploring it. It is both a fog and an interminable dark. On the way, we do discover beautiful things, and capricious conclusions might come from that beauty. These things were there whether or not we had found them, and they are not ours to keep, even when we act like they are. Solnit's answer is that the rewriting of history is an act of reconciliation. We can change the story we tell in order to better respect those it affects, having concluded, but as well to honor these affected and those who took action against or toward those effects. Here, I think Powers has little to say. I heard he did a press tour for the book that oriented toward saving the oceans. I'm not sure why: he seemed in Playground to think this is a fantasy some AI will tell us to placate the end, a reality we can escape by telling ourselves an alternate history. This is maybe nothing more than escapism - but I think this is typical of Powers: skilled as he may be at coming up with a story, his most notable works offer a concerning conclusion that maybe the only path forward is annihilation and slow remove. So does Arco. Solnit looks as the rubble and says instead 'how can I help?' It is ironic that this is the ultimate conclusion of which Powers convinces us, because we could hope some of his character believe otherwise. Evelyn doesn't, despite her love of the sea - she spends most of her career in teh selfish pursuit of observation and cataloguing. Nowhere in the book does Powers descrive what sahe is doing as 'activism' or 'advocacy'. Maybe Powers does think the world will keep spinning without us - but I think it is short sighted in nearly an ignorant and dangerous sense to sculpt a reader's attention toward a subject that matters and conclude that 'well, it's probably all going to die anyway, allowing all of his characters to continue on in the same vein of vague individual humanistic pursuit. Solnit doesn't do this because she's actually seen what people can do. From what I can tell Powers hasn't done much but stand by, observe, drain out a conclusion, then cry about its beauty through beautiful prose, never having taken his own conclusion to heart as a course of action. It is the stories we tell which help us understand how to do better. Beautiful as Playground is, -- as a work of literature, that is --, it is not an act of advocacy. It's an observation, maybe made a little too close to the subject matter to be respectful of it. I should be clear, and I do so because I mean so genuinely: I am not saying that Powers is a poor writer - but at the heart of the writing, he makes the same mistake most men do: they see the problem, grow conscious of the cause (usually them), then make little headway on actually preparing a solution. I think he knows this, too -- he is self aware enough to articulate the perspectives of minorities despite his whiteness and gender, and he is genuinely skilled in guiding the reader to some conclusion or other: that being different from the people for whom society is built is difficult, and escaping that difficulty is harder than not having to live with it. Than being prototypically 'normal', that is. Those observations written into character hardly go anywhere, however: Evie realizes she's a lesbian. So what? Her husband dies, her children no longer exist to her, and nothing happens. Rafi dies of blackness, maybe. So what? There is not redemptive quality to this happening, it's merely a sad outcome. The residents of Makatea are smarter than globalistic noble savage perspectives of ther capacity to overcome conditions. So what? We don't know what happens next when Ina, who isn't even from Makatea (an emphasis Powers himself hamfists into a commentary on being third culture) gets all the money that Todd Keane leaves her. This conclusion, far more than the 'gotcha' nature of Playground's conclusive arc, is what most frustrated me in hindsight. It shares the same disappointment I felt in reading the Overstory: after absolutely living in these books rich with detail, characters, settings, and thought-provoking risk - none of these provoked thoughts really concluded in anything. They don't go anywhere. I didn't learn anything. (well, that's not true, I did learn about oceanography's relatively recent inclusion into the scientific record) If literature is meant to convince us not only of the relateability of the human experience but as well to provoke new ideas, Playground only does one of those things. I was deeply affected by the most human aspects of his writing,and for this I want to extend Powers immense credit as a scholar of letters -- but to couch this relateability in the landuage and context of needful chance without drawing out a conclusion or even a lesson in this other, more pressing dimension is careless and again, specifically dangerous. It as a result becomes nothing more than thoughtful observation and unfortunately (yes, I'm going to say it) exactly as flat and predictable as what any other self-proclaimed conscious white man might have come to as a conclusion. It is advocacy without action. I'm not surprised to realize this, bathing in the afterglow of what I truly would consider a work of art. I've been steadily drawin my own conclusion that even the most compassionate of those who observe the world from a position of (granted, unelected) power don't know what future exists beyond willfully ceding it. They lack the imagination because it does not progress the only story they have ever been told, or that they tell themselves. I also want to express my own compassion for coming to this conclusion: it is terrifying, bewildering, and altogether stymying to realize that maybe you were actually the baddie this whole time. That's as far as most of the culpable can g. It requires a staggering amount of workl to reconcile; and people in power are used to having other people do that work for them. Playground is destines to bear that same tragic subtitle of many period works; it is a product of its time: a time in which men are realizing that they caused all the failure that is steadily being brought to shore by the tide, but still haven't quite come up with what they should do in response. So they do what all the hopeless are wont to doing: nothing at all, making art out of scraps, when maybe what they should have done was keep listening.

I do have a certain fear for men. I think broadly the attitudes of Adrienne Rich and Sontag and all of those we look up to with so much zeal was the right one - that we as women do not have the responsibility to care for men. I agree with this. When the male gender has been in a position of control and power for so long then are caused to lose this power at which point the entire gender flails in public in some display of disaparagement and self-pity - we as women, again, are not responsible for this flailing. We do not need to coddle them. Yet I still fear for them: I do find myself hoping that if we have abandoned them in the ways we have chosen to do in the last fifty years since the turning of feminism, we must pay at least some attention to what they have done in response to this abandonment. Not as a question of responsibility, but rather as a responsive measure, if nothing else. The reason for this is that I don't think it is right to think that we can utterly abandon the social fabric that has shaped modern society (read: I am writing this from the West, so I can only speak to how it has shaped the West), we do in some senses have a responsibility to steel ourselves and our children to the impact of men not knowing what to do with the assertion of will by women over society. Read: we have made tremendous progress, as women. What I mean by this is that today, we are debating not whether or not women are equal (we are not, there is still work to be done) but whether or not some women are 'women enough' to be included in the canon of womanhood. What a privilege, comparative to the progress that has been made, and to our general standing in the annals of time, across our societies. Not only can women vote, but we have earned many more needful freedoms, and we have far more freedom to orient toward so many other forms of success. It is magnificent! Women are solidly represented across the workforce (if unequally in terms of profession, but as I said, there is work to be done here). However we do not yet earn more than our 'counterparts', despite the rumors that some think we do. Presently, the work to be done still has women overrepresented in low-wage jobs, which skews the data southward in terms of total money time women have to work in order to make as much as their male counterparts, with the glaring impact of bonuses making up for the largest disequaling for closing the gap - men are rewarded for their work at a level that women have few ways of fighting for. Despite this the 'controlled gap' (measured as an averaging of women/men rated against equal qualifications and jobs) brings the gap much closer, which is great! However the former gap is usually described as the 'opportunity gap', reflecting how much harder it is, generally, for women to seek these same opportunities available to men. That is to say, women are in a better position than ever before, but there is still much to work on - and it is not the purpose of this essay. What I seek to write about instead is the importance of paying attention to what then men 'do' when they are abandoned. I fear for the fact that when men are 'abandoned' they do not know what to do, chiefly when a part of a society that has structured itself around the servile role of women in relation to men. this is why men are pining for a previous era. There is a book that I think of often; the book is the origin of the phrase 'paradigm shift'. Thomas Kuhn wrote this book in the 7-'s, in the wake of a scientific reimadining of reality iunder the advent of relativity and quantum technologies. Whet he discerned was that when a society is fiven enough information to change its mind, it will resist the urge to do so until the fate of the change is inevitable. I think we are in this time. I think we are in this time because as e watch men capriciously try toremake the world into what they had wanted it to be, they are doing so in response to what they most fear: the loss of their power. They fear the possibility that they might have to be responsible for themselves, and they fear that the order that was established which alloed thm not to have to make that effort is an event that they will have to respond to - and so they have handily rejected it, trying to bring in the previous order. The really cool thing about Kuhn is that he believes paradigm shifts are inevitable, no matter how much rejection the system tries to push upon the opposition to the norm. He believes that when there is a systemic rejection to a sort of science by the zeitgeist, this is an inoculating gesture before the system is forced to assimilate in the new norm and progress forward. Because of this, I am optimistic, but I am still concerned. I am concerned because I don't want men to flail. I am seeing certain kinds of men appear that people are calling 'performative' and my immediate reaction is to exclaim 'even when they are trying, they are wrong? what do you want from them?' I see them and they give me hope because performance is all we have to cause change. At some point pretension gives way to the performance becoming the norm. In his work 'Pretentiousness: Why It Matters', Dan Fox makes a compelling argument that outlines exactly this requirement - it is important if not an obligation of every person to perform what it is that they expect to be. Why should men not 'perform' in this way? The performance gives way to actually acting the right way, if even there is a period of time where this performance does not take hold. I am optimistic because watching the power system flail feels just as it should. It has collateral damage, as with any flailing. However, I do think the flailing is an indication. What I am worried about is that the men who don't follow the change find themselves entrenched and depressed because they are depressed, and this is the more terrifying component of it all. Angry men are violent in their desire to have the right to be violent, but it doesn't mean that they will win.

Jobs are search problems it's important to make yourself visible and promote the work you do as part of who you are I don't really agree with this - because it means that in order to succeed, you can't merely be good at your job; you are also required to tell everyone that you're good at your job somehow. Some people are not able to do that, as much as we might aspire otherwise. "getting a job” [means] finding someone with a problem and convincing them you can solve it." the question becomes asking of oneself what problems one wants to solve rather than 'what do I want to do' I think this makes sense - 'a company is a group of people trying to make something happen in the world' "They have obvious jobs, which become job posts, and illegible jobs, which hover around the edges as unsolved tension." Core to this is asking oneself: What do I care about? Who is doing work I care about? What are they trying to make happen? Where are they stuck? What do I know ow to do, or what could I learn to do, tha would help? Who would be delighted, relieved, or intrigued if I showed up with something useful? Side doors create a different kind of signal because it shows you people who are not trying to work through traditional means, and might solve problems in non-traditional ways as well this is how you set yourself apart this is also the reason that the work with Prineha Narang - Meeting Prep shows me I was willing to solve her problems, and SHE saw that I was the sort of person who knows how to look at problems and understand how I might be able to solve them. There are two kinds of side doors: Outbound You put it out into the world that you're interested in working on x style problems by reaching out to the people that you want to work with you sent thoughts to founders / people you want to work with that are insights into what you think are their problems. this is how informational interviews can turn into work. you're getting information about their problems Inbound you put it out into the world that you want to work these problems by SHOWING people that you know how to solve them What kinds of 'bounds' to make "An essay can be a small ambassador for your mind." showing people through engagement is a great way to get noticed - it's a way of letting people know that you're paying attention and that you're thinking critically about the problems that they're encountering, then finally that you might be able of solving these problems in novel ways or with novel thinking. it's what sets you apart when there's a need to do so.

What is Quantum Computing? In the complicated sense, quantum computing is a system of computation that takes advantage of relativistic physics to drastically increase the processing power of computers. In a simpler sense, quantum computers are several times faster than their predecessors, and importantly that when saying they are several times faster, it's by orders of magnitude. A quantum computer can process information that would take a normal computer several hundred years in just a few hours. The implications is boggling, because that last sentence almost doesn't make sense. There's a law in computing (Moore's Law) that describes the accelerated growth of compute, also known as 'processing power'. In general, it had predicted the the speed of computation to increase substantially based on the silicon chips that had existed before, but quantum computing speed is essentially unprecedented to anyone other than those who literally work in the field of quantum computing. What was the breakthrough that happened this week? Historically, any time you have a massive increase in computing ability, you also have a required increase in the energy needed in order to use that processing power; faster processing speed means more things happening, and more things happening means more energy in the system. While breakthroughs in quantum computing over the last 15 years were astounding, they were generally tucked away as the success of energy-intensive laboratories at universities or the research division of companies. Recent historical quantum computers have been described as near-holy copper and glass artifacts extending several floors up into laboratories - not anything that could be described as accessible to the public. This week, however, Google gave notice of progress on their quantum solution, a chip known as 'Willow'. Willow proclaims to be 10^42 times more powerful than traditional silicon chips and is expected to be significantly more energy efficient, although precise comparative data on energy consumption has not been disclosed. What this means is that Google has essentially transformed the trajectory of Moore's Law into a vertical spike. If, with Willow, Google has made progress toward what is known as 'practical quantum computing' (which often implies more stable and efficient quantum processing), then quantum computing could eventually become a consumer-accessible product — something that those with the resources might one day be able to purchase. While this is unlikely to happen in the immediate future, it significantly reduces the technological and energy-related barriers required to meet the processing demands of the chip. What does it matter to Crypto? How is Crypto protected today? While this is a significant achievement in the progress of computation, it makes so many things possible that it's important to examine and explore the effects it has on many other industries. In particular, it has implications for what happens to encryption. In general, encryption is a technology based on code-breaking. It takes normal information and obfuscates, or 'encrypts' it using key information so that only a key holder can unlock it and understand the original contents. The point here is that the 'security' of encryption is mostly based on the time it would take to break a code - where 'breaking' a code essentially means 'trying things until you get the answer'. Encryption helps you guarantee that what you are looking at is the thing you intend to look at: if you know that you were sent information from only the person you intended to receive it from (even if it's just yourself), you know you are receiving or viewing the same information that was input. If you know no one else could affect that information in any way, this also guarantees that the information can't be tampered with. These two points combine to how crypto benefits from and is built around encryption. Crypto benefits from this on the principle that financial applications depend on an "agreed upon constant for unit value", or the idea that you can trust that your money is actually your money. Crypto was created because it turns out that if you trust a third party (banks) to hold your money and you don't retain control of what is done with it, they can go off and do things with it themselves. This is a component of what led to the 2008 financial crisis. Crypto itself is protected by encryption standards, the "time it takes to break a code and reveal information" as a safeguard for showing that the money you own is tied to a set of keys providing the evidence that the money is only yours and that you are the only person who can use it. Most of crypto is protected by SHA256 encoding, which would take 12 "unvigintillion" years to break (that's 1.27 with 67 zeroes after it). This means that with modern computation methods it is practically impossible to reverse a 'hash' (the encoding) in order to get the original result. It's this encoding that allows people to 'own' crypto - you can feel very certain that you are the only owner of information on the basis that you are the only person in control of the hash that secures your currency. Where quantum computing matters to crypto is in what it offers as an accelerant for processing power. Even though the 1.27x10^67 year limit is an inconceivably large number for 'breaking' SHA256, if you have a computational system that can increase computational efficiency by 10^42 over traditional silicon chips, then it now only takes 1.2710^25 years to break. Without getting into the numbers, what this means is that you go from traditional silicon being able to break crypto's encoding in 10^52 times more time than the age of the universe to quantum computing being able to break it in 10^14 times the age of the universe. That is a drastic improvement in computation; it means that Willow would take [data] less time to do the work. Roughly speaking, it means that while yes, Willow can drastically increase the speed at which crypto could be broken, it would still take several times the age of the universe to do it. That is a drastic improvement in computation; it means that Willow would take [data] less time to do the work, but at this end of the calculation, the time needed (orders of magnitude older than the age of the universe), there's almost no reason to deploy Willow on this technology in a way that could make tractable progress. It would simply still take too long. Could new Quantum Crypto emerge? It could--there are projects working on this, remarkably--but it's not a real threat.. At least, not until Willow or some other even better technology figures out how to get the time needed to break down the encoding down to an order of time that actually means something to humans. Humans have only been around for the last fraction of a millisecond that the universe has existed. Until Google can come up with something that can break encoding in a way that makes it a problem that we can worry about on our timescale (rather than the timescale of 'the age of the universe' then crypto will have to worry.

The concept of 'feeding the monkey' is the expectation that tasks are often someone's responsibility, but a manager's role is to assign these tasks a degree of initiative and to ensure that the monkey stays on the DR's back. The justification for this is that work on the manager's part can only happen if subordinates have ownership over their roles and responsibilities. Otherwise, ownership of tasks is constantly shifted to the manager for completion, such that the 'monkey' always ends up on the manager's back. Link: 'Who's Got the Monkey' - Walter Onckler Core question: Where is the monkey? Three kinds of management time: Boss-imposed time required, delegated tasks System imposed time required, active support within working group Self-imposed time Manager-originated, but also taken up by imposed time from DRs (but not required) discretionary time - remaining portion of a team's time. - The correct approach is to increase discretionary time by decreasing imposed time "Monkey on your back" means: Whose job is it to get this task done? - i.e work that a subordinate needs to get done being blocked resulting in a manager taking on the task, such that the 'monkey' leaves the subordinate's back and instead is on the managers. -- Key term then, do not let someone else make their work your job, because then you become the blocker. Burnout involves three distinct symptoms: energy depletion and exhaustion, depersonalization and cynicism, and reduced efficacy. Burnout Symptoms Energy Depletion and Exhaustion We have all had those days when it is hard to get out of bed in the morning and get started on work. We also know what it is like to push hard on a particular project and look forward to a few days off to recuperate. But the kind of exhaustion associated with burnout is more chronic and nonspecific. It doesn’t go away after a vacation, and it is not tied to a particular project or deadline. It feels like a persistent fog weighing you down mentally and physically. Depersonalization and Cynicism In addition to that kind of debilitating exhaustion, burnout is associated with feeling detached and distanced from a job or even becoming cynical about it. Importantly, burnout is associated with a change in those sentiments. For example, perhaps you are a doctor and you used to find great joy in helping others, but now you feel more numb, or less empathetic, toward your patients. You might even start to question whether anything you are doing is making a difference. In a business context, you might begin to feel disinterested in your work or start to question the motives and intentions of your company. Simply put, what used to motivate and inspire you about your job no longer has the same effect. Reduced Efficacy The third component of burnout is a drop in work performance. Perhaps you used to be great at your job and now you feel yourself slipping. It may not even be something that your boss or clients notice, but you know the difference in your work quality. Or you may be maintaining the same peak performance but at a greater cost: it now takes more work, more concentration, and more effort than before. ⤴️ Mark Mortensen [an associate professor at INSEAD] and I surveyed global executives in December 2019 and January 2020. At that time, 76 percent of the executives reported that they had difficulty making connections with their work teammates, and 58 percent agreed with the statement, “My social relationships are superficial at work.”

A trade credit agreement between individuals is a mutual arrangement where two parties agree to exchange goods or services without immediate monetary transactions. Instead, they extend credit to each other, allowing one party to receive goods or services upfront while deferring payment to a later date, often with agreed-upon terms and conditions for repayment. This informal arrangement enables individuals to facilitate transactions without the immediate need for cash or external financing.

Why do I want to be a leader?

I believe that leadership is how someone can move energy through a system and away from the places where it gets stuck. I've been a natural leader much of my life - I was always the kid that people picked to lead projects when someone needed to do it, and I've also always worked to never be the smartest person in the room because I'm always curious about how I can be in the service of the change that I want to see. I'm now in a place in my career where I have significant leadership responsibility that is wholly undirected, and I want to take charge of this opportunity to both see out what I think success is in this situation and to hone in on the leadership qualities that I know I possess as a person so that they can be developed and despite any lack of support in doing so. Further, I see a lot of opportunity in my current position because of the lack of accountability, and I want to optimize for my wants and desires in the opportunity while still urging the work toward the best possible version of success. In all, I'm reaching out because I want to develop personal accountability, discipline, and the ability to celebrate my success as a leader, while also growing this skill to greater and more important heights in the future. I was apparently born to use these skills, so now I want to make the effort to use them.

Private Library, 29 August 2023: privacy as the foundation of trust

Discussing Taking Trust Seriously in Privacy Law - Hartzog et al, The 230829 Private Library call concerned itself the most with how to pull ourselves away from a cultural paradigm of privacy pessimism toward one of privacy optimism by engaging in Privacy as foundational to Trust with others, thus as the basis for building relationships and community. At the highest level - well-founded communities built on trust and the relationships that they share form the basis of the most resilient communities. Signaling more widely is a function of the information we have chosen for others to know, but there is no reason to broadcast widely that which we are not ready to share with others. privacy pessimism is the framing of individualistic privacy being that which protects the individual from the horrors of a world that seeks to impose itself upon us - further decrying a 'death of privacy' in a time where the world has crept in to consume all of our individuality. Pessimism is a tool that can be used by intermediaries to navigate control over your privacy away from the tools that you use and toward the control illusion - wherein you as the individual are fully responsible for your own privacy. Within the scope of our interactions with other tech, we 'give up' our privacy in order to have certain benefits - which means that we 'pay' for free things not just with that which should be private to us and while having our right to choose whether or not we want to engage in this trust taken from us. the Control Illusion makes it such that we have to do things like read entire privacy policies in order to be 'responsible' for our privacy It was pointed out by a community member that "education" is necessary for individuals to appreciate their responsibility to their own privacy This was responded to by asking if this unduly places a burden on the individual to engage in this education, rather than navigating toward building better relationships between those things we are forced to trust and the individuals that use these things. In previous discussions, we highlighted that 'total privacy' is isolating - meaning that there must be some function within which privacy must act as a shield toward engagement with others. when we build relationships with others, we engage in building trust, because trust is a function of the information that is shared between parties - when we choose not to build trust, we do not have relationships with others. This is true of technology as well - when we spoke to how auditors earn their reputations, the incumbency of a first mover advantage was brought up - but with the understanding that new entrants can win out in the long term provided they build a relationship, through trust, with those they audit - and this is an optimistic approach. In the use of most modern internet technology, we are coerced into trusting what they do with our information, and truly do not know what they do with it. This asks the question of whether or not we should establish a new paradigm of accountability and data stewardship among those that should be held accountable for their use of our information - and we should! Not mentioned: part of the article concerned itself with the pathos of Privacy as a sacrifice - that our experience on the internet is one of giving up our privacy in order to have 'a good experience' on the internet, meaning that privacy somehow is argued as not being a positive user experience. privacy optimism, by contrast, engages in the ideal that we can disclosure of private information (or a crucial volume) is foundational to trust, because the more information that someone holds about you, the more vulnerable you are as an individual. The implications of this are that all interactions between individuals and the technologies and other parties with whom they interact are build on the basis of loyalty and trust. While we work to build trust-minimized technology, we seek to build a foundation for decreasing vulnerability in the users that participate in its use. This requires accountability on the part of the parties with whom we interact and build relationships, whether people or otherwise. A culture of privacy optimism requires equal parts transparency and autonomy built on trust, so (as mentioned by StellarMagnet) - the relationships that you build with your community should be intentional. What if who you truly are is distasteful to those that you interact with? - asked by dismad Answering this, the question of your 'reach' is not to be called into view, because a community is not built on trying to get as many people as possible to listen to you, but rather those with whom you develop a network of relationships based on trust. Workin from a position of privacy optimism means that working on Namada is a function of those who choose to continue working on it and the relationships they have built in order to do so.
Discussing the Community Builder Epoch 1 RPGF results

Ahead of anything further, I want to thank all Community Builders (CBs) for being a part of the first Community Builders RPGF round. An impressive collective effort was made by those who stayed on. I'm personally very pleased with both the results and the final crop of those who remain a part of the program, in addition to what the results show us, which will be what we discuss here. The final group that currently comprising the program ended up being some 172 candidates offering varying levels of contributions across several skill sets. This made qualitative evaluation difficult, but the voting structure that I spoke to the program employing in this article did a fair job of using social consensus. The results speak for themselves, barring some fuzzy edges to the logic of the program's execution - some of which I hope to address in this article - and the results from this voting round (epoch) will aid us in understanding what we hope to see in the community we foster around Namada. There's a fun exercise that you can play with a jar of sweets - you ask a room full of people (usually it's a classroom) to cast an estimation on the number of sweets that are inside the jar. Usually, this is a competition to see which single person can guess the correct answer for individual payout (sometimes the sweets themselves!), and is intended as a demonstration of estimation. However, the secondary effects of having a whole room make a guess are a little bit more fascinating: if the estimations made by the collective of students who submitted their guesses are summed and divided by the number of people in the classroom, in a perfect setting this estimation is usually shockingly close to the actual number of sweets in the jar. This phenomenon was popularized by James Surowiecki's studies on the 'Wisdom of Crowds' - showing that collective computation can often lead you to results that are harder to discern on an individual level. This was the same logic behind proposing we allocate 40% of the allocation power to the community of CBs who participated. While having an evaluation of contributions centrally executed could have led to the highest level of quality control overall, approaching the results from an involved perspective means collecting an aggregate opinion. As a result, the contributions of the program were not assessed by only Early Stewards, but by 172 community participants whose opinions were valued and whose votes were counted as valuable. I expect that the results reflect an accuracy that I didn't think the Early Stewards could perform on their own. As a reminder, the first round of Community Builders social consensus voting used the Web3 application Coordinape to allocate differing vote weights to the community's opinion of contributors to the program. This was proportioned with 60% of the vote weight in the hands of the Early Stewards (ES - a hand-selected collective of core contributors to Namada) and 40% of the vote weight allocated to the CBs themselves. Program participants had 1 week to allocate their votes to one another, with the ES ineligible to receive tokens due to their relationship to the protocol's development. With the votes finally in, our first pass of the results shows that the community did favor community members who have been a part of the Namada community for a long time and who have staked their name within the community by being strong collaborators. This is evidenced by the following graph, with 40% of total vote GIVE weight allocated to the top 17 (or 10%) of Community Builders. Chart showing the distribution of GIVE across individual CBs These results are astounding! It's apparent to anyone looking on that there was a strong concentration of votes toward a small set of CBs. It's important to control for the ES votes to account for having tipped the scales of this distribution, it still reflects an analytically useful outcome for signaling toward those who merited the most attention, and we envision that the effect of ES votes will decrease as the total GIVE percentage allocated to ES decreases in proportion to the community At first glance, the distribution shows us that the contributions distribution is a reflection of certain community members having been very active members of our community and being recognized for this by others, and it's important to center this before adding other level of interpretation. Second, it's not quite a question of accumulated points - the allocation of GIVE reflects community sentiment around what all 176 voting members found to be valuable to the future of Namada. This is fundamentally a very good thing that we should encourage far more of. Nothing is saying that Namada will continue on using Coordinape as a method for allocating NAM for Community Builder programs (that will be the subject of discussion with those who stay on), but for now, these results are extremely promising because they show us who the community sees as being the most impactful, and they orient us positively toward understanding who we should be asking to stay within the Community Builders' Program. This is evidenced as well by the contrast in distribution for how many givers allocated to select CBs: Chart showing the number of CBs who allocated to any one Community Builder Without naming names, we can see that the distribution of voting actions is overall more normalized than individual token amounts - it reflects a well-connected network. There are some exciting implications for this that I'll discuss in a future article, but it suffices to say that the distribution of tokens AND voting actions reflect that the CB program served to at least initially connect many of those who participated in the CB program. Ahead of voting, I received messages from a few CBs worried that implementing the voting structure used in the program would encourage the formation of cartels (cartelization, as I'll refer to it from here on out) of individuals who would vote only for one another rather than - likely encouraged on by an expectation of the accumulation of rewards. It looks as though people did actually do this, but I'd guess anything the effects were marginal due to the fixed number of votes per participant. A DM from a CB sent directly to me outlining cartels forming during the voting period. Despite these cartels, it looks as though the results played out as expected - we still have the signals necessary to determine who we want to stay on in the program by using the voting metric and weighing against qualitative assessments such as contributions and collaborative skill-will. The equal distribution of votes likely normalized votes into the lowest possible tiers of GIVE allocation (e.g. the bottom 40% (69) of CBs only received 10% of total GIVE (10231) at an average of 148GIVE each - a lot of effort for little return, where collusion what is their midst). The net effect of any defections I expect to see in the final analysis will be interesting because of this - but so far the results effectively met the expectations I had starting. For the most part, the best contributions trended toward useful, meaningful, and mission-aligned work, with most others either falling into a camp of 'high quality but inaccurate' or 'low quality and accurate' through 'low quality and inaccurate', which unfortunately wasn't revealed until Early Stewards went through everything that was submitted (managing ongoing work by 250 initial participants, it turns out, is really difficult). From here, the Early Stewards will have to get together to assess which Community Builders will be asked to stay on in the program based on these voting results and some secondary qualitative assessments, which should lead us toward the next stage of what Namada's community will become. Many more projects are on the horizon for Community Building, and Namada's future is particularly bright having found people who want to be there to make it happen.

A canary network is a vital trial environment that allows protocols to both test the stability of major applications in real-world use conditions, allowing developers to execute high-iteration applications stress tested against the conditions that exist in the real world and the incentives that come from embracing a chaotic system with a higher degree of risk. Related to: blockchain Polkadot Kusama The name 'canary network' comes from the an extension of a 'mining' analogy used throughout blockchain - the extraction of information from a set of executable hash results in verifiably unique and scarce data, much in the same way that real world resources are 'mined' from the earth's surface. The 'canary in the coal-mine' provides a miner with an appreciation for the conditions of safety in a mine; since birds in general are notoriously sensitive to changes in conditions, the death of a 'canary' while down in the mine would be an indication of volatile or dangerous gases in the air during the operation of a mine. We usually understand an object path from test network to main network, from 'testnet'to 'mainnet'. Test networks use test currency, while main networks operate with fungible tokens that represent immutable value. In the Polkadot/Kusama ecology, the path from testnet to mainnet includes another interstitial layer - the canary network. The canary network is intended to offer a similar purpose - it allows a set of developers participating in the execution of a network to check for the safety of an active execution environment - though fortunately in this situation they dispense with the cruelty on birts. By operating a canary network on Kusama before launching to a primary slot on Polkadot, a prospective Polkadot network can test the viability of the network in a real-world setting in order to see if the intended model executes similar to the manner in which it does in a testing environment. So why might someone choose this model rather than stress-testing an industrial scale model outright? There are two main reasons: canary networks create a real economy you can never plan for the conditions of the real world The essential difference between a test network and a canary network is that a test network never operates with any fungible assets; all assets that operate on a test network have no value - and so tests can only reflect prediction of how transactions will take place on the network. While running a test environment can account for the lion's share of issues that may be experienced on a main network, there is always a degree of interaction that will not be evidenced in testing and for which real-world testing can account. In order to prevent a steep increase in failures - having an actively labeled and far more volatile proving-ground is an instrumental step in ensuring that a network is ready to deploy with the scaling solutions that Polkadot strives to offer. Kusama provides network operators the opportunity to examine the outcomes of real retail and institutional users in order to examine the results of their intended execution. The assets that are traded on Kusama are fully fungible and the transactions that result from their exchange are a representation of real value for their users, which means that the incentives for transactions and deployment are just as real as the insights their results provide. The question here is whether or not this approach has any value - why might someone decide to execute with real world transactions in the Kusama ecology, rather than wait to deploy directly onto Polkadot? Chaos flies in the face of prediction. It often does more than one would expect - outcomes are unpredictable, and no amount of testing can account for these outcomes. This design language has been adapted by a number of organizations without the tech sector, in a practice known as Chaos Engineering Because the interactions of users with a canary protocol maintain real world risk, users do not act as though they are in a test environment. Instead, they act as real users would, taking on risk in a blind setting that allows the protocols to act as they will when they are fully launched. This means that the course of execution by protocols that launch a canary network prepare them dutifully for the institutional-scale execution available to protocols that eventually launch on Polkadot. The options for parachains to pick from on Kusama are at this time plentiful, and the competition is fierce. As of writing, Kusama parachain slot auctions are in full force, and all slots appear on route to being filling in the near future. The total value locked in crowdloans and self-bond for parachain slots on Kusama is currently a total of 9.2mKSM (about 2.9bUSD) tokens locked in either active auctions or in crowdloans. Barring this, there is a tremendous amount of development that is happening on the Kusama network - with some projects launching and seeing immediate utility. The Moonbeam/Moonriver team were seen to have an immediate effect on the Polkadot ecosystem through their support of an EVM-compatible substrate chain that allows users to deploy fully Ethereum native Solidity applications with minimal alterations to code, which in turn resulted in a high valuation for Moonriver's MOVR toke

Polkadot is an industrial scale blockchain solution acts as a metaprotocol for the implementation of Web 3 applications, providing ease of interoperability, shared security, and infinite scaleability. Validator election on Polkadot happens through use of the weightedPhragmén electionalgorithm, wherein the algorithm selects the winner of election cycles based on the number of tokens that a nominator holds, and the number of votes that a validator has received. In practice, a nominator can select up to 16 validators with whatever number of tokens that they have bonded to an account for nomination. The nominations are then distributed relative to the number of validators available, the scores that they have in accumulated token votes, and a distribution of the votes that ensures the largest possible amount of validators are elected with the tokens available. While this can seem quite confusing, the votes are distributed in a deterministic fashion, and it's possible to follow the logic once you've wrapped your head around the voting mechanism, known as the Phragmén election algorithm. It's useful to understand this as an election mechanism that allocates votes based not solely on the number of votes that a particular validator has, but also the 'weight' of the other votes allocated by other parties to a validator in previous elections. In practice, this means that even if a validator has a higher amount of direct votes in a round, the weight of votes from previous elections can influence the current election, meaning that a less-allocated validator (in terms of cumulative votes) can be elected based on the distribution of votes from nominators. If you're running a private validator set, chances are that we can arrange the election mechanism in a way that we'll be able to elect the maximal number of validators for the amount of DOT or KSM available. Assuming that there is enough of the asset to elect multiple validators, we will manage election through a controller account that we will rebalance on your behalf. However, there's no function on Polkadot or Kusama to permission only specific wallets - the only way we can do so is by setting commission at 100% for the validator and then settling rewards balances off-chain. For public elections, the method for election becomes a little more chaotic to predict - but it's still deterministic within a certain threshold (otherwise, how would the validators get elected?). The primary determining factor for getting a validator elected is the minimum stake required in order to be in the 'active set'. This is the minimum amount of DOT tokens required for nomination on a particular validator is a factor of two variables: The number of available slots for validation (as of writing this, 297 slots for validation are available on Polkadot) The amount of DOT staked by lowest staked validator in waiting. To simplify, let's posit that there are 5 slots available to validator and 10 validators hoping to fill the slots. The top five are elected based on each validator's total stake. The lowest staked validator in the top five determines the threshold for what is necessary in order for a validator to get elected if the 5th highest staked validator has 5 DOT nominating it if another validator is nominated with 6 DOT, this validator can take their place as the 5th highest in the next election. In this situation, the 5 DOT limit would be considered the Minimum Stake Required. In order for a validator to be elected into the active set, Minimum Stake Required threshold that must be crossed before a validator will be a part of the set of 297 validators Polkadot distributes rewards equally to all active validators, such that no matter the amount of tokens staked to a validator from nominators, the amount rewarded and distributed to all active validators is roughly^1 equal. Validators are selected for block production using the NPoS consensus mechanism that rotates through all active validators Rewards are also not distributed on a constant basis per epoch (roughly ~1d) but rather per era (~4 hours) - so at times it can appear that a validator is not earning rewards. At the end of each epoch, all validators will have been selected for validation, roughly equalizing the total stake distributed to all elected validators. 1- It is 'roughly' because validators can also receive network fees and tips that accrue over time, resulting in variations. Accessibility verification would be a method of using a verification technology like blockchain to ensure compliance in all web-connected applications against an open standard of accessbility rules. The point of this technology would be to check the UI and UX rules of a web-connected system for violations of coded characteristics representing successful accessibility. So long as the web-app follows these elements of compliance, it will not fail verification and present itself as quantifiably inaccessible in its interaction format. What this would require is that the rules of the system be hard-coded as a component of another structure - the structure cannot exist without this verification element in place, because if the verification metric is failing to execute, the system is not in compliance with the rules. The question is whether or not work could happen at a low enough resolution to provide meaningful verification - an acceptable minimum standard by which accessibility verification is defined. How would verification take place, and is the role of decentralizing this process to make it as acceptable as possible as a useful part of buiilding an open web?

The Cosmos SDK is an interoperable blockchain ecosystem facilitating simple connection of blockchains with one another using the Inter Blockchain Communication (IBC). Cosmos makes this easy and straightforward, additionally providing common ground around which protocols can build their protocols within what is provided by the SDK. Most importantly, access to building in the space is 'rent free' - in that those who build within it only need to spin up nodes in order for other protocols to interact with their protocol. While the SDK offers a slew of options that allow protocols to interact more easily, the freedom with which they are able to do so comes at the cost of shared security, which must be built ad-hoc and electively within the relationships between protocols, unlike Polkadot, which offers this by virtue of being connected to their relay chain. A validator is a worker node that that engages in the practice of consensus-building on proof-of-stake networks with a number of other worker nodes who then continuously script the consensus into a distributed ledger so that transactions can be publicly trusted and act as a record of intermediation between parties without having to hold the assets of the exchange itself. Validators are offered incentives in the form of There are four types of validators: in-house validator institutional validator retail validator activist validator An in-house validator is often a validator operation that has been subsumed by a parent organization, usually a cryptocurrency exchange that is seeking to support a token internally and hopes to provide a reward rate to their customers on this basis, as well as skimming off of this inflationary reward to prevent the dilution of their own holdings against the market. In these situations, the holdings of an exchange are often delegated to a single or a small number of accounts and the accounts internal to the exchange are not represented on the network for which the exchange's validators provide their services. The margins are, in this way, extremely low, since these validators do can dictate commission on the basis of total asset holdings delegated to their operating validators. The requirements for participating in protocol governance are as well low, since the customers that an in-house validator serve are the retail token holders who custody their assets within the cryptocurrency exchange, thus there being little incentive to involve themselves in the development of the protocols they support themselves, since they are likely more focused on a cohesive product experience for their customers. An institutional validator is often an operation whose profit margins depends on delegation by institutional-level holders of tokens in blockchain and cryptocurrency networks. The targets of this type of validator are individual wallet accounts, usually investors in protocols themselves, or foundations that are holding portions of the assets for a network. As such, this kind of validator is primarily concerned with a small-but-mighty clientele that is interested in the success of the networks that they support, but as an infrastructure provider, do not feel any real obligation to the maintenance of the network from a protocol governance perspective, due to a lack of incentive to do so. Institutional validators can operate white-label validator nodes at 100% commission on-chain, then settle with the investor off-chain. Institutional validators may operate on a large number of chains of varying complexity on the basis of the desires and demands of institutional-level tokenholders. A retail validator seeks to make their margins off of the percentage of commission that they earn from their stakers. As such, much of their success is contingent on how a community of tokenholders who are not at the institutional level and the reputation that they hold as an operator within the community of operators. The means through which they can do this is through garnering popularity, participation in protocol governance, and core contribution to protocol research - since the reputation and margin for the operation of a retail validator increases with the amount of stake delegated to their node. An activist validator operates at the scale of, usually, a single or only a few chains. They operate with the full intention to act committed to the success of the chain that they are a part of, and their main market are the community of tokenholders who hold a middling but self-custodied number of assets. In this sense, activist validators play the volume game, hoping to have as many assets custodied to them by members of the community so as to earn the support that they merit. Paradoxically, activist validators are often the most value-aligned with the success of a particular blockchain - they are normally highly active in protocol governance, especially in systems that employ token-based governance under delegated proof-of-stake. The counter-play of this kind of validator is that they are often the most aligned with the vision of the chain, but are not rewarded accordingly other than by the hopes that the community recognize their contributions to the protocol even while often proselytizing the most on the value of the technology that they are supporting. blockchain, Figment, proof-of-stake

A voting system that aims to demonstrate not only the support for a particular position, but also the direction and conviction of the the vote. This voting system requires that voting takes place in a voting market, in which voters use tokens to support their positions, and the number of votes that can be used by a single individual increases in cost for each vote that is posed on a quadratic curve: number of votes cost of vote --------------- ------------ 1 1 2 4 3 9 4 16 5 25 As a result, each vote is more expensive than the last, meaning that the cost of influencing a market-based democratic environment becomes that much more expensive to perform with each subsequent vote. The direct benefit of this is that if someone has voted multiple times, the cost of the votes goes up exponentially so that conviction from a single party becomes obvious, and credibility of the position may become more apparent as a result of that conviction.

Data availability is a core tenet of the available space for a set of transactions - in that there must be sufficient space in a transactional environment for a number of transactions or computations to be authorized for the computational environment to proceed. In the context of blockchain, data availability is a limitation on blockspace - where the number of transactions in a block decreases as the complexity of the transactions increases. As a result, an inability to change the structure of the block environment or to displace portions of the transactions taking up a block to a difference scaling solution (such as rollup) becomes a scaling limitation on a particular block structure. A good example of this is the Ethereum blockchain, whereing execution and smart contracts occupy the same block space and as a result the execution potential of the chain can become limited by smart contract execution, which on average takes up larger amounts of available data in a block. A potential solution to this is the Celestia blockchain, which aims to remain an execution-only environment for blockchains, with independent rollups connecting with the execution layer and smart contracts (or other transaction types) remaining in the rollup environment. In computer science, message passing is a technique for invoking behavior (i.e., running a program) on a computer. The invoking program sends a message to a process (which may be an actor or object) and relies on that process and its supporting infrastructure to then select and run some appropriate code. Message passing differs from conventional programming where a process, subroutine, or function is directly invoked by name. Message passing is key to some models of concurrency and object-oriented programming. Message passing is ubiquitous in modern computer software. It is used as a way for the objects that make up a program to work with each other and as a means for objects and systems running on different computers (e.g., the Internet) to interact. Message passing may be implemented by various mechanisms, including channels. Access Source(s):

A parachain is a sharded blockchain equivalent that earns the shared security of the Polkadot or Kusama networks, not having to engage in settlement in its own right through collation of transactions that are then validating by the Polkadot or Kusamabase chain. The great advantage of a sharded format is that the chains that connect to the relay chain can depend on the base chain for their security, and therefore do not need to exhibit their own consensus, while the base chain is able to validate transactions and keep the data availability of the base chain at a maximum while smart contracts are executed on the parachains themselves. In order to earn access to the relay chain for both message passing and execution, parachains must participate in slot auctions, wherein the parachain raises locked DOT in order to secure slot access to the base chain.

A slot auction is the process by which a parachain earns access to the Polkadotor Kusama execution layers. Chains that want to leverage the shared security of the base chain must raise funds in DOT or KSM to be locked for predetermined periods of time (dependent on the desired slot duration). Toward the end of the auction period, the auction enters a 'candle period' wherein the tokens that are raised for each chain can increase but a post-determined block is chosen at which the balances are proven in order to select a winner. This is in an effort to prevent bid sniping by parachain communities as the auction comes to a close, encouraging contributors to contribute the most toward the beginning of the candle period.

XCMP stands for Cross-chain message passing format, a format that allows chains connected by the Polkadot ecosystem to communicate with one another using the relay chain, which in turn provides a closed interoperability environment for all connected parachains. One of the core problems encountered by running XCMP is that it requires you to work within the Polkadot ecosystem in order to chain the advantages of shared security. XCMP is not available to sovereign chains that have not gone through the process of securing a parachain slot on either Polkadot or Kusama. What does it mean for cryptocurrency protocols to be conceived of as public goods? The most mature example example that we've seen at scale is the Kusama network. Kusama is Polkadot's 'cousin' canary network blockchain, providing fast-paced execution and settlement with a shared security model that allows for sharded chains to test the functions of a Substrate-based metaprotocol. (If that seems jargony, don't worry too much, it's not really the point of this article). What this means is that people who want to release large-scale projects that benefit from Polkadot's network effect, a good way to gain exposure to the true-market conditions So why build on a canary network? Why not first deploy on an active testnet, then launch into a mainnet standard? The answer to this question lies in exploring new design languages for how to build out software implementation - a discipline known as 'Chaos Engineering'. One of the first major entities to take an approach along these lines. The study of this phenomenon has lead to an expansion of the field of "Learning from Incidents" - study that concludes that a lack of coordination is where a failure insight usually emerges from - a lack of coordination over problem solving often causes the failure in the first place. Sagan intends to be canary network for the Cosmos development space, a space that intends to offer locally sanctioned shared security from a permissioned set of vetted validators. Since this design language is so early in implementation, many criticisms of the model argue that canary networks are really just an expansion on incentivized test networks, and claim that there isn't really a strong argument for the longevity of canary networks once a network goes fully live. Running a canary network has some distinct advantages, some disadvantages, but is otherwise an unproven system in the context of blockchain network scaling. Celestia a base Data Availability layer designed to offer a new paradigm in blockchain architecture - the modular blockchain ecosystem. As a data availability layer, Celestia offers networks that use it to prove the existence of a dependent network’s data without having to store and verify the data on their own chain. Importantly, Celestia introduces the concept of a ‘stack’ in the construction of blockchain networks - meaning that the services of a network can be dependent on another network in order to make more efficient the scaling and construction of whatever the dependent network decides to work on. With IBC (Inter-Blockchain Communication) compatibility on by default, Celestia is biased toward interoperability by default, meaning that all networks using it as a part of their stack can easily communicate with any other part of their stack. A modular blockchain world moves us out of a paradigm in which blockchains were required to build out the entirety of their component architecture within a single chain, introducing scalability issues and coordination fault in a single team attempting to support and build out every part that is needed in order to run their network. The Data Availability layer functions through the care of a party of contributors whose function is to provide light verifiability to the data that has been posted to the Celestia base layer. Using statistical logic, clusters of light nodes verify the availability of information that has been posted to the DA layer, a much more efficient verification method than what has been required in past constructions for blockchains in the monolithic paradigm. With a stack-based blockchain architecture, components that are required for the basic functions of data availability, settlement, and execution can abstracted into separate elements that can be serviced by entirely different and separate teams focused on building out the best version for that part of blockchain architecture. In the long term, this means that teams can focus on the construction of pure utility implementation while using elements of an accessible modular stack to meet all the other requirements of running settlement architecture. Little is known about the TIA token, but there is high likelihood that Celestia's construction around the Tendermint SDK ensures a standardized staking approach for tokenholders, wherein tokenholders will delegate to providers who will serve the function of validating the transactions posted by light nodes to the Celestia record.
