An activist validator operates at the scale of, usually, a single or only a few chains. They operate with the full intention to act committed to the success of the chain that they are a part of, and their main market are the community of tokenholders who hold a middling but self-custodied number of assets. Paradoxically, activist validators are often the most value-aligned with the success of a particular blockchain - they are normally highly active in protocol governance, especially in systems that employ token-based governance under delegated proof-of-stake.

An in-house validator is often a validator operation that has been subsumed by a parent organization, usually a cryptocurrency exchange that is seeking to support a token internally and hopes to provide a reward rate to their customers on this basis, as well as skimming off of this inflationary reward to prevent the dilution of their own holdings against the market. In these situations, the holdings of an exchange are often delegated to a single or a small number of accounts and the accounts internal to the exchange are not represented on the network for which the exchange's validators provide their services. The margins are, in this way, extremely low.

An institutional validator is often an operation whose profit margins depends on delegation by institutional-level holders of tokens in blockchain and cryptocurrency networks. The targets of this type of validator are individual wallet accounts, usually investors in protocols themselves, or foundations that are holding portions of the assets for a network. As such, this kind of validator is primarily concerned with a small-but-mighty clientele that is interested in the success of the networks that they support, but as an infrastructure provider, do not feel any real obligation to the maintenance of the network from a protocol governance perspective, due to a lack of incentive to do so. Institutional validators can operate white-label validator nodes at 100% commission on-chain, then settle with the investor off-chain.

A retail validator seeks to make their margins off of the percentage of commission that they earn from their stakers. As such, much of their success is contingent on how a community of tokenholders who are not at the institutional level and the reputation that they hold as an operator within the community of operators. The means through which they can do this is through garnering popularity, participation in protocol governance, and core contribution to protocol research - since the reputation and margin for the operation of a retail validator increases with the amount of stake delegated to their node.

In the context of blockchain accounts, account-level privacy is a question of where it is that your assets are being held - meaning, what identifiable information does a particular account hold on a particular user. Ideally, account-level privacy should be a question of the information that is being revealed to those with whom you transact, or at the least is an account of what it is that an individual stores and have the ability to decide that which is available to those who use the information held by an individual account.

Information leakage happens whenever a system that is designed to be closed to an eavesdropper reveals some information to unauthorized parties nonetheless. In other words: Information leakage occurs when secret information correlates with, or can be correlated with, observable information. For example, when designing an encrypted instant messaging network, a network engineer without the capacity to crack encryption codes could see when messages are transmitted, even if they could not read them.

Writing with a slip box is a process that acts like a funnel for information capture, allowing insight to emerge from the act of aggregating information and refining which information is important to the process of synthesizing subject matter. The outcome of this approach is to create a repository that links ideas together, allowing writing to flow freely from pre-written content and it's connections to other subject matter. It was initially established as a thinking system by Luhmann, an archivist who used it to create connections between ideas, resulting in over 90k individual notes. There are six steps to the process of writing with a slip box: 1. Make Fleeting Notes Any ideas that strike you - just so long as they are documented somewhere. They don't need to be referenced, they just need to be captured. Referencing structure comes later. 2. Make Literature Notes Notes that require bibliographic attention and help you trace the roots of the knowledge you are looking to document. A reference system starts here. 3. Make Permanent Notes These are shorter notes that are used to relate thinking. Go through notes once or twice a day and think about how the information learned relates to other ideas and concepts. Exactly 1 note per idea, as a jumping off point. 4. Add permanent notes to the slip box File it 'near' other related notes, add links to notes that are less associated, make sure the note can be found from other places as well, whether through discussion or topic. You want to be able to 'stumble' on the subject. 5. Look through connections to a 'topic' This was you're not trying to come up with an idea, but rather extablishing connection in an idea you already have. Add to these connections and build our the weaker connections. Let the slip box do the brainstorming for you. 6. Flesh out a structure 7. Fill out the written connection as a draft 8. Edit and Proof read the manuscript Ask constantly "how does this connect to what I already know" - all of your thinking must be in context. Work to explain simply, and have everything someone needs up front. Whitehead "Civilization advances by extending the number of important opeartions which we can perform without thinking about them." A Markov blanket is a set of variables that contains all the necessary information to predict the behavior of a specific variable in a probabilistic graphical model. It includes the variable's parents, children, and the parents of its children. By knowing the values of the variables in the Markov blanket, accurate predictions can be made about the target variable, without considering the rest of the variables in the system.

A Turing Complete system means a system in which a program can be written that will find an answer (although with no guarantees regarding runtime or memory). To show that something is Turing-complete, it is enough to show that it can be used to simulate some Turing-complete system. For example, an imperative language is Turing-complete if it has conditional branching (e.g., "if" and "goto" statements, or a "branch if zero" instruction; see one-instruction set computer) and the ability to change an arbitrary amount of memory (e.g., the ability to maintain an arbitrary number of data items). No physical system can have infinite memory, but if the limitation of finite memory is ignored, most programming languages are otherwise Turing-complete. Access Source(s): "Turing completeness"
Can financial instruments save the world?

If humans are really and truly economic creatures, they would be rational. Being that they aren't - it should be evident that the work humans have put into changing the planet are in alignment with irrationality, not rationality. It is because of this that our use of the climate is something that has lead us to be fundamentally wasteful creatures - we don't know how to use what we have efficiently, because we've never had to consider the possibility of scarcity. This may be the fundamental issue that we run into when considering the logic of our own collapse. Scarcity is baked into nature. When a biome reaches a state of scarcity, one of two things happen: either the community dependent on the scarce resources disbands in search of other resources, or there is competition over the resource. The latter is less likely - because it is a battle over something that will disappear, so being capricious as it disappears does not result in outsized reward. In fact, humans are the only species that prizes what are known as 'ephemeral goods' - resources that have no intrinsic value but for their scarcity. Gold, diamonds, even bitcoin, are not examples of naturally occurring events in nature. They are wholly human in design and logic - a capriciousness imposed by rarity alone. If economic arguments outline several strains of logic, especially those of supply and demand, of cost and benefit - we leave out too much information that is important to the system. Let's get the frustrating part of this conversation out of the way first - there's no world where creating a financial incentive for working on human-caused climate change will lead to solving 'the problem'. Truthfully, the one greatest thing that will solve this issue is collective action, by all parties at all levels of society, working to prevent the worst from happening - because yes, climate change is here, and we basically don't have a feasible way of stopping it. With this out of the way, we can address the next question: can financial instruments contribute to solving issues with climate change? If the key term here is contribute - then yes, absolutely. In fact, there are innumerable projects that are doing just that, backed by strong theory, really requiring nothing more than adoption to get them started. Let's consider one of the greater barriers to solving the issue of climate change - financial incentives to those who have done the brunt of the damage to this planet. Oftentimes the blame is laid on a collective ignorance of the effect we have been having on the climate, so with that collective blame has been a collective call to action that conveniently sidesteps the most egregious culprits of carbon dioxide emissions (corporations and industry) and focuses instead on individuals as the place where change 'can happen'. Regardless of the political ire that this can inspire, the other structure waylaying measurable action is economy - there's just too much money in putting useful resources to work. The most profitable economies on the planet are resource extraction and utilization. A whopping [number] worth of raw materials are mined/extracted/processed each year. We've seen distinct advantage in the use of these resources - fossil fuels are a dream material. The chemical qualities of raw oil are so tremendous in utility that, were they not actively destroying the planet, everyone would champion them. There's almost no denying this. There is almost nothing you can't do with oil, and it has accelerated the progress of our human race tremendously in a short period of time. This has come at a cost of creating an extremely wasteful culture around the material that we are now finally clawing back, in addition to the contributions that petroleum as a fuel source adds to the atmosphere in terms of carbon dioxide emissions. Second to this is coal, which still constitutes an extremely high portion of electricity generation worldwide, followed quickly by minerals extraction and refinement for use in industry (which happens in most cases to use electricity and/or materials generated by the prior two in processing). There's a lot of money in raw material extraction and use - it's essentially what we do as a species. There's little wonder that we can be quite closely compared to ants in that regard. We use the world around us to build things that serve us. We have done all of this in the name of growing our footprint as a species, and it turns out we've been largely successful - it's just that it was a carbon footprint, and it's getting bigger all the time. Despite what stock tickers will tell you, the underlying economic value of operating our resource-driven economy is enormous, and will be (has been) extremely difficult to deviate from. It's a tale that is drilled into us, that price meets where demand is high, and demand will not go down any time soon. After considering all of this it's actually a little hard to imagine that there's anything that will stop us from prioritizing extraction. But that's also only if we approach everything from a pure economic mindset, which (luckily) humans required to think within. Those who hold the most influence over the decisions of how money is used in our society (and how they make more of it) have the greatest impact on these numbers, rather than any number counted within the gross majority of society that cannot come close to conceiving of such wealth. With economic mindset comes an incentives-based approach to modeling intention - and here we do indeed see how human these decisions can be. The issue I have with this thinking is that asking if wealth is good. I think it is? I don't think we really have a choice about having it - we're not going to see massive wealth redistribution, because we've seen that experiment and it just doesn't work. Give people enough to survive with and you lift the bottom, that's really the most important work you could do. Would a financialized climate incentive market make rich people richer? Yeah, maybe, but at least we'd save the planet, and I'm (for the most part) willing to put up with that so that Montana isn't constantly on fire when I want to go see mountains.

The robust-ness (or resilience) of a network is a function of the number of internal self-preserving cycles that exist within it. According to navigations of Katz Centrality and the Jain-Krishna model of networks, if there is high internal network diversity, it is implied that the likelihood of collapse is low due to the number of cycles existing within the diversity of internal connections for the system. A core indicator of a collapsing system is the absence all of internal self-feeding cycles but one. That is - if the system becomes fully linear and energy is not redistributed through cycles within the system, energy accrues at one end of the system and other cycles connected to it die out. Proposed that in scale free systems resilience is only found in the preservation of the most connected nodes - in that networks are dependent on their best connected members, while the pruning of the least connected members does not have a measurable impact on network performance. The reason for this is that the removal of the most connected members of a network results in connection 'islands' wherein some members are isolated from all other connection, therefore unable to distribute any of their communication through the otherwise highly connected nodes. A complex adaptive system is a form of structure in which the interactions of internal components allow it to dynamically respond to changes in the environment around it, but the behavior of the system is not predictable according to the behavior of the individual components. A good example of this would be an ant colony - ant colonies are capable of responding to novel situations by virtue of the inflows that individual ants can bring into the larger colony response mechanism - but an individual ant will not reveal what the larger systemic response of the colony will be. Changes at the level of the individual ant can, however, have larger ecosystemic impacts, but the result is nonlinear. complex adaptive system Thinking in Systems - Meadows, D 2008 Lorenz,complexity,network growth

A mass coordination problem is when a problem's tractability is a product of coordinating the parties needed in order to solve the core issue that joint parties need to solve. As the scale of a given problem grows and the parties are increasingly abstracted or insulated from the problem's effects, it becomes increasingly difficult to coordinate a sufficient number of parties to work on the problem to any measurable effect. Examples of particularly intractable mass coordination problems are issues with climate change, wealth inequality, and/or market incentive misallignments. Depending on the mode and level of abstraction of parties connected to the whole, MCPs are particularly difficult to solve as those who have the most outsized effect on the system become increasingly isolated from their own effects. Is it possible that parties whose influence expands to sufficient enough a level become their own ecosystems that the effects of inflows necessary to sustain them on other systems remain sustainable enough for core motivators to be abstracted from their effects, leading to systemic parasitism? question How would one solve for this question? The Karadshev Scale represents the levels of progression through which society may optimally utilize locally available energy. The scale proceeds as follows: Type 1 - The civilization has taken full advantage of all energy that hits their planet Type 2 - The civilization has taken full advantage of all energy released by the star in it's solar system. Type 3 - The civilization has taken full advantage of all possible stars available in it's neighborhood, or entire galaxies, white holes, and gamma ray bursts. Interestingly, humanity is unlikely to reach Kardashev scale level 1 any time in the near future and is currently a solid Kardashev type 0 civilization. solarpunk,cyberpunk,network profligacy,network growth, speculative fiction

A core tenet of network growth is recognizing the importance of small-world systems in growing/maintaining a network. Strogatz references this in Sync when he mentions that small-world networks (strong convictions, weakly held) with a low degree of randomness and high clustering are best positioned for network resilience. Therefore networks that establish a number of small-world connections are able to sustain their network volume more comfortably. Highly-connected individual nodes act as information highways for local clusters, so that the network has strong long-distance connections across shorter path length, leading in turn to small-world connectivity as information travels across less steps to get to it's destination. This allows the network to be well-connected across distances and increases resiliency, though only if the small number of well-connected individuals are kept safe from disconnection to the rest of the network. Models have proven that the removal of highly-connected individuals has an outsized effect on the stability of the network as the smaller sub-networks they are a part of become unconnected islands, while the removal of less connected nodes has very little effet on overall network stability. Scalability is the ability for a system to operate at multiple scales - it's not a natural process and is something exclusive to fabricated systems. The core idea behind building a scalable system is to predict a system's ability to function at all scales by designing it so that it is not fragile as it grows. One issue with this way of thinking is believing that scalability means robusticity, which it does not. A scalable system can grow quickly, but because it relies heavily on short path length, no complexity can emerge throughout the network due to the distributed nature of the paths between connections - it is not unified. Scalability as a rule banishes the ability for system to change as they grow, since a scalable system is really just a simple set of rules governing connections - if there is an issue with this path connection when it is at 'scale' - the system is highly vulnerable. self 'The Mushroom at the End of the World( - Tsing, A Scalability banishes systems changing as they grow - meaning that there is no capacity for a system to change in response to the environments it encounters at difference sizes. A book written by Miguel Benasayag detailing the rise of the automated whole - such that the human experience is one resulted from being directed rather than directing. Benasayag argues for a need to uncenter immediacy, since rationality has become the dominant narrative in our evaluation of action; just as we've been able to deduce the linearity of cause and effect, so must be understand that the relationship between the two is not necessarily linear and instead is comprised of a plurality of contextual probabilities that engender the outcome. complexity here reigns over the outcome of our desire to "change the world" through a desire to seek out some sense of complimentarity in our actions to their outcomes - when in fact the only means through which we can hope to create meaningful change must be through the recognition of multiple futures that are held loosely. Bensayag speaks of democracy as being a process that must be defined wholly in terms of conflictuality - that we must continually orbit a moving center between beliefs. Democracy is intented the live around this conflictuality and indeed to mediate it rather than live through the immediacy of our actions and intentions, leading us to think not much further than the rationalized immediacy of our actions and intentions. Democracy is by contrast far more conflictual - it is meant to mediate through conflictuality, so that the moving center demonstrates qualities of complimentarity rather than polarity. Polarity leads us to believe in opposites that must supercede one another, a swinging of a pendulum rather than the complex action of movement that unites either side of the swing. Benasayag writes with the intention to have us understand the "tyranny" with which being directed removes our ability to be autonomous and take part in the decisions that surround us - using often the example of GPS and it's influence on our ability to conceive of time and space in meaningful terms. We are instead moved into a context of immediacy due to the automation of our transit and our actions, everything being only that which is directly before us. A paradigm is a state of norms that exist within a system wherein the state of the system accepts these norms to be the rules of the interpretive mechanisms necessary for acting within the system. In a scientific setting, the current 'paradigm' is the system of interpretive rules and laws that explain knowledge up to the most complete state of interpretation. In laymen's terms, it means that the current paradigm is the most up to date 'science'. The context for this is that there were times where the information necessary to explain the world was incomplete, but those who wished to study it were interpreting the world through the tools they had available, such that those were the 'laws' of nature. When new evidence was discovered to indicate that these laws were incomplete, the weight of this evidence eventually instigated a paradigm shift wherein the previous science was seen as incomplete, requiring that the new set of rules be fully explored as an interpretive basis for the world. Interestingly, Thomas Kuhn concluded in his 1969 book 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions' that science undergoes similar a similar state to that of politics, where the previous science exists in a state of incumbency due to the pervasiveness of the ability for previous natural laws to explain the phenomena that we see in the universe. The most explanatory version of this is the shift from Classical Physics (those that came about in the time of Isaac Newton) and Quantum Physics (those that came about in the time of Albert Einstein). The previous science in the time of Newton explained the physical phenomena of the universe in a sufficiently accurate way so as to 'work' for almost all frames of reference, but it didn't work at certain levels of resolution. When digging into that level of resolution, it was clear that the rules of the previous system were incomplete, spurning a need by Einstein (and many of his contemporaries) to further explore physical phenomena at this state of resolution. The science that emerged from this period of time is what we consider to be some of the most 'accurate' science, in that is provides the most complete picture of the natural laws that explain the physics of the universe. This said, shifting over to this new form of science was met with with resistance as Quantum Physics was required to gather evidence of its accuracy, until the evidence was overwhelming and the understanding of the most accurate underlying paradigm was accepted as the new paradigm, hence causing a 'paradigm shift'. --- --- The Structure Of Scientific Revolutions - Kuhn, T See also: complexity or phase transition or phase state or philosophy of science

The halting problem is the question of determining from a description of arbitrary inputs, whether or not a program will finish running, or if it will keep running forever. The issue with a halting problem wherein it continues on forever has primarily to do with a question of whether or not the components of the program end up in a state of recursion, where there the program continues to re-work the same issue over and over, meaning that the program's output is undecidable.

If the future is one in which we are connected to everything, we must not let that connection consume us. Being connected does not mean allowing yourself to be seen in entirety, it means choosing what it is that people see of you and keeping the rest sacred. This is the reason that the act of sovereignty is one of allowing oneself to acknowledge that which is completely ours - to release this and allow it to be consumed by any passer-by is to give up our internal sanctified space and allow it to be devalued. Does this track with the idea that there are cultures where privacy is not a concept shared by the community? I think so, and I think that they exist. In those communities, the concept of privacy is one that acts in opposition to the liminal nature of the whole and what it is up against. Knowing this, it is crucial to understand that the act of privacy is one of preserving a sense of sovereignty not as a fundamental right (because it is not, in times of survival, a full sense of vulnerability is Pareto optimal), but in the face of systems that seek otherwise to consume us. Privacy is an act of self-preservation and rebellion against forces that seek otherwise to make us into their tools - as such we need to ensure that the act of privacy as one of self-preservation is one of establishing a sacred space between ourselves and the systems to which we are a part. Privacy allows us to modulate the energy that is taken from us so that only what is necessary for a system to exist is consumed - this being the case, privacy is an act of self-liberation. The notion of system design comes from examining the interaction of all parts in a system and working to guarantee that there is a degree of sustainable interaction between the sum of parts. design as a notion in and of itself can be either emergent or intentional - an intentional design being one that was put into motion by an agent. All system design can result in highly complex architecture, though to some degree intentional system design seems to leave out a lot of interaction with surrounding ecosystems, often leaving out sufficient examination of impact on surrounding ecosystem services 1. Unintentional system design, by contrast, tends to emerge from interaction with the environment on the part of an agent, such that a system will be designed in response to the pressures put upon the system. The latter tends to be much more sustainable and much more complex, since the system exists in concert with the environment and flow bias is at least to some degree in equilibrium between energy flowing from the environment into the system, then from the system back into the environment.

Started realizing yesterday in my conversation with Patrick that I actually know so much more about networks than I realize - which really has me reeling. There's a split in definition between what a network is and what a system is, and what most people mean when they say network is actually system. This being true, I'm not sure it's difficult to re-orient public definition toward the latter, but I could see it being possible given the correct set of definitions placed in motion as a result of the work that goes into it. That's really the best way I can think to explain it, any sufficiently reductive explanation without at the very least analogous context eventually results in a description that is so coarse-grained as to seem unintelligible and requiring additional description. That's just one of those things. In any case, there's a lot of thinking there that is worth exploring, especially when considering that some of the top thinkers in the space are still navelgazing over the possibility that a path-dependent course of analysis is the way to examine things like community, so being able to generalize a science of systems from first principles is at least in some ways a valid pursuit, especially when considering the possibility that a sufficiently developed science would be one in which the thinking that comes from it can provide a framework to re-think how it is that we consider the growth, stability, and death of systems as they are. Pursuing something along these lines is a valid analysis and can be done neutrally in order to recognize that at some point it requires an appreciation of more remote concepts such at negative and positive externalities and carrying capacity of a system - the notion of cannibalization or prey-predator dynamics as characteristic of a system are easy to zoom out from if you understand to a sufficient degree what is actually needed in order for a system to exist. So what are these fundamental rules of system design, I wonder - how much have they actually been thought out, and what kind of information is actually necessary in order for a system to exist successfully? There's an interesting question there around sufficiency - what is the smallest unit of lossless information in a system? It should in theory be possible for a system to exist without needing above a certain degree of fidelity necessary in order to function. Coarse-grain information in certain bounds is probably sufficient in most contexts, but I do wonder what might be needed when it comes to the specifics, i.e. are there scenarios in which the complex work that is done at one level needs to be shared in all of its complexity at the next in order to function? At some degree this will require trust between parties and becomes a game theory question within the bounds of a system occupied by autonomous agents. How often is this actually the case? I think in most systems, the autonomy is bounded - all we mean by autonomy in the contexts where it is necessary is the the agents can choose to or not to participate in the particular topology of interaction necessary for their role or scope of interaction. It makes me think about how the role of an analyst is actually to act as an information summary mechanism - something whose role is actively to fold through the effort necessary to synthesize information that exists within a system and reduce it to that which is necessary to disseminate. In this context, even though there was a large amount of work done in the components of the system, the amount of information necessary for success between parties and/or tiers of a system does not require this level of fidelity, i.e. this is the reason that an executive summary for a report is sufficient for most contexts, or why it is that an electrician who knows which screw to turn is a valid synthesis of their experience. Both are equally valid ways through which information is being moved through a system, because the work that is being done at one level is being compressed down to a single action that is relevant to the next level. That's an interesting realization - most information passed between systems is actually compressed in order for the system to function. Is this true in nature? Do we have lossless communication between components? Is there actually an analogue? The first thing that comes to mins is the possibility that there's some sort of compression between what a part of an ecosystem feels and what it communicates to the rest of the system; a tree that has fallen ill can use a mycorrhizal network to communicate a threat to the rest of the system, but the way that it does so is through a set of chemical triggers that cause a basic set of responses by the rest of the system.

Rooted in the field of anthropology, an ecosystem service is the quality of a contingent environment that might provide some good to a system. Ecosystem services are inherently passive in nature up to the point that there is no or marginal general maintenance required in order for a system to benefit from this service - an example might be the quality of clay from a surrounding landscape and it's utility as part of building supplies, or simply having a source of fresh water nearby. Ecosystem services are often under threat once interaction is an ecosystem passes a point of sustainability 1, wherein flow bias is one-sided and there is either no replenishment mechanism to return energy from the system to the surrounding environment in a sustainable fashion, or there is an outsized degree of inapplicable energy (non-replenishment energy) that flows from the system into the environment (a material example of this is pollution. When this happens, ecosystems tend to fall into a state of degradation wherein flow bias is entirely negative and the energy held within the ecosystem dwindles. Oftentimes this causes contingent systems to fail or reorient where they gather the energy needed for survival in the context of the environment. --- Related to:

in a signal-based network maintenance system, a 'loss of relevance' is a given network's ability to connect to its surrounding environment on the basis of a continually decreased number of connections; however well-developed the internal structure of a system is, its relevance to surrounding networks is a function of sufficient information exchange with surrounding conditions. As such, a closed system that has no influence on nor can be influenced by its surroundings must eventually die as the entropic state of the system leads toward disorder. For example: if a sufficiently developed science has found its place in explaining a set of phenomena through the ability to offer informed solutions toward the solving of research questions in the subject matter, then it is a "relevant science". If, however, the explicative power of a branch of science falls out of favor as the predominant explicative force for a course of study, then the science becomes irrelevant. The same could be said for a number of phenomena, but the concept broadly applied explains well how well a system can or should be either connected to or resolve for its surrounding conditions.

A network is closely related to and exhibits all the characteristics of a system, though a network is simply a map of connections between these components and does not necessarily require any energy flow between these components. A network becomes a system at the point which there are energy flows between components and s degree of interdependence between these components. A network acts as a map of associations between components on the basis of whatever pre-defined set of characteristics; networks that are defined through one set of characteristics may have overlap with another network that defines these components through another set of characteristics.
A system is an atomic set of interacting components, where there is some degree of energy flowing between them. --- Related to:

The term "small-but-mighty" refers to the concept of highly-connected individual nodes in a network that act as information highways for local clusters. These nodes have a low degree of randomness and high clustering, making them crucial for network resilience. They play a significant role in maintaining strong long-distance connections across shorter path lengths, leading to small-world connectivity. The term emphasizes the importance of these well-connected individuals in the stability and resilience of the network.

Economic systems are emergent properties of resource use by a society - as the complex needs of a society begin to increase, the system fragments at the level of individual contribution, and the concept of self-sufficiency becomes less important in giving way to interdependence. In small tribal settings, this isn't true - the concept of self-sufficiency can go one of two ways - either the independent hunter-gatherer consumes their own goods (unlikely, since for the most part the act of hunting does not predicate the idea of meat preservation), or they work within a small collective to collaborate toward mutual self-sufficiency - which is far more likely. Since this is a basic aspect of social groups in any species that has the ability to hunt or gather, it's probably not a stretch to say that as a social group scales to the degree of 'society' the contributions from individuals to the whole can become increasingly fragmented, as the 'society' continues to evolve its set of needs less toward provision to the individual and more toward provision of needs for the emergent structure that depends on their input. This is part of what is wrong-headed about how humans thing of society; society does not care for individuals when at sufficiently large scales - they contribute to an overarching structure that seeks its own self-preservation. In many ways, the writing and thinking of Ivan Illich in his approach to thinking about Tools for conviviality is the most salient - a recognition that beyond a certain scale, there are emergent qualities of a tool for coordination that will result in the tool seeking to only serve the tool. --- Related to:

A primitive is a constituent module within a system that performs an atomic purpose - its use can be more widely adapted, but it has differentiated such that the utility of the primitive serves a function in the context of the wider system. Primitives, as a rule, do not change much - relative to the wider system they are a rather simple part of the network of interacting parts, and the system being analyzed cannot be broken down further than the primitive parts that make up the wider system. However, this is not to say that the construction of a primitive is itself necessarily simple (a mitochondria is an oft-raised example of a primitive), but relative to any particular examined system, a primitive can be seen as a crucial and constituent part that cannot and does not vary much. Understanding the behavior of primitives in the context of the wider system affords a much more clear understanding of how parts interact in order to result in order for a system to sustain itself - both in the analysis and in the design of the system. Primitives are differentiable, but not often designed for and usually a result of iteration that leads to their necessity within the larger system.

Infrastructure is any important piece of a system such that it is necessary to how that system works. A primitive might be used as a component of a system, but the system will only function if these primitives articulate into infrastructure for maintaining the larger system. --- Related to:

a bit of a ramble on the direction I think the internet might be headed. I think we'll see two things. 1. Consumer internet most people will spend their time here, but generally speaking it will lack in much social depth. I think in part this will be the realm of the creator economy and adspace, where the goal is to make things that people want, or to find things that you want. It will mostly be a domain of parasocial interaction or direct consumerism, and will orient itself mostly around good user experiences and not much user input. It is generally not interoperable because it is a domain where platforms compete for market share, and the best way to do so will be to silo interactions into walled gardens. Users will generally not contribute their thoughts and opinions here, and the computer literacy will stay low in general. General examples: Instagram, TikTok, Pinterest, YouTube, Snapchat, etc. 2. Community internet These will be smaller corners of the internet where people who are literate in how to use all different manner of communication will create community across any number of platforms; the social layer will act (acts) as an interoperability mechanism since those who are in this space take their time to build relationships with one another, agnostic of medium. The barrier to access will be some degree of internet-native computer literacy, both socially and practically. Tech that is used here is a means to an end, and those involved will always be communities of intention. It's from these communities that new social coordination mechanisms will form that can operate on a digitally local level that does not care about the limitations of meatspace. More "interesting" things will be made here that generally will work to bring people closer to ideals Examples of this kind of internet are most of crypto and true FOSS, some science communities, Farcaster, Mastodon, and many subject area Discords and Subreddits, and will work best when they do not aim for popularity but rather functionality, since too large of anything becomes operatively diluted in utility. -- Both of these are ultimately good things, and characteristic of humans slowly evolving back toward tribal tendencies while using technologies that we made but did not have the social tools to adapt to. A consumer internet could result in people spending less time online, since they realize that they are not truly interacting with others and will spend more time interacting in meatspace, but it's equally likely people will doomscroll these environments. My hope is that socially we'll evolve past this, but that's just optimism. The countervailing force could be a heterogenous Community Internet, where select people who want to find their people can move with intention toward those who hold similar ideals, and will make meaningful things together. These communities will be small-bit-mighty, and will likely have enormous areas of effect on a Consumer Internet, since it will be a place for people to organize. I could also foresee competition between these internets, mostly due to a Consumer Internet wanting eyeballs and despising the organizational effects of there being spaces to organize online (this, I think, is actually what the purchase of X was about). -- Time will tell, but I think the greatest differentiating factor between the types of people that will occupy these internets will be based on the many forms on literacy, sociality, and collaborative tendencies. People will occupy both spaces in many cases, one out of obligation to a society that has integrated internet-as-media and the other out of a desire to find our tribes - but I hope that this works broadly in our favor. Generally, I think it will. Crucial to this working is developing a sense of what online culture can look like in its many facets and how people can learn to navigate online spaces as either newcomers or as collaborators. Some communities will operate privately and only by invitation, while others will be inviting and places where others are attracted to feeling included - but I think all of this will evolve out of a human desire to create communities around mutually assured survival. I think there is a high potential that a good Community Internet might work toward better coordination despite individual differences in belief, in stark contrast to the feed-based internet that we had in the Social Media era that amplified discontent bringing us back to a time when humans simply dissociated from one another in situations of discontent. It will be difficult to determine whether or not it's working - tribes can still go to war with one another, after all - but maybe we'll have just a few less reasons to oppose those we're in community with than we do when faced with a feed of literally every other person on the planet.

Aniara was a movie I specifically watched on the question of the loss of meaning - a population living on a generation ship grapples with the loss of an artificial intelligence that was put on board to therapize those who were traveling. The artificial intelligence reaches a point of saturation and can’t cope with the amount of negative energy created by humans, eventually leading to the deterioration of it’s will to live. The artificial intelligence commits suicide by overloading its circuits, then the population of the ship attempts to create a new sense of society despite the loss of the one mechanism that was keeping them moored in reality. This is coupled with the fact that the generation ship is off-course from its destination, or rather is going to have to travel at sub-light speeds in order to get there. This means that asking can artificial intelligence commit suicide is an important question to ask, at least from the perspective of thinking about being too overwhelmed with the human state and its vicissitudes. The search for meaning is in this regard one that asks whether or not harboring the emotional state of others is something that can be performed tenably, and it seems that the story for Aniara is that it can’t.
